In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surat Bani Isra'il (17)**

It is also called al-Isra' and Subhan. According to what Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is a Meccan surah. That it is entirely Meccan is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). The author of al-Ghaniyan said it is Meccan by consensus (ijma'). It has been said that two verses are excepted: ﴿And indeed they almost tempted you﴾ and ﴿And indeed they almost drove you out﴾. It has also been said that four are excepted: these two, ﴿And [remember] when We told you that your Lord encompasses the people﴾, and His words ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance﴾. Muqatil added His words ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ and so on to the end of the verse.

According to al-Hasan, five verses are excepted: ﴿And do not kill the soul﴾ and so on to the end of the verse; ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾ and so on; ﴿Those are the ones who call upon﴾ and so on; ﴿Establish prayer﴾ and so on; and ﴿And give the relative his right﴾ and so on. Qatadah said that eight verses are excepted, namely His words ﴿And indeed they almost tempted you﴾ through to the end of them. It has been said other than this. The surah has one hundred and ten verses according to the majority, and eleven according to the Kufans.

It is narrated in Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i and others, on the authority of 'A'ishah, that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, used to recite it and al-Zumar every night. Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Durays and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said of this surah, al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta-Ha and al-Anbiya': "They are among the first of the old ones (al-'ataq al-uwal), and they are among my ancient possessions (tilad)." This is one view on their order.

The connection of this surah with al-Nahl, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, is that when Allah, glorified is He, said at the end of al-Nahl: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾, He mentioned in this surah the law of the people of the Sabbath which He had prescribed for them in the Torah. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The whole Torah is in fifteen verses of Surat Bani Isra'il." In it He mentioned their disobedience, their corruption, their destruction of their sanctuary, their attempt to provoke the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, their intention to expel him from Madinah, and their asking him about the Spirit. Then He concluded it, exalted is His majesty, with the nine signs of Musa, peace be upon him, and His address to Pharaoh. He informed that Pharaoh wished to drive them out of the land, so he was destroyed, and the Children of Israel inherited after him. In this there is an allusion to them that they will suffer what Pharaoh suffered, since they intended against the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, what he intended against Musa, peace be upon him, and his companions. Since this surah begins with the story of the destruction of the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa), it opens with the mention of the Night Journey of the Chosen One, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, as an honour to him by the arrival of his noble mount, as a consolation for what happened to his sanctuary.

Abu Hayyan said concerning this: Allah, exalted is He, when He commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to be patient and forbade him to grieve over the disbelievers and to be distressed by their plotting, and among their plotting was their ascribing to him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, lies, sorcery, poetry and other things with which they accused him, though he was far above them, then followed this with the mention of his nobility, his excellence and the loftiness of his station with Him, exalted is His majesty.

It has also been said that the connection is that the surah includes mention of blessings, some specific and some general. In Surat al-Nahl was mentioned of the blessings what made it called "the Surah of Blessings," and it includes mention of the glorious Qur'an as that one does. In that place, in al-Nahl, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿There comes out from their bellies a drink of varying colours, in which is healing for mankind﴾.

[Page 3]

And here in the Qur'an He mentioned: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers﴾. In that surah He mentioned the command to give to the relative, and here He commanded it with an addition in His words: ﴿And give the relative his right, and the needy, and the traveller, and do not squander wastefully﴾. This comes after He commanded, exalted is He, kindness to the two parents, who are the origin of kinship, and to other things that cannot be counted. So let this be considered. And Allah is the Granter of success.

**﴿Glorified is He who took His servant by night﴾**

Subhan here, according to what some of the scholars of verification (al-muhaqqiqin) held, is a verbal noun (masdar) of sabbaha, tasbihan, in the sense of nazzaha, tanzihan (declaring Him free of imperfection), not in the sense of saying "Subhan Allah." Indeed tasbih has come in the sense of the aforementioned saying many times, so much so that some thought it was restricted to that meaning. To this view went the author of the Qamus in his commentary on the preface of the Kashshaf, and he made subhan a verbal noun of sabaha, lightened, but this is not so. It may be used as a proper name for tanzih, and then it is cut off from the genitive construction (idafah), because proper names are not put in the genitive by analogy, and it is not declined (la yunsaraf) because of its being a proper name and its extra letters. This is supported by the verse of al-A'sha:

*Indeed I said, when his boasting came to me: "Glory be to the one of 'Alqamah the boaster."*

Al-Radi said: There is no proof that it is a proper name, because it is most often used in the genitive, and so it is not a proper name. When it is cut off it has come in the poetry declined (munawwan), as in his saying:

*Subhanahu thumma subhanan nu'udhu bihi / wa-qablana sabbaha al-Judiyyu wal-Jumudu*

It has also come with the definite article, as in his saying: "Subhanaka Allahumma dhu al-subhan." There is no obstacle to saying, in the verse they cited as proof, that the genitive complement has been omitted but is intended, since it is known, and the genitive construction has been kept in its state, following the most common of its conditions, namely being free of tanwin, as in the saying: "Khalata min Salma khayashimu wa-fa." The end of his words.

The apparent sense of the words of al-Zamakhshari is that it is a proper name for tasbih always, and it is a generic proper name (alam jins), because a generic proper name is assigned to things and to meanings alike, so there is no distinction in his view. Sahib al-Kashf defended it and said: What the scholar (al-'allamah) went to is the correct view, because when the proper-name status is established by its evidence, the genitive construction does not contradict it, and it is not like "Zayd al-ma'arik" so as to be anomalous, but like "Hatim Tayyi'" and "'Antarah 'Absi." He mentioned that it indicates thorough tanzih, from the standpoint of derivation from sabaha, which means going off and going far away in the land; then what its transfer to the pattern tafil gives; then the shift from the verbal noun to the name specific to it, especially since it is a proper name that points to the reality present in the mind; and what is in it of standing in place of the verbal noun together with the verb, for its accusative is by a verb that is left unexpressed. For this reason it is not permitted to use it except for Him, may His names be exalted and His majesty be great. It is as if it were said: How far is He who has this power from all deficiencies, so His choosing of His special servant for Himself is nothing but wisdom and rightness. The end.

It has been objected to what he mentioned first that whoever forbade the genitive construction of a proper name by analogy did not distinguish between one genitive construction and another. If it is claimed that some proper names have become known for a meaning, such as Hatim for generosity, then the genitive construction is permitted in such a case for the purpose of specification and removing a general sense that has arisen. What we are discussing is not of this kind, as is not hidden. And what was mentioned of its indicating tanzih from all deficiencies is what the transmitted report supports. In al-'Iqd al-Farid, on the authority of Talhah, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, about the explanation of "Subhan Allah," and he said: "It is the declaring of Allah free of every evil."

Al-Tibi said, concerning al-Zamakhshari's words that it indicates thorough tanzih from all the ugly things that the enemies of Allah ascribe to Him, that this is something the context of the Night Journey rejects, as a thirsty camel rejects the waterings. This is refuted. Rather its meaning is wonder (ta'ajjub), as he said in al-Nur: The origin of this is that Allah, exalted is He, is glorified when one sees a marvellous thing of His creation, and then it became common until it was used for everything one marvels at. And it is not so. In al-Kashf it is said that tanzih does not contradict wonder, as was supposed and objected, and that making it the basis, with wonder following, is the sense here, unlike the verse of al-Nur. Some have mentioned that the apparent sense of al-Kashf in several places is that he does not accept combining tanzih and wonder because they are contradictory; rather because each of them is an independent meaning, so combining them is combining the meanings of a shared term (mushtarak). If combination is taken, the view mentioned is the sense; understand it.

It has been said that subhan is not a proper name at all, without distinction, so there are three views on it. Some have mentioned that in the verse it carries the sense of a command, that is: declare Allah free of imperfection and absolve Him of all deficiencies, and this includes incapacity to what is far away, or from incapacity to that. The more evident reading is taking it as a present-tense form.

Al-Isra' is travelling by night specifically, like al-Sura. Asra and sara have the same meaning. The hamzah in asra is not for transitivity (ta'diyah), as Abu 'Ubaydah said. Ibn 'Attiyah said: the hamzah is for transitivity and the object is omitted, that is: His angels made His servant travel by night. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: He needed this claim only because he believed that if asra means sara, then, given that the ba' is for transitivity, the doer would share in the object, and this is a matter that al-Mubarrad held. So if you say qumtu bi-Zayd, it implies your standing and Zayd's standing with him. If you make the ba' like the hamzah, this does not follow, as is not hidden. He also said: It is possible that asra means sara with an omitted genitive complement and the genitive being put in its place; the original is "asra malaikatuhu," and this is also based on that belief. Al-Layth said: It is said asra for the beginning of the night and sara for its end. As for sara, the majority hold that it is general, not restricted to night or day. It has been said that it is restricted to the day and is not a transposed form of sara.

The choice of the word "servant" ('abd) is to signify that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was entirely devoted to His worship, and that he reached in it the furthest extreme and the ultimate end, as is indicated by the starting point and the end point of the Night Journey. Servanthood, as the gnostics (al-'arifun) have stated, is the most noble of attributes and the highest of ranks, and lovers take pride in it, as it has been said:

*Do not call me except "O servant of Her," for indeed it is the noblest of my names.*

Another said:

*By Allah, if they ask you about me, say to them: "My servant, the possession of My hand, and what I have freed."*

It is narrated on the authority of Abu al-Qasim Sulayman al-Ansari that he said: When the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, reached the lofty ranks and exalted stations, Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: "O Muhammad, with what shall We honour you?" He said: "With my ascription to You in servanthood." So Allah, exalted is He, sent down ﴿Glorified is He who took His servant by night﴾. And there is the report: "Say: the servant of Allah and His messenger." It has been said that the use of the word "servant" here, rather than "beloved" for example, is a barrier against exaggeration concerning him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, as happened to the Christians concerning their Prophet, peace be upon him. They mentioned that Allah, exalted is He, did not refer to anyone as "His servant" in a construction with a pronoun of absence pointing to the essence, except the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and in this there is what there is of indication. Whoever reflects even briefly on the difference between His words ﴿Glorified is He who took His servant by night﴾ and His words ﴿And when Musa came to Our appointed time﴾ will find the complete distinction between the station of the Beloved and the station of the one who spoke with Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. Allah willing, what indicates this distinction will come soon in this surah. So do not be heedless.

The genitive construction of "subhan" with the relative clause mentioned is to indicate that what is in the relative clause's scope is the cause of the thing governed. For that is among the evidences of His complete power, perfect wisdom, and utmost tanzih from attributes of deficiency. His words ﴿by night﴾ are an adverb of time for "took." Its purpose, by the indefiniteness of the word, is to indicate the shortness of the duration of the Night Journey, and that it was part of the parts of the night. For this reason 'Abd Allah and Huzayfah read "min al-layl," meaning "part of it," as in His words ﴿And from the night, pray the tahajjud with it﴾.

It is objected that the partitiveness derived from the partitive min is partitiveness in the parts, while the partitiveness derived from the indefinite is partitiveness in individuals and particulars. So how is it derived from the indefiniteness that the Night Journey was in part of the parts of the night? The correct view is that its indefiniteness is to remove the assumption that the Night Journey happened on several nights, or to give it grandeur, as is suitable to the context and the preceding passage. That is: a night, what a night, in which the lover drew near to the beloved and won the sought-after goal in the station of witnessing.

Some of the accomplished scholars answered this with what its deficiency is not hidden. Some of the verifiers said: What was mentioned has been explicitly stated by Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir in Dala'il al-I'jaz, and the objection does not arise against it from the start.

[Page 6 of the source]

Its verification, as clearly stated by the eminent al-Yamani, citing Sibawayh and Ibn Malik, is that "the night" (al-layl) and "the day" (al-nahar), when they are definite, serve as a measure for generalization and as a bounded time-frame. Therefore you do not say, "I accompanied him tonight," while you mean an hour of it, unless you intend hyperbole, as when you say, "The people of the world came to me," meaning some of them. This is in contrast to the indefinite form, which does not convey that. Since the definite form was deliberately avoided here, it is known that the intention was not to encompass the entire night for the journey. This is the meaning of the "partiality" mentioned, and there is no need to make "the night" a metaphor for part of it, just as when you say, "I sat in the market," your sitting in some of its places does not make "the market" a metaphor, as is clear. The meticulous scholar in al-Kashf has also pointed to this. It has been said:

The purpose of its indefiniteness is that it occurred in the middle and most of the night, as one says, "So-and-so came to me at night," meaning in the greater part of its darkness. This also conveys partiality. What contradicts this is what will come, God willing, in the hadith. As for the claim that the mention of "laylan" (at night) is for emphasis, or to strip "the journey" of its meaning and intend mere travel, it arises from a lack of resources, as is clear. God willing, the wisdom behind the journey taking place at night will be explained later.

﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾.

The apparent meaning is that it refers to the mosque well known among the elite and the common people, in its specific sense. At that time the Prophet ﷺ was in al-Hijr adjacent to it. Al-Bukhari and Muslim (the two Shaykhs), al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i reported from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "While I was in al-Hijr (and in another narration, in al-Hatim), between sleep and wakefulness, a comer came to me and split what is between this and that, and extracted my heart, washed it, then returned it. Then I was brought an animal, less than a mule and more than a donkey, white, called al-Buraq, and I was mounted upon it..." and the hadith continues.

In some narrations it is said that Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them both, came to him while he was lying down in al-Hijr between his uncle Hamza and his cousin Ja'far. The angels, peace be upon them, carried him and brought him to Zamzam, laid him on his back, and Jibril split his chest from the hollow of his throat to the bottom of his belly, without any instrument, without bleeding, and without any pain. Then he said to Mika'il, "Bring me a basin of Zamzam water," and he brought it. He extracted his noble heart and washed it three times, then returned it to its place, filled it with faith and wisdom, and sealed it. Then he went out with him to the door of the mosque, and there was al-Buraq saddled and bridled, and he mounted it. (The report continues.)

From this it is known that there is a reconciliation between what has been mentioned, that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was at that time in al-Hijr, and what has been said, that he was between Zamzam and the Maqam. It has also been said that the meaning of "the Sacred Mosque" is the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and it was applied to it because it encompasses the mosque. So it is a metaphor by the relation of sensory proximity and encompassing, or because the whole Haram is a place of prostration and is forbidden (muharram), not permitted (laysa yahill), so it is a linguistic literal meaning. The subtle point in this expression is the correspondence between the starting point and the endpoint.

At that time the Prophet ﷺ was in the house of Fakhita, Umm Hani bint Abi Talib.

For al-Nasa'i reported from Ibn Abbas, and Abu Ya'la in his Musnad, and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, from her hadith, that "he, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, was sleeping in her house after the 'isha prayer, then he was taken on the Night Journey and returned in the same night, and he related the account to her, and said, 'The prophets were displayed to me, and I led them in prayer.' Then he went out to the mosque and informed the Quraysh of it. Some clapped their hands and put their hands on their heads in amazement and denial, and some people who had believed in him apostatized, peace be upon him. Some men went to Abu Bakr, and he said, 'If he said that, then he has spoken the truth.' They said, 'Do you affirm him in that?' He said, 'I affirm him regarding something even more remote than that: I affirm him regarding the news from heaven, morning or evening.' Therefore he was named al-Siddiq (the Truthful). There was among the people one who knew Bayt al-Maqdis, so they asked him to describe it to them, and it was made manifest to him, and he began to look at it and describe it to them. They said, 'As for the description, he has hit the mark.' They said, 'Tell us about our caravan, for it is more important to us. Did you encounter anything of it?' He said, 'Yes, I passed by the caravan of so-and-so, and it was at al-Rawha, and they had lost a camel of theirs and were searching for it, and in their saddlebags there was a vessel of water. I became thirsty so I took it and drank, then I put it back as it was. Ask them: did they find the water in the vessel when they returned?' They said, 'This is a sign.' He said, 'And I passed by the caravan of so-and-so and so-and-so, riding a she-camel, and their camel bolted from me and broke.' Ask them about that. They said, 'This is another sign.' Then they asked him about the number, the loads, and the appearances, and the caravan was displayed to him, and he informed them of all of that and said, 'It will arrive on such-and-such a day at sunrise, and with it so-and-so and so-and-so, and in front of it will be a grey camel upon which are two sacks sewn together.' They said, 'This is another sign.' So they went out running that day toward al-Thaniyya, and they began looking to see when the sun would rise, to disprove him. Then one said, 'This is the sun that has risen!' Another said, 'This is the caravan that has come, with a grey camel in front of it, and in it so-and-so and so-and-so, as he said.' But they did not believe, and said, 'This is manifest magic.' ﴿God fight them! How are they deluded?﴾"

In some reports: "Umm Hani said: I missed him, peace be upon him, and he had been sleeping with me, so sleep withheld me, fearing that some of the Quraysh had waylaid him." It is also said: "The sons of Abd al-Muttalib scattered, seeking him, and al-Abbas reached Dhu Tuwa, calling out, 'O Muhammad! O Muhammad!' He answered him, peace be upon him, and said, 'O son of my brother, you have worn out your people! Where were you?' He said, 'I went to Bayt al-Maqdis.' He said, 'In the same night?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Did the Last (night) reach you?' He said, 'The Last did not reach me.'" And other things have been said.

Just as the starting point of the Night Journey has been disputed, so too its year has been disputed. Al-Nawawi mentioned in al-Rawda that it was ten years and three months after prophethood. In al-Fatawa (it is stated) that it was in the fifth or sixth year of prophethood. Al-Fadil al-Mulla Amin al-Umari, in his commentary on Dhat al-Shifa, transmitted from him the definitive statement that it was in the twelfth year after the mission (al-mab'ath). Ibn Hazm claimed a consensus on that. What is stated in al-Fatawa was weakened on the grounds that Khadija, may God be pleased with her, did not live to the fifth year, as she died three years before the Hijra. It has been said that it was one year and five months before the Hijra, and it has been said three months. In the hadith of Shurayk ibn Abi Namir from Anas, it occurred that it was before revelation came to him, peace be upon him, and many have criticized him for that. The Hafiz Abd al-Haqq, in his book al-Jam' bayn al-Sahihayn, transmitted the hadith of Shurayk in which this occurs in full, then said: "This hadith, with this wording, from Shurayk's narration from Anas, has added an unknown addition and brought unfamiliar expressions."

The Hadith of the Night Journey has been transmitted from Anas by a group of the memorizers, the precise, and the renowned imams, such as Ibn Shihab, Thabit al-Bunani, and Qatada. None of them brought what Shurayk brought, and Shurayk is not considered a memorizer (hafiz) by the people of hadith.

Muhyi al-Sunna and others answered this with what you will hear, God willing. Likewise, its month and night have been disputed. Al-Nawawi said in al-Fatawa that it was in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal. He said in his commentary on Muslim, following al-Qadi Iyad, that it was in the month of Rabi' al-Akhir. He affirmed in al-Rawda that it was in Rajab. It has been said that it was in Ramadan, and it has been said in Shawwal. According to what has been said, it was on the twenty-seventh night of the month, and it was a Saturday night, as Ibn al-Mulaqqin transmitted from the report of al-Waqidi. It has been said it was a Friday night because of its virtue and the virtue of the Night Journey. This was refuted on the grounds that Jibril, peace be upon him, led the Prophet ﷺ in the noon prayer on the first day after the Night Journey, and if it had been a Friday, its obligatory prayer would not have been the noon prayer. This was stated by Muhammad ibn Umar al-Sufayri. In this there is a point: al-Umari mentioned in his commentary on Dhat al-Shifa that Friday prayer and funeral prayer became obligatory after the five daily prayers. In the commentary on al-Minhaj by the scholar Ibn Hajar, it is said that the Friday prayer was enjoined in Makka but was not established there due to the lack of the required number, or because its distinctive mark is public display, and he, peace be upon him, was there in hiding. The first to establish it in Madina before the Hijra was As'ad ibn Zurara, in a village at a distance of a mile from Madina.

Al-Damiri transmitted from Ibn al-Athir that he said: "The correct view in my opinion is that it was the night of Monday," and Ibn al-Munir preferred this. In al-Bahr it is said: "It has been said that the Night Journey was on the seventeenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, when the Messenger of God ﷺ was fifty-one years, nine months, and twenty-eight days old." He related from al-Jurmi that it was the night of the twenty-seventh of Rabi' al-Akhir, and it is, according to what al-Sufayri transmitted from the majority, the most virtuous of nights, even above the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) absolutely. It has been said that it is more virtuous with respect to the Prophet ﷺ compared to his community, peace be upon him.

So it is more virtuous absolutely. Yes, worship was not legislated for it, whereas worship on the Night of Power is legislated until the Day of Resurrection. And God knows best.

It was also disputed whether it took place while awake or in a dream. From al-Hasan (al-Basri), it is that it was in a dream. This was reported from Aisha and Mu'awiya, may God be pleased with them both, but it is likely that this was not authentically reported from her, as in al-Bahr. At that time Aisha, may God be pleased with her, was a little girl, and she was not yet his wife, peace be upon him. Mu'awiya was then a disbeliever. It has been argued for this by the words of God: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾, because "ru'ya" (vision) linguistically pertains to sleep. The hadith of Shurayk mentioned above has something that supports this. The majority hold that it was while awake, in his body and his spirit, peace be upon him, and "ru'ya" can mean "seeing" while awake, as in the words of the shepherd describing a hunter:

He exclaimed at the sight, and his heart was stirred,
And it gladdened a heart whose flocks were abundant.

Al-Wahidi said: It is the seeing of wakefulness, at night only. The report of Shurayk is not relied upon, as transmitted from Abd al-Haqq. Al-Nawawi said:

As for what occurred in a narration from Shurayk, that he was sleeping, and in another from him: "While I was by the House, between sleep and wakefulness," one who holds it to be a dream may argue with it. But there is no proof in it, since that may have been the first arrival of the angel to him, and there is nothing in the hadith indicating that he was asleep throughout the whole account. The majority argued for their view by saying: If it had been a dream, the Quraysh would not have been amazed at it, nor would they have deemed it impossible, because the sleeper may see himself in the heavens and travel from east to west, and no one finds that far-fetched. Also, "the servant" (al-'abd) is evident as referring to the spirit and the body together.

A group, including al-Qadi Abu Bakr and al-Baghawi, went to the position of affirming both those who say it was a dream and those who say it was in wakefulness, and they authenticated both hadiths on that basis, that the Night Journey happened twice: one of them while he, peace be upon him, was asleep before prophethood, when he was taken by night in his spirit as a preparation and facilitation for what human powers are weak to bear. To this is the allusion in the words of God: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾. Then he was taken by night in his spirit and body after prophethood. In al-Kashf it is said: "This is the truth, and by it the reports are reconciled."

Al-Mazari, in his commentary on Muslim, transmitted a fourth view by which he reconciled the two views. He said: The Night Journey was with his body, peace be upon him, while awake, to Bayt al-Maqdis, so it was a seeing with the eye. Then he was taken with his noble spirit, peace and blessings be upon him, from there to what is above it, so it was a vision of the heart. For this reason the disbelievers ridiculed him for his saying: "I came to Bayt al-Maqdis in this night of mine," and they did not ridicule him for what was other than that, nor were they amazed by it, because a dream is not a matter of amazement. And the meaning of the Night Journey is not...

[Page 8 of the source]

with the spirit, a waking ascent like the "stripping away" (al-insilakh) that the Sufis and the philosophers (al-Hukama') have adopted. For although it breaks the normal course of things and is also a source of wonder, it is a matter that the Arabs did not recognize, and none of the early generations (al-Salaf) held it. Most scholars hold that the Mi'raj (Ascension) was, like the Isra' (Night Journey), with both the spirit and the body, and there is no impossibility in that. It has been established by geometry that the diameter of the body of the earth is 2,545 farsakhs (parasangs, a unit of distance) and a half farsakh, and that the diameter of the sphere of the sun is five and a half times the diameter of the earth's body, which is 14,000 farsakhs. Its far edge reaches the place of its near edge in two-thirds of a minute, so the sun, by the motion of the Great Sphere (al-Falak al-A'zam), covers 14,000 farsakhs in two-thirds of a minute of an equal hour.

Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned in al-Arba'in that bodies are equal in their essences and realities, so whatever applies to one of them as an accident (ard) applies to the others. For if the receptivity (qabiliyya) of that accident is among the necessary attributes of that quiddity (mahiyya), then wherever it occurs, that receptivity occurs necessarily, and so whatever applies to one applies to the other. If it is not among its necessary attributes, then it is among its accidental attributes, and the argument returns to the start. If this is granted, well and good; otherwise it is either circular or an infinite regress, and both are impossible. So the aforementioned validity must be affirmed. God, exalted is He, is capable of all possible things, and so He is able to create a movement as swift as this in the body of the Prophet (ﷺ) or in what carries him.

Al-'Allama al-Baydawi said:
"The impossibility is refuted by what has been established in geometry: that the distance between the two edges of the disc of the sun is twice the distance between the two edges of the sphere of the earth, one hundred and sixty-some times over. Then its lower edge reaches the place of its upper edge in less than a second," and so on to the end of what he said.

What we have mentioned is the correct way to put it, because the two premises he cited are both open to objection. As for the first, the ratio he mentioned is in fact the ratio of the body of the sun to the body of the earth, as they demonstrated in the chapter on the magnitudes and distances of bodies in the books of astronomy (hay'a). But they said: the body of the sun is one hundred and sixty-six and a quarter and an eighth times the body of the earth. Al-'Allama took this to be the ratio of diameter to diameter, since that is what is immediately understood from "between the two edges," and taking it to mean the body is far from the apparent meaning. Had he wished that, it would have sufficed for him to say: "The disc of the sun is twice the sphere of the earth," so what meaning does his addition have?

As for the second premise: if by "second" he means the second of the minute of the celestial degree, which is sixty minutes, then it is refuted by what al-'Allama al-Qutb al-Shirazi wrote in Nihayat al-Idrak, where he said: "The measure of one degree of the concave surface of the Atlas sphere is 9,343,593 miles. The highest sphere covers, in the time it takes for one fifteenth of an equal hour, which is one third of its fifth, this distance of miles. So when it moves for a minute, which is one part of nine hundred parts of an equal hour, the distance it covers is 155,718 and a sixth of a mile and a fifth of a quarter, or a quarter of a fifth of a mile. And because the time from when the horn of the sun appears until it has fully risen is equal to counting from one to three hundred, then in the time it takes to count to thirty, the sphere moves 155,718 miles, which is one thousand seven hundred and thirty-two farsakhs from its concave side. God knows best what its convex side moves in that time. Glory be to God, how great is His affair." End of quotation.

The summary of this is that the Great Sphere moves from the start of the rising of the body of the sun until it has fully risen, a sixth of a degree, which is ten minutes out of sixty minutes of a celestial degree. The measure of the area of these minutes is 519,600, that is, five hundred and nineteen thousand six hundred farsakhs. If we make these minutes seconds, they become six hundred seconds. So where is the "less than a second"?

If by "second" he means the second of the minute of the hour, which is a quarter of the celestial degree, then the sixth of a degree here is two-thirds of a minute, and if we make the two-thirds of a minute seconds, they are forty seconds. These are the same six hundred seconds, except that the astronomers, when they made the hour sixty minutes for ease of calculation, and an hour is equivalent to fifteen celestial degrees, required that the celestial degree and each second of the minute of the hour be fifteen seconds of the minute of the celestial degree. So the difference between the seconds of the minutes of the celestial degree and the seconds of the minute of the hour is a merely verbal distinction.

'Abd al-Rahman al-Kurdi, known as al-Fadil, answered that the second is a part of sixty parts of a minute; and the minute is sometimes applied to a part of sixty parts of a degree, sometimes to a part of sixty parts of an hour, and sometimes to a part of sixty parts of a day and night. What al-'Allama al-Baydawi meant by "second" is the third second, not the first second, which is clear; nor the second second, as Sa'di Jalabi held and Ibn Sadr al-Din followed him. But in this there is the implication that astronomers divide the day and night into sixty minutes just as they divide it into hours, degrees and minutes, a division by which the parts of time are distinguished. No one among them has said this. Rather, some of them mentioned it to facilitate knowing the fractional excess over the complete days of the year, so that a leap year may be known every three or four years. This has nothing to do with what we are discussing, namely crossing a great distance in a small amount of time. Even if we accept what he claimed, it would fall short of the duration of the motion of the Great Sphere from the start of the rising of the disc of the sun to its end, which is two-thirds of a minute, namely forty seconds. That is a part of ninety parts of an equal hour, as al-'Allama al-Shirazi determined. As for what he mentioned, that the second of the minute of the day and night is equal to twenty-four seconds of the seconds of the minute of the hour, which is less than two-thirds of a minute by sixteen seconds, it is an error upon an error. That is an unjust division (qisma dayza). Indeed, he was right in his refutation of the two scholars, but the first scholar erred in other matters in this context, as will not be hidden from anyone who has read his words and has a little acquaintance with the books of these people. Because this topic is discussed among students and they do not find anyone to quench their thirst, we have addressed it with what we hope will quench it. Scholars are of different ranks, and God, exalted is He, is the one who grants success in understanding subtleties. So reflect once, twice, and a third time, and perhaps God will open for you something other than this.

As for what has been mentioned about the equality of bodies, it is based on what is said about their composition from indivisible atoms (al-jawahir al-fard), and this is disputed by al-Nazzam and the philosophers. The discussion of this is lengthy. The impossibility cannot be argued from the necessity of tearing and rejoining (al-kharq wal-iltiam), and they have proven the impossibility of that. We say: their proof for this is weaker than a spider's web, as explained in its proper place. The verse does not address whether the Prophet (ﷺ) was carried on anything during the Night Journey. But the reports are sound that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was taken by night on the Buraq (a heavenly steed) "to the farthest mosque" (al-Masjid al-Aqsa), which is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is described as "farthest" (al-aqsa), that is, most distant, relative to those in the Hijaz. Many have said that it was so named because it is the most distant of the mosques that are visited from the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), and between them is about forty nights' journey. It was also said that it is because there is no place of worship beyond it, so it is the most distant of places of worship. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that by "farthest" is meant distant, without comparing it to others, and it is indeed distant in itself for those who visit it. It was also said that the intended meaning is its distance from filth and evils.

There is disagreement about whether Jibril (peace be upon him) rode with him. It was said that he rode behind him, upon him be blessings and peace. The correct view is that he did not ride, but rather took hold of his stirrup, while Mika'il led the Buraq. There is also disagreement about whether he, upon him be blessings and peace, remained upon it during his ascent to the heavens. It was said that he ascended upon it. The correct view is that a ladder (mi'raj) was set for him and he ascended upon it. What has been related about its description and greatness is what has been related. Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir considered wrong, as al-Halabi said, those who say, including the author of al-Hamziyya, that his ascent (ﷺ) was upon the Buraq. Among the famous fabrications is that when he, (ﷺ), wanted to ascend, he climbed onto the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis and mounted the Buraq, and the rock tilted and rose to follow him, but the angels held it. On one side of it is the mark of his noble foot, and on the other side the marks of the fingers of the angels, peace be upon them. So it stands suspended in the air, cut off from every direction, held by none but He who holds the heavens from falling to the earth, glory be to Him and exalted is He.

Al-'Ala'i mentioned in his tafsir that the Prophet, peace be upon him, had five vehicles on the night of the Isra': the first, the Buraq, to Bayt al-Maqdis; the second, the mi'raj from there to the lowest heaven; the third, the wings of the angels from there to the seventh heaven; the fourth, the wing of Jibril, peace be upon him, from there to Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary); and the fifth, the rafraf (green cushion) from there to Qab Qawsayn (the distance of two bow-lengths). Perhaps the wisdom in riding is to display honor, for otherwise God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is capable of bringing him to any place He wills in less than the blink of an eye. It was also said that there was only the Buraq from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, and the mi'raj from there to wherever God willed. He had ten ladders: seven to the heavens, the eighth to the Lote Tree, the ninth to the level where he heard the scratching of the pens, and the tenth to the Throne. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

Among the wonders is what I heard from the mystic (Kashfiyya) group, though the responsibility rests on the narrator, that the spirit has two bodies: a body from the world of the unseen, subtle, in which the elements have no part; and a body from the world of witness, dense, composed of the elements. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was ascended, he cast off each element of the elemental body into its own sphere, so that by the time he reached those heights all the elements had been cast off and nothing remained with him but the subtle body. He then rose with it wherever God willed. Then, when he, upon him be blessings and peace, returned, what he had cast off returned to him, and what had been scattered gathered again in him. By my life, it is a tale of fable, with no basis in Revelation or reason.

Mawlana 'Abd al-Rahman al-Dashti, then al-Jami, mentioned that the ascent to the Throne was with the spirit and body, and to what lies beyond the Throne, with the spirit alone. He recited in Persian:

When the Rafraf was honored by His existence,
the Throne's Rafraf snatched it swiftly from his hand.
The body, like a robe, was set aside at the hand of the Throne,
and the spirit, unclothed, raised its banner above the placeless.
A call came from that threshold:
"Hand upon hand, at that lofty court."
He freed the piece from the checkered square of direction,
and made the place a steed that outran the lands.
He found a place empty even of place,
where the body was not admitted, nor the spirit either.

I have not found any textual support for this from the reports. It seems he considered that ascent beyond the Throne with the body would require a place, and it has been established among the philosophers that beyond the Throne there is neither void nor plenum, and with it places end and directions are cut off. Some have said: the matter of the Mi'raj is too great to be described. What more can be said, except that the Loving, Capable One, whom nothing can overpower, called His beloved, whom He created from His light, to visit Him, and sent to him whom He sent of His chosen angels; so Jibril was the one who took hold of his stirrup, and Mika'il the one who held the reins of his mount, until he reached what he reached. Then He, glory be to Him, took charge of his affair in what He willed until it was accomplished. What distance could be long for that Lordly beloved, and what body could refuse to be torn open for that luminous body?

Pass through Hazwa, for there is a world of gentleness,
from whose bodies the spirits remain.

[Page 11]

Whoever reflects on the eye and its perception of near and far, even if he lacks sight and is told of its condition, would deny it with a denial beyond which there is no further degree. Likewise in other matters, the manifest signs of God Most High's power in the souls and the horizons, and in what occurs, despite their great magnitude, leave one with no choice but to accept what the verses have stated and the reports have authenticated. The words of this group resemble what one of the Persian poets said, though there is in it an inclination toward the doctrine of the Ahl al-Wahda (the monists), and it is his saying:

*Qissa-yi bayarn-i mi'raj az man bi-dil mursa*
*Qatra-yi darya gasht u baygham nami-danam ki shud*

The apparent meaning is that the distance he (peace be upon him) traversed on his journey remained as it was in its extent. This is supported by what al-Tha'labi mentioned in his tafsir describing the Buraq: when it came to a valley, its forelegs lengthened and its hind legs shortened, and when it came to a steep ascent, its hind legs lengthened and its forelegs shortened. The distance was then extremely long. In *Haqa'iq al-Haqa'iq*, the distance from Mecca to the place where God Most High revealed to His Prophet (peace be upon him) what He revealed was about three hundred thousand years, and it is said fifty thousand, and other things have been said. There is no folding of distance (*tayy al-masafa*) of the kind that the Sufis and some jurists affirm as a karamah (a wondrous gift granted to saints) for the awliya' (saints). Some Hanafis declared its affirmers ignorant, and others declared them unbelievers. It has no clear basis, and it may well entail for its affirmers the view of the interpenetration of substances. The philosophers and the theologians, apart from al-Nazzam, deem it impossible and argue for its impossibility. Some of them claimed it to be a matter of necessity and said: "Denying it is mere obstinacy." The Sufis have attributed to the awliya' the folding of time, and they have marvelous accounts about it, but God Most High knows best their soundness. I have not seen any of the lawyers (*mutasharri'in*) address this, and it is a matter beyond our intellects, which are mixed with illusions. Similar to this is the saying of one who said: "Eternity a-parte ante and eternity a-parte post are one point; the difference between them is only by consideration." Understanding this, in my view, belongs only to those stripped of the garments of their bodies, and they are few. God willing, under the section on allusion (*al-ishara*) there will come the report of the denial of the folding of distance too, and mention of what it contains. God Most High is the Granter of success.

The reason he (peace be upon him) was taken on the Night Journey (*isra'*) at night is the greater honoring of him (peace be upon him), for the night is the time of seclusion, privacy, and the company of kings. A king hardly summons anyone to his presence at night unless he is especially close to him. God Most High has honored among His prophets, peace be upon them, some with various kinds of marvels at night, and it is like the root of the day. Also, guidance toward the destination is more eloquent at night than during the day. Also, they said: a traveler covers at night what he does not cover in the day, and from here came the saying: "Travel by night, for the earth is folded by night what is not folded by day." Also, he was taken by night so that what he ascended to, from the world of pure light, would be further removed from resemblance to what he ascended from, the world of darkness; and this is more eloquent in wonder.

Ibn al-Jawzi said concerning this: the Prophet (peace be upon him) is a lamp, and a lamp is lit only at night, and a full moon, and likewise the moon's course through the darknesses; and other wisdoms that none knows but God Most High. Then, the verse is not an explicit text about his (peace be upon him) entering the Farthest Mosque, but the sound reports are explicit about it.

His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Around which We have blessed﴾ is a qualifying adjective of praise, and in it is the removal of a superficial ambiguity. Its blessing lies in what it was specially granted: that it is the place of worship of the prophets, peace be upon them, and their qiblah, and the abundance of rivers and trees around it. In a hadith, God Most High blessed what lies between al-'Arish and the Euphrates, and singled out Palestine for sanctification. It is said: its blessing is that God, glorified is He, made the waters of the whole earth gush from beneath its rock, and God Most High knows best the soundness of that. It is one of the three mosques to which the saddles are bound (*tushaddu al-rihal*), and one of the four that the Dajjal is prevented from entering. Ahmad reported in the *Musnad* that "the Dajjal will traverse the earth except four mosques: the Mosque of Medina, the Mosque of Mecca, the Aqsa, and al-Tur, and prayer in it is multiplied." Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah also reported from Maymuna, the freed slave-woman of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), that she said: "O Prophet of God, give us a fatwa concerning Bayt al-Maqdis." He said: "It is the land of the gathering and the resurrection; come to it and pray in it, for a prayer in it is worth a thousand prayers."

In a narration of Ahmad from one of his wives (peace be upon him): she said, "O Messenger of God, if one of us cannot go to it—" He said: "If one of you cannot go to it, let her send oil to be burned in it, for whoever sends oil to be burned in it

[Page 12]

is as one who prayed in it." Abu Dawud related part of it. It is the second mosque established on earth, according to the report of Abu Dharr: "I said: O Messenger of God, which mosque was first established on earth? He said: 'The Sacred Mosque.' I said: Then which? He said: 'The Farthest Mosque.' I said: How much time is between them? He said: 'Forty years. Then wherever prayer overtakes you, pray, for the merit is in it.'"

Ya'qub (peace be upon him) founded it after Ibrahim (peace be upon him) built the Ka'ba, as is mentioned in the hadith, and Sulayman, or he completed the renovation of his father, peace be upon them both, long after that. The discussion of what relates to this is detailed in its proper place. ﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾: that is, that We might raise him to the heaven so that he would see the great marvels there. It is established that "he (peace be upon him) was taken up from the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis," as mentioned before, and in each heaven he met with one of the prophets, peace be upon them, as in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and others. He (peace be upon him) was shown the states of Paradise and Hell, and he saw among the angels what no one knows the number of except God Most High.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that on the night of the Mi'raj he (peace be upon him) saw, in the kingdom of God Most High, a creation in the form of men upon piebald horses, bearing weapons, each of them a thousand years tall, and the horse likewise, following one another, their first and last not seen. He said: "O Jibril, who are these?" He said: "Have you not heard His saying, Most High: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord but He﴾? I descend and ascend, and I see them passing like this; I do not know from where they come nor where they go." He (peace be upon him) led the prophets, peace be upon them, in prayer at Bayt al-Maqdis. In *al-'Aqa'iq* it is said: his prayer with them (peace be upon him) was two rak'as; in the first he recited "Say, O disbelievers," and in the second, "Sincerity." Some said it was supplication. It is mentioned that the prophets were seven rows, three of whom were messengers, and that the angels, peace be upon them, prayed with them. This is one of his distinctive features (peace be upon him), as Qadi Zakariyya said in his commentary on *al-Rawd*. The wisdom in that is to manifest that he is the imam of all (peace be upon him). Did he pray with their spirits alone or with them together with their bodies? There is a difference of opinion about it. Likewise, it is disputed whether he (peace be upon him) prayed with them before the ascent or after it. Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir affirmed that it was after, while Qadi 'Iyad and others affirmed that it was before. In a narration it came that "he (peace be upon him) prayed two rak'as in every heaven, leading their angels." The Night Journey and the ascent were within part of one night, and his return was like his going. The extent of that part is not specified. However it was, what happened in it is among the most wondrous signs and the strangest of created things.

In some reports: "When he (peace be upon him) returned, he found his bed had not cooled from the warmth of sleep." It is also said that a branch of a tree caught his turban on his way, and when he returned he found it still moving. Some claimed that the night of the Isra' is other than the night of the Mi'raj, but the apparent meaning of the verse, as you have heard, requires that they were in one night. He (peace be upon him) was taken first to Bayt al-Maqdis and was then ascended from it, so that his arrival at the noble places would be gradual; for the nobility of Bayt al-Maqdis is less than the nobility of the Presence to which he ascended, according to what is said. It is said: to accustom him (peace be upon him) to the great strangeness of the Mi'raj, which the Isra' does not have, though the Isra' is also strange. It is said: so that the Land of the Gathering would be honored by him, going and returning. It is said: because the gate of the heaven called the ascent-place of the angels, peace be upon them, lies opposite the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis. It is related from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: "God Most High has an open gate from the lowest heaven to Bayt al-Maqdis, through which seventy thousand angels descend each day, asking forgiveness for whoever comes to Bayt al-Maqdis and prays in it." So he (peace be upon him) was taken there first, then ascended from it, so that his ascent would be in a straight line. It is said: the pillars of the mosque said: "Our Lord, we have obtained from every prophet a portion, and we have longed

[Page 13]

for Muhammad (peace be upon him); grant us his meeting." So the Night Journey to the mosque began with him, to hasten the answer. It is said other things as well.

The expression "from" (*min*), which indicates partiality, is used because showing all of God Most High's signs is not something that could happen, since they are endless. Had it said "Our signs," the totality would have been understood immediately. It may be supported by the context in favoring this meaning. It was objected: how does our Prophet (peace be upon him) see only some of the signs, while Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is shown the dominion of the heavens and the earth, as His saying states: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾? And there is a difference between the Beloved and the Intimate Friend. It was answered that some of the signs ascribed to Him, Most High, are nobler and greater than the dominion of the heavens and the earth, as He said: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. Al-Khafaji said: the objection is not valid, because what Ibrahim (peace be upon him) saw was the proofs and arguments in them, and that is not comparable to the Mi'raj. So consider this carefully.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is possible that the meaning of the verse is: "That We may show Muhammad (ﷺ) to the people as a sign from Our signs"; that is, that he (peace and blessings be upon him) would be a sign that God Most High does this with a human being, and by this the aforementioned question is dispelled. However, this is an interpretation that is extremely far-fetched. Then, it is not hidden that there is no indication in the verse that he (ﷺ) saw his Lord on the night of the Isra'. For it is not true of Him, exalted is He, that He is one of His signs; indeed, it is not even true of Him, glorified is He, that He is a sign. Yes, those who affirm the vision (of God) argue from other than this, and it will come, God willing, Most High. Likewise, the verse is not an explicit text concerning the Mi'raj (the Ascension); rather, it is an explicit text concerning the Isra' (the Night Journey) without the Mi'raj, since it is possible to interpret some of the verses as referring only to what happened to him (ﷺ) in the Isra'. Indeed, some of them said: there is nothing at all in the verses that is an explicit text on that. From here they said: The Isra' to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) is a definitive matter established by the Book, so whoever denies it is a disbeliever; but the Mi'raj is not like that, so whoever denies it is not a disbeliever but an innovator (mubtadi'). It seems that He, glorified is He, did not state it explicitly as He stated the Isra', out of mercy to those of limited understanding, as it has been said. In the Tafsir of al-Khazin it is stated that the benefit of mentioning only the Masjid al-Aqsa and not the heavens is that if his (peace and blessings be upon him) ascent had been mentioned, their denial of it would have been intensified. So when He informed them that he was taken by night to Bayt al-Maqdis, and that for them there was a confirmation in what he told them of the signs that were in it, and they affirmed him regarding them, He then informed them of his ascension to the heavens; thus the Isra' was like a preparation for the Mi'raj. End of quote. This is evident in the report that came in this matter, not in the verse itself, because He did not inform in it of the Mi'raj as He informed in it of the Isra' explicitly. It has been said: the allusion after that explicit statement is sufficient, so reflect.

The shift of speech from the third person, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night﴾, to the first person of majesty in: ﴿We have blessed﴾ and "that We may show him Our signs," is to magnify the blessings and the signs, for just as they indicate the magnificence of what the pronoun refers to, they also indicate the greatness of what is attributed to Him and proceeds from Him, as it is said: "Only the great does great things." They have mentioned a particular subtle point for this variation: that His saying, Most High: ﴿The One who took His servant by night﴾ indicates his (peace and blessings be upon him) journey from the world of witnessing to the world of the unseen, so the third person is more fitting for it. His saying, Most High: ﴿We have blessed around it﴾ indicates the descent of blessings, so it suits the magnification of the One who sends them down, and the expression with the pronoun of majesty fulfills that. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿That We may show him﴾ implies remoteness of connection and the honor of presence, so speaking in the first person with him is appropriate. As for the third person, it is because at that time he (ﷺ) was not of the world of witnessing; and for this reason it has been said: in it there is a return to the station of secrecy and withdrawal from this world, and the third person is most suitable for that. His saying, Most High: ﴿of Our signs﴾ is a return to magnification, as the allusion to it has already passed. As for the third person in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, on the assumption that the pronoun refers to God Most High, as is most apparent and what most have held, it is so that it agrees with His saying, Most High: ﴿His servant﴾. The specification corroborates this, with what makes this shift best placed and what fits the reason most perfectly, for the meaning is: He brought him near and singled him out with this honor, because He, glorified is He, is aware of his conditions and knows his worthiness for this station. Al-Tibi said: "Indeed He is the All-Hearing" of the words of that servant, "the All-Seeing" of his deeds, being refined and sincere, free from the taints of desire, joined with truthfulness and purity, deserving of nearness and closeness.

As for the assumption that the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), as Abu al-Baqa' transmitted from some of them, and said: that is, the All-Hearing of Our speech, the All-Seeing of Our essence. Al-Jalabi said: it is not far-fetched, and the meaning according to it is: My servant whom I have honored with this honor is the one worthy of it, for he is the All-Hearing of My commands and prohibitions, acting upon them, the All-Seeing who looks with the gaze of contemplation at My creatures and so takes heed, or the All-Seeing of the signs that We showed him, as in His saying, Most High: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. It has been said: it is for the agreement of the pronouns referring back to him. Likewise, when He expressed it by it from Him, in His saying, glorified is He: "His servant." It has been said: it is for the indication of his (ﷺ) being singled out with gifts and nearness, and the absorption of his witnessing into a single eye: by Me he hears, and by Me he sees. The application of "All-Hearing" and "All-Seeing" to other than God Most High is not impossible, as it has been imagined, neither absolutely nor here. Al-Tibi said: Perhaps the secret in the pronoun's coming with the possibility of both meanings is the indication that he (ﷺ) saw the Lord of Might and heard His speech, by Him, glorified is He, as in the hadith referred to just above. So understand: you will hear and you will see. The insertion of the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) is either because His hearing, exalted is He, is without an ear, and His sight without an eye, in a manner in which none shares with Him, exalted is He, anyone; or to indicate the specialness of him (ﷺ) with that honor.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya claimed that His saying, Most High: ﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ is a warning to the disbelievers for their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the matter of the Isra'; that is: Indeed He is the All-Hearing of what you say, O deniers, the All-Seeing of what you do, so He will punish you for that.

al-Hasan recited: "Liyurayahu" with the third-person ya' (لِيُرِيَهُ), and thus in the verse there are then four shifts of speech (iltifatat).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 2:

﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾, that is, the Torah, ﴿and made it﴾, that is, the Book, which is the apparent reading, or Moses (peace be upon him), ﴿a guidance﴾, a great one, ﴿for the Children of Israel﴾. The phrase "for the Children of Israel" is connected either to "guidance" or to "made," and the lam is causal (ta'lil). The waw is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), or it is coordinating, conjoining it to the sentence ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾, not to "took by night," as Abu al-Baqa' al-Ukbari's view is reported by Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr al-Muhit.

A similar view is reported from Ibn 'Atiyyah, but it is distant and forced. He followed the verse of the Night Journey with this one as a digression (istitrad), preparing for the mention of the Qur'an. The common element is that Moses (peace be upon him) was given the Torah through his journey to Mount Sinai, and that journey was like his ascent (mi'raj), for there he was granted direct speech and was honored with the title "the one who spoke with God" (al-Kalim). The request to see God is embedded in it. There is a difference between the two books and the two men to whom they were revealed. If you wish, compare: ﴿He took His servant by night﴾ and ﴿And We gave Moses﴾ with ﴿a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾ and ﴿It guides to that which is most upright﴾.

﴿Lest you take﴾, that is, that you not take. Here "an" is explanatory (tafsiriyyah) and "la" is prohibitive (nahiyah). The explanation, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is of what the Book contains of commands and prohibitions. It is also said that it is for an omitted element, meaning: We gave Moses the writing of a thing, which is: "do not take." Although the Book is intended to mean the Torah, it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and it is clearly contrary to the apparent meaning.

Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr allowed that "an" be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), with the preceding preposition omitted, and "la" be negative, meaning: so that you do not take. It is also said that "an" and what follows it may be in apposition (badal) to "the Book." Abu al-Baqa' allowed that "an" be superfluous and that "la tattakhidhu" be the object of an omitted verb of saying, with "la" prohibitive: We said, "Do not take." Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that this position is not among the places where "an" is superfluous.

Likewise he allowed that "la" be superfluous, as in His saying, ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾, and the estimate would be: out of dislike that you take. The problems with this are not hidden.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Isa, Abu Raja' and Abu 'Amr among the Seven read: (an la yattakhidhu) with the third-person yā' (the verb in the absent form). Many scholars made "an" in this reading a verbal-noun particle and did not mention the possibility that it is explanatory. Shaykh Zadah said: there is no basis for "an" being explanatory on the reading with the yā' of absence, because what falls within the scope of an explanatory "an" must be speech in meaning, and the one to whom speech is addressed must be a addressed person; likewise there is no basis for it being a verbal-noun particle on the reading with the second person, because the Children of Israel are absent. Reflect upon this. The preposition in their view, when "an" is a verbal-noun particle, is omitted, meaning: so that they do not take ﴿besides Me as a guardian﴾, that is, a lord to whom you entrust your affairs other than Me. Thus "wakil" is an intensive form (fa'il) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), meaning the one to whom affairs are entrusted, that is, the one to whom authority is delegated, who is the Lord. Ibn al-Jawzi said: the Lord is called "wakil" because of His sufficiency and His management of the affairs of His servants, not in the sense of the elevation of the rank of the one who entrusts and the lowering of the status of the agent. ("Min" is the sword of an orator.) "Dun" is in the sense of "ghayr" (other than), and its use in this sense has been stated explicitly in more than one place. It is the second object of "tattakhidhu," and the first is "wakilan."

It is also allowed that "min" be partitive, but the first (exclusive) sense is preferred, and the intended meaning is the prohibition of associating anyone with Him, exalted is He:

[Page 16]

"Dhurriyyata man hamalna ma'a Nuh" (the descendants of those whom We carried with Noah) is in the accusative, either as a specification (ikhtisas) or as a vocative (nida'). The intended meaning is to remind them of the blessing of God, Exalted is He, upon them, in that their forefathers were saved from drowning in Noah's ark, when they had no protector (wakil) to rely upon other than God, Exalted is He. Makki specified the vocative for the reading in the second person. He said: "Whoever reads 'yattakhidhu' with the third-person ya' (yattakhidhu) makes the vocative remote, because the ya' indicates the third person while the vocative indicates the second person, so the two cannot come together except with distance." He said well. As for the statement of some of them, "It is not as he claimed, for a person may address one individual and report about another, saying: 'O Zayd, Bakr goes out, and I did such-and-such, O Zayd, let 'Amr do such-and-such,' and so on," this does not remove the remoteness that Makki claimed.

It is also permitted that one of the two objects of "tattakhidhu" (you take) and "wakilan" (a protector) be the other, namely that the word, being a fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive participle), is used in the same form for the singular masculine and others. Thus there is no objection that how can it be a second object when the second object is, in meaning, a predicate, and this does not agree here. "Min dooni" (other than Me) is a circumstantial (hal) clause relating to it, and "min" may be an initial (ibtida'iyyah) "min."

It is also permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for "wakilan," because the substituted element is not in the position of being discarded in every respect. That is: "Do not take, other than Me, the descendants of those whom We carried" as a protector. The intended meaning is the prohibition of them from taking 'Uzayr and Jesus, peace be upon them both, and their like, as lords. In the expression with what has been mentioned there is an allusion to the reason for the prohibition in several respects. The first: reminding them of the blessing in the salvation of their forefathers, as has been mentioned. The second: reminding them of their weakness and their condition, which required carrying. The third: that they are weaker than them, because they are born of them. In the choice of the word "dhurriyyah" (descendants), which in common usage applies to children and women, there is a complete suitability to what has been mentioned.

Abu al-Baqa permitted that it be a substitute for "Musa" (Moses), but this is very remote. A group read "dhurriyyatu" with a nominative case (raf'), on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "he is the descendant," and there is no remoteness in this, as it is thought, or on the basis that it is a substitute for the pronoun in "yattakhidhu." Abu al-Baqa said: "On the reading with the ya' of the third person." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is not permitted on the reading with the ta' of the second person, because the pronoun of the addressee is not replaced by an apparent noun." Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticized him, saying that the matter requires detail. That is: if it is a substitute of part from whole (badal ba'd min kull) or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), it is permitted without disagreement. If it is a substitute of one thing from another, and both refer to one entity, then if it conveys emphasis, it is permitted without disagreement too, like: "I passed by you, your young and your old." If it does not convey emphasis, then the view of the majority of the Basrans is prohibition, while the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans is permission, and this is the correct view, because this occurs in the language of the Arabs. He cited evidence for its soundness in Sharh al-Tashil.

Zayd ibn Thabit, Aban ibn 'Uthman, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Mujahid, in one narration, read "dhirriyyata" with a kasrah on the dhal. In another narration from Mujahid, he read it with a fathah. And from Zayd ibn Thabit also, he read "dharriyyata" with a fathah on the dhal, a lightened ra', and a shaddah on the ya', in the pattern fa'iliyyah, like "matiyyah" (mount).

"Innahu" (indeed he), i.e., Noah, peace be upon him, "kana 'abdan shakuran" (was a grateful servant), greatly thankful in all his states.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Salman al-Farisi that he said: "When Noah, peace be upon him, wore a garment or ate food, he praised God, Exalted is He, and so he was called a grateful servant." 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad narrated in the Zawa'id al-Zuhd from Ibrahim, who said: "His thankfulness, peace be upon him, was that he would say the name of God when he ate, and praise God, Exalted is He, when he finished."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Mu'adh ibn Anas al-Juhani, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "God, Exalted is He, only named Noah a grateful servant because when he entered the evening and the morning he would say: 'So glory be to God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning. And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the evening and when you enter midday.'"

al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from 'A'ishah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Noah never rose from the place of relieving himself except that he said: 'Praise be to God who let me taste its pleasure, kept in me its benefit, and removed from me its harm.'"

This is among the parts of his thankfulness, peace be upon him.

In this sentence there is an allusion that the salvation of those who were with him, peace be upon him, was by the blessing of his thankfulness, and an exhortation to the descendants to follow his example, and a warning to them against polytheism (shirk), which is the greatest level of disbelief. This is the aspect of its suitability to what came before. al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permitted that this be said about his mention by way of digression (istitrad), and then its suitability with what the speech preceded is not sought except insofar as it was part of the matter of the one mentioned, namely Noah, peace be upon him." It was also said: the pronoun in "innahu" refers to Moses, peace be upon him, and the sentence is brought in the manner of causation (ta'lil), either for the giving of the Book, or for making him, peace be upon him, a guidance, based on the view that the pronoun in "ja'alnahu" (We made it) refers to him, or for the prohibition of taking. In this there is remoteness, so reflect.

**Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 17, verse 4:**

﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel﴾. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and others related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it means: We informed them. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) added: and We revealed to them a firm revelation. Many scholars stated that *qada'* (decree) includes the meaning of *iyha'* (revelation), and for this reason it is followed by *ila* (to). Revelation to them means informing them, even through an intermediary. It was also said that *ila* here means *ʿala* (upon), and this too is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: That is, We decreed upon them. ﴿in the Book﴾, that is, the Torah, or the category of books, as evidenced by the recitation of Abu al-ʿAliya and Ibn Jubayr, "*al-kutub*" (the Books) in the plural form. The apparent meaning is the first one according to the first view, and the Preserved Tablet according to the last view. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim related from Tawus, who said: I was with Ibn ʿAbbas, and with us was a man from the Qadariyya (the Qadariyya). I said: Some people say there is no divine decree (*qadar*). He said: Is there anyone among them? I said: If there were, what would you do with him? He said: If there were anyone among them, I would have seized his head, then recited to him: ﴿And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Book that you would surely cause corruption in the land﴾.

The clause ﴿you would surely cause corruption﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, and the object of the decree is also omitted because it is known. The estimated meaning is: And We decreed to the Children of Israel regarding their corruption and their arrogance: By God, you will surely cause corruption, etc. This would be an emphasis of the connection of the decree. It is also permissible to make it the answer to "*qada'na*" (We decreed), by treating the decree as an oath, so that it is followed by what follows an oath, like the saying "*qada'a Allah ta'ala la-af'alanna kadha*" (God the Exalted has decreed: I will surely do such-and-such). The word "land" here means the category (of land), or the land of al-Sham and Jerusalem.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Nasr ibn ʿAli and Jabir ibn Zayd recited *latufsadunna* (with the first letter pronounced with a ḍamma and the sīn with a fatḥa, in the passive voice), meaning: others will corrupt you. It was said: by leading you astray; and it was said: by overpowering you. ʿIsa (ibn ʿUmar) recited *latafsudunna* (with a fatḥa on the first letter and a ḍamma on the sīn), meaning: you will be corrupt by your own selves by committing sins. ﴿twice﴾ is in the accusative case because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) not derived from the word ﴿you will surely cause corruption﴾. The meaning is two acts of corruption. The first, as al-Suddi related from his teachers, was the killing of Zakariyya, peace be upon him.

This is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Mas'ud. The reason was that when the king of their people died, they competed for the kingship, and some of them killed others. They did not listen to Zakariyya, so God the Exalted said to him: Stand among your people and deliver revelation through your tongue. When he finished what he had been revealed, they rushed at him to kill him, so he fled. A tree split open for him and he entered it, but Satan caught up with him and took a thread from his garment and showed it to them. They then placed the saw in the middle of the tree and sawed it through its middle.

It was also said that the cause of his killing was that they accused him regarding Maryam, peace be upon her. It is said: They said when she became pregnant: "He neglected the daughter of our master until she committed fornication," so they sawed him with the saw in the tree. Ibn Ishaq said: The first (corruption) was the killing of Shaʿya (Isaiah), peace be upon him, who was sent after Musa (Moses), peace be upon him. When the revelation reached them, they wanted to kill him, so he fled and was killed. He is the owner of the tree. Zakariyya, peace be upon him, died a natural death and was not killed.

In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari): The first was the killing of Zakariyya and the imprisonment of Armiya (Jeremiah), and the last was the killing of Yahya and the intent to kill ʿIsa, peace be upon them both. This applies to those who held that the death of Zakariyya came before that of Yahya, peace be upon them both, and this is the narration of Ibn ʿAsakir in his history from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face.

Then (al-Zamakhshari) combined that with the imprisonment of Armiya in one sentence, which is not sound, because Armiya lived in the time of Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar), and between him and Zakariyya there were more than two hundred years.

Some scholars chose, and it was said that this is the truth, that the first (corruption) was the altering of the Torah, not acting upon it, the imprisonment of Armiya, and his wounding when he admonished them and gave them good news of our Prophet ﷺ. He was the first to give good news of him after the good news in the Torah. The second was the killing of Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both. Whoever says that Zakariyya died in his bed limits it to Yahya, peace be upon him.

There is disagreement about the cause of his killing. From Ibn ʿAbbas and others it is related that the cause was that a king wanted to marry a woman whom it was not lawful for him to marry, so Yahya, peace be upon him, forbade him. The king had accustomed that woman to grant her whatever she wished from him on every festival. Her mother taught her to ask him for the blood of Yahya on one of the festivals. She asked him, but he refused. She pressed him, so he called for a basin and slaughtered him into it. A drop fell on the ground and kept boiling until seventy thousand people were killed because of it.

Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: Yahya, peace be upon him, was very handsome and beautiful. The wife of the king sought to seduce him, but he refused. She said to her daughter: Ask your father for the head of Yahya. She asked him, and he gave it to her.

Al-Jubba'i said: God the Exalted mentioned their corruption in the land twice and did not specify it, so nothing of what has been mentioned can be asserted with certainty. ﴿and you will surely become exceedingly arrogant﴾, that is, you will become arrogant toward obedience to God the Exalted, or you will overpower people with injustice and transgression and will go to an extreme in that, exceeding all limits. The original meaning of *ʿuluww* (exaltation) is elevation, which is the opposite of lowliness, and it is used figuratively for arrogance and domination in the manner of injustice. Zayd ibn ʿAli, may God the Exalted be pleased with both of them, recited *ʿiliyyan kabiran* (with a kasra on the ʿayn, the lām, and a shaddah on the yāʾ). In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan) it says:

The sound form (without the doubling) in the verbal noun pattern *faʿūl* is more common, unlike the plural, where the altered form is the regular one. The sound form in *lahw* and *mahw* is anomalous, contrary to al-Farra' who took it as a rule.
