Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 5:

﴿So when the promise of the first of them comes﴾, i.e., the first of the two (marratayi) occasions of corruption.

The "promise" (al-wa'd) here carries the sense of "what was promised," meaning the punishment (al-'iqab), as in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit). The sentence contains an implied element: i.e., when the time for the promised punishment arrives. It has also been said that "promise" means "threat" (al-wa'id), with an implied element as well. It has further been said that it means "promise" in the sense of the appointed time, i.e., when the appointed time for the punishment of the first of them arrives. ﴿We sent against you﴾, i.e., We dispatched to take you to account for that deed, ﴿servants of Ours﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "We left them free to do what they did, and did not prevent them," and there is in this a hidden Mu'tazili (i'tizal) insinuation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that Allah, exalted is He, sent to the king of those servants a messenger ordering him to raid the Children of Israel, so the dispatch would be by a command from Him, exalted is He." Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them) read: (ʿabīdan), ﴿possessors of great might﴾, i.e., people of strength and violent force in wars. Al-Raghib said: al-bu's, al-ba's and al-ba's'a are hardship and what is disliked, except that al-bu's is more common for poverty and war, while al-ba's and al-ba's'a are for inflicting harm. From here it has been said that describing al-ba's as "shadid" (great) is an intensification, as if it were said: "possessors of a great might," like "a shade that is shady" (zill zalil), and there is no problem with that. It has also been said that this is tajrid (a rhetorical device of abstraction), and that is also correct.

People differed about identifying these servants. From Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada: they are Jalut al-Jazari and his armies. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Ishaq said: they are Sanjarib, king of Babylon, and his armies. It has also been said they are the 'Amaliqa (Amalekites). In al-A'lam by al-Suhayli: they are Bukhtansar, governor of Lahrasif, one of the Kayanid kings of Persia, over Babylon and the Romans, and his armies were sent against them when they denied Armiya (Jeremiah), wounded him and imprisoned him. It has been said: this is the truth.

﴿So they roamed through the houses﴾, i.e., they moved about in their midst searching for you. Al-Raghib said: "Jasu al-diyar" means they penetrated its midst and moved back and forth among them, and close to it are hasu and dasu. Abu al-Sammal and Talha read (ḥāsū) with ḥāʾ; it has also been read (tajawwasū) with jīm, on the pattern of (takassarū). Abu Zayd said: al-jaws and al-haws mean seeking a thing with thoroughness. The word ﴿khilal﴾ is singular in form; for this reason al-Hasan read (khalal). It is also possible that (khilal) is the plural of (khalal), like (jibal), the plural of (jabal). The words of Abu al-Su'ud point to his preference for this, and the words of al-Baydawi point to preference for the first reading.

﴿And it was a promise fulfilled﴾, i.e., the promise of the first of them was a promise ﴿mafʿūlan﴾ (carried out), its action being certain. The pronoun in (kāna) refers to the earlier promise; it has also been said it refers to the roaming (al-jaws) understood from (jāsū). The majority hold that in this dispatch these servants destroyed the Temple of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), a devastating slaughter, exile and captivity befell the Children of Israel, and the Torah was burned. But from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid it is reported that this did not happen; rather the raiders merely roamed through the houses and departed without fighting.

Page 18

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 6:

﴿Then We gave you back the return (karrah) over them.﴾ That is, the dominion (al-dawlah) and the victory (al-ghalabah). The original meaning of al-karr is turning back and returning, and the use of "karrah" for what has been mentioned is a common metaphor, as one says: "the matter returned" (tarajaʿa al-amr). The lam in "lakum" is for transitivity (li-l-taʿdiyah), and it has been said that it is for causation (li-l-taʿlil). The words of the Exalted, ﴿ʿalayhim﴾, that is, "over those who did to you what they did," are connected to "al-karrah" because of the meaning of victory contained in it, or they are a circumstantial clause (hal) of it. It has also been permitted that it be connected to "radadna." According to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan), this is a report from Him, exalted is He, in the Torah to the Children of Israel, except that He placed "radadna" in the position of "naruddu" to affirm that the event would occur. It is said that between the raising (al-baʿth) and the return there were one hundred years, and this was after they repented and turned back from what they had been upon.

The cause of this has been disputed. It is narrated that Ardashir Bahman ibn Isfandiyar ibn Kishtasp ibn Lohrasp, when he inherited the kingdom from his grandfather Kishtasp, God Most High cast into his heart compassion for the Children of Israel, so he returned their captives whom Bukhtansar had brought to Babil, and sent them to the land of Syria, and he installed Daniel over them, and they gained control over whoever among the followers of Bukhtansar was there. Some have considered among the effects of this return the killing of Bukhtansar, but this is not established.

In al-Bahr: a king attacked the people of Babil, and Bukhtansar had killed forty thousand of the Children of Israel, of those who recited the Torah, and had left a remnant with him in Babil. When that king attacked them and overcame them, he married a woman from the Children of Israel, and she asked him to return the Children of Israel to their homes, and he did so. After a period, prophets arose among them and they returned to the best of what they had been. It has also been said that the "return" was by God Most High empowering David, peace be upon him, so that he killed Goliath (Jalut). This has been objected to on the ground that the words of the Exalted, ﴿and that they may enter the Masjid﴾, etc., refute it, since the intended masjid is the Bayt al-Maqdis, and David, peace be upon him, began its construction after the killing of Goliath and his being given prophethood, but did not complete it, and Solomon, peace be upon him, completed it; so there was no masjid before David, peace be upon him, for them to enter the first time. It is answered that the true meaning of masjid is the ground, not the building, and the words of the Exalted, ﴿they entered it﴾, are to be understood by way of istikhdam, which is, as you see, far-fetched. The truth is that the masjid existed before David, peace be upon him, as we have previously mentioned.

﴿And We aided you with wealth﴾ abundant, after your wealth had been plundered, ﴿and sons﴾ after your children had been taken captive, ﴿and made you more numerous in manpower (nafir)﴾ than you were before, or than your enemies. Al-nafir, according to what Abu Muslim said, is like the one who goes forth (al-nafir) with a man from his clan and household. Al-Zajjaj said: it may be the plural of nafr, like kalb and kulayb, and ʿabd and ʿabid, and they are those who gather to go to the enemy. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning more outgoing to raiding, as in the words of the poet:

So honour Qahtan for their forefather, and Himyar; honour a people of nafir.
It is also narrated: "bi-l-Himyariyyin akrim nafiran." Al-Suhayli held that it is a collective noun (ism jamʿ), because of its predominance in its uses and the non-regularity of its singular.

﴿If you do good﴾ in your deeds, whether they are for your own benefit or extend to others, that is, you perform them in the praiseworthy and fitting manner, [or you do good] ﴿you do good to yourselves﴾, that is, for their benefit, through the reward that follows from it. ﴿And if you do evil﴾ in your deeds, whether they are self-directed or extend to others, by performing them in an unfitting manner, or by committing evil, ﴿then it is against yourselves﴾, that is, the evil falls upon them, through the punishment that follows from it. The lam here means "upon" (ʿalā), as in the line: "He fell prostrate upon his hands and his face" (fakharra ṣarīʿan li-l-yadayni wa-li-l-fami). It is used here for the sake of mushākalah (harmonizing with the preceding phrasing).

Al-Ṭabarī said: it means "to" (ilā), in the sense that its evil returns to them.

It was said: it is for entitlement (istiḥqāq), as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾.

In al-Kashshāf [of al-Zamakhsharī], it is for exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ). This has been criticized on the grounds that it contradicts what is found in the reports about the harm of evil extending to one who did not commit the wrong. Unless it is said that the harm of these people, from among the Children of Israel, did not reach beyond them. But this is a strained interpretation that is not needed, because the reward and punishment in the Hereafter do not extend to others, and these are what is meant here.

It was said: the lam is for benefit, like the first one, but in the manner of mockery (tahakkum). The generalizing of "good" and its opposite so that they include both the transitive and intransitive deeds is what some verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) have favored. Good is explained as doing what is considered praiseworthy for oneself and others, and evil as the opposite of that. He said: this is more fitting and more complete. For this reason it was said: the repetition of "good" in the noble verse, but not of "evil," indicates that the side of good is predominant, and that when it is done it should be repeated, unlike its opposite.

It has been reported from ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face, that he said: "I never did good to anyone, nor did I do evil to anyone," and he recited the verse.

As for the connection between this verse and what precedes it, according to al-Quṭb: when they disobeyed, Allah the Exalted empowered over them those who targeted them with plunder and captivity. Then, when they repented and obeyed, their condition became good. It thus became clear that the goodness and evil of deeds pertain specifically to them, and the verse includes this. It also contains, in exhortation to good and warning against evil, what is not hidden. So reflect.

﴿Then when the promise of the last﴾ time, of the two times of your corruption, ﴿comes﴾, ﴿to distress﴾: the phrase li-yasūʾū is connected to a verb that has been omitted because what preceded it indicates it, and it is the response of idhā (when). That is: We sent them so that they would distress ﴿your faces﴾, that is, so that the servants who were sent would make the traces of distress and sorrow evident upon your faces. For the psychological states appear in the face: with joy, brightness and radiance appear, and with sorrow and fear, gloom and blackness appear. So the faces are taken in their literal sense. It was said: it is possible that "face" is used to denote the whole person, for they distressed them through killing, plunder and captivity, so distress reached all the persons. This is supported by His words: ﴿And if you do evil, then it is against yourselves﴾. It is also possible that by "faces" the leaders and their chiefs are meant. But how do you see it?

This reading was chosen over "to distress you" (li-yasūʾukum), even though the latter is more immediate and clearer, to indicate that the pain of both the soul and the body was gathered upon them, as indicated by His words: ﴿and to destroy﴾, etc. It was said: ﴿then when it comes﴾ here, although it is part of the detailed explanation of the summary in His words, glorified is He: ﴿You will surely corrupt the earth twice﴾, the apparent [expression] would be "then when it comes," and "when it comes" is used to indicate that the coming of the promise of punishment for the last time did not delay from their multitude and gathering, indicating the severity of their stubbornness in ingratitude for blessings, and that whenever they increased in number and power, they increased in transgression and arrogance, until the means of wealth and abundance were complete. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, surprised them while they were heedless. We seek refuge in Allah, glorified is He, from the sudden onset of His punishment.

Abū Bakr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamzah read: li-yasūʾa (in the singular), with the pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted, or to the promise, or to the sending indicated by the omitted response. The attribution is figurative in the last two cases and literal in the first. This is supported by the reading of ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face, and of Zayd ibn ʿAlī and al-Kisāʾī: li-nasūʾa, with the plural "we" of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah), for the pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted admits of no other meaning. Ubayy read: li-nasuʾnna, with the lam of command (lam al-amr) and the nūn of majesty at the beginning, and the light emphatic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd al-khafīfah) at the end. The lam of command entered upon a verb of the speaker, as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿and let us carry your sins﴾. The response of idhā in this reading is the imperative clause, with the fāʾ assumed, because it cannot be a response without it.

It is also reported from ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face: li-nasūʾanna and li-yasūʾanna, with the nūn and the yāʾ at the beginning, and the heavy emphatic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd al-shadīdah) at the end.

The lam in all of that is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), and the clause is the answer to the oath, standing in place of the response of idhā. The lam in His words, the Exalted: ﴿and that they enter the mosque﴾ is the lam of purpose (lam kay). The prepositional phrase is conjoined to the prepositional phrase before it, and it is connected to the omitted "We sent" as well. It is also permitted that it be connected to another omitted verb, in which case the conjunction is of one clause over another. In the readings with the lam of command or the lam of oath mentioned earlier, it is permissible that the lam be the lam of command, or the lam of purpose. "The mosque" here means Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and it is the object of "enter." In al-Ṣiḥāḥ [of al-Jawharī] it is stated that the correct usage in phrases like "I entered the house" is that you mean "I entered into the house," so the preposition was omitted and "the house" was put in the accusative as a direct object. Its verification is in its proper place. ﴿as they entered it﴾, that is, an entering like their first entering of it. ﴿The first time﴾: this is in the position of an adjective to an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar). It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: being as they entered it. "First" (awwal) is in the accusative as a time adverb. The meaning of the comparison, according to al-Baḥr [al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ], is that they enter it with the sword, with force, with domination and with humiliation. In it there is also the implication that this refutes the view of those who held that the first of the two times involved no fighting, no killing and no plunder.

﴿And that they may destroy﴾, that is, they may ruin. Qutrub said: they may demolish. He cited the poet's line: "And people are none but two agents: one agent destroys what another builds, and another raises." Some said: demolition is also destruction. Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that tatbīr (destruction) is a Nabataean word.

﴿What they overpowered﴾, that is, what they dominated and seized control of. So mā is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, and it is either an object or a prepositional complement, as has been said. It is also permitted that mā be a verbal-temporal (maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah) particle, meaning: so that they may destroy for the duration of their lasting, dominant and prevailing. ﴿With a dreadful destruction﴾, one that cannot be described.

There has been disagreement about identifying these servants who were sent, after they mentioned the killing of Yaḥyā, peace be upon him, in the final corruption. Many said: they were Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his armies. Al-Suhaylī criticized this, saying it is not correct, because the killing of Yaḥyā was after the raising of ʿĪsā, peace be upon them both, while Bukhtnassar was a long time before ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. It was said: they were Iskandar (Alexander) and his armies. He also criticized this, saying that between Iskandar and ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, there were about three hundred years. Then he said: but if it is said that their corruption the last time was by the killing of Shaʿyā (Isaiah), it is permissible that the one sent against them was Bukhtnassar and those with him, because he was alive at that time.

It was reported from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the one who raided them was the king of Khardūsh, and that the one who undertook to kill them for the blood of Yaḥyā, peace be upon him, was a commander under him, and so the matter subsided. In some reports it is stated that the commander of the army entered the place of their sacrifices and found in it blood boiling. He asked them about it, and they said: "It is the blood of a sacrifice that was not accepted from us." He said: "You have not been truthful with me," and he killed thousands of them upon it, but the blood did not calm down. Then he said: "If you do not tell me the truth, I will leave none of you alive." They said: "It is the blood of Yaḥyā, peace be upon him." He said: "For such a thing your Lord takes vengeance upon you." Then he said: "O Yaḥyā, my Lord and your Lord knows what has befallen your people because of you. So calm down, by Allah's permission, before I leave none of them alive." So it calmed down. Al-Kashshāf chose, and said it is the truth, that the one sent against them the second time was Birdus, one of the kings of the Ṭawāʾif (the Parthian dynasty), and it seems that he is the same as Khardūsh mentioned just before, for it was mentioned that he was king of Babylon from among the kings of the Ṭawāʾif. It was said: his name was Juzur.

These kings appeared after the killing of Dārā (Darius) by Iskandar and his seizure of the kingdom of the Persians. That occurred through Iskandar's doing, following the opinion of his teacher Aristotle (Arisṭū). Their number exceeded seventy kings, and the duration of their rule, according to some histories, was five hundred and twelve years. After this period the Persians gathered upon Ardashīr ibn Bābak, willingly and unwillingly, and one of the kings of the Ṭawāʾif was at Istakhr. On this basis, the king sent to corrupt the Children of Israel by killing Yaḥyā, peace be upon him, was one of the last of the kings of the Ṭawāʾif, as is not hidden. And between this sending and the first sending, according to the view that the one sent was Bukhtnassar and his followers, there was a very long period. In some histories it is stated that the killing of Dārā by Iskandar was four hundred and thirty-five years after Bukhtnassar. And after about three hundred years from Iskandar's conquest, the Messiah, peace be upon him, was born. There is no doubt that the killing of Yaḥyā, peace and blessings be upon him, was after his birth by some time, and the sending after the killing likewise. So between the two sendings there is more than seven hundred and thirty-five years.

What the Jews hold is that the first one sent was Bukhtnassar, and he was in the time of Armiyā (Jeremiah), peace be upon him. He had explicitly warned them of his coming after forbidding them from corruption and the worship of idols, as his book states. So they imprisoned him in a well and wounded him. His destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis took place in the nineteenth year of his reign. Between that and the descent of Adam there were three thousand, three hundred and thirty-eight years. It remained in ruin for seventy years. Then Asbiyānus (Vespasian), Caesar of the Romans, sent his minister Ṭūṭūz (Titus) to its ruin, and he destroyed it in the year three thousand eight hundred and twenty-eight. So, according to them, the period between the two sendings is four hundred and ninety years. The detailed discussion of that is in their books. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best the reality of the matter.

How well what has been said: knowing the peoples who were sent by their individual identities, the date of the sending, and similar matters, is not of great concern, since the purpose is that when their disobedience multiplied, Allah the Exalted empowered over them those who took vengeance upon them time after time.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires that the ones sent first and second be the same. Whoever does not hold this makes the return of the pronouns to "the servants" like the return of the pronoun to "dirham" in your saying: "I have a dirham and its half." So understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 8:

﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾ after the second sending, if you repent and desist from sins. ﴿But if you return﴾ to corruption after what has preceded from you, ﴿We shall return﴾ to punishment, and We punished you in the world in the same manner as We punished you in the first two instances. This is also among what was decreed for them in the Book, and likewise the following sentence. They returned by denying the Prophet (ﷺ) and intending to kill him, so God, exalted is He, returned by giving His Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) power over them. He killed Qurayzah, expelled Banu al-Nadir, and imposed the jizyah (poll tax) on the remainder. It was also said: they returned, so God, exalted is He, returned by setting the Kisras (Persian kings) over them, and they did to them what they did, such as imposing the itawah (tribute) and the like. The first view is related from al-Hasan and Qatadah. The expression with (an) [in ﴿an yarhamakum﴾, "it may be that"] is to indicate that they should not return.

﴿And We have made Hell a prison (ḥaṣīr) for the disbelievers﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: that is, a prison. He cited in al-Bahr the verse of Labid:

"And an assembly with subdued necks, as though they were jinn standing at the door of a ḥaṣīr."

If ḥaṣīr is a noun for the well-known place, then it is a fixed noun and its feminine and masculine forms do not need to agree. If it means ḥāṣir, i.e., encompassing them, and fa'īl in the sense of fā'il requires agreement, then the lack of agreement here is either because it is of the type of nisba, like laabin and tamir, meaning "possessor of confinement," and on this basis is the verse ﴿the heaven will be split asunder thereby﴾ [al-sama' munfaṭir bihi], meaning "possessor of splitting"; or because it is taken as fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl. It was also said: the masculine is used in view of Hell being interpreted as a place, and it was said: because its feminine form is not real. Abu al-Baqa' transmitted this, and it is, as you see, weak.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from al-Hasan that he explained it as bedding and resting place. Al-Raghib said: it seems he took ḥaṣīr to mean a woven mat, and applied that term to it because some of its parts are confined by others. So ḥaṣīr in this sense means maḥṣūr (confined). In the statement there is an eloquent simile. The word ḥaṣīr also came to mean authority/sovereignty. Al-Raghib cited the previous verse in this regard, then said: its being named so is either because it is confined, like muḥajjab (veiled), or because it is confining, i.e., preventing whoever wishes to prevent him from reaching it, end quote.

Taking what is in the verse in this sense is something I have not seen anyone address, and taking it that way is extremely remote; so it should not be taken that way, even though it contains a subtle meaning that is grasped through reflection. The apparent expectation was that it should say "for you" instead of "for the disbelievers," but it was turned away from this to record their disbelief through returning, to censure them for it, and to indicate the cause of the ruling.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an﴾ which We have given you. This is connected to the opening of the surah, as the reference to it has already passed. In pointing to it with "this" there is an exaltation of what the chosen Prophet (ﷺ) brought. ﴿Guides﴾, i.e., guides people in general, not a particular group among them, as was the practice with the Book which We gave to Musa (peace be upon him). ﴿To that which﴾, i.e., to the path which ﴿is most upright﴾, i.e., the most upright and straightest of paths, namely the religion of Islam and monotheism. So "allati" is an adjective of a noun that has been omitted for brevity. Some scholars supplied it as "the state" (al-ḥāla) or "the religion" (al-milla). Whichever you supply, you will not find with the affirmation the taste of eloquence that you find with the omission, because of the vagueness it contains, which indicates that the flood has run and covered the villages. ("Aqwam") is an elative (af'al al-tafḍīl), according to what many have pointed out.

Abu Hayyan said: What appears from the standpoint of meaning is that it is not intended as a comparative, since there is no shared basis in the derivation between the path to which the Qur'an guides and other paths, such that one would surpass the other. The meaning is therefore: "to that which is upright" (qayyima), i.e., straight (mustaqima), as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Therein are upright books﴾ and ﴿That is the upright religion﴾. End of quote.

Al-Imam al-Razi went to this view.

﴿And gives good tidings to the believers﴾ of what it contains of rulings and laws.

Abdullah, Talha, Ibn Thabit and the two brothers (al-Akhawan) read ﴿yubashhiru﴾ with a light pronunciation, as the present tense of bashara (the unemphasized form), and it has come as bashartuhu, basharathu and abshartuhu. ﴿Those who do﴾ the deeds ﴿righteous﴾ ones, which are explained in it, ﴿that for them is﴾, i.e., that for them, in exchange for their deeds, ﴿a great reward﴾, according to its essence and, by way of multiplication, ten-fold or more. Ibn Jurayj explained "a great reward," and likewise "a noble provision" wherever it occurs in the whole Qur'an, as Paradise.

[Page 23]

"And as for those who do not believe in the Hereafter" [﴿وأنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ﴾] and its rulings explained in this Qur'an, concerning resurrection (al-ba'th), reckoning (al-hisab), and recompense (al-jaza'), including reward (al-thawab) and punishment (al-iqab), both spiritual and physical. The Hereafter is singled out for mention from among all the things the disbelievers did not believe in, because it is the greatest of what they were commanded to believe in, and in consideration of the correspondence between their deeds and their recompense, which is indicated by His saying, ﴿We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾, namely the punishment of Hell. That is, We have prepared and readied for them, for what they disbelieved in and denied the existence of, of the Hereafter, a painful punishment. This is more effective in deterrence, because punishment that comes from where it is not expected is more terrible and more grievous. Perhaps the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab, the Jews and Christians) are included in this ruling, because they do not affirm physical recompense and they hold beliefs about the Hereafter for which there is no basis. Thus they have not believed in the Hereafter and its rulings explained in this Qur'an with true faith, so understand this.

The conjunction here is with ﴿that for them there is a great reward﴾ [﴿أنَّ لَهم أجْرًا كَبِيرًا﴾]. So the preparation of a painful punishment for those who do not believe in the Hereafter becomes a matter of good news, just as the establishment of a great reward for the believers who do righteous deeds is. The misfortune of an enemy is a joy that is given as good news. It is as if it were said: "He gives good news to the believers of their reward and of the punishment of their enemies." It is also possible that "good news" (bishara) is used as a metonymy (majaz mursal, a figurative usage based on a non-metaphorical connection) in the sense of general informing (mutlaq al-ikhbar), which includes informing of what brings joy and informing of what does not. In this there is no combining of the meanings of a homonym (mushtarak) or of the literal and the figurative, so as to say that it falls under the generality of metaphor. Even if it refers to this, or it is coordinated with ﴿gives good news﴾ or ﴿guides﴾, with the implied verb "informs," so that it is the coordination of one clause with another clause. It is not hidden what there is in the verse of giving preference to promise over threat.

[Page 23]

He, glory be to Him, drew attention to what is in the good news by describing the believers as "those who do righteous deeds," in their complete state, so that the believer may adorn himself with that. You know that if the great reward is interpreted as Paradise, then it is established for the believer who does righteous deeds and for the believer who is negligent (mufarrit), since the essence of faith guarantees entry into Paradise by the grace and mercy of God, the Exalted. Yes, what is prepared in Paradise for the one who does righteous deeds is greater than what is prepared for the negligent. If it is interpreted as what God, the Exalted, has prepared in the Hereafter of Paradise, the high ranks, and the various kinds of honours in it, which mere faith does not guarantee, then it is evident that this is not established for the negligent believer. So a qualification is necessary, and this does not imply that the negligent one will not enter Paradise. Yes, it implies that the great reward in the previously mentioned sense is not established for him. The verses from which his entry into Paradise is understood are many, and perhaps this verse also indicates that. The context required not explicitly stating his ruling.

In al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari) it is said that He, the Exalted, mentioned the righteous believers and the disbelievers, and did not mention the wicked (al-fasaqah), because at that time people were either a pious believer or a polytheist, and those of the intermediate position (ashab al-manzila bayn al-manzilatayn) only emerged after that.

Abu Hayyan responded to this, saying that it is obstinacy (mukabara), for there occurred in the time of the Messenger ﷺ among some of the believers lapses and slips, some of which are mentioned in the Qur'an and some in the authentic hadiths. End of quotation. What is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul) is that the majority hold the uprightness (adalah) of the Companions, and whoever among them had an impairing matter arise, such as theft or fornication, was dealt with according to its requirement. Then, what he mentioned of the intermediate position between the two positions apparently means what his fellow Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilah, a theological school) held, that the one who commits a grave sin is neither a believer nor a disbeliever, and if he dies without repentance he will abide forever in the Fire. This has been refuted in the science of theology (ilm al-kalam), so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 11:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And man prays for evil﴾. Shaykh al-Islam said: This is a description of the state of the one who is guided, following a description of the state of the guide, and a showing of the contrast between the two. By "man" is meant the species, and the state of some of its individuals, namely the disbeliever, is ascribed to it. The words of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, point to this, or he related his state at some times, as is suggested by what is narrated from al-Hasan and Mujahid. The meaning on the first reading is that the Qur'an calls man to the good, which has no greater good beyond it, namely the great reward, and warns him against the evil, which has no greater evil beyond it, namely the painful punishment. And some of them, that is, the disbeliever, prays for himself for what is evil, namely the punishment mentioned, either with his tongue literally (haqiqatan), like the practice of those among them who said: ﴿O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾, and who said: ﴿Bring upon us what You threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾, and other such things related from them. Or with their evil deeds, which lead to it and make it obligatory, figuratively (majazan), as is the custom of all of them. Some have also taken the prayer with the tongue to be figurative for hastening, in mockery.

﴿His prayer﴾, that is, a prayer like his prayer. The qualified noun was omitted, along with the particle of comparison, and the genitive noun was put in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdariyya). This is what is meant by the one who said: "like his prayer." ﴿For good﴾ mentioned, supposedly, not in reality, for he is far from praying for it. This contains an allusion that it is what befits his state.

﴿And man has been ever hasty﴾, that is, the one to whom the aforementioned prayer is ascribed from among its individuals, ﴿hasty﴾: he hastens to seek everything that occurs to his mind, heedless of its harm, or he exaggerates in haste, seeking evil and punishment, though it will surely come to him. In this there is a kind of mockery of him. On the reading that the prayer refers to their deeds, haste is taken to mean persistence and continuance in incurring punishment through those deeds. The meaning on the second reading is that the Qur'an calls man to what is good, but at some times, such as in anger, he abandons it and prays to God for himself, his family and his property for what is evil. Man, by his natural disposition, is hasty and impatient, not waiting until what afflicts him passes away.

Al-Waqidi related in al-Maghazi from 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to her with a captive and said to her: Keep watch over him."
Page 24
She said: "I became occupied with a woman, and he went out without my noticing. The Prophet (ﷺ) came in and asked about him. I said: 'By God, I do not know,' and I had neglected him, so he went out and said: 'May God cut off your hand.' Then the Prophet (ﷺ) went out and cried out to them, so they went out in search of him until they found him. Then he came back to me, saw me turning my hand over, and said: 'What is the matter with you?' I said: 'I am waiting for your supplication.' He raised his hands and said: 'O God, I am only a human being. I become angry and wrathful as humans become angry. Whichever believing man or woman I curse with a curse, make it for them a purification and a means of purity.'"

Or he prays for what is evil while supposing it to be good. Man is hasty, not discerning, not reflecting upon his affairs with due reflection, so that what is truly good, deserving of prayer, might be realized, while what is truly evil, deserving of seeking refuge from, might be avoided. End, with some addition and alteration.

Some researchers (muhaqqiqun) chose that the "man" in the first place refers to the disbeliever. In explaining the connection of the verses, they said: when He, Exalted is He, explained what He had singled out His Prophet (ﷺ) with, namely the Night Journey, and the giving of the Torah to Moses, peace be upon him, and what He did to the rebellious disobedient ones by sending affliction upon them, this served as a warning that obedience to God, Exalted is He, brings every good and honor, and disobedience to Him, glorified is He, brings every calamity and penalty. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides﴾, etc., then He joined to it:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 12 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And We made the night and the day﴾ etc., with the common thread of the proof of reason and of revelation, or the two blessings of religion and of this world. As for the connection of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾ etc., it is that when He, glorified is He, described the Qur'an to the highest degree of guidance, He mentioned those who excessively denied this greatest blessing, saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ etc.

Similar to this is what has been said: that after describing the Qur'an with what He described, He censured Quraysh for not seeking guidance through it, and for their request that stones be rained down upon them or that a painful punishment be brought upon them, if it were true. In al-Kashf it is said that His saying ﴿And man prays for evil﴾ etc. explains that the Qur'an guides them to what is most upright, but they refuse anything except what is most blameworthy. This is an aspect of connection in general. All that they have mentioned in this regard is close in meaning. It is objected that interpreting "prayer" as prayer for (evil) deeds, and "hastiness" as persistence and insistence in incurring punishment through those deeds, is contrary to what is apparent, as is clear. Some interpreted the second "man" as Adam (peace be upon him), on the basis of what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Salman al-Farisi, who said: "The first thing Allah the Exalted created of Adam (peace be upon him) was his head. He began to look while he was being created, and his two legs remained. When it was after the afternoon, he said: 'My Lord, hasten (the creation of) the rest before the night.' This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾." Something similar is narrated from Mujahid. Al-Qurtubi related, and the responsibility for it lies with him, that when the soul reached his eyes he looked at the fruits of Paradise, and when it entered his body he desired them, so he leapt hastily towards them and fell. The connection of ﴿And man has ever been﴾ etc. according to this view is that it conveys that his haste in praying for others, or his lack of reflection, is part of his nature, and that it is inherited from his origin, and a disposition (shanshana) recognised in him from Akhzam (a proverb). Thus it is an interjected concluding clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyil), and a causal statement (kalam ta'lili). The better view is that the word refers to the species (al-jins), although the wording of the verse does not rule out that Adam (peace be upon him) is meant, as Abu Hayyan claimed. Furthermore, the particle "bi" in both places is in its apparent sense, governing the verb "yad'u" (to pray). It has also been said that it means "fi" (in), and the meaning is: he prays in a state of evil and harm just as he prays in a state of good, so the thing prayed for is not the evil or the good. It has also been said that it is causal, i.e., he prays because of that. Both of these views contradict the apparent sense and are not relied upon. The verse has been used as evidence for some of the possibilities of prohibiting a man from praying against himself, his property or his family, and the prohibition on this has indeed come explicitly in some reports.

For Abu Dawud and al-Bazzar related from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not pray against yourselves, do not pray against your children, do not pray against your property, lest you coincide with an hour from Allah, the Exalted, in which there is an answer, and He answers you." With this it is refuted what has been said, that such a prayer is not answered, out of grace and generosity from Allah, the Exalted.

It has been objected that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed against his family, as you have heard in the report of al-Waqidi. It has been answered that this was for deterrence, even if it was in a time of anger. The Prophet (ﷺ) had stipulated with his Lord, glorified is He, that in such a case it should be a mercy. For it is established that he (peace be upon him) said: "I have made a condition with my Lord, for I said: 'I am only a human being; I am pleased as human beings are pleased, and I am angry as human beings are angry. So whichever of my community I curse with a curse that does not deserve it, make it for him a purification, a means of purification (zakah) and a means of drawing near (qurbah).'"

Al-Nawawi, in answer to what is said, namely that the apparent meaning of the hadith is that the prayer and the like were due to anger, mentioned what al-Mazari said: it is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) meant that his prayer, his cursing and the like were among matters in which he was given a choice between two things: one of them is what he did, and the second is to restrain him by another matter. Anger for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, moved him to one of the two options he was given. This is not outside the ruling of the Shari'ah. The meaning of his (peace be upon him) saying "it does not deserve it" is that it does not deserve it before Allah, the Exalted, in the inner reality of the matter, but in the outward sense it is deserving of that. Such a judgement may be derived from legal indicators, and he (ﷺ) was commanded to judge by what is apparent, while Allah, the Exalted, takes charge of hidden matters. It has also been said that what issued from him (peace be upon him) of prayer and the like was not intended. Rather it is among what the custom of the Arabs has run in joining their speech without intention, like (may your hand be dust) and (may she be barren, may she be unfortunate). But he (peace be upon him) feared that some of that might coincide with an answer, so he asked his Lord, glorified and exalted is He, and besought Him that He make that a purification and a means of drawing near. Yes, in mentioning the report of al-Waqidi and the like, such as the hadith that al-Baydawi mentioned in the place where it was mentioned, there is something to consider, so reflect.

Then, by analogy, the wāw should be retained in "yad'u al-insan" (﴿يَدْعُ الإنْسانُ﴾), since there is no apocopating particle requiring its deletion. But the Noble Qur'an was transmitted as it was heard, and the transmitter did not alter it according to the measure of his understanding or the strength of his intellect.

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾. This, according to what has been said, is a beginning of explaining some of what was mentioned of guidance, by directing to the method of reasoning through the signs and the evidences of the horizons, each of which is a clear proof without doubt and a plain path that whoever follows it will not go astray. For the aforementioned making and what is conjoined to it, although they are among the creational guidances, the report of this is among the Qur'anic guidances that alert to those guidances.

The Imam mentioned several aspects of the connection. The first: when He, exalted is He, explained in the previous verse what reached creation of the blessings of religion, namely the Qur'an, He followed it with explaining what reached them of the blessings of this world, so He said: ﴿And We made﴾ etc. Just as the Qur'an is composed of the clear (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih), so too time comprises night and day. And just as the purpose of the obligation is not complete except by mentioning the clear and the ambiguous, so too time is not fully benefited from except by day and night. The second: He, exalted is He, described man as "ajul", i.e., one who moves from one attribute to another and from one state to another, and He explained that all the states of the world are like this: the movement from light to darkness and the reverse, and the movement of the light of the moon from increase to decrease and the reverse. The third is like what we related first, and it is perhaps the better one. The night is mentioned first in order to observe the existential order, since the day is stripped away from it, and the beginnings of the Arabic months appear in it, and so that the end of the day is ordered upon it without intermediary. What increases the goodness of mentioning the night first is the opening of the surah with His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Glorified is He who took His servant by night﴾. The making (al-ja'l), as conveyed from al-Samin, is either in the sense of "making into" (taṣyir), transitive to two objects, or in the sense of "creating" (khalq), transitive to one object, and "two signs" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥal muqaddara).

Al-Kirmani objected to the first view, saying that it requires that the night and the day existed in one state and then moved from it to another. This is not so. It is answered that it is of the type of "narrow the mouth of the well", which is a well-known figurative usage (majaz), and Abu Hayyan preferred this. The meaning is: We made the two luminaries, with their forms, their succession and their difference in length and shortness, on a wondrous regularity, two signs that indicate that they have a wise, powerful and knowing Maker, and that guide to what the Noble Qur'an guided to, namely Islam and monotheism.

﴿Then We erased the sign of the night﴾. The annexation here and in what follows is either explanatory (bayaniyya), as in the annexation of a number to what is counted, like "four women", meaning: We erased the sign which is "the night", i.e., We made the night erased of light, obliterated, dark, such that nothing in it is clearly discerned, just as what is on an erased tablet is not discerned. This is the view taken by the author of al-Kashshaf.

It is also narrated from Mujahid, and it is of the same type as "narrow the mouth of the well". The particle "fa" is explanatory (tafsiriyya), because the erasing mentioned and what is conjoined to it are not things that occur immediately after the making of the two renewed things as signs; rather they are part of that making and its completions. It has also been said that the meaning of erasing the night is removing its darkness by light. This has been preferred on the ground that it keeps the erasing in its literal sense, namely the removal of a thing that is established, and that is not what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. One should not depart from the literal sense without necessity. It has been objected that what follows is sufficient as an indication of that intended meaning, for the erasing of the night in opposition to it is the making of the day to be seeing. According to the literal meaning mentioned, the erasing of the night has no additional benefit beyond what follows it. It has been said in response that darkness is the original state and light is an incidental addition, so the night's being created with its light obliterated is taken for granted, and the intended meaning is to show that Allah, the Exalted, created time as a dark night, then made some of it day by producing brightness, for a benefit that He, glorified is He, mentioned. The fact that the erasing of the night is in contrast to making the day luminous does not necessitate taking it in a figurative sense, for the benefit of showing that some of the time was left in its darkness and some of it was made luminous. End of quotation. There is no concealing the artificiality in this, and that the context does not suit it. So what is relied upon is what is in al-Kashshaf.

﴿And We made the sign of the day﴾, i.e., the sign which is the day, ﴿seeing﴾, i.e., luminous. So it is a figurative usage (majaz) by a relation of causation, or the predication is figurative, as in "his day is fasting", meaning: its people see. Or the form indicates attribution, i.e., possessing their sight. Or it is from the transitive "abṣarahu", i.e., made him seeing and observant, and the predication to the day is also figurative, being predication to a customary cause, while the real agent is Allah, the Exalted. Or it is of the form "af'ala" in which the meaning is other than the one to whom it is predicated, as in "ḍa'ufa al-rajul" (the man's mounts became weak) when his beasts are weak, and "jabuna" (became cowardly) when his people are cowards. So "the sign became seeing" means its people became perceptive.

This is narrated from Abu Ubayda, and it is a lexical meaning, not a figurative one.

Qatada and Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "mubṣirah" as "mabṣarah" with a fatḥa on the mim and on the ṣad. It is a verbal noun put in place of another, and such usage is frequent in descriptions of places, like "arḍ masbaʿa" (a land full of lions) and "makān maḍabba" (a place full of lizards). Or it is a possessive annexation (idafa lamiyya), and the two signs of the night and the day are their two luminaries, the moon and the sun. In that case, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾, one needs to assume an elided noun in the first and the second, i.e., We made the two luminaries of the night and the day two signs, or We made the night and the day possessors of two signs. And the making (ja'l) is transitive to two objects, the night and the day being the first object and "two signs" the second. But if it is reversed, as Abu Hayyan preferred, and the night and the day are taken as accusative of place in the position of the second object, i.e., We made in the night and the day two signs, namely the two luminaries, no assumed elision is needed. This is also the case if the making is taken as transitive to one object, and the night and the day are in the accusative of place, as the grammarians allowed. The erasing of the sign of the night, which is the moon, according to what the traditions indicate, is the removal of the light that it had on the day it was created. For Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "The moon used to shine as the sun shines, and it is the sign of the night, so it was erased. Hence the blackness that is in the moon is a trace of that erasing."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others related from Ikrimah that he said: "Allah, the Exalted, created the light of the sun as seventy parts and the light of the moon as seventy parts. Then He erased from the light of the moon sixty-nine parts and added it to the light of the sun. So the sun has one hundred and thirty-nine parts, and the moon has one part." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: "There was a sun by night and a sun by day. Allah, the Exalted, erased the sun of the night, and that is the erasing that is in the moon."

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 12 (part 2 of 3)]

Al-Bayhaqi related in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwah* (The Proofs of Prophethood), and Ibn 'Asakir from Sa'id al-Maqbari, that "'Abd Allah ibn Salam asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the blackness that is in the moon. He said: 'They were two suns.' And he said: 'God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs, then We effaced the sign of the night﴾. So the blackness you saw is the effacement.'"

In a long hadith that Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related with a weak chain (*sanad wahin*) from Ibn 'Abbas, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ): "God, exalted is He, created two suns from the light of His Throne. He sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who passed his wing over the face of the moon, which was then a sun, three times, and so the light was obliterated from it, while its radiance remained in it. That is His saying: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾, to the end of the verse."

There are other reports besides these. According to this view, the *fa'* (ف) in the verse indicates sequence (*li-l-ta'qib*). He made the sign of the day, which is the sun, "making things visible" (*mubsirah*), in the manner already mentioned, so reflect on this. It has also been said that the effacement of the moon is either: (a) that God created it dulled, its light obliterated, not shining of its own essence, as the astronomers (*ahl al-hay'ah*) mention, that it does not give light in itself but its light is derived from the light of the sun. In this case the *fa'* is explanatory (*tafsiriyyah*), as has passed. Or (b) that it gradually decreased what it derived from the sun, bit by bit, according to sight and perception, until it vanished entirely, which is the meaning of effacement. In this case the *fa'* indicates sequence.

The Imam mentioned two views about its effacement. One is that its light diminished little by little until the period of waning (*al-mihaq*). The other is that it became marked with spots (*kalaf*). Then he said: "Taking it in the first sense is preferable, because the *lam* in the two verbs after it (*li-tabtaghu*...) relates to what was mentioned before it, namely the effacement of the sign of the night and making the sign of the day visible. The effacement of the sign of the night only affects the seeking of God's bounty if we understand the effacement of the moon as the increase and decrease of its light, since the cause of this sign's occurrence varies with the states of the moon's light. And those who study experiments (*ahl al-tajarib*) have established that the variation in the states of the moon, in the measures of its light, has a great effect on the conditions of this world and its benefits, like the states of the seas in tide and ebb, and like the states of ... (*al-bahranat*), as the physicians mention in their books. Also, by the increase and decrease of the moon's light the months come about, and by the recurrence of the months the Arabic years come about, which are based on the sighting of the crescent (*al-hilal*), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And that you may know﴾, etc."

You know that whenever a sound report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) indicates what we mentioned first, it is not proper to claim that something else is preferable. By my life, this is an interpretation without any dulling (*kalaf*) for one who has a seeing eye. The philosophers have a lengthy discussion about this visible effacement on the face of the moon, and there is no harm in acquainting oneself with it in outline. So we say: The Imam mentioned in *al-Mabahith al-Sharqiyyah* that the refusal of some parts of the moon's face to accept full light is either due to a cause external to the body of the moon or not external to it. If it is due to an external cause, then it is either like what happens to mirrors, in which the images of things fall, so that when those things are seen they do not appear shining. Likewise, when the images of mountains and seas were imagined in the moon, those places had to be not seen as fully illuminated. Or it is due to a veiling cause.

The first is false. Firstly, because images do not keep their form when the mirror moves, and even if it is still, those images do not settle in it when the positions of the viewers differ, whereas the marks on the face of the moon are not like that. Secondly, because the light is reflected from the moon to the eye, and what is so does not suit imagination. Thirdly, because those marks would have to be like spheres, since mountains on the earth are like irregularities or roughness on the surface of a sphere, and they have no magnitude sufficient to affect the roundness of the earth. So how could their images be visible in a mirror?

As for the case of a veiling cause, that veil is either elemental or celestial. The first is false. Firstly, because the hidden places of the moon's body would have to vary according to the positions of the viewers. Secondly, because that veil could be neither pure air nor pure fire, since both are transparent and do not obstruct. It must rather be composed, either vapour or smoke, and that is not permanent. If the veil is celestial, then it is the truth. That happens only through the presence of celestial bodies very close to the moon, and so small that each one is not seen, but their totality is in a particular shape. Some of them have no light, and the first of them has a light weaker than the moon's, so that it appears dark while the moon is shining.

If the cause is due to the moon itself, then that place's substance either is identical with the substance of the illuminated places of the moon in essence, or it is not. If it is not, then this is due to celestial bodies of a different kind from the moon embedded in its body, as we mentioned before, and that is close to it. If those places are identical in essence with the body of the moon, then their being singled out for those marks is impossible except by an external cause. But it has become clear to us that celestial bodies are not affected by anything elemental. By this, the view of those who say that the effacement is due to the wearing away of the moon's surface through contact with fire is refuted. Firstly, because this would require that over long periods it would come to total non-existence and corruption, whereas continuous observations contradict that. Also, the moon is not in contact with fire, because it is set in its epicycle (*falak tadwir*), which is in its carrier (*hamil*), and between it and the fire there is a great distance. The proof is that if the fire were in contact with its carrier, it would move with its motion to the east, and that is not the case, because the motions of the meteors (*shuhub*) are mostly toward the west. That motion follows the motion of the fire, and circular motion is not intrinsic to fire, since its motion is straight, so that circularity belongs to it only accidentally, following the motion of the whole. So what they said is refuted. End.

Al-Amidi mentioned in *Abkar al-Afkar* additional views beyond what is understood from what has been mentioned. Among them are those who said: what is seen is an imagined thing with no reality. He refuted this by saying that if it were so, observers would differ about it. Among them are those who said: it is the blackness present in the moon on the side not facing the sun. He refuted this by saying that if it were so, it would not be seen dispersed. Among them are those who said: it is the face of the moon, for it is formed in the shape of a human face, with two eyes, two eyebrows, a nose and a mouth. He refuted this by saying that, with its distance, it would require that the work of nature in their view be idle of benefit, because in their view the benefit of the eyebrows is to ward off the harm of sweat from the eyes, the benefit of the nose is smelling, and the benefit of the mouth is the entry of food, and the moon has none of that. May God have mercy on him; he refuted all their other claims as well.

The Imam mentioned in *al-Tafsir* that the last thing the philosophers said about this is that small bodies of little light became embedded on the face of the moon, like the embedding of the stars in the bodies of the spheres. Since those bodies were of less light than the body of the moon, they were necessarily seen on its face like freckles on a human face. Their embedding in some parts of it and not others, though its parts are uniform in their view, is evidence of a free Creator, just as the singling out of some of its parts with strong light and others with weak light, though its parts are uniform, is evidence for that. A similar singling out in indication is the singling out of some sides of the sphere, which in their view is also a simple body uniform in its parts, by the embedding of the stars in it and not others.

Some people of the traditions (*ahl al-athar*) claimed that it is written on the face of the moon: *There is no god but God*. It has also been said: a beautiful word, and other things were said. And that the visible effacement is that writing. None of this is relied upon. Yes, *There is no god but God* is written on everything, and likewise "beautiful," but that is in another sense, as is not hidden.

It was related to me that the new astronomers (*ahl al-hay'ah al-jadidah*) claim that the moon, like the earth, has mountains, valleys, trees and seas, and that they witnessed this in their observations. They say the places where no effacement is seen are seas, and those where there is effacement are uneven land. They claimed that if anyone reached the moon he would see the earth the same way. From this they said: it is not far-fetched that it is populated with creatures, the same as the earth is populated. Rather, they said that all the stars are like it, by analogy with it, even if what is seen on it cannot be seen in them because of their great distance. It is far from wisdom that God, exalted is He, would populate the earth with creation despite its smallness, and leave great bodies, most of which are larger than the earth, empty of creation despite their size. Since the moon deceived them, they have clung to its ropes in devising stratagems for ascending to it. They built ships of quicksilver and ascended in them, but before they reached the sphere of vapour, their bodies swelled and their understandings went astray as they had gone astray before. So they turned back humiliated and descended in defeat.

You know that their discourse on this subject contradicts the principles of philosophy, and they have no proof for it except foolishness. Its source is purely that they saw something on the moon, did not verify it, and assumed what they assumed. And what is to prevent God, exalted is He, from making the effacement in a way that gives the impression of that? Indeed, on our principles there is no obstacle to saying: God, exalted is He, placed in the moon bodies resembling what they supposed. But nothing has come about this from the truthful one (ﷺ), who was taken up to *qab qawsayn aw adna* ("two bow-lengths away or nearer"). As for their claim that it is far from wisdom for God, exalted is He, to populate the earth, etc., it entails that what lies between the stars, like the stars of the Great Bear for example, should be populated with creatures like the earth as well, and it is many times larger than the earth. They do not say this. Moreover, we say: it has come in a hadith: "The heaven has creaked, and it has a right to creak. There is not a space of a foot in it except that there is an angel bowing or prostrating." So it is possible that on the body of the moon there are angels worshipping God, exalted is He, in whatever way and manner He wills. Indeed, it is possible that at every particle of its particles there is such an angel, and this is a kind of populating with creation. For one whose time is precious, the best course is to not give heed to such superstitions and not waste time refuting them. And God, glorified is He, is the Granter of success.

Now, what preceded, that the effacement diminished what the moon had derived from the sun bit by bit, contains the claim that the light of the moon is derived from the light of the sun. Most scholars have counted that among the conjectural matters (*hadsiyyat*), and they mentioned that the sun shines by its own essence. Both matters are among what the philosophers mentioned, and there is no basis for them in the Law (*shar'*) to rely upon. Al-Amidi related it and then criticised it, saying: "They mentioned that the sun is luminous in itself. What prevents it from being black in body, with God, exalted is He, creating light in it at the times we observe it? And it may be luminous from other stars above it, which are hidden from us by some dark celestial bodies, as happens to the sun during an eclipse. And even if we grant that it is luminous in itself, we do not grant that the light of the moon is derived from it. What prevents the Lord, exalted is He, from creating light in the moon at one time and not another, or from its being embedded in its sphere, turning around its own centre, with one of its faces luminous and the other dark, just as some parts of the sphere were transparent and some luminous? It moves with a motion equal to the motion of its sphere, and its luminous face is toward the sun when it is in opposition to it, and that is the face facing us. The increase and decrease that appear to us follow its distance and nearness from the sun, so it is not luminous from the sun." End.

[Page 30]

It has been objected that if the eclipses are added to the increase and decrease of the moon, measured by nearness and distance, then what he mentioned is not complete, and what they mentioned about the benefit is correct.

It is answered: what prevents the eclipse from being caused by a heavenly body coming between us and it, rather than by the earth coming between it and the sun? Negating that requires proof, so understand this. And God Most High knows best, and He is the one who disposes of His dominion as He wills. ﴿That you may seek﴾ is connected to the words of God Most High, ﴿And We made the sign of the day﴾, and there is an implied element in the sentence, meaning: We made the sign of the day to give sight, so that you may seek for yourselves in it.

﴿A bounty from your Lord﴾, that is, provision, since that cannot be achieved at night. In expressing provision as "bounty" and earning as "seeking," and in referring to the attribute of Lordship, which indicates the gradual progression toward completion, there is an indication, as Shaykh al-Islam said, that the servant has no effect in obtaining provision except seeking. The giving is entirely from God, glorified be He, not by way of obligation upon Him Most High, but as a favour by the authority of Lordship. The effect of seeking is like the effect of ordinary causes, for it is one of them, and provision does not in reality depend upon it.

In a report: "Your provision seeks you just as your term seeks you." And how well the poet said, by God Most High:

I know, and excess is not my character, that what is my provision will certainly come to me.
I strive toward it, and its seeking does not weary me; and if I sit still, it comes to me and does not tire me.

﴿And that you may know﴾ is connected, as has been said, to both actions together, namely the effacing of the sign of the night and the making of the sign of the day to give sight, not to either one alone, since that by itself would not be the basis of the stated knowledge. That is: so that you may know, through the difference of the two new moons or their two luminous bodies in essence, in respect of darkness and light, along with their succession, or their movements and positions, and all their other states, ﴿the number of years﴾ which has a scientific purpose connected to establishing your religious and worldly interests, ﴿and the reckoning﴾, that is, the reckoning connected to the times contained within them, namely the months, nights, days, and other things to which some of the stated interests are attached. The year itself, in respect of its realization, is among what the reckoning organizes; what is connected to counting is a portion of it, and its connection in that regard to each one of them is not from the aspect of its realization and attainment from a number of months, each of which is attained from a number of days, each of which is attained from a portion of hours, for example. That belongs to the function of the science of reckoning. Rather, it is in respect of its being a unit from the group of counted years after it, that is, the year itself, without taking into account the attainment of any specific thing, as Shaykh al-Islam verified.

It has also been said: the meaning is, so that you may know, through their difference and their succession in a single order, or through their movements, the number of years, and so on. By "the reckoning" is meant its kind, that is, what operates in transactions such as leases, sales on credit, and other things. Some scholars have mentioned that the apparent and fitting meaning is that what is intended is: so that you may know through the night, for the number of legal years and the legal reckoning are known by it mostly, or through the moon, according to His words concerning the crescents: ﴿Say, they are timings for the people and for the Hajj﴾ (2:189). You know that years are solar and lunar, and both are acted upon. So if it were said that one of the two verses explains one of them and the other explains the other, there is no objection to it. That the Law relies on one of them does not harm this. The placing of the number before the reckoning, given that the order between their objects, as you heard earlier, is reversed in existence and in non-existence, is to alert from the outset that the object of the reckoning is what lies within the periods of the years, or because the knowledge connected to the number of years is a general knowledge of what the reckoning connects in detail, or because the knowledge connected to the first is the highest of levels and so deserves precedence in the context of favour, or because number descends from reckoning to the position of the simple relative to the compound, based on what has been verified: that reckoning is the enumeration of what has a discrete quantity by repeating its like, such that a certain portion of it attains a specific limit with a particular name and an independent ruling, whereas number is its enumeration by the mere repetition of its like without anything attaining such a limit. Because the years are among the things in which no specific limit with a particular name and an independent ruling has been taken into account, number was added to them and the reckoning was connected to what is other than them. So reflect.

﴿And everything﴾ that you need in your livelihood and your return, apart from what has been mentioned concerning the making of night and day as two signs and what follows from them of religious and worldly benefits. It is in the accusative governed by a verb which is explained by His words: ﴿We have detailed it in detail﴾. This is from the class of ishtighal (the construction in which a verb is suppressed in favour of a pronoun, grammatically "occupation"), and the accusative is preferred because a verbal clause precedes it. It is also permitted that it be coordinated with "the reckoning," and the clause ﴿We have detailed it﴾ is a description of "thing," but this is distant in meaning.

Tafsil (detailing) is from fasl in the sense of cutting off, and what is intended by it is complete clarification. The verbal noun is used for emphasis. So the meaning is: We have explained every thing in the Noble Qur'an with an eloquent clarity admitting no ambiguity, as in His words: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of everything﴾ (16:89). Thus it becomes clear that it is a guide to what is most upright, with manifest clarity.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 17, verse 13:**

﴿And every person﴾ is in the accusative, as in the construction of (every thing), meaning: and We have bound to every responsible person ﴿his omen⁠﴾, that is, his deed which proceeds from him by his own choice, whether good or evil, as if it flew to him from the nest of the unseen and the hollow of destiny.

In the *Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), it is mentioned that they used to take omens from birds, calling this *zajr*. When they travelled and a bird passed by them, they would scare it off. If it passed by them *sanih* (from left to right), they took it as auspicious, and if it passed *barih* (from right to left), they took it as inauspicious. For this reason it was called *tatayyur* (augury). When they attributed good and evil to the bird, the word was borrowed by way of an explicit metaphor (*isti'ara tasrihiyya*, a metaphor in which the borrowed term is stated outright) for something resembling them, namely the decree of God Most High and the action of the servant, because the deed is the cause of good and evil.

From this usage comes the phrase "God's bird, not your bird," meaning: the decree of God, exalted is His majesty, which prevails and to which good and evil are ascribed, not "your bird" by which you take omens as inauspicious or auspicious. Their practice of this became so widespread that they did it with gazelles and all other wild animals, and they called all of that *tatayyur*, as is mentioned in *al-Bahr* (al-Andalusi's commentary). Interpreting *ṭā'ir* here as "deed" is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Bayhaqi related it in *Shu'ab al-Iman* from Mujahid, and a number of scholars adopted it. Some of them interpreted it as what befalls the servant in the eternal allotment, which is made according to what he deserves in eternal knowledge, from the expression: "the arrow of such-and-such flew to him." From this comes: "So 'Uthman ibn Maz'un flew to us from among those who came," that is, his share fell to us. The meaning is: We have bound to every person his portion and his lot, which We apportioned to him from eternity. ﴿around his neck⁠﴾ is a depiction of the intensity of the attachment and the completeness of the bond. This is also the sense of the saying: "I have a need from you," and he replied: "Between my ear and my shoulder, whatever you want." The neck is singled out because what is upon it is visible, whether adornment such as necklaces and collars, or disgrace such as shackles and fetters. It is also because it is the limb that remains exposed, displaying what is on it, and to which rank and honour are attributed. It is used to express the whole and the chief of a people. So the meaning is: We have bound his yoke upon him such that it never leaves him, but clings to him as a necklace or a shackle clings, never separating from him in any way.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hudhayfa ibn Usayd, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The drop from which the living soul is created flies in the womb for forty days and forty nights, and nothing of it remains—neither hair, nor skin, nor vein, nor bone—without entering into it, until it even enters between the nail and the flesh. When forty nights and forty days have passed, God Most High sends it down into the womb, and it becomes a clot (*'alaqa*) for forty days and forty nights, then it becomes a lump of flesh (*mudgha*) for forty days and forty nights. When four months have been completed for it, God Most High sends to it the angel of the wombs, who creates through his hand its flesh, its blood, its hair and its skin. Then the Glorified says: 'Form it.' He says: 'O Lord, shall I form it as something excessive or deficient? Male or female? Beautiful or ugly? Curly-haired or straight-haired? Short or tall? White or dark-complexioned? Sound or unsound?'
[p. 32]
He then writes down of these what God Most High commands. Then he says: 'O Lord, is it wretched or fortunate?' If it is fortunate, He breathes into it happiness at the end of its term; if it is wretched, He breathes into it wretchedness at the end of its term. Then He says: 'Write its traces, its provision, its afflictions and its deeds, whether obedience or disobedience.' So he writes of these what God Most High commands him. Then the angel says: 'O Lord, what shall I do with this book?' The Glorified says: 'Hang it on its neck until My judgement upon it.'"

This is the meaning of His words, Exalted: ﴿And every person We have bound his omen around his neck⁠﴾.

It should not be overlooked that the apparent meaning of this report is that the mention of the neck is not for the depiction mentioned, and that the "omen" is an expression for the book in which whatever was written has been recorded.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas that he explicitly interpreted it in that way. The domain of metaphor is broad, and we believe in the hadith if it is sound, and we entrust the manner of what it indicates to the Subtle, the All-Aware, exalted is His majesty. The apparent meaning of it also does not restrict "person" to the responsible (*mukallaf*). This is supported by what Abu Dawud recorded in the *Book of Qadar*, and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid that he said regarding the verse: "There is no child born except that upon its neck is a paper on which is written 'wretched' or 'fortunate'." The end of the verse, however, is apparent in restricting it.

Mujahid, al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read (*ṭayrahu*) and it was read (*'unqihi*) with the *nun* sukun ﴿and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection⁠﴾, and the raising (*ba'th*) is for the reckoning, ﴿a book⁠﴾, which is the scroll of his deeds. It is in the accusative because it is the object of (*nukhriju*). It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from an omitted object of (*nukhriju*), which is a pronoun referring to the omen, meaning: We bring it out for him while it is a book. This is strengthened by the reading of Ya'qub, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin: (*wa-yukhraju*) with a *ya'* and in the active form from *kharaja yakhruju*, with the accusative (*kitaban*), for its subject then is the pronoun of the omen and (*kitaban*) is a circumstantial accusative of it. The principle is the agreement of the two readings. Likewise is the reading of Abu Ja'far: (*wa-yukhraju*) with a *ya'* in the passive form from *akhraja*, with the accusative (*kitaban*) also. The way in which it strengthens is that in (*yukhraju*) in this case there is a hidden pronoun, which is the pronoun of the omen, which was the object. As for the possibility that (*lahu*) is the deputy subject, so that it is not strengthened, this is not to be considered, because placing a non-object in the position of the subject while the object exists is weak. And there is nothing that could be a circumstantial accusative of (*kitaban*), so what was mentioned is definite, as stated by Ibn Ya'ish in his commentary on the *Mufassal*. From him also it is narrated that it was read (*yukhraju*) in the passive, with the raising of (*kitabun*) as deputy subject. Al-Hasan read (*yakhruju*) in the active from *al-khuruj*, with (*kitabun*) raised as subject. A group read (*wa-yukhriju*) with a *ya'* in the active from *al-ikhraj*, where the subject is the pronoun of God Most High, and in it there is a shift (*iltifat*) from the first person to the third person.

Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Harun, who said regarding the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: (And every person We have bound his omen around his neck; he will read it on the Day of Resurrection, a book) ﴿he will meet it⁠﴾, meaning he will meet the person, or the person will meet it, ﴿open⁠﴾, not folded, so that its reading is possible, and in this is an indication that this is something prepared for him, not forgotten. The clause ﴿he will meet it⁠﴾ is a qualifier of (*kitaban*), and ﴿open⁠﴾ is a circumstantial accusative from its pronoun. It is also permitted that both be qualifiers of it. The placing of a clausal qualifier before a single-word qualifier is contrary to what is apparent. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari and al-Hasan, with a variant from him, read (*yulaqqahu*) with a *ya'* vowelled *damma*, the *lam* vowelled *fatha*, and the *qaf* doubled, from *laqqaytuhu kadha*, meaning: the person encounters it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan that he said: O son of Adam, I have spread for you a scroll, and two noble angels have been assigned to you, one on your right and the other on your left. When you die, your scroll is folded and placed around your neck in your grave, until you come on the Day of Resurrection and it is brought out for you.

[Page 33]

﴿Read your record.﴾ Its implied meaning is: it will be said to him, "Read." This clause may be a qualifier (ṣifah), a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a new independent clause (mustaʾnafah).
