The apparent view is that the clause ﴿Sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ is part of the content of the implied saying. Here (kafā) is a past-tense verb, and (binafsika) is its subject (fāʿil). The bāʾ (here the redundant particle) is "the sword of an orator" (a figure of speech for its emphatic force). Its omission with the noun in the nominative is also attested, as in the line: "Gray hair and Islam have sufficed a man as a restrainer." And another line:

"His guidance informs me about the absent man's [inner state]; guidance suffices, about what a man has hidden, as an informant."

The verb does not take the feminine marker, although a similar verb may take it, as in the verses ﴿No town believed before them﴾ and ﴿No sign came to them﴾. It has been said that this is because the subject is a metaphorically feminine noun. But this does not satisfy the question, because the subject of the verbs mentioned is also a metaphorically feminine noun, governed by a redundant particle, and the verb still takes the feminine marker. At most, in such cases, the feminine marker is optional, and its omission is not what is preserved. As al-Baḥr notes, the feminine marker is not attested with (kafā) when the subject is feminine and governed by the redundant bāʾ. For this reason it has been said that the subject of (kafā) is a pronoun referring to self-sufficiency (ikhtikāʾ), meaning: "it suffices, that is, self-sufficiency, with yourself." It has also been said that it is an ism al-fiʿl (a verb-like noun) meaning "be sufficient," and the subject is the pronoun of the addressee, and the bāʾ in both views is not redundant. The view preferred by the majority is what we have mentioned earlier. Their insistence on the masculine form is contrary to analogy.

Some scholars explained this by the frequency with which the subject is governed by the redundant bāʾ, to the extent that its omission is found only in a few known examples. Thus its rank has fallen below the rank of [normal] subjects, and the verb is therefore not made feminine for it. This is similar to what has been said about "murra bi-Hind" (he passed by Hind). Other explanations have also been given.

(al-yawma) is an adverb of time (ẓarf) for (kafā). ﴿Reckoner﴾ (ḥasīban) is a specification (tamyīz), as in the verse ﴿And excellent companions are they﴾, and as in the saying "God bless his horsemanship" (li-Llāhi taʿālā darruhu fārisan). It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). (ʿalayka) is connected to it and was placed first for the sake of the rhyme endings (fawāṣil). It takes the preposition (ʿalā) because it means "reckoner" (ḥāsib), and the one who counts (ʿādd) takes (ʿalā), as you say, "he enumerated his offences against him" (ʿaddada ʿalayhi qabāʾihahu). The form faʿīl as an adjective derived from faʿala yafʿilu (with a kasra on the ʿayn in the imperfect) occurs, like ṣarīm meaning ṣārim (sharp) and ḍarīb al-qidāḥ meaning ḍāribuhā (the one who strikes the arrows), but this is rare. Or it may mean "sufficient" (kāfin), and in that case it is used figuratively to mean "witness" (shahīd), because the witness suffices the claimant for what concerns him, so it takes (ʿalā) as the witness does. It has also been said that it means "sufficient" without figurative use, but it takes the construction of "witness" because its meaning necessarily involves it, as in "a lion against me" (asadun ʿalayya). This is a cold and forced view.

The masculine form of the adjective (faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil) is a qualifier of the self (nafs), which is feminine in grammar, because reckoning and testimony are typically associated with men. Thus the description is applied to its most common state, as if it were said: "Sufficient is yourself as a male reckoner." Or because the word "self" (nafs) is interpreted as "person" (shakhṣ), as one says, "three souls" (thalāthat anfus). Or because the masculine faʿīl is treated as faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil. The apparent meaning of "self" is the essence (dhāt), so it is as if it were said: "Sufficient are you as a reckoner against yourself."

Some have considered this a case of tajrīd (abstraction, where a speaker treats a part of himself as a separate party). It was said that this is a serious error, but it has been objected that there is something to examine here, because the witness is different from the one witnessed against. If one considers that the person in that state is like another person, then it is tajrīd, but this has no bearing on the purpose here.

It is reported from Muqātil that the "self" here means the limbs, since they bear witness against the servant when he denies [his deeds]. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. It is reported from al-Ḥasan that when he recited the verse he would say: "O son of Adam, God has been just to you who made you the reckoner of your own self." The apparent view is that this is said to both the believer and the unbeliever. As for what Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Suddī, that on the Day of Resurrection a book is brought out for the unbeliever, and he says, "My Lord, You have decreed that You are not unjust to the servants, so let me reckon my own self," and then it is said to him, "﴿Read your record; sufficient is yourself﴾" and so on, this does not indicate that it is specific to the unbeliever, as is clear. It is also reported from Qatādah that on that Day whoever was not able to read in this world will read.

It has been reported that the believer first reads his good and bad deeds written on the back of his record, which the people of the gathering see but he does not see, and they envy him for them. When he finishes reading the bad deeds and thinks that he is ruined, he sees at the end: "These are your bad deeds, which We have forgiven you." His face brightens, his joy grows, and then he reads his good deeds, so his light increases and he returns to his people joyful, saying: ﴿"Here, read my record! Indeed I thought I would meet my reckoning."﴾

As for the unbeliever, he first reads his good and bad deeds written on the back of his record, which the people of the gathering see, so they seek refuge from them. When he finishes reading the good deeds, he finds at the end: "These are your good deeds, which We have returned to you." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿"And We will turn to the deeds they did and make them scattered dust."﴾ His face blackens, his distress grows, then he reads his bad deeds, so his affliction is added to affliction, and he returns with increased loss and wretchedness, saying: ﴿"Would that I had not been given my record, and had not known my reckoning!"﴾ May God the Exalted make us of those who read and are elevated, not of those who read and are wretched, by His bounty and generosity.

This is the view. Some interpreted "the Book" (al-kitāb) as the self imprinted with the traces of deeds, its "publication" (nashr) as its being made manifest to himself and others, and its "reading" as the manifestation of that to him and to others. Its explanation is that whatever comes from a person, good or bad, produces in the spirit a specific trace, which is hidden as long as the spirit is attached to the body and occupied with the impressions of the senses and faculties. When its attachment is severed, its resurrection occurs, as the veil is lifted by its connection to the higher world. Then the trace of everything he did in his life appears imprinted on the tablet of the self, and this is the meaning of writing and reading. It is not hidden that this is a Sufi and speculative approach, far from being apparent and close to being hidden. It also amounts to interpreting the Resurrection as the lesser resurrection, which is also contrary to the apparent meaning. The narrations clearly state what is understood from the apparent meaning of the verse. True, they do not deny that the self may be imprinted with the traces of deeds, and that this appears on the Day of Resurrection, so there is no objection to affirming both. For this reason the Imam said: "The truth is that the apparent states mentioned in the narrations are true and genuine, without doubt, and the verse's capacity to bear these spiritual meanings is also evident. The straight method and the right path is to affirm all of them." Excellent is what he said, except that whether that capacity is evident is itself not evident. Al-Khafājī said: "There is nothing in this that contradicts the transmitted report." It has been applied to what is reported from Qatādah, that on that Day whoever was not a reader will read. There is no basis for counting it as supporting this view. You know that interpreting Qatādah's words in that way is also an interpretation. Perhaps Qatādah and his like among the early community did not have such interpretations in mind. Arabic speech is like a camel with a flexible nose [that can be led anywhere], and God the Exalted knows best the realities of things.

As for the arrangement of the discourse (kayfiyyat al-naẓm), the Imam mentioned three aspects.

The first: when God the Exalted said ﴿And everything We have detailed with explanation﴾, it implied that everything needed of the proofs of Divine Unity, prophethood, and the return has been mentioned. Given this, the excuses have been removed and the causes eliminated. Thus everyone who arrives at the plain of Resurrection has had his "omen" (ṭāʾir) fastened around his neck.

The second: when He showed that He, glorified is He, brought to creation kinds of things beneficial to them in religion and in worldly life, such as the signs of night and day and others, it was as if He had bestowed upon them the forms of His blessings. This requires that they occupy themselves with serving and obeying Him, the Exalted. Thus everyone who arrives at the plain of Resurrection will be questioned about his words and deeds.

The third: when God the Exalted made clear that He did not create creation except for His worship, as He said: ﴿"I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me."﴾ When He explained the conditions of the sun, the moon, the day and the night, it was as if He said: "I created these things so that you would benefit from them, and become able to occupy yourselves with obeying Me." Given this, everyone who arrives at the plain of Resurrection will be asked whether he performed that obedience or rebelled and disobeyed. End of the Imam's words.

It may also be said that the connection is this: earlier the discourse explained the state of the Book of God, which contains the explanation of what is beneficial and harmful among deeds. Here the discourse explains the state of the servant's record, which leaves out no small or great deed without recording it. Its goodness and badness follow from taking what is in the first Book or not. Whoever takes it is guided, and whoever turns away from it has gone astray.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 15 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for his own self﴾ is a summary (fadhlaka) of what preceded concerning the Qur'an being a guide to that which is most upright, and to the binding of deeds upon their doers. That is: whoever is guided by its guidance, acts upon what is within its contents of rulings, and refrains from what it forbids, then the benefit of being guided by it returns only to his own self; it does not pass beyond him to others who were not guided. ﴿And whoever strays﴾ from what it guides him to, ﴿then he strays only to his own loss﴾. That is: the burden of his straying is only upon him,
[p. 35]
not upon one who did not engage in it, so that the deed could be separated from its doer. ﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾: this is an emphasis on the second clause. That is: no soul bearing a burden bears the burden of another soul, such that the second soul could be freed of its burden, and the necessary connection between the doer and his deed would be disrupted. The emphasis is specifically given to the second clause to cut off vain hopes, since they used to claim that if they were not upon the truth, the responsibility would fall on their forefathers who had imitated them.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira when he said: "Disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ) and I will bear your burdens." This verse is not contradicted by what is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will have a portion of it﴾, nor by His saying: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾. This is about one person bearing another's burden and benefiting from his good deed or being harmed by his evil deed. For in reality this is a benefit from one's own good deed and a harm from one's own evil deed, since the reward of the good and evil deeds that the doer performs is necessarily his. What reaches the intercessor is the reward of his intercession, not the reward of the original good or evil deed. Likewise, the reward of misguidance is restricted to the misguided, and what the misleaders bear is only the reward of misleading, not the reward of straying. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyya).

It was on the basis of this verse that 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, criticised the authenticity of the report of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the deceased is punished for the weeping of his family over him." For it contains the taking of a person to account for the sin of another, which contradicts what this verse states.

It has been answered that the hadith is to be understood as applying when the deceased had bequeathed that (weeping), so that the punishment would be of the kind of the reward for misleading. It was also said: the intended "deceased" is metaphorically the one at the point of death, and "punishment" means punishment in this world; that is, the dying person suffers pain from his family's weeping over him, so they should not weep. Also on the basis of this verse, a group of the early jurists prevented the diya (blood money) from being imposed upon the 'aqila (paternal kin), because it involves holding a person accountable for the act of another. It has been answered that this is an obligation that falls by way of original imposition; otherwise, the one who erred himself is not held accountable for that act, so how could another be held accountable for it?

Al-Jubba'i used this verse to argue that the children of polytheists are not punished; otherwise they would be held accountable for the sins of their fathers, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning of the verse. Some claimed that it was revealed concerning them, but this is not correct. Indeed, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr reported in al-Tamhid, with a weak chain, from 'A'isha who said: "Khadija asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the children of the polytheists, and he said: 'They are from their fathers.' Then she asked him again after that, and he said: 'Allah knows best what they used to do.' Then she asked him after Islam had become firmly established, and the verse was revealed: ﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾, and he said: 'They are upon the fitra,' or he said: 'They are in Paradise.'"

The matter is disputed and there are various positions. The majority said: they are in Hell, following their fathers. It is cited in support of this what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported in Nawadir al-Usul, "from 'A'isha also, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the children of the Muslims, where are they? He said: 'In Paradise.' And I asked him about the children of the polytheists, where are they? He said: 'In the Fire.' I said: O Messenger of Allah, they did not reach the (age of) deeds, and the pens did not record upon them. He said: 'Your Lord knows best what they used to do. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you wish I will let you hear their wailing in the Fire.'"

In response: this report has been declared weak by Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, so it cannot be used as proof. Indeed, it is authentically established that "he (ﷺ) was asked about the children of the polytheists and he said: 'Allah knows best what they used to do.'" There is no explicit statement in this that they are in the Fire. The literal meaning of his words, "Allah knows best what they used to do," applies whether they would have reached maturity or not, and obligation only applies upon reaching maturity.

al-Bukhari, the authors of the Sunan, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "al-Sa'b ibn Jaththama told me: I said, O Messenger of Allah, we sometimes attack at night and hit the offspring of the polytheists. He said: 'They are from them.'" According to the opponents, this is to be understood as meaning that they are from them in worldly rulings, such as enslavement.

A group withheld judgment concerning them, and among these is Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him. It was also said: among them are those who enter Paradise and those who enter the Fire, based on what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported in al-Nawadir from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about the offspring of the polytheists who died while young. He lowered his head for a while, then said: 'Where is the questioner?' He said: 'Here I am, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'When Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has judged between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, and none remain but them, they will cry out and say: O Lord, our Lord, Your messengers did not come to us, and we knew nothing. So He will send to them an angel, and Allah knows best what they used to do. He will say: I am the messenger of your Lord to you. Go, and they will follow until they reach the Fire. He will say: Indeed Allah commands you to plunge into it. A group of them will plunge in, then they will be brought out from where their companions do not see, and they will be placed among the foremost and those brought near. Then the messenger will come to them and say: Indeed Allah commands you to plunge into the Fire. Another group will plunge in, then they will be brought out from where they do not perceive, and they will be placed among the companions of the right. Then the messenger will come and say: Indeed Allah commands you to plunge into the Fire. They will say: Our Lord, we have no strength for Your punishment. So He will command concerning them, and their forelocks and feet will be gathered together, and they will be thrown into the Fire.'"

The verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) held that they are among the people of Paradise, and this is the correct view. It is supported by several things, among them the verse according to what you have heard from al-Jubba'i. Among them is the hadith of Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him in Paradise with the children of people around him. They said: O Messenger of Allah, and the children of the polytheists? He said: "And the children of the polytheists." Reported by al-Bukhari in his Sahih.

Among them is what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi also reported in al-Nawadir, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, "from Anas who said: We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the children of the polytheists, and he said: 'They are the servants of the people of Paradise.'"

Among them is the verse that follows, since it indicates that there is no punishment before accountability, and that obligation does not apply to a newborn; and the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him, binds, "until he reaches maturity." No one has disagreed that the children of the Muslims are in Paradise, except some of those who are not counted, who withheld judgment concerning them, based on the hadith of 'A'isha: "A child from the Ansar died, and I said: Blessed is he, a sparrow from the sparrows of Paradise, who did not do evil and did not reach it. He (ﷺ) said: 'Or other than that, O 'A'isha? Allah, Exalted is He, created for Paradise people, whom He created for it while they were in the loins of their fathers, and He created for the Fire people, whom He created for it while they were in the loins of their fathers.'"

The scholars answered this by saying that perhaps he, peace be upon him, forbade her from hastening to a definitive judgment without a conclusive proof, just as he rebuked Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas for his saying: "Give him (the gift), for I see him as a believer." He said: "Or a Muslim." The hadith is long.

It is possible that he (ﷺ) said that before he knew that the children of the Muslims are in Paradise; then when he knew, he said what he said in his saying (ﷺ): "No Muslim has three children die who have not reached the age of puberty except that Allah, Exalted is He, admits him into Paradise by His grace and mercy towards them."

And besides that from the hadiths. The Qadi said: the verse indicates that the burden is not of Allah's doing, for if it were, it would be impossible for the servant to be held accountable for it, just as he is not held accountable for the burden of another. And because the burden would have to be entirely removed, since the one who bears a burden is described as such only when he is acting by choice and is able to guard against it; for this reason a child is not described as bearing a burden. You know that this only holds against the Jabriyya (determinists), not against the group who say: there is neither compulsion nor delegation.

﴿And We are never punishing﴾: this is an explanation of the divine care following the explanation that the effects of guidance and misguidance are restricted to their possessors, that the one who is guided is not deprived of the fruits of his guidance, and that a soul is not held accountable for the crime of another. That is: it is not valid, nor proper, from Us, but rather it is impossible, in Our custom founded upon profound wisdoms; or it is not in Our past judgment and previous decree that We should punish anyone with any kind of punishment, whether worldly or otherworldly, for doing or leaving anything, whether fundamental or derivative, ﴿until We send﴾ to him ﴿a messenger﴾ who guides to the truth, warns against misguidance, establishes proofs, and lays down the laws; or until We send a messenger of this kind whose call reaches him, whether he was sent to him or not, as you will learn, God willing, from the disagreement. This is a limit to the impossibility of the punishment occurring at its appointed time, not a limit to its non-occurrence absolutely. How could it be so, when the otherworldly punishment cannot occur immediately after the sending, and the worldly punishment does not take place except after the realization of what requires it of sin and disobedience? Do you not see how the punishment that befell the people of Noah, peace be upon him, was delayed from them for about a thousand years?

The Mu'tazila, who hold the rational obligation (wujub 'aqli) before the sending of a prophet, were refuted by this verse, for He, Exalted is He, negated punishment absolutely before the sending, and this is a necessary consequence of obligation, on condition of abandoning the obligatory act according to them, since they do not permit pardon. So obligation is negated before the sending because its necessary consequence is negated. The gist of it is: if there were a rational obligation, it would be established before the sending, and there is no doubt that rational people used to abandon obligatory acts at that time, so it would follow that they would be punished before it, and this is false by the verse.

It has been objected that this is only complete if punishment is understood to include both worldly and otherworldly punishment, as has been indicated; but what fits what follows is that the intended punishment is the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal) in this world. And from the negation of worldly punishment before the sending it does not follow that obligation is negated, because the necessary consequence of obligation according to them is the otherworldly punishment. It was answered, granting that what fits what follows is worldly punishment: the verse, since it indicates that it is not befitting His wisdom to bring the lesser punishment for abandoning an obligation before the warning through the sending of a messenger, its indication that the greater punishment is not brought for abandoning it before that is more fitting.

Al-Asfahani, in his commentary on al-Mahsul, raised several objections against those who used the verse to negate rational obligation before the sending. First: the intended meaning of "messenger" in it is reason. Second: even granting that the intended meaning is the prophet sent, the verse indicates the negation of punishment for direct action before the sending, and it does not follow from this the negation of punishment in general. Third: granting that, there is no indication in the verse that punishment before it is negated for every sin. Fourth: granting the indication, it does not follow from the negation of being held accountable that the liability is negated, since the removal of being held accountable through forgiveness is permissible.

Then he answered the first: the true meaning of "messenger" is the sent prophet, and the original in speech is the literal meaning. He answered the second: it is characteristic of the great in status to express the negation of punishment absolutely by the negation of direct action. He answered the third: as we pointed out, the sentence is to be understood as "and We are never punishing anyone," and from this follows the negation of the punishment of each one of humankind; and that is what is sought, because the opponent does not hold that.

And on the fourth point: the verse indicates the negation of punishment before the sending of a messenger, and the negation of punishment before it apparently indicates the absence of obligation before it. So whoever claims that the obligation is established, and that forgiveness has overlooked it, must provide the proof. End quote.

You know that if the argument is *ilzami* (a reasoning that binds the opponent by his own premises), as many have said, the fourth point does not arise at all, because the Mu'tazilah do not permit pardon for abandoning the rational obligation (*al-wajib al-'aqli*). We have already pointed to this. Yes, al-Maraghi said in his commentary on the *Minhaj al-Usul* of al-Qadi: "There is no need to make the proof ilzami. Rather, it can be completed even on the assumption that pardon is permissible, by saying: the occurrence of punishment, even if it is not necessarily entailed by the obligation, nevertheless entails the absence of security from its occurrence by necessity, since punishment for abandoning an obligation is permissible according to us even if it is not obligatory. And this entailed consequence, namely the absence of security, is negated by the verse's indication that it does not occur. So the antecedent is negated by the negation of the consequent."

This was refuted, first, by denying that the absence of security from the occurrence of punishment is a necessary consequence of abandoning the obligation in every case. Rather, the absence of security holds only when the non-occurrence of punishment is not known with certainty by another proof. Second, the negation of the absence of security is only through the verse, for if its revelation is accepted, punishment would be permissible. There is no doubt that its negation through the verse is a negation through pardon, because the meaning of pardon is the absence of punishment, and the verse indicates this. So the proof is not complete on the assumption that pardon is permissible, and this is, as you see, [unconvincing]. It was also said: "We take the consequent to be the permissibility of punishment, so the proof is completed in a verified manner, because the permissibility of pardon

[p. 38]

does not contradict the permissibility of punishment." It was refuted by saying that the implication, namely that if the obligation were established before the Law, the abandoner of the obligation would be punished, even if it is accepted at that point, nevertheless the falsity of the consequent is disputed, because the verse only indicates the negation of the occurrence of punishment, not the negation of its permissibility.

But it may be said that the meaning of "We would not be punishing [anyone] until We sent a messenger" is that [punishment] is not permissible, and the meaning of the negation is the negation of permissibility. This construction is frequently used in that sense, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وما كُنّا ظالِمِينَ﴾ ("We were not wrongdoers") and ﴿وما كُنّا لاعِبِينَ﴾ ("We were not playing"), and so on. Had the negation of occurrence been intended, it would have been said: "We do not punish until We send a messenger."

Al-Imam [al-Razi] weakened the use of the verse as proof by saying: "If the rational obligation is not established, the legal obligation is never established at all, and this is false, so that is false too." He said: The implication is shown in several ways. The first: when the Lawgiver comes and claims to be a prophet from Allah, exalted is He, and manifests a miracle, is it obligatory for the hearer to listen to his speech and to reflect upon his miracle, or is it not obligatory? If it is not obligatory, then the claim of prophethood is invalid. If it is obligatory, then either it is obligatory by the Law or by reason. If it is obligatory by reason, then the rational obligation is established. If it is obligatory by the Law, that is invalid, because that Lawgiver is either that claimant or someone else. The first is invalid, because the result of the statement returns to his saying: "The proof that it is obligatory to accept my word is that I say: it is obligatory to accept my word," and this is establishing a thing by itself. If it is someone else, the discussion about him is as in the first case, and it leads either to circularity (*dawr*) or to infinite regress (*tasalsul*), and both are impossible.

The second: when the Law comes and makes some acts obligatory and forbids others, there is no meaning to obligation and prohibition except that [the Lawgiver] says: "If you leave such-and-such, or do such-and-such, I will punish you." So we say: either it is obligatory upon him to guard against punishment or it is not obligatory. If it is not obligatory, the meaning of obligation is not established at all. If it is obligatory, then either it is obligatory by reason or by revelation (*al-sam'*). If it is obligatory by reason, that is what is intended. If it is obligatory by revelation, the meaning of obligation is not established except through the ordaining of punishment for it, and then the first division returns and infinite regress follows, which is impossible.

The third: the position of the People of the Sunnah is that Allah, exalted is He, may permissibly pardon the punishment for abandoning an obligation. If that is so, the quiddity of obligation (*mahiyyat al-wujub*) is present along with the absence of punishment. So there remains only that it be said: the quiddity of obligation is established only through the arising of fear of punishment, and this fear arises through reason alone. Thus it is established that the quiddity of obligation arises only through this fear, and that this fear arises through reason alone. It follows that obligation is present through reason alone. If they say: the quiddity of obligation is established only through the arising of blame, we say: if He, exalted is He, pardons, the blame falls away. So the quiddity of obligation is established only through the arising of fear of blame, and that arises through reason alone. Thus it is established by these aspects that rational obligation cannot be repelled. End quote.

Al-'Ibadi criticized this: It is possible to answer the first point by saying that when [the messenger] manifests a miracle as proof of his claim to be a messenger, his truthfulness is established, as is settled in its proper place. So it is obligatory to accept his word in everything he reports from Allah, exalted is He, without entailing any of the faults of establishing a thing by itself, or circularity, or infinite regress. And if the establishment of what is reported by the Law is in the sense that its establishment is by the report of one whose messengership has been established by a miracle, from Allah, exalted is He, that it is so. The sum of the argument on this view is not that he says: "The proof that it is obligatory to accept my word is that I say: my word is obligatory," so that what follows follows. Rather its sum is that he says: "It is obligatory to accept my word, because it has been established that I am the messenger of Allah, exalted is He, so my truthfulness and the affirmation of me in everything I claim is obligatory." There is none of the earlier objectionable consequences in this. The Sayyid al-Sanad [al-Jurjani] explicitly stated in his commentary on the *Mawaqif* that the Law is established and following it becomes obligatory by the mere claim of messengership, together with the accompaniment of a miracle and the capacity of the addressed rational person to reflect, even if he does not reflect. He mentioned that in that case it is not permissible for the responsible person to ask for delay, and if he asks for delay, delay is not obligatory, because it is the custom that knowledge is created after reflection, which he is capable of. So it is known that by the mere claim of messengership together with what has been mentioned, the obligation is established by his report,

[p. 39]

namely the establishment of the Law, because the meaning of establishment by it is establishment by report from Allah, exalted is He, actually or by ruling. On this view, the dilemma he mentioned with his words, "because that Lawgiver is either..." etc., cannot arise. So consider this carefully. As for the second point, the obligation to guard against punishment is not something foreign to the obligation of such-and-such, so that the dilemma he mentioned could be directed at it. Rather it is the very obligation of such-and-such or its necessary consequence, since guarding is only by doing such-and-such, which is the obligatory act. So the obligation to guard is either the obligation of such-and-such or its consequence, and its obligation is by its obligation. Thus the mentioned dilemma does not follow.

As for the third, if by his saying that the quiddity of obligation is established only through the arising of fear of punishment he means that the actual occurrence of the obligatory act in external reality, by performing it, is only through the arising of fear, then that is not the subject of discussion. Moreover, we do not accept that performing the obligatory act depends on the arising of fear. If he means that the realization of the obligation of the obligatory act, that is the attachment of its obligation to the responsible person, which is the actual (*tanjizi*) command, depends on the arising of the said fear, then this is disputed, as is evident. End quote. So consider this carefully.

You know that the use of the verse as proof, if it is complete, is not restricted to the Mu'tazilah. It is shared by one of the two groups of the Hanafiyyah among the People of the Sunnah, namely the Maturidiyyah and the general body of the shaykhs of Samarqand. For although they do not say, as the Mu'tazilah do, that reason judges by good and evil, which they both affirm, they say that reason is an instrument for knowing them, so Allah, exalted is He, creates that knowledge after reason's correct reflection. They also made the belief in Allah, exalted is He, and His exaltation obligatory, and forbade attributing anything shameful to Him, glory be to Him. It is narrated from Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "If Allah, exalted is He, had not sent a messenger, it would still have been obligatory upon creation to know Him."

Several of their scholars have explicitly stated that reason is one of the proofs of Allah, exalted is He, and that reasoning with it is obligatory before the revelation of the Law. They argued for this by what Allah, exalted is He, reported about Abraham, peace be upon him, saying to his father and people: ﴿إنِّي أراكَ وقَوْمَكَ في ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ ("Indeed I see you and your people in clear error"), where he said this without saying "It was revealed to me." And [they cite] his reasoning by the stars, and knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, through them, and making them a proof against his people. Likewise all the messengers argued with their peoples by proofs of reason, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿قالَتْ رُسُلُهم أفِي اللَّهِ شَكٌّ فاطِرِ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ ("Their messengers said: Is there doubt about Allah, Creator of the heavens and earth?"), and the verse ﴿ومَن يَدْعُ مَعَ اللَّهِ إلَهًا آخَرَ لا بُرْهانَ لَهُ بِهِ﴾ ("Whoever invokes with Allah another god, for which he has no proof"), where He did not say: "Whoever invokes with Allah another god after it was revealed to him or the call reached him." And by His saying, glory be to Him, reporting about the people of the Fire: ﴿وقالُوا لَوْ كُنّا نَسْمَعُ أوْ نَعْقِلُ ما كُنّا في أصْحابِ السَّعِيرِ﴾ ("And they will say: Had we been listening or reasoning, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze"), where they reported that they came to the Fire because they abandoned benefiting from hearing and reason. And there is more.

It may be replied that if they had benefited from reason in knowing the Creator before the revelation of the Law, they would not have entered the Fire. Also, the revealed proofs were not proofs except through rational inference. Also, calling all the disbelievers to the religion of Islam is obligatory upon the community, and it is known that the Dahriyyah cannot be argued against with the speech of Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. So nothing remains but the proofs of reason. And then it may be said to them:

If it were obligatory upon creation to know Allah, exalted is He, and to believe in Him before the sending of a messenger, the punishment of the disbeliever before it would follow, because He, exalted is He, reported that He does not forgive associating partners with Him. But He has negated punishment in the verse, so there is no obligation by necessity, the negation of the necessitated being by the negation of the necessitating, in the manner done with the Mu'tazilah.

Al-Imam al-Razi, after he had weakened the use of the verse as proof and established the rational obligation, mentioned two aspects regarding the verse. The first: taking "messenger" to mean reason. The second: restricting the general (*takhsis al-'umum*), by saying: the intended sense of "We would not be punishing" is in the matters that cannot be known except by the Law, until after the coming of the Law. Then he said: "What we accept and hold to is that mere reason is a cause for it to be obligatory upon us to do what benefits and to abandon what harms, and it is impossible that reason should judge that God, exalted is He, is obligated to do or to refrain from doing anything." End quote.

You know what has been said about taking "messenger" to mean reason, which is contrary to the usage of the Noble Qur'an. It is also made distant by the rebuke of the guardians [of Hell] to the disbelievers with their words: ﴿أوَ لَمْ تَكُ تَأْتِيكم رُسُلُكم بِالبَيِّناتِ﴾ ("Did there not come to you your messengers with clear proofs?"), and they did not say: "Were you not rational?" And taking "messenger" in it to mean reason is something that reason itself does not accept. He himself excused the restriction by saying that although it is a departure from the apparent meaning, it is necessary to turn to it when evidence for it exists, and he claims that evidence exists.

Abu Mansur al-Maturidi and his followers interpreted the verse as negating the punishment of annihilation (*ta'dhib al-istt'sal*) in this world. These [others] went to the punishment of the people of the *fatrah* (the interval between prophets) for abandoning faith and monotheism. They are everyone who lived between two messengers, where the first was not sent to them and they did not reach the second. Al-Nawawi, in his commentary on Muslim, relied on the view that they are punished, and said: "Whoever died in the *fatrah* upon what the Arabs were upon, the worship of idols, is in the Fire, and there is no censure in this before the call reached them, for these people had been reached by the call of Abraham and other messengers, peace be upon them." The apparent meaning is that al-Nawawi is satisfied, for the obligation of faith upon everyone, with the call of one who came before them from the messengers reaching them, even if he was not sent to them. So there is no contradiction between his ruling that they are people of the *fatrah* in the earlier sense and his ruling that the call reached them, contrary to al-Abi's claim in that regard. Indeed, the contradiction would arise only if he claimed that those messengers who preceded them were sent to them, and that is not the case.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 15 (part 3 of 3):

To this view al-Halimi (Abu 'Abd Allah al-Halimi) went. In his *Minhaj* he said: Whoever is an intelligent discerning person, when he hears any call to God Most High, and abandons using his reason to establish its validity, while he is among the people of reasoning and reflection, becomes by that one who turns away from the call, and so he disbelieves. It is far-fetched that there could exist a person to whom the report of any of the Messengers has not reached, despite their great number, the long duration of their missions, the abundance of those who believed in them and followed them, and of those who disbelieved in them and opposed them. For the report may reach through the mouth of an opponent just as it reaches through the mouth of a supporter. And even if it were possible that someone had never heard of a religion, or of the call of a prophet, or had no knowledge that there are people in the world who affirm a God, and we do not think that this would occur, then his case would fall under the disagreement over whether faith is obligatory by reason alone or whether the transmitted report must be added. This is explicit in establishing that every person is obligated to believe after the call of any one of the Messengers has come, even if he was not sent to him. Some have gone to excess in relying on this, to the point that one of them said: Whoever has been reached by the call of any of the Messengers (upon them be peace) in any way, and then neglects to investigate it, is an unbelieving person among the people of the Fire. So do not be deceived by the statement of many people about the salvation of the people of the interim period (*ahl al-fatra*, those who lived in the gap between prophets), together with the reports of the Prophet (ﷺ) that their fathers who died in the time of ignorance are in the Fire. End of quotation.

What the Ash'ariyya among the theologians and jurists (*usul*), and the Shafi'is among the jurists (*fuqaha'*), hold is that the people of the interim period are not punished, and they stated this without qualification. It is, however, authentically established that a group of the people of the interim period were punished. It has been answered that their reports are solitary reports (*ahad*), which cannot contradict the certainty of there being no punishment before the mission (*ba'tha*). It has also been answered that it is possible that those among them who were authentically reported to have been punished were punished for a matter specific to them that required this, a matter known to God Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ), similar to what has been said regarding the ruling of the disbelief of the boy whom al-Khidr (upon him be peace) killed despite his youth. It has also been said that the punishment of these persons mentioned in the reports is restricted to those among the people of the interim period who altered and changed their religion in a way that cannot be excused, such as worshipping idols

[Page 41]

and altering the laws, as 'Amr ibn Luhayy did. It is not hidden that this does not accord with the unqualified statements of these imams, nor with the view that there is no obligation except through the Shari'a. And if it were possible that those whose punishment is established were followers of a law that was still in force at that time, such as the law of 'Isa (upon him be peace), then no difficulty would remain at all. Some who hold that they are punished without qualification have relied on what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported in *Nawadir al-Usul*, and al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: ««On the Day of Resurrection there will be brought the one who was made deficient in reason, the one who died in the interim period, and the one who died as a child. The one made deficient in reason will say: O Lord, if You had given me reason, the one You gave reason would not have been happier with his reason than I would have been. The one who died in the interim period will say: O Lord, if a covenant from You had come to me, the one to whom a covenant from You came would not have been happier with Your covenant than I would have been. The one who died as a child will say: O Lord, if You had given me a lifespan, the one You gave a lifespan would not have been happier with his lifespan than I would have been. The Lord, blessed and exalted, will say to them: Go and enter Hell. Even if they entered it, it would not harm them at all. Then there will come out upon them spurts of fire, and they will think that it has destroyed everything God created. So they will return hastily and say: O our Lord, we came out, by Your might, desiring to enter it, but spurts of fire came out upon us, and we thought it had destroyed everything God created. Then He will command them a second time, and they will return for it and say the same. Then the Lord, exalted, will say: I created you upon My knowledge, and to My knowledge you return. O Fire, seize them. And the Fire will seize them.»»

Some reports indicate that among them there are those who are punished and those who are not punished.

Ahmad, Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Hurayra that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ««Four will argue on the Day of Resurrection: a deaf man who hears nothing, a fool, an aged decrepit man, and a man who died in the interim period. As for the deaf man, he will say: O Lord, Islam came and I heard nothing. As for the fool, he will say: O Lord, Islam came while the children were pelting me with dung. As for the decrepit one, he will say: O Lord, Islam came and I did not understand anything. As for the one who died in the interim period, he will say: O Lord, no messenger of Yours came to me. Then He, glorified be He, will take their covenants that they will surely obey Him, and He will send to them a Messenger saying: Enter the Fire. Whoever enters it, it will be cool and safe for him, and whoever does not enter it will be dragged into it.»»

Qasim ibn Asbagh, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: ««On the Day of Resurrection four will be brought: the newborn infant, the mentally impaired, the one who died in the interim period, and the aged decrepit old man. All of them will speak with their argument. The Lord, blessed and exalted, will say to a neck of Hell: Emerge! And He will say to them: I used to send Messengers to My servants from among themselves, and now I am My own Messenger to you. Then He will say to them: Enter this. The one for whom wretchedness was written will say: O Lord, will You make us enter it, when it is from it that we were fleeing? But the one for whom happiness was written will proceed and plunge into it. Then the Lord, exalted, will say: You have seen Me and you disobeyed Me, so you are even more severe in denying and disobeying My Messengers. Thus these will enter Paradise and those will enter the Fire.»»

Besides these reports and others, those who hold that the children of polytheists, and even the children of believers, are divided (into those who enter Paradise and those who enter the Fire) rely on them. Yet there is some doubt in the heart about their authenticity, although Ibn Hajar in *al-Isaba* said that they were transmitted by several chains. Even supposing they are authentic, their contradictory report is more authentic than they are. What the heart inclines to is that reason is a proof for knowing the Creator, may He be exalted, and His oneness, and His transcendence above having offspring, glorified be He, even before the coming of the Shari'a, by the earlier evidences and others, although some of them may be open to objection. The sending of Messengers and the revelation of Books is a mercy from Him, exalted be He, or it is for explaining what cannot be attained by reason of the kinds of worship and the prescribed limits. Thus it is not objected that if reason were a proof, God Most High would not have sent a Messenger and would have been satisfied with it. It has been said in reply to this: Since the matter of resurrection and recompense is one that is problematic for reason alone, except through great reflection, which is a hardship for which a person may be excused, and without which there is no faith, God Most High sent the Messengers (upon them be peace) to explain what completes the religion, not to supply the bare knowledge of the Creator, for that is attained by the first stirrings of reason. A dung-pellet indicates the camel, and a track indicates the traveler. Is not a sky with constellations, an earth with wide paths, and seas with waves, indicative of the Subtle, the All-Aware?

Also, God Most High did not leave us without a Messenger from the beginning to the end, and the proof was established through one (Messenger) just as it remains established through Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Day of Resurrection. This does not indicate that the first was not a sufficient proof. Likewise He did not leave us, glorified be He, and the explanation through a single sign, but rather favored us, may His majesty be exalted, with repeated signs. This does not indicate that a single sign was not a sufficient proof.

As for His saying, reporting the words of the guardians to the people of the Fire: ﴿Did not messengers come to you with clear proofs?﴾, it is a rebuke in its most evident sense, and it does not indicate that the other (proof) is not a proof. And His saying: ﴿So that people will have no argument against God after the Messengers﴾ means: so that they will have no pretext to argue with their claim that they would say: ﴿Why did You not send us a messenger?﴾. And His saying: ﴿That is because your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly while their people are heedless﴾ is to be understood as referring to destruction by the punishment of total annihilation in this world for denying the Messengers. As for the recompense of disbelief, it is the Fire in the Hereafter. The same applies to the verse under discussion, given how much it calls to (reflection). There is no excuse for whoever among the people of the interim period did not know his Lord, glorified be He, if he was intelligent, discerning, and able to observe and reason, especially if the call of one of the Messengers (upon them be peace) reached him. It is hardly found that anyone has not been reached, as you have heard from al-Halimi. It has been said that such people exist in America, which is called Yekī Dunyā (the New World), before it was conquered around the year 1000 after the Hijra by Christopher Columbus, known as Colombo, for as we have been informed, its people at that time had never heard the call of any Messenger at all. Then, what is understood from the words of the eminent scholars is that the dispute concerns only the rulings of faith in God Most High, unlike the branches (*furu'*), about which there is no disagreement that they are not established except for one who has been reached by the call of the one sent to him. This is the apparent meaning. Yes, regarding what the religions agree upon of the branches, is it like faith, so that the dispute mentioned above applies to it? There is room for consideration. As for belief in our Prophet (ﷺ), it is not obligatory for one who has not been reached by his call, since reason has no scope in that, as is not hidden from anyone of intellect. Indeed, the proof of Islam, al-Ghazali, said: After his mission (ﷺ), people are of several categories. One category has not been reached by his call and has never heard of him at all; those are decreed to Paradise. A second category has been reached by his call and by the manifestation of the miracle at his hand, and by the noble character and praiseworthy qualities he possessed (ﷺ), but they did not believe in him, like the disbelievers who are among us; those are decreed to the Fire. A third category has been reached by his call (ﷺ) and has heard of him, but as one of us hears of the Antichrist, and far be his noble station (ﷺ) from that; I hope for these Paradise, since they did not hear what would encourage them to believe in him. End of quotation. Perhaps the decree of Paradise for the first group and the hope of it for the second apply only if they are believers in God Most High; but if they are not, they are in a different state. Furthermore, the question of the non-obligation before the revelation of the Shari'a can be established by this verse only according to those who argue with it, as al-Isfahani said: If the aim is to obtain a predominant assumption from it, then if it is a matter of certainty, it cannot be established by probabilistic proofs. And according to them there is a kind of sufficiency in it, i.e., ﴿And We would not punish nor reward until We send a Messenger﴾. They said: He dispensed with mentioning the reward by mentioning its counterpart, the punishment, and did not reverse it, because the punishment is more evident than the reward in realizing the meaning of obligation. So reflect.

**Page 43**

﴿And when We intend to destroy a city﴾ explains how the punishment takes effect after the sending of a messenger. The intention meant here is not the eternal will related to the occurrence of the willed thing at its predestined time, since the consequent punishment does not accompany that eternal will, nor is it realized in fact, since the willed thing does not lag behind it. Rather, it means the approach of the time, as in His saying, ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ (16:1), meaning: when the time approaches for Our will to be related to destroying it, by punishing its people with the mentioned punishment of total annihilation (*al-istiʾsal*), which we have shown cannot be inflicted by Us before the sending of a messenger, or with some type of the general punishment whose nature we have mentioned. Namely, the punishment of total annihilation, because of their wrongdoing and sins, at an approach that wisdom requires, without having a specific fixed limit. ﴿We command﴾ them to obedience, as Ibn Jarir and others have transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr, through the tongue of the Messenger sent to its people.

﴿Its affluent ones﴾ means its pampered ones, its tyrants, and its kings. They are singled out for mention, although the command is directed to all of them, because they are the leaders of depravity and the heads of misguidance, and whatever occurred from others occurred by following them; and because the directing of the command to them is more emphatic. What indicates the supposed obedience is that *fasaqa* (to transgress) and *ʿasa* (to disobey) are close in meaning linguistically, even though *fisq* is restricted in the Sharia to a specific sin. The mention of the opposite indicates the opposite, just as the mention of the like indicates the like. Thus the mention of transgression and disobedience indicates the supposed obedience, as has been said regarding His saying, ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ (16:81). The meaning is like: "I commanded him, so he did evil to me," that is, "I commanded him to do good," by the contextual opposition between the two, supported by reason, which indicates that one is not commanded to do evil just as one is not commanded to transgress, and by transmission, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not command immorality﴾ (7:28). It is also permissible that the verb be treated as intransitive, as in "he gives and withholds," meaning: We directed the command.

﴿So they transgressed therein﴾ means they went out of obedience and became rebellious. Al-Zamakhshari preferred that the original sense is "We commanded them to transgression, so they transgressed," but the literal meaning is impossible because of the evidence, so it is taken as a metaphor, either through the figurative metaphor (*istiʿara tamthiliyya*) by likening their state, in their turning about in blessings while disobeying and being insolent, to the state of one who was commanded to that; or through the figurative metaphor (*istiʿara tamthiliyya*) by likening their state, in their turning about in blessings while disobeying and being insolent, to the state of one who was commanded to that; or through the explicit subordinate metaphor (*istiʿara tasrihiyya tabaʿiyya*) by likening the pouring of the insolence-inducing blessings upon them to commanding them to transgress, with the common element being driving them to it and causing it. The metaphor in both forms is completed by what is not hidden. It has also been said: the command is a metaphor for driving and causing, because they are both shared in leading to something. He (al-Zamakhshari) also held that the supposition "We commanded them to obedience, so they transgressed" is not permissible, on the claim that it is the deletion of what has no evidence for it; rather, the evidence stands against it. Because the expressions "I commanded him, so he stood" and "I commanded him, so he sat" are understood only as a command to stand and sit, and if you intended the opposite of that, you would have been demanding from your interlocutor knowledge of the unseen. There is no objection from expressions like "I commanded him, but he disobeyed me" or "he did not comply with my command," because since that contradicts the command, it is known that it is not suitable as an indication of the omitted element, so the verb in that case is of the type of "he gives and withholds." It has been objected: why could it not be of the type of "I commanded him, so he disobeyed me," given what you have heard of the closeness of *fasaqa* and *ʿasa*? And why would the phrase ﴿Indeed, Allah does not command immorality﴾ not suffice as an indication for the supposition "We directed the command," so that transgression occurred from them, rather than the object of the command needing to be supposed? Then why could the sequence with the opposite not be an indication of the other opposite? Such examples are more than can be counted. Al-Kashshaf answered these: As for the first two, the author of al-Kashshaf prevented the meaning "We commanded them to obedience," but as for the meaning "directing the command," he did not prevent it on this path; rather, what prevents it is that the specification of the affluent then remains without clear reason, and likewise the restriction by the time of the intention to destroy, since His command is in effect at every time and for everyone; and because of its evident nature he did not address it. As for the third, the fame of *fisq* in one of its two meanings prevents counting it as the opposite of disobedience. Moreover, what we mentioned of the remoteness of the context from absolute usage applies to restriction by obedience. In this there is a statement of sound judgment and a view with the eye of satisfaction and heedlessness of the aspect of specification that we mentioned, which is clear and free of blemish. Likewise the aspect of restricting by the mentioned time. The truth is that what al-Zamakhshari mentioned about the figurative reading is a fine aspect, but his not accepting what the trustworthy transmitters related from the interpreter of the Qur'an (Ibn ʿAbbas) and others, of supposing obedience, despite the evidence being evident and the context of rebuking misguidance and urging guidance supporting it, has no basis, as is not hidden from one who has a heart.

**Page 44**

Abu Hatim transmitted from Abu Zayd that ﴿amarna﴾ means "We multiplied," and al-Farisi preferred it. Abu ʿUbayda cited for the validity of this usage what Ahmad and Ibn Abi Shayba in their *Musnads* and al-Tabarani in *al-Kabir* transmitted from the hadith of Suwayd ibn Hubayra: "The best wealth is a steadfast path and a fertile mare." (*Khayr al-mal sikkatun maʾburatun wa muhratun maʾmurah*.)

That is: abundant in offspring. And *amara*, as has been said, is of the category of what is intransitive and made transitive by variation of vowel, so one says *amartuhu* with a fatha on the *mim*, and it becomes *umira* with a kasra on it. This is like *shatara Allah ʿaynahu* (Allah blinded his eye) and it became *shutira*, *jadaʿa anfahu* (he slit his nose) and it became *judiʿa*, and *thalama sinnahu* (he chipped his tooth) and it became *thulimat*. It has also been said that the kasra form is transitive too, and that al-Hasan, Yahya ibn Yaʿmur and ʿIkrima recited it thus, and al-Nahhas and the author of al-Lawamih transmitted this from Ibn ʿAbbas. The rejection of it by al-Farra' is not to be heeded, because the transmission is sound. In al-Kashshaf, that *amara* in the sense of *kaththara* is common. As for the transitive *amartuhu*, al-Zamakhshari said in al-Faʾiq something to the effect that: this speaker relied only on what came in the report, namely "a fertile mare," and this is nothing but from *amr* (command), which is the opposite of *nahy* (prohibition), and it is also a metaphor, as in the verse. It is as if Allah, the Exalted, said to her, "Be abundant in offspring," and she was. So she is commanded contrary to being forbidden. It has also been said: its origin is *muwmara*, and it was changed to *maʾmura* to seek rhyme, like His (ﷺ) saying: "Those who bear burdens, not those who are rewarded" (*maʾzurat ghayr maʾjurat*), where he did not say *mawzurat*.

ʿAli (may Allah honor his face), Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Rajaʾ, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Zayd and al-Kalbi recited *āmarna* with a long vowel (*madd*). The same was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu al-ʿAliya, Ibn Hurmuz, ʿAsim, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafiʿ, and it is the preference of Yaʿqub. Its meaning according to all is "We multiplied," and with this the earlier interpretation is supported against the well-known recitation.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi, al-Suddi, Zayd ibn ʿAli and Abu al-ʿAliya recited *ammarna* with doubling (*tashdid*). It is also transmitted from ʿAli, al-Hasan and al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with them.

And ʿAsim and Abu ʿAmr. Its meaning according to this recitation has been said to be "We multiplied" also. It has also been said: "We made them rulers and appointed them as commanders." The intransitive form of this is *ummira* with a damma, assimilating it to the innate qualities, that is, he became a commander. What is meant by it is one who commands and is obeyed, whether he is a king or not, since there is no objection even if the king is meant by it, contrary to al-Farisi's view; because when a pampered man is made king over a city and he transgresses, then another transgresses after him, and so on, corruption multiplies, disbelief follows, and the punishment descends upon them through the last of their kings.

﴿So the word became due against it﴾ means: the word of the punishment previously decreed, by its power, or by the manifestation of their disobedience, or by their immersion in it. ﴿So We destroyed it with complete destruction﴾, which cannot be fully comprehended in its reality and cannot be described. Destruction (*tadmir*) is annihilation together with the obliteration of traces and the demolition of buildings. The verse indicates the destruction of the people of the city in the most complete manner, and the destruction of all of them, because transgression came from all of them, for the non-affluent usually follows, especially if the affluent one is one of the scholars of evil. From here it has been said: the meaning is: "And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones, so they transgress therein, and others follow them, so the word becomes due against it," and so on. It has been said: the destruction of all does not depend on following, for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who wronged﴾ (8:25).

It is authentically related from the Mother of the Believers Zaynab bint Jahsh that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her and said, supplicating: "There is no god but Allah. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near! Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Yajuj and Majuj like this," and he made a ring with his thumb and the finger next to it. Zaynab said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases."

Now, the apparent meaning is that ﴿We command﴾ is the answer to *idha* (when), with no preposition or postposition in the verse. The well-known difficulty in it on this supposition is that it indicates that He, glorified is He, wills to destroy a people from the outset, and so He reaches it by commanding them, whereupon they transgress and He destroys them; and willing harm to others from the outset without their deserving harm, as harm of this kind, is something He is exalted above, since it contradicts wisdom. The answer to this has already been pointed out. Some have answered it by saying that there is inversion and reordering in the verse, and the original is: "When We command the affluent of a city and they transgress therein, We intend to destroy it, so the word becomes due against it," and its parallel, as has been said, is His saying: ﴿And when you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you﴾ (4:102). Others said that His saying ﴿We command﴾ and so on is in the position of a qualifier for *qaryah* (city), and the answer to *idha* is omitted, being dispensed with by what in the speech indicates it, as has been said regarding His saying: ﴿Until, when they came to it and its gates were opened﴾ up to His saying: ﴿How excellent is the reward of the workers﴾ (39:73), and the words of the Hudhali poet, from the end of a qasida:

*Until, when they drove them into the wasteland, lame, as the camel-drivers drive the scattered camels.*

Other answers than these have been given regarding this, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 17:

﴿How many generations have We destroyed﴾, meaning: We have destroyed many. ﴿of the generations﴾ is a specifier (tamyiz, a grammatical term for a noun that clarifies the meaning of a preceding quantity word) for "how many." The word *qarn* (generation), according to al-Raghib, means a people who coexist in one time period. It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa that it is a period of one hundred and twenty years. It is narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Mazini, and it is reported with a traceable chain to the Prophet (ﷺ), that it is one hundred years. It has also come that the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated for a man, saying: "Live a qarn," and he lived one hundred years or one hundred and twenty. It is narrated from al-Kalbi that it is eighty years, and from Ibn Sirin that it is forty years. ﴿after Noah﴾, meaning after his time, peace be upon him, such as ʿAd and Thamud and those after them, among those whose circumstances are recounted in the Mighty Qur'an and those whose circumstances are not recounted. Noah, peace be upon him, is singled out for mention and it does not say "after Adam," because he was the first messenger whose people harmed him, and so the punishment uprooted them. Therefore there is in it a threat and a warning to the polytheists. And because the condition of his people was manifest, they were not classed among the destroyed generations. Moreover, the mention of him, peace be upon him, is a symbol pointing to the mention of them. The first *min* (from) is explanatory (lil-tabyin), not superfluous, and the second is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghaya). Therefore it is permissible for their two complements to be the same. Al-Hufi said: the second *min* is a substitute for the first, but this is not sound.

﴿And sufficient is your Lord﴾, meaning: sufficient is your Lord. The discussion of this construction has already been treated in detail just above. ﴿as one who is aware of the sins of His servants, Seeing﴾, meaning encompassing their outward and inward aspects, so He will punish them for them. The placing of *khabiran* (aware) first is due to the precedence of its object, namely the beliefs and intentions which are the origins of outward actions, a precedence of existence. It was also said: a precedence of rank, because what matters is what is in the heart, as is indicated by the hadith: "Indeed God, Exalted is He, does not look at your forms or your actions, but He looks at your hearts and your intentions."

And indeed, actions are by intentions, and the intention of the believer is better than his action, and so on. Or it is for its generality, in that it relates to things that are not visible as well. The prepositional phrase is connected to "aware, Seeing" by way of the grammatical dispute (tanazu').

Al-Hufi said: it is connected to *kafa* (sufficient), and this is a mistake. In concluding what has preceded with what has been mentioned, there is an indication, as has been said, that the sending of messengers, the command, and what follows them of their immorality are not for the purpose of acquiring knowledge of the sins that proceeded from them, for that knowledge already exists before that. Rather, it is for cutting off excuses and establishing the proof from every direction. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that He, glorified be He, by His saying ﴿And sufficient is your Lord﴾ etc., indicated that the sins are the causes of destruction only and nothing else. Its explanation, as in al-Kashf, is that when He, majestic is His glory, followed their destruction with His knowledge of their sins with a more complete knowledge, this indicates that He requited them for them, otherwise the speech would not be coherent. As for the restriction (hasr), it is because if anything else had a part in it, the apparent thing would be to mention it in the context of the threat, and then the cause would not be complete and the speech would fall short of conveying the intended meaning. So the restriction is necessary, and that is what is sought. I do not see his speech as free of a trace of Mu'tazilite insinuation, which becomes apparent upon reflection. Perhaps for this reason the scholar al-Baydawi did not address it.

[Page 46]

﴿Whoever desires﴾ — that is, by His knowledge, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak — ﴿the immediate [world]﴾ alone, without desiring the Hereafter along with it, as indicated by the continuity conveyed by the addition of (kana) here, together with the restriction to absolute desire in its two divisions. It has been said: if it were not restricted, it would apply to one who desires both the immediate world and the Hereafter, and division contradicts partnership. The indication of this from desire is that desire is the heart's resolve toward a thing, and the exclusivity of one's concern with it is not quite that. By "the immediate [world]" is meant the worldly abode, as was also reported from al-Dahhak. Desiring it means desiring the various kinds of its aims, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿And whoever desires the tilth of this world﴾. It has also been permitted that the intended meaning is "the immediate life," as in His Exalted saying: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾. The first interpretation has been preferred, because it is more fitting with His Exalted saying: ﴿We hasten for him therein﴾, i.e., in that immediate [world], since that life and its continuity are among what is hastened. Therefore the more fitting particle here is (min) ("from"), as in the Mighty and Majestic saying: ﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it﴾. ﴿What We will﴾, i.e., what We will to hasten for him of its bounties, not everything he desires.

﴿For whomever We will﴾ — hastening for him what We will. Abu Ishaq al-Fazari said: that is, for whomever We will to destroy; but no word in the verse indicates this. The prepositional phrase (lahu, "for him") is a substitute (badal, a grammatical apposition) for the earlier prepositional phrase, namely (lahu), so it needs no resumptive pronoun, since it is a substitution of single words. Or the prepositional phrase ﴿for whomever﴾ is a substitute for the earlier pronoun in the genitive case, by repeating the governing particle, and its estimated form is: "for whomever We will to hasten for him from among them." The pronoun refers back to (man, "whoever"), which is either a relative or a conditional. On both estimates, it indicates plurality, so it is a substitute of part for whole. It is reported from Nafi' that he read (ma yasha'u, "what He wills") with the letter ya', so it is said that the pronoun in it refers to God Most High, and the two readings then agree. It is also said that it refers to (man), so it would be specific to those whom God Most High wills this for, such as Nimrod and Pharaoh, and those who were aided by God Most High in what they willed as a respite for them. This has been supported by the argument that on the first reading there would be a shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical person) within a single clause, and a shift within a single clause, if it is not prohibited, is not favored, as he elaborated in ʿArus al-Afrah. The restriction of what is hastened and of its recipient by the will and desire mentioned is because the wisdom on which the cosmic order turns does not require that every seeker reach his goal, nor that every one who attains something receive all that he seeks in full. By "their deeds" in His Exalted saying: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they therein will not be denied﴾, is not meant all their deeds, nor every one of their deeds. The discussion of this has already preceded, so remember it. The mention of "will" (mashi'ah) in one and "desire" (iradah) in the other, if they are said to be synonyms, is a stylistic variation (tafannun, variety of expression).

﴿Then We have made for him﴾ — in place of what We hastened for him — ﴿Hell, he will burn in it﴾, i.e., he will suffer its heat, as al-Khalil said, or he will enter it, as has been said. The clause, as Abu al-Baqa said, is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (lahu, "for him"). Abu Hayyan said it is a circumstantial clause from (Jahannam, "Hell"), which is the first object of (ja'alna, "We made"), and (lahu) is the second object.

It has also been permitted that the clause is a new, independent sentence. The author of al-Ghaniyan said: the second object of (ja'alna) is omitted, and the estimated word is "a destination" or "a recompense," but there is no need for that. ﴿Blameworthy﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of (yasla, "he will burn"). It is from blame, the opposite of praise, and its verb is (dhamma), and (dhammatuhu, "I blamed him") and (dha'amtuhu, "I censured him") have the same meaning. ﴿Rejected﴾, i.e., expelled, distanced from the mercy of God Most High. Al-Imam said: punishment is an expression for a harm combined with humiliation and blame, on the condition that it be lasting and free of any benefit. So His saying: ﴿We have made for him Hell, he will burn in it﴾ is an indication of the great harm; ﴿blameworthy﴾ is an indication of humiliation and blame; and ﴿rejected﴾ is an indication of distance and expulsion from His mercy. This indicates that the harm is free of any admixture of benefit or mercy, and it indicates that it is lasting and free of any change to comfort and deliverance. End. It is not hidden that this is apparent in showing that the verse indicates eternity, and in that case it is necessarily clear to us that this seeker is one of the disbelievers.

In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim: ﴿Whoever desires﴾, i.e., by the deeds he performs, whether the attainment of what he desires follows from them as a recompense, as with deeds of righteousness, or by way of the effects following from causes, as with means, or by deeds of the Hereafter. So the one who desires is, on the first reading, the disbelievers and most of the wicked; on the second, the people of showing off and hypocrisy, the one who emigrates for worldly gain, and the one who fights for booty. You know that including the wicked person, the one who emigrates for worldly gain, and the one who fights for booty, if he is a believer, within this illustration, on the view that the verse indicates eternity, is not consistent with our principles. Yes, it is valid according to the principles of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school). Al-Zamakhshari included the wicked person in this, and the subtle stratagems of Mu'tazilism from him, may God Most High deal with him by His justice, are more than can be counted. The apparent position of Abu Hayyan's statement is to favor the view that the one who desires is one of the disbelievers, where he said: "the immediate [world] is the worldly life, and desiring it means preferring it over the Hereafter, and there must be an omitted element, indicated by the opposing term in..."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 19:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾, etc. That is: whoever desires the immediate (worldly life) and strives for it its due striving while he is a disbeliever, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish. It has also been said that what is meant is whoever desires the immediate (worldly life) by means of the deeds of the Hereafter, such as the hypocrite, the show-off, the fighter who seeks the spoils of war and renown, and the emigrant who seeks worldly gain, and so on to the end of what was said. Thus he (al-Alusi) related a view other than the first view, which necessarily requires that the one who desires be a disbeliever, after he introduced it with "it has been said." It is supported by Kathir's explanation of ﴿whoever desires the immediate (worldly life)﴾ as "whoever's concern is confined to it, desiring nothing else at all." For this hardly applies to a believing sinner, since if he had no desire for the Hereafter he would not have believed in it.
