And according to the view that the sinner and the like are included, of those for whom we do not judge eternity (in the Fire), the claim that the verse proves eternity is rejected, and it is said of whoever is admitted to the Fire that he is distanced from the mercy of Allah the Exalted for as long as he is in it. Thus it applies to the sinner for as long as he is in it, just as it applies to the eternal disbeliever.

Some have claimed that the one who desires is the hypocrite who fights alongside the Muslims for the spoils and not for reward, for the verse was revealed concerning him. In this there is an objection: what has preceded, that the surah is Meccan apart from certain specific verses which this is not one of, rejects that. Moreover, the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not the specific cause (of revelation). So understand.

﴿And whoever desires﴾: the apparent meaning, in line with what passed from al-Dahhak, is that his deed is also directed at ﴿the Hereafter﴾, that is, the Abode of the Hereafter and the lasting bliss within it. ﴿And strives for it its striving﴾, that is, the striving that is fitting and suitable for it, as the specifying genitive (idafa) indicates. Whether "striving" is the object, meaning "he performed its deed," or an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq, a verbal noun that is the object of its own verb), the meaning holds. This is realised by doing what Allah the Exalted has commanded and refraining from what He, glorified is He, has forbidden. Thus it excludes those disbelievers who worship by means of innovated opinions and claim that they are striving for it. The purpose of the lam, whether it denotes purpose or specification, is to make the intention and sincerity to Allah the Exalted in the deed a consideration. Some scholars chose, and it is not without merit, that there is no need for what al-Dahhak considered; rather, it is better not to consider it, because of "and strives for it its striving." In that case, nothing is considered in what preceded either, and the verse, on this reading, contains, as anyone who reflects will see, a belittling of worldly affairs and a magnifying of the status of the Hereafter.

﴿And he is a believer﴾, a sound belief not mixed with anything that corrupts it. The mention of belief in a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya, a clause that describes the state of the subject) indicates that its concomitance with what was mentioned within the scope of "whoever" is a condition, so neither desire nor striving benefits without it. In reality, belief is that from which the desire for the Hereafter and the striving for salvation in it and the attainment of reward arise. It is reported from one of the early scholars: "Whoever does not have three things, his deed will not benefit him: firm belief, a sincere intention, and a correct deed." And he recited this verse. ﴿Those﴾ refers to "whoever," with the designation of his being characterised by what has preceded. The distance implied by "those" is to indicate the loftiness of their rank and the eminence of their station. The plural is used in consideration of the meaning, indicating that the reward implied by the report occurs in a collective manner. That is: those who combine the praiseworthy qualities that have passed, namely the desire for the Hereafter, the fine striving for it, and belief, ﴿their striving is appreciated﴾, rewarded for it and accepted by Him, the Exalted, with good acceptance. Some explained "striving" here as the deed expressed by a verb, which includes all that has preceded; this is different from the earlier striving. Others said it is the same. He attached appreciation to it alone, not to its two companions, indicating that it is the chief element in that. The origin of "striving," as al-Raghib said, is brisk walking, which is less than running, and it is used for earnest effort in a matter, whether good or bad, but it is used most often for praiseworthy actions. The poet said:

If I reward Alqamah ibn Sa'd for his striving,
I will not reward him for the trial of a single day.

[p. 48]

The tanwin (nunation) in ﴿كُلا﴾ is, according to the well-known view of the grammarians (al-nuhat), a tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad) for the genitive noun that is added to it, not a tanwin of tamkin (tanwin al-tamkin, the nunation that marks a noun as fully nominal). The meaning is "each of the two groups." It is the object of ﴿نُمِدُّ﴾, placed before its verb. The meaning is: We increase them time after time, such that each later gift becomes an increment to the earlier one. What is given as increase is what is hastened to each of the two groups of worldly gifts, and what is prepared for the other group of deferred gifts, which is indicated by the fact that their effort is appreciated (mashkuriyyat al-sa'y). The verse did not state this explicitly because it relies on what was previously stated, both explicitly and allusively, and on what follows, both in expression and in indication.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿هَؤُلاءِ وهَؤُلاءِ﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿كُلا﴾, a substitution of the whole (badal kull) in the manner of detailed specification. The meaning is: We increase these, for whom the gift is hastened, and these, whose effort is appreciated. The demonstrative indicates the very referent together with its characteristic designation, not merely the entity as a pronoun does. Thus it reminds of that by which the increase occurs, and it specifies the omitted genitive noun, to block the supposition that it refers only to the last group, those who desire the true good and are deserving of assistance. It also serves to confirm the restriction (qasr) derived from fronting the object.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿مِن عَطاءِ رَبِّكَ﴾ means: from His vast giving, which has no end. It is a verbal noun (ism masdar) occupying the position of the passive participle, and it is connected to (numuddu). It dispenses with mention of that by which the increase occurs, and it draws attention to the fact that the increase mentioned is not by way of earning through effort and action, but purely by bounty, as has been said.

﴿وما كانَ عَطاءُ رَبِّكَ﴾ means: whether it is worldly or otherworldly.

The explicit noun in place of the pronoun serves to give greater attention to its matter and to indicate that it is the cause of the ruling. ﴿مَحْظُورًا﴾ means: prevented from those who seek it. Rather, it overflows upon whoever has been decreed for it, according to the requirement of a will founded on wisdom, even if there is present in him what calls for prohibition, such as disbelief. This has the sense of a causal explanation for the inclusiveness of the increase to both groups. The mention of the title of Lordship (ruboobiyyah) indicates that it is the origin of each of the increase and of the absence of prohibition.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 21 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Behold how We have favoured some of them over others.﴾ "Kayfa" (how) is in the accusative position, as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) governed by "faddalna" (We have favoured), and it is not a noun governed by a clause as some have supposed. The whole clause is in the accusative position governed by "unzur" (behold), and it is here suspended (mu'allaq). The purpose, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is to clarify what preceded concerning the provision (imdad) and that giving is not restricted, by drawing attention to the degrees of one of the two gifts and inferring from them the degrees of the other. That is: look with the eye of consideration at how We have favoured some of them over others in the deferred gifts that We have bestowed upon them, and the disparity among their recipients, by way of inference from the state of the lower to the state of the higher, as He, exalted is He, made clear in His saying: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.﴾ That is, greater than the degrees and preferences of this world, because the disparity in the Hereafter, through Paradise and its lofty degrees, cannot be measured in extent nor comprehended in essence.

It is reported in some narrations that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, between the highest of the people of Paradise and the lowest in rank is a distance like the star that is seen in the eastern and western horizons. Allah, exalted is He, has pleased all of them, so none envies another."

And from al-Dahhak: the one above sees his favour over one below him, and the one below does not see that anyone is above him. It is also established that Allah, exalted is He, has prepared for His righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr narrated in al-Isti'ab from al-Hasan who said: A group of people came to the door of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), among them Suhayl ibn 'Amr al-Qurashi, who was one of the nobles in the Jahiliyyah, and Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, and those elders of Quraysh. He gave permission to Suhayb, Bilal, and the people of Badr, whom he loved, and he had given them a grant. Abu Sufyan said: "I have never seen a day like this; permission is given to these slaves while we sit and no one pays attention to us." Suhayl, who was the most intelligent of them, said: "O people, by Allah, I see what is in your faces. If you are angry, then be angry at yourselves. The people were called and you were called, and they hastened while you were slow. By Allah, what they have been given of virtue is harder on you to miss than this door for which you compete."

In al-Kashshaf it is said that he said: "We were only brought low from our side, that they were called and we were called, and they hastened while we were slow. And this is the door of 'Umar, so how could there be disparity in the Hereafter? And if you envy them for the door of 'Umar, then what Allah, exalted is He, has prepared for them in Paradise is greater." It is also read: (akthar tafdilan) with the thaa' (with three dots), meaning "more in preference."

Moreover, it is permissible that what is meant by "that" (ma) in "by which We provide" are only the immediate gifts. The restriction mentioned is understood as rebutting the assumption that they are restricted to the first group, since the specification of their desire for them and their attaining them, mentioned without any reference to the relation between them and the second group in desire and attainment, gives the impression that they are restricted to the first. So the meaning is: both groups We provide with immediate gifts, not only those whose desire for them We mentioned from the first group, from the gift of your Lord, which is abundant; and His worldly gift was never forbidden to anyone, whether one who desires it or one who desires other than it. Behold how We have favoured, in that gift, some of each of the two groups over some others of them... and so on. This view was also held by al-Hasan and Qatadah, for it is reported from them that they said regarding the verse: Allah, exalted is He, provides in this world both those who desire the immediate life, the disbelievers, and those who desire the Hereafter, the believers, and He provides all of them with sustenance. The mention of sustenance among what is provided is said to be by way of example, and it is said to be a specification indicated by the context.

It is also permissible that what is meant by it is its linguistic meaning, so it includes rank and the like, as one says: "Happiness is provisions." The majority considered that giving is not forbidden with respect to the first group, in order to establish that provision includes them, saying: "He does not prevent the sinner from it because of his sin." It was objected that this requires the restriction to be to rebut the assumption that worldly provision is restricted to the second group, although nothing in the speech had preceded that would suggest its being established for them, let alone suggesting its restriction. There is consideration in this. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the meaning of "from the gift of your Lord" is from the acts of obedience, and He provides with them the one who desires the Hereafter and with the acts of disobedience He provides the one who desires the immediate life. So the gift would be a term for what Allah has apportioned to the servant of good or evil. You know that it is extremely far-fetched to take acts of disobedience as meant by "gift," and perhaps the attribution of this to the scholar is not correct, so do not be heedless.

Know that the division contained in the verse is not exhaustive, and that is not harmful. The exhaustive division is that every doer either intends by his act the immediate life alone, or the Hereafter alone, or both together, or intends nothing. The first two kinds have had their rulings known from the verse. The third kind divides into three sorts: either the intention for the Hereafter is stronger, or it is weaker, or the two intentions are equal. Regarding the acceptance of the deed in the first sort there is a discussion according to the Imam, who said: It is possible that it is not accepted, because of what is reported from the Lord of Might, exalted is His majesty: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners from association. Whoever performs an act in which he associates another with Me, I leave him and his association."

It may be said: if the intention for the Hereafter is stronger than the intention for the world, the two equal weights cancel each other out, and the remaining excess remains sincerely for the Hereafter, so it must be accepted. To non-acceptance went al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam, while Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali inclined to the view of the basic reward, saying: If people's observing him were a factor in strengthening his energy, and if it were absent he would not abandon the worship, and if the intention of showing off alone prevailed he would not have undertaken it, then what we think, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He, is that it does not nullify the basic reward, but he is punished according to the measure of the intention of showing off and rewarded according to the measure of the intention of reward. This is clear in that showing off, even if forbidden, does not prevent the basic reward in his view when the motive for worship is predominant. Ibn Hajar mentioned that what appears preferable is that whenever the showing off accompanying the intention of worship is permissible, it does not require the cancellation of its reward from its root, but one is rewarded according to the measure of the intention of worship, however weak it is; but if it is forbidden, it requires its cancellation from its root, on account of the reports. The verse, "So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it," may not conflict with this, because his shortcoming by intending what is forbidden has required the cancellation of the intention of reward, so no atom's weight of good remains in him, and the verse does not include him. They agreed on the non-acceptance of what has the motive of the world predominant in it, or in which the two motives are equal. Al-Ghazali restricted the reports that by their apparent meaning indicate non-acceptance absolutely to these two kinds. The full discussion on this point is in al-Zawajir 'an iqtiraf al-kaba'ir.

As for the fourth kind, according to those who hold that the occurrence of an act by a capable agent depends on the arising of a motive, it is impossible to occur. Those who said it does not depend on it said: that act has no effect inwardly, and it is forbidden outwardly, because it is vain. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

* * *

Among the allusive (ishari) meanings in the verses: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾. In it there are four allusions. The allusion of sanctification in "Glory be" (subhan): it is an exaltation of Him, exalted is He, above material attachments, deficiencies of likeness, and all that is imprinted in minds. The allusion of jealousy in not naming the apparent name of His beautiful names, exalted are His names, and likewise in not naming His Prophet (ﷺ). The allusion of the unseen in using the pronoun of the absent. The allusion of secrecy in mentioning the night, for it is the place of secret and intimate converse. It is reported from one of the great ones: "Were it not for the night, I would not have loved to remain in this world." Many have mentioned that in choosing the title of servanthood there is an allusion that it is the highest of stations, and this has been alluded to earlier. Its root is humiliation and submission, and since humbling oneself before something is only after knowing it, servanthood to Allah indicates knowledge of Him, glory be to Him, and its completeness indicates the completeness of that knowledge. From here Ibn 'Abbas explained His saying: ﴿And I did not create jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ as: "except that they should know Me." And it is ninety-nine parts, corresponding to the number of the divine names, of which whoever counts them enters Paradise. For each divine name there is a particular servanthood specific to it, which those created beings who worship it worship. None has realized this station in its full perfection like the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he was a pure servant, ascetic in all states that would take him out of the rank of servanthood. Allah, exalted is He, bore witness for him that he is a servant attributed to Him in respect of his lofty aspiration here, and his comprehensive name in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And that when the servant of Allah stood up﴾. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to describe his station on the Day of Resurrection, he qualified it, saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say so without boasting."

(With the letter ra' or zay, according to the two differing narrations.) It cannot, given what you know of its meaning, be a divine attribute at all, but is a special quality in which there is no sharing. Abu Yazid al-Bistami said: "I found nothing by which one draws near to Him, exalted is He, since I saw that every attribute by which one draws near to divinity has an entry into it. So I said: 'O Lord, by what shall I draw near to You?' He said: 'Draw near to Me by what is not Mine.' I said: 'O Lord, and what is it that is not Yours?' He said: 'Humility and neediness.'"

It is mentioned that the servant with the Real in the state of his servanthood is like the shadow with the person facing the lamp: whenever he comes near the lamp, the shadow grows large, and there is no nearness to Allah, exalted is He, except by what is your more particular attribute, not His, glory be to Him. And whenever he moves away from the lamp, the shadow shrinks. For what distances you from the Real is only your leaving your attribute which befits you and your desire for His attribute, exalted is He. Thus Allah seals every proud and tyrannical heart. These are two attributes of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Taste it; indeed you are the Mighty, the Noble﴾, and these two are likewise. To this the Prophet (ﷺ) alluded by his saying: "I seek refuge in You from You."

Some have interpreted the night as the darkness of the bodily veils and natural attachments, and said: ascent and elevation can only occur through the body. They have explicitly stated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken by night, and likewise ascended while awake, without his body leaving it. But the gnostic Jami said that this reaches the Muhaddad, then the body was cast there, and this has been mentioned earlier. In Asrar al-Qur'an it is said that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was taken by night from seeing his actions to seeing his attributes, and from seeing his attributes to seeing his essence; so he saw the Real through the Real, and his form was his spirit, his spirit was his intellect, his intellect was his heart, and his heart was his secret. It seems he intended that this night journey occurred to him, otherwise to claim that the night journey mentioned in the verse is this is not fitting.

It is not hidden that the night journey (isra') is other than the ascension (mi'raj). Yes, they sometimes apply the term isra' to the mi'raj, indeed it is said: when the two are combined they separate, and when

They parted, yet they came together. It has been mentioned that all the heirs (of the prophets) have a ascension (mi'raj), but it is an ascension of spirits, not of bodies, and a night journey of secrets, not of walls, and a vision of the heart's gardens, not of direct sight. It is a path of tasting and realization, not a path of distance and road, to the heavens of meaning, not of emptiness. This ascension varies according to the varying ranks of men. Al-Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn al-Arabi), may God sanctify his secret, mentioned in his own ascension what bewilders minds and produces an astonishing wonder. That was not considered strange from him, on the basis that he sealed the Muhammadan wilayah (the saintly guardianship derived from the Prophet ﷺ) in their view.

Among the strange events that occurred in our time is that a man called Abd al-Salam, deputy of the judge in Baghdad, who was bold in issuing rulings based on falsehood, began to translate the ascension of the Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, into Turkish, together with an explanation of some of its obscure points. He was not among those who knew the hidden corners of these matters. Before he could complete his aim, he was afflicted, and we seek refuge in God Most High, with a flesh-eating ulcer in his mouth, which ate him up to his ears, and he died. His spirit was taken up to wherever God Most High willed. We ask God, glorified is He, for pardon and well-being in religion, in this world, and in the Hereafter.

It is transmitted from the Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, that the night journey (isra') happened to the Prophet ﷺ thirty times. In the words of Shaykh Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani, his night journeys, upon him be blessings and peace, were thirty-four: one of them with his body and the rest with his spirit. They have declared explicitly that the first of them was among his special distinctions ﷺ.

In al-Khasa'is al-Sughra (the Lesser Book of Special Distinctions): The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, was singled out with the night journey and what it included of piercing the seven heavens and ascending to "the distance of two bow-lengths" (cf. ﴿Or nearer still﴾), and his treading a place that no prophet sent nor any near angel had trodden, and that he covered a long distance in a short time, which is among the miracles (karamah) of the saint. The commonly known term for this is "folding of distance" (tayy al-masafa), and it is among the greatest of the breaks in customary order. The Hanafiyyah denied that it is established for the saints, and among them is Ibn Wahban, who said:

"Whoever says that a saint can fold distance,
is an ignorant one, and some of them disbelieve him."

This is from them, together with their saying: if a child is born to a man of the west from his eastern wife, for example, he is attributed to him, even if they did not meet outwardly, which is strange. The books are full of reports from trustworthy narrators of this miracle for many of the righteous. It seems that the one who called its speaker ignorant based his judgment on the notion that this involves the view of the interpenetration of substances (tadakhul al-jawahir). The theologians (mutakallimun) deemed it impossible, against al-Nizam, and they proved its impossibility with what admits of no addition. Some of them claimed that it is a matter of necessity (darura). You know that covering a long distance in a short time does not depend on the interpenetration of substances, since it may occur by speed, as they said regarding the night journey. So let it be affirmed for the saints in this manner. Moreover, miracles (karamat) like the miracles of prophets (mu'jizat) have an unknown mode (kayfiyyah), so we believe in what is authentically transmitted of them, and we entrust their mode to Him to whom nothing is impossible, glorified and exalted is He.

Like the folding of distance is what they relate of the folding of time (nashr al-zaman). I believe, and to God Most High belongs praise, in whatever of the two is validly transmitted. The one who declares them disbelievers is ignorant, and the one who calls them unknown is not a messenger (of truth). God Most High is the granter of success to what is right, and to Him is the return and the final place.

The Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) is interpreted as the station of the respected heart, lest the polytheists of the bodily powers circle around it and the abominations and sins of those powers be committed in it. The Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa) is interpreted as the station of the most remote spirit from the corporeal world. ﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾, i.e., the signs of Our attributes, insofar as they are attributed to Us, and We are the ones witnessing through them; otherwise, the origin of witnessing the attributes is in the station of the heart. ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return (to sin), We will return (to punishment)﴾. Sahl said: that is, if you return to disobedience, We return to forgiveness; if you return to turning away from Us, We return to turning toward you; if you return to fleeing from Us, We return to laying the path upon you so that you may return to Us.

Al-Warraq said: if you return to obedience, We return to facilitation and acceptance, and other things have been said.

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ (the verse). That is: this Qur'an makes its people know, by its light, the most upright ways to God Most High, which is the path of obedience and of following him to whom it was revealed, upon him be blessings and peace, for there is no path that leads (to Him) except that. And by God Most High's gift is the one who said:

"You are the gate of God; whoever comes to Him
from other than you will not enter."

They have mentioned that the Qur'an guides by its outward meaning to the meanings of its inner dimension, and by the meanings of its inner dimension to the light of its reality, and by the light of its reality to the root of the attribute, and by the attribute to the essence. So blessed is the one who seeks guidance from the Qur'an, for it leads him to God Most High. Well has said the one who said:

"When we travel by night and you are before us,
your light suffices as a guide for our mounts."

It gives good news to its people who follow it that they have the reward of witnessing and of its unveiling without a veil. ﴿And man invokes evil as he invokes good; and man has always been hasty﴾. In this is an allusion to one of the etiquettes of supplication, which is not being hasty. So the wayfarer should be patient until he knows what befits his state, and then supplicate with it. Sahl said: the safest of supplications is remembrance (dhikr) and giving up choosing, for in remembrance there is sufficiency, and a person may ask for what is his ruin without perceiving it. In a report: "God, may His glory be exalted, says: whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance rather than asking Me, I give him the best of what I give those who ask."

﴿And We made the night﴾, i.e., the night of existence and the darkness of the body, ﴿and the day﴾, i.e., the day of origination and spirit, ﴿two signs﴾ by which one arrives at knowledge of the essence and the attributes. ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾ by corruption and annihilation, ﴿and We made the sign of the day visible﴾, bright and remaining in its perfection, seeing realities by its light. ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾, which is your perfection that you are prepared to attain. ﴿And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾, i.e., that you may count the number of stations and ranks from your beginning to your end, by ascending through them, and the reckoning of your deeds, character, and states, so that you may replace the evil of these with good. ﴿And every thing﴾ of the sciences and wisdoms ﴿We have detailed﴾ by the light of your Furqanic intellects, which are attained for you when perfection is reached, in a detail without any vagueness, unlike the station of the Qur'anic intellect attained at the beginning. ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ (the verse). What may be suitable as an allusion in it has already been mentioned.

﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾. For the Sufis, regarding this messenger, like others, there are two views: some said he is the messenger of intellect, and some said he is the messenger of the Law (shar').

﴿And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones, and they defy therein﴾ (the verse). In it is an allusion that when He, glorified is He, intends to ruin the heart of the aspirant, He sets upon him the armies of his self's desire and the hosts of his devils, and it is ruined by the hooves of the horses of passions and the calamities of natural dispositions. We seek refuge in God Most High from that. ﴿Whoever desires the immediate﴾, because of the turbidity of his preparedness and the dominance of his caprice and nature, ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have made for him Hell, which he will enter, blamed and banished﴾ from the people of intellect, ﴿banished﴾ in the wrath and subjugation of God Most High. ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾, because of the purity of his preparedness and soundness of his nature, ﴿and strives toward it with the striving due to it﴾, which is striving along the path of uprightness and what the Law approves. Some said: striving toward the world is with the bodies, striving toward the Hereafter is with the hearts, and striving toward God Most High is with the aspirations. ﴿While he is a believer﴾, of firm faith, whom the gusts of doubts do not shake, ﴿those, their striving is appreciated﴾, accepted and rewarded for it. It is transmitted from Abu Hafs that the appreciated striving is that which is not mixed with showing off, nor with reputation, nor with seeing oneself, nor with seeking a return, but is sincere for His Face, glorified is He, with nothing sharing in it. So do not be heedless.

﴿To each of these and those We extend from the gift of your Lord﴾. Their will and striving have no effect in this; rather they are indicators and signs of what We have decreed for them of gift. In al-Futuhat al-Makkiyyah I saw that this verse is similar to His saying, Most High: ﴿And He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾, and it is similar to what was previously reported from Ibn Abbas, may God Most High be pleased with both of them. I have heard what is in it.

﴿And the gift of your Lord is not restricted﴾ from anyone, whether obedient or disobedient, because His way, glorified is His way, is to bestow according to what wisdom requires. ﴿Observe how We have favored some of them over others﴾ in this world by the dictate of will and wisdom. ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favor﴾. There is that which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human. May God Most High grant that to us and to you. Indeed, He, glorified is He, is the Generous, the Owner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 22:

﴿Do not set up another god alongside Allah﴾. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community (ummah), in the manner of the saying: "It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour" (إيّاكِ أعْنِي فاسْمَعِي يا جارَةُ). Or the address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed, as in the verse ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand﴾ [6:27].

﴿So you will sit (fa-taqʿuda)﴾, with the verb in the subjunctive (naṣb) as a prohibition (nahy). As for quʿūd (sitting), it has been said that it means staying (al-mukth), as you say: "He is seated (qāʿid) in the worst condition," meaning he remains and stays, whether standing or sitting. It has also been said that it means inability (ʿajz), as the Arabs say: "What has kept you (aqʿadaka) from noble deeds?", meaning what has made you unable to attain them. It has also been said that it means becoming (al-ṣayrūra), from their saying: "He sharpened the blade until it became (qaʿadat) as if it were a spear," meaning it became so. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that the use of qaʿada in the sense of ṣāra (became) is, according to the scholars, restricted to this example and is not a general rule. Some of them said: even if it is a general rule, it applies only in the same context in which the Arabs first used it, namely the saying mentioned above. So one does not say qaʿada kātiban (he sat as a writer) meaning ṣāra kātiban (he became a writer), but one may say qaʿada ka-annahu sulṭān (he sat as if he were a ruler), because it is like qaʿadat ka-annahā ḥarba (it became as if it were a spear). Perhaps whoever interpreted qaʿud here as ṣayrūra followed the view of al-Farra', for he, as Abu Hayyan and others said, held that this usage is general, and he cited as an example the verse of the rajaz poet mentioned in al-Bahr and in the Hawashi al-Shihabiyya, but there is no proof in it.

Al-Kisa'i related: "qaʿada does not ask for a need except that it fulfils it," and the usage of the Baghdadis is based on this.

Then they differed about quʿud in the sense of inability. Some said it is a metaphor (majāz) derived from quʿud, the opposite of standing (qiyām), like al-muqʿad meaning one who is unable to stand, and then the term was extended to mean inability in general. Others said it is a metonymy (kināya) for inability, since whoever wants to take something rises for it, and whoever is unable sits down. As for quʿud in the sense of disability (zamāna), it is literal (ḥaqīqa), and iqʿād (causing to sit) is a metaphor, as if his illness had caused him to sit. This quʿud in the sense of staying has been taken to be literal, but this was objected to, unless one means a customary literal meaning (ḥaqīqa ʿurfiyya) rather than a lexical one (lughawiyya), since it is the opposite of standing.

If quʿud here is taken to mean inability, the verb is intransitive, and its complement is omitted, i.e. "you will be unable to attain the desired goal," for example. And ﴿blamed and forsaken (madhmūman makhdhūla)﴾ are either two predicates for taqʿudu according to the last opinion, or two synonymous circumstantial clauses (ḥāl), meaning: "so you will sit, bringing upon yourself abandonment (khidhlān) from Allah the Exalted and blame (dhamm) from the angels and the believers, or from people of intellect, for having taken as a god a needy, dependent being like yourself, who possesses no power to benefit or harm himself, and for having attributed to him what is not fitting for him, and for having made him a partner to the One who has essential perfection, who created you, provided for you, and bestowed favours upon you, as well as upon everything else."

Abu Hayyan permitted that quʿud may be understood in its literal meaning, because it is characteristic of one who is blamed and forsaken to sit bewildered and reflecting. This is an expression by the usual condition (al-ḥāl al-ghāliba).

In the verse there is an indication that the one who affirms the oneness of Allah (al-muwaḥḥid) combines praise and support.

[Page 53]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 23:**

﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated, through Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "It means: He commanded." ﴿That you worship none but Him﴾, meaning: "that you should not worship..." etc. Here "an" (أن) is a verbal particle (masdariyya), the preposition before it is understood, and "la" (لا) is a negation, with the intended sense being a prohibition. It is also permissible for "la" to be a prohibitive particle, as has been mentioned, and this does not conflict with the interpretation of "an" as forming a verbal noun, as we have previously stated. Or the meaning is: "Do not worship, etc.," with "an" being explanatory (mufassira), because what precedes it contains the sense of speech without its letters, and "la" is purely prohibitive. Some have permitted that "an" be a lightened form (mukhaffafa) with an omitted pronoun of the matter (damir sha'n) as its subject, and "la" likewise prohibitive, but as you see, this is weak. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "an" be a verbal particle and "la" be superfluous, and the meaning would be: "Persist in worshipping your Lord." But the exception (istithna') contradicts this.

In al-Kashshaf, the verb "qada" (قضى) is explained as "amara amran maqta'an bihi" (commanded a definite command). Many scholars considered this to be from the category of tadmin (implicit meaning, where a verb is used with the sense of another verb). The implied verb was taken as the principal and the implying verb as a qualifier. Some said: He intended that "qada" is a metaphor for a firm command that does not admit abrogation (naskh). If this were tadmin, the object of "qada" would be the command and not the one commanded, otherwise it would follow that no one would worship anyone other than Allah the Exalted. Thus it would be necessary to specify the address as being to believers. This is refuted by the statement that all the commands of Allah the Exalted are by His decree, so there is no reason for specification.

It has been objected that this applies only if "qada" is intended in the sense of its brother, "qadar" (decree). But if it is intended in its linguistic meaning, which is firm determination and decisiveness, as indicated, then what he mentioned does not apply. Furthermore, the implication that no one would worship anyone other than Allah the Exalted was claimed by Ibn Abbas regarding "qada" without detail, for Abu Ubayd, Ibn Mani', Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through Maymun ibn Mihran from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Allah the Exalted sent down this letter upon the tongue of your Prophet: 'And your Lord has commanded that you worship none but Him.' Then one of the two waws adhered to the sad, and so people read: '﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾.' Had it been revealed as 'qada', no one would have associated anything with Him."

A group also narrated the same from him through Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it through al-Dahhak. This reading was also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with them both. If this is authentic, it is strange from Ibn Abbas, since the problem is removed by understanding "qada" as "amr" (command), and this is also what is narrated from him. Yes, it has been said that this meaning is metaphorical for "qada," and it has been said that it is literal. In al-Mufradat of al-Raghib, it is said: "Qada is the decisive separation of a matter, whether by speech or by action, and each of these may be divine or human." From divine speech is His statement: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾, meaning: "Your Lord has commanded," and so on to the end of what He said.

Furthermore, this command is, according to some, in the sense of absolute request, so as to include the request to abandon worship of other than Allah the Exalted. This metaphorical usage may be dispensed with, as has been said, by understanding "do not worship other than Him" as "worship Him alone," so that it is a command by way of its necessary implication. This was chosen to indicate that clearing the ground by abandoning all else is an important preliminary here. And He, glorified be He, commanded that they not worship other than Him, because worship is the utmost of glorification, and it is fitting only for one who is at the utmost of greatness and who bestows great blessings, and none other than Allah the Exalted is like this. This and what is joined to it of good deeds are like an elaboration of striving for the Hereafter.

﴿And to parents, kindness﴾, meaning: "and that you show kindness to them," or "be kind to them with kindness." Perhaps, when the change to singular address that follows is considered, the verb was supposed and "be kind" is also in the singular. The prepositional phrase is connected to the supposed verb, which is the view of al-Zamakhshari, who prevented its connection to the verbal noun because its complement cannot precede it. Al-Wahidi connected it to the verbal noun. Al-Halabi said: "If the verbal noun is resolved into 'an' and a verb, then the view of al-Zamakhshari is correct; if it is made to stand in place of the omitted verb, then the view of al-Wahidi is correct." The opinion of many grammarians is that the complement may be placed first when it is a circumstantial adverb (zarf) without restriction, because they take a wide latitude with it, and the prepositional phrase is its counterpart.

﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. "Imma" (إمّا) is composed of "in" (إنْ), the conditional particle, and "ma" (ما), the added particle that reinforces it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "For this reason the emphatic nun (nun al-ta'kid) may attach to the verb, and if 'in' were alone, its attachment would not be valid." There is disagreement regarding its attachment after the addition. Abu Ishaq held that it is obligatory, while from Sibawayh comes the view that it is not obligatory. He cites in support the verse of Abu Hayya al-Numayri:

*"So if you see my locks like this, they have overtaken the young women, guarding them."*

And upon this is the verse of Ibn Duraid:

*"Do you not see my head, whose color resembles the streak of dawn beneath the skirts of darkness?"*

The meaning of ﴿with you﴾ (عِنْدَكَ) is "in your care and guardianship." Its placement before the object, although its proper place is after it, is for the sake of arousing anticipation of what follows, since it is the seat of multiplying care and kindness. ﴿One of them﴾ (أحدهما) is the subject of the verb, and its delay after the adverbial phrase and the object is so that the sentence is not lengthened by it and what is joined to it. ﴿Both of them﴾ (كلاهما) is joined to it by conjunction.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: ﴿If both of them reach﴾ (إمّا يَبْلُغانِ). Then "ahaduhuma," according to what is in al-Kashshaf, is an apposition (badal) of the alif of the pronoun, not the subject, and the alif is the sign of the dual, according to the dialect of "akalūnī al-baraghīth" (the fleas ate me). This was refuted, because that is conditional on the dual verb being attached to a subject such as "qama akhawāka" (your two brothers stood), or to a separated subject by the conjunction "wa" alone, according to a difference of opinion, as in "qama Zayd wa 'Amr" (Zayd and Amr stood). What is here is not like that.

The apposition was also questioned, on the grounds that "ahaduhuma," on this reading, is an apposition of part from whole (badal ba'd min kull), not a whole from a whole, because it is not identical to it, and "both of them" is joined to it, so it would be an apposition of whole from whole. But this is devoid of benefit. Furthermore, the conjunction of a whole apposition with other than itself is something we have not found. It was answered: We grant that the apposition added no further meaning beyond the thing it replaces, but this is not harmful, because that is the nature of emphasis. Even if it were stipulated that this must occur, there is benefit in it, because it is a divided apposition (badal muqassam), as Ibn Atiyya said, and it is like his saying:

*"So I became like one with two legs: one healthy, and the other, time has struck it and it is paralyzed."*

It was objected that this is not of the aforementioned type of apposition, because its condition is conjunction by "wa," and that the replaced thing must not apply to one of the two divisions, whereas here it applies to one of them. In sum, this view is not free from dispute. Abu Ali al-Farisi held that "ahaduhuma" is an apposition of the dual pronoun, and "both of them" is an emphasis of the pronoun. It was objected that emphasis cannot be conjoined to an apposition, just as it cannot be conjoined to anything else; that "ahaduhuma" is not suitable as an emphasis for a dual or any other; so what is conjoined to it is likewise unsuitable; and that there is an incompatibility between making an apposition of partial sense and emphasizing it, because emphasis removes the intention of a part. From here, the author of al-Durr al-Masun said: "It must be corrected by making 'ahaduhuma' an apposition of part from whole, and a verb is supposed after it, bearing the dual pronoun as subject, and 'both of them' is an emphasis of it. The sense is: 'or both of them reach.'" Then it is a conjunction of sentences, but there is in this the omission of the emphasized and the retention of its emphasis, which some grammarians forbade. There is discussion of this in the detailed works of Arabic grammar. Perhaps the preferred view is to suppose a verb to which the dual pronoun is not attached, and to make "both of them" its subject, for it is free of what you have heard in other views. For this reason al-Bahr chose it.

The singular address of the pronoun in ﴿with you﴾ and in what follows, although what was explicitly stated earlier was in the plural, is to avoid confusion of the intended meaning, which is the prohibition of every individual from saying "uff" to his parents or scolding them. If the plural were matched with the plural, or the dual with the dual, that would not be achieved. It was mentioned that He used the singular address in ﴿do not say﴾ for emphasis, and the plural in ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ because it is more suited to glorifying the matter of decree.

﴿So do not say to them﴾, meaning: to either one of them, whether alone or together, ﴿"uff"﴾. It is a sound word (ism sawt) indicating annoyance, or a verbal noun (ism fi'l) meaning "I am annoyed." A verbal noun with the meaning of the present tense is common, and with the meaning of the past tense is rare, while most have the meaning of the imperative. About this there are roughly forty dialects. Of those that occur in the readings, there are seven: three are mutawatir (widely transmitted) and four are shadhdh (irregular).

Nafi' and Hafs read it with a kasra and tanwin, which indicates indefiniteness, so the meaning is: "I am annoyed with some annoyance." If it is not given tanwin, it indicates a specific annoyance. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read it with a fatha without tanwin. The rest read it with a kasra without tanwin, which is according to the basic principle of meeting two unvocalized letters, while the fatha is for lightness. There is no disagreement among them regarding the doubling of the fa'. Nafi', in one transmission from him, read it with a damma and tanwin, and Abu al-Sammal with a damma without tanwin, following the vowel of the letter after it. Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read it with a fatha and tanwin, and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, read it with sukun (no vowel).

The sum of the meaning: Do not be annoyed at what is disgusting from them, and do not find their burdens heavy. The prohibition of this implies the prohibition of all other kinds of harm by clear analogy (qiyas jali), because it is understood by the way of priority (bi-tariq al-awla), and it is called "mafhum al-muwafaqa" (implicit meaning of agreement), "dalalat al-nass" (indication of the text), and "fahwa al-khitab" (the import of the address). It has been said that it indicates that by way of literal meaning and explicit statement in the custom of the language, as when you say: "So-and-so does not possess a date-stone or its membrane," for it indicates likewise that he does not possess anything, small or great. Some kinds of harm were singled out for mention in His statement: ﴿and do not scold them﴾, for the sake of giving attention to its importance. Scolding, as al-Raghib said, is harsh rebuke. In al-Kashshaf: "Nahy (prohibition), nahr (scolding), and nahm (reproach) are siblings," meaning: do not rebuke them for what they do that does not please you.

The Imam said: "What is meant by His statement, ﴿So do not say to them 'uff'﴾, is the prohibition of displaying annoyance, whether little or much. What is meant by His statement, glorified be He, ﴿and do not scold them﴾, is the prohibition of displaying opposition in speech by way of answering back to them and contradicting them. For this reason this order was observed. Otherwise, the prohibition of saying 'uff' implies the prohibition of scolding by way of priority, so mentioning it after would be pointless. So reflect."

﴿And speak to them﴾ in place of the "uff" and the scolding, ﴿a generous word﴾, meaning: a beautiful word, without harshness in it. Al-Raghib said: "Everything that is honored in its category is described as generous (karim)." Some of the researchers considered this to be describing a thing by the name of its owner, meaning: a word issuing from generosity and gentleness. In the end it returns to the beautiful speech that good manners require and that the dignity of conduct demands, such as saying: "O my father!" and "O my mother!" and not calling them by their names, for that is coarseness and bad manners. A generous word is not restricted to that, as the restriction of al-Hasan in what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him might suggest, for that is by way of example. Likewise what he narrated from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad, who said regarding it: "When they call you, say: 'Here I am at your service, and at your command.'"

He and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Hadday that he said: "I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: 'Everything that Allah the Exalted mentioned in the Qur'an about kindness to parents I have known, except His statement, glorified be He: ﴿And speak to them a generous word﴾. What is this generous word?' Ibn al-Musayyib said: 'The speech of a sinful servant to a harsh master.'"

﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾ means: be humble toward them and submit yourself to them. There are two possible readings. The first is that it is to be understood as "your humbled wing," so that ﴿the wing of humility﴾ is a figurative depiction (*tamthil*) of humility, and the lowering of the wing is the image itself. It may also be a metaphor (*istiʿara*) in the single word "wing," with the lowering as a complementary image (*tarshih*), either subordinate or independent. The second reading is that it belongs to the type of the saying of Labid:

*"On a day of wind and cold, when I bared myself to it, when its reins had come into the hand of the north wind."*

In that case the speech contains a implicit metaphor (*istiʿara makniyya*) and an imaginative metaphor (*istiʿara takhyiliyya*): humility is likened to a bird that has descended from a height, an implicit comparison (*tashbih mudmar*). A wing is attributed to it imaginatively, and the lowering is a complementary image. For when a bird wishes to fly and rise, it spreads its wings and raises them so that it may ascend; when it abandons that, it lowers them. Also, when it sees a predator it fears, it presses itself to the ground and draws in its wings, which is the utmost of its fear and submission. It has also been said that by lowering the wings is meant what the bird does when it gathers its young to nurture them, and that this is more fitting to the context. In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: in the speech there is a metaphor by way of allusion (*istiʿara bi'l-kinaya*), arising from making the wing be the humility, and then the whole [image] as is the proverb for the utmost humility. Since he attributed a wing to his humility, He commanded him to lower it, for completeness. As for what may occur to some minds, that since He attributed a wing to his humility, the command to raise that wing would be more eloquent in strengthening humility than lowering it, because the perfection of a bird is in raising it, this is an error: when the whole is taken as a figurative depiction, it is evident that [raising] would be a fall, since the purpose is to portray humility as if it were seen and perceived. As for the reading of complementary image, it is a mistake, because making the lowered wing stand for humility indicates submission; but making the wing alone [stand for it] is nothing, and for this reason it was taken as a figurative depiction earlier.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited: ﴿mina'l-dhill﴾ with a kasra on the dhal, meaning submission and compliance. Its root is in beasts of burden, and its adjective is *dhalul* (tractable). As for *dhull* with a damma, its root is in human beings, and it is the opposite of honour (*izz*), and its adjective is *dhalil*. ﴿From mercy﴾ means: from the abundance of your mercy toward them. So "min" is for origin (*ibtida'iyya*) in the sense of causation (*ta'lil*). *Al-Kashshaf* says: it does not admit of explanation in the sense that "if it were so, the metaphor would revert to a comparison, since the wing of humility is never from mercy; rather the lowering of the wing of humility may be called mercy." This is clear. The emphasis is derived from making the genus of mercy the source of humbling oneself, for it arises only from perfect mercy. It has also been said that it derives from the definite article being for totality (*istighraq*), but this is not the case. They needed this because they depend on one who was the neediest of creation toward them, and a person's need for one who was needy of him is the utmost of supplication and humbleness, so he requires the most intense mercy. May God the Exalted be pleased with the wisdom of al-Khafaji, when he says:

*"O you who came asking about my poverty, how is the state of one who asks of his own asker?*
*The humiliation of a sultan is only when he becomes in need of his own agent."*

Page 57

﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy upon them﴾: call upon God the Exalted to have mercy on them with His enduring mercy, which is the mercy of the Hereafter, and do not be content with your own perishable mercy, which is what the preceding command and prohibition contained. The otherworldly mercy was singled out for the desire because it is the greatest, and it is fitting to ask it of the Great One. Also, worldly mercy is generally attained by everyone. It has been permitted that what is meant is that which encompasses both mercies. Whatever the case, this mercy in the supplication has been said to be specific to the two Muslim parents. It has also been said that it is general and abrogated (*mansukha*) by the verse prohibiting seeking forgiveness [for polytheists]. It has further been said that it is general and there is no abrogation, because that verse concerns after death and this is before it. Among God the Exalted's mercy upon them is that He guide them to faith, so supplicating for this mercy entails supplicating for that, and there is no harm in it. The claim of abrogation was recorded by al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, and Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from several routes from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both): ﴿as they raised me when I was small﴾. The *kaf* is for comparison, and the prepositional phrase is a description of an implied verbal noun, meaning: a mercy like their rearing of me, or like their mercy upon me, on the ground that rearing is mercy. It is permitted that both mercy and rearing be meant together, and that one is mentioned on one side and the other on the other side, as is indicated by the mention of the title of lordship at the opening of the supplication, as if it were said: "My Lord, have mercy upon them and lord over them as they had mercy upon me and reared me." ﴿When I was small﴾, but this is far-fetched.

It has been permitted that the *kaf* is for causation, that is, for the sake of their rearing of me; but this has been objected to, on the grounds that it contradicts its well-known meaning, and that comparison conveys what causation conveys. al-Tibi said: the *kaf* is for emphasizing existence, as if it were said: "My Lord, have mercy upon them with a realized mercy, manifest and without doubt," like His saying: ﴿just as you speak﴾. *Al-Kashshaf* says: this is a good reading. As for interpreting the *ma* as a verbal *ma* that is made a temporal clause, meaning "have mercy upon them at a time when they are most in need of mercy, like the time of their mercy upon me when I was a child, and I was like a piece of flesh on a fire", and this is only in the Resurrection, and the mercy is Paradise, and the claim that this is the verification, I wonder whether it is upright in Arabic, or whether he approved it, or whether it fits the context and the grandeur of its meaning, and so on. As he pointed out, it is nothing worth relying upon. The apparent reading is that the command is for obligation, so a child must supplicate for his parents for mercy. The implication that a command does not imply repetition is that it suffices in obeying to do it once. Sufyan was asked: how often should a person supplicate for his parents, once a day, or in a month, or in a year? He said: we hope that it will suffice if he supplicates for them at the end of the tashahhud, just as God the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him﴾, and they used to see that the tashahhud suffices for sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), just as He said: ﴿And remember God during numbered days﴾, and then they would say takbir after the prayers.

Moreover, He, Mighty and Majestic, has emphasized the recommendation of the two parents in ways that are not hidden. Even if there were nothing but that He paired kindness to them with His own monotheism and joined the judgment regarding them together, it would suffice.

Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim related, and al-Hakim said: it is sound according to the condition of Muslim, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The pleasure of God the Exalted lies in the pleasure of the two parents, and the wrath of God the Exalted lies in the wrath of the two parents."

It is authentically reported that a man came asking the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to fight alongside him, and he said: "Are your parents alive?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then strive for them."

It has also come that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "If God the Exalted knew of anything less than 'uff, He would have forbidden it. So let the disobedient child do whatever he wishes, he will never enter Paradise, and let the dutiful one do whatever he wishes, he will never enter Hell."

Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both) saw a man circumambulating the Kaʿba carrying his mother on his neck, and said: "O Ibn ʿUmar, do you think I have repaid her?" He said: "No, not even with a single contraction (of labour pain). But you have done well, and God the Exalted will reward you abundantly for little."

Page 58

Muslim and others related: "No child can repay his parent, unless he finds him a slave, buys him, and frees him."

al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* and *al-Saghir* related, with a chain containing one who is not known, from Jabir, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of God, my father has taken my wealth. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: Go and bring me your father. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: God the Exalted sends you His greetings and says: When the old man comes to you, ask him about something he said to himself that his ears did not hear. When the old man came, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What is the matter with your son, complaining of you, wanting to take his wealth?' He said: Ask him, O Messenger of God: did I spend it except on his paternal and maternal aunts, or on myself? The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Come now, leave this aside, tell me about something you said to yourself that your ears did not hear.' The old man said: By God, O Messenger of God, God never ceases to increase us in certainty through you. I did say something to myself that my ears did not hear. He said: Say it, and I am listening. He said: I said:

*I nursed you as an infant, and I nurtured you as a youth, you were ill from what I suffered for you, and you were sick.*
*Whenever a night brought you sickness, I did not sleep, but kept vigil, turning restlessly because of your sickness.*
*As if I were the one afflicted by what you were afflicted with, not I, and my eye sheds tears.*
*My soul fears for you from death, and it knows that death is an appointed time.*
*When you reached the age and the goal to which I had hoped to attain,*
*you made my reward harshness and roughness, as if you were the benefactor and the bestower.*
*Would that when you did not honour my fatherhood, you had acted as a neighbour who is near does,*
*you see him ready to oppose, as if he were appointed to reject those who are right.*"

He said: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) seized his son by the collar and said: "You and your wealth belong to your father."

The mother takes precedence over the father in goodness, for Bukhari and Muslim related: "O Messenger of God, who among people has the greatest right to my good companionship? He said: Your mother. He said: Then who? He said: Your mother. He said: Then who? He said: Your father."

Goodness is not restricted to life, but continues after death as well. Ibn Majah related: "O Messenger of God, is there anything left of the goodness to my parents that I can do for them after their death? He said: Yes: praying for them, seeking forgiveness for them, fulfilling their pledges after them, maintaining the ties of kinship that are only maintained through them, and honouring their friend." Ibn Hibban related it in his *Sahih* with the addition: "The man said: How much this is, O Messenger of God, and how good! He said: Then act upon it."

al-Bayhaqi related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A servant may die while his parents, or one of them, are being disobeyed by him, and he continues to supplicate for them and seek forgiveness for them until God the Exalted records him as dutiful." He also related from al-Awza'i, who said: It reached me that whoever disobeys his parents during their lifetime, then pays their debt if they had one, and seeks forgiveness for them, and does not revile them, is recorded as dutiful; and whoever is dutiful to his parents during their lifetime, but does not pay their debt if they had one, and does not seek forgiveness for them, and reviles them, is recorded as disobedient.

He also related, as did Ibn Abi al-Dunya, from Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man, raising it to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever visits the grave of his two parents, or one of them, every Friday, is forgiven and recorded as dutiful."

Muslim related: "Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both) was met by a man on the road to Mecca, and Ibn ʿUmar greeted him, placed him on a donkey he was riding, and gave him a turban that was on his head. Ibn Dinar said: I said to him: May God set you right, they are Bedouins, and they are content with little. He said: The father of this man was a friend of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'The greatest goodness is maintaining the ties of a child with the friends of his father.'"

Ibn Hibban related in his *Sahih*, from Abu Burda (may God be pleased with him), who said: "I came to Medina, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar came to me and said: Do you know why I came to you? I said: No. He said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever wishes to maintain his father in his grave, let him maintain the brothers of his father after him.' And there was a bond and friendship between the father of ʿUmar and your father, so I wished to maintain that."

Page 59

There are countless hadiths on the excellence of goodness. It is authentically established that disobedience to parents is counted among the greatest major sins, and that it is among them is what they agreed upon. The apparent sense of most scholars, indeed its explicit sense, is that there is no difference in this between the parents being disbelievers or being Muslims; the restriction to Muslims [appears in the hadith below].

In the fair hadith: "He (ﷺ) was asked about the major sins, and said: 'Nine: the greatest of them is associating partners with God, killing a believing soul without right, fleeing from battle, slandering chaste women, sorcery, consuming the property of orphans, consuming usury, and disobedience to the two Muslim parents.'"

This is either because their disobedience is more reprehensible, and the discussion there concerns mentioning the greatest on one of the two interpretations in the conjunction with killing a believer and what follows; or because they were mentioned for the usual case, as in other similar instances.

Al-Halimi has a distinction here, based on a weak opinion of his: disobedience (*'uquq*) is a major sin (*kabira*). If it involves something like cursing, it is a grave sin (*fahisha*). If his disobedience consists of resenting their commands and prohibitions, frowning in their faces, showing impatience with them while still obeying and remaining silent, it is a minor sin (*saghira*). If what he does compels them to withdraw so that they abandon their command and prohibition and suffer harm from this, it is a major sin.

Among the scholars there is disagreement over the definition of disobedience. In the *Fatawa* of al-Bulqini there is a question with which people have been afflicted, and it has been necessary to expand on it and on its branches, so that the purpose may be achieved within that. It is the question of the criterion by which the disobedience of the two parents is recognized. Referring to custom (*'urf*) without an example does not achieve the purpose, since people's interests lead them to treat what is not custom as custom. So there must be an example that can be woven upon. For instance: if he has a legitimate right against his father and chooses to bring him before the judge to take his right from him, even if this involves imprisonment, is that disobedience or not? He answered: Some of the great scholars said about this matter that it is difficult to pin down. Allah the Exalted has opened with a criterion, which I hope, by the bounty of the Opener, the All-Knowing, will be sound. I say: Disobedience toward one of the two parents is to harm him by an act which, if done to another person, would be forbidden as one of the minor sins, so that in relation to him it becomes a major sin. Or it is to oppose his command or prohibition in a matter in which the child may fear for his own life or a limb of his body, provided the parent is not accused in that. Or it is to oppose him in a journey that is burdensome to the parent and not obligatory for the child, or in a long absence in a matter that is not beneficial knowledge and brings no gain, or in which there is a slander of honour that has an effect.

The explanation of this criterion is that our phrase "to harm one of the two parents by an act which, if done with someone other than one's parents, would be forbidden" has the example: if he insults someone other than one of his parents, or strikes him in a way that the insult or blow does not reach the level of a major sin. Then the forbidden act, if the child does it to one of his parents, is a major sin. Our phrase "to harm" excludes taking a fils or a small amount of one of the parents' property, for this is not a major sin, even though taking the same from another person's property without a lawful means would be forbidden. This is because one of the parents is not hurt by such a thing, given their compassion and tenderness. But if he takes a large amount such that the one from whom it is taken, of the parents, is hurt by it, then it is a major sin with regard to the stranger, and so likewise here. However, the criterion for what is forbidden but minor in relation to people other than the parents is as follows. Our phrase "what, if done with someone other than one of the parents, would be forbidden" excludes, for example, demanding a debt, for this is not disobedience, because if he does it with someone other than the parents, it is not forbidden. Understand this, for it is precious.

As for imprisonment: if we base it on the permissibility of imprisoning a parent for a child's debt, as a group of scholars have affirmed, then he has sought what is permitted, and there is no disobedience. If we base it on the prohibition of imprisoning him, which is affirmed by others,
*(page 60)*
then the judge, if his belief is that, will not comply with it, and the child is not disobedient by seeking it if he holds the first view. But if he believes in the prohibition and proceeds with it, it is like seeking the imprisonment of someone who may not be imprisoned, from among strangers, for insolvency or the like. So if the child imprisons him while believing in the prohibition, he is disobedient, because if he did it to someone other than his father where it is not permitted, it would be forbidden.

As for the mere permissible complaint and the permissible demand, these are not disobedience in any way. Some of the sons of the Companions complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) did not forbid him, though he is the one who does not approve of falsehood. As for when he shouts at one of his parents, if he does this with someone other than his parents and it is forbidden, then with regard to one of the parents it is a major sin. If it is not forbidden with others, then it is not a major sin. Likewise "uff," which is a minor sin with regard to one of the parents. The prohibition concerning them, given the situation mentioned, does not necessarily mean they are major sins.

Our phrase "or to oppose his command and prohibition in a matter in which there is fear..." etc. is intended to refer to travel for jihad and similar dangerous journeys, where there is fear for the child's life or a limb of his body, because of the parents' intense grief over that.

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, concerning the man who came asking the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to go for jihad, that he (ﷺ) said to him: "Are your parents alive?" He said: Yes. He said: "Then strive (jahid) in service to them."

In another narration: "Return to them, for in them is the striving (mujahada)." In another: "I came to pledge allegiance to you for emigration, and I left my parents weeping." He said: "Return and make them laugh as you made them weep."

In its chain is Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, but the narration is from Sufyan on his authority.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that a man emigrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Do you have anyone in Yemen?" He said: My parents. He said: "Have they given you permission?" He said: No. He said: "Return and ask their permission; if they permit you, then strive; otherwise, be dutiful to them." Abu Dawud narrated it, and in its chain is one whose reliability has been disputed.

Our phrase "provided the parent is not accused in that" excludes the case where the parent is a disbeliever, for then the child does not need his permission for jihad or the like. Wherever we consider the parent's permission, there is no difference between whether the parent is free or a slave.

Our phrase "or to oppose him in a journey..." etc. is intended to refer to a voluntary pilgrimage (hajj al-tatawwu') where there is hardship, and it excludes the obligatory pilgrimage (hajj al-fard). If the journey involves sea travel, which must be undertaken when safety is predominant, then the apparent position of jurisprudence is that seeking permission is not obligatory. Even if it were said to be obligatory, because of the parent's fear over sea travel even if safety is predominant, it would not be far-fetched. As for his journey for obligatory knowledge or a communal obligation (fard kifaya), there is no prohibition on it, even if he can learn in his own city, contrary to those who make that a condition, because in travel he may expect a free heart, the guidance of a teacher, and the like. If he expects none of that, he needs to seek permission. Wherever the maintenance of the parent is obligatory upon the child, and his journey involves neglecting this obligation, the parent may forbid it. As for when the child's journey results in a slander of honour that has an effect, such as when he is a young beardless man and his journey carries a fear of accusation, he is forbidden from it; this applies with even greater force to a female.

As for opposing his command and prohibition in a matter that does not harm the child at all, but is merely guidance for the child, it is not disobedience, though not opposing is better. This is the end of al-Bulqini's words.

"Some of the researchers mentioned" that disobedience is doing to them, or to one of them, something that results in harm which is not light by custom. It is possible that the criterion is the one who is harmed. But if the parent, for example, is extremely foolish or weak-minded, and commands or prohibits his child in a matter in which opposing him is not regarded by custom as disobedience, the child does not become a sinner by opposing him in that case, because of his excuse. Accordingly, if he is married to a woman he loves, and the father commands him to divorce her, even for lack of her chastity, and he does not comply, there is no sin upon him. Yet it is more virtuous to divorce her in obedience to his father.

Ibn Hibban in his *Sahih* narrated that a man came to Abu al-Darda' and said: My father has not ceased to press me until he married me to a woman, and now he commands me to separate from her. He said: I am not one who commands you to disobey your parents, nor one who commands you to divorce your wife. But if you wish, I will tell you what I heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "The parent is the middle gate of Paradise." So preserve that, if you wish, or leave it.

*(page 61)*

The authors of the four Sunan and Ibn Hibban in his *Sahih* narrated, and al-Tirmidhi said: a hasan sahih hadith, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: I had a wife whom I loved, and Umar disliked her. He said to me: Divorce her. I refused, so Umar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Divorce her."

Likewise, all his commands which have no motive except the weakness of his intellect and the foolishness of his judgment, if they were presented to people of intellect, they would count them as trivial matters, and they would see that opposing them does not cause harm. Then he said: This is what is correct in establishing the definition.

Al-Bulqini's view has been criticized on the ground that restricting disobedience to committing a forbidden minor sin with regard to others is questionable. Rather, the rule should be what has been mentioned: that if one does to the parent something that harms him in a way that is not light by custom, it is a major sin, even if it would not be forbidden if done to another person. For example, one meets him and frowns in his face, or comes upon him in a gathering and does not stand up for him, or pays him no regard, and similar things which people of intellect and dignity among the people of custom judge as causing great harm. So reflect.

Now, the reason for magnifying the matter of parents is that they are the apparent cause of his existence and his livelihood. Hardly is any creature's blessing upon the child like the blessing of his parents upon him. It may not be said against this: the parents only sought to obtain pleasure for themselves, so that the child's entering existence and his entering the world of afflictions and dangers followed from it; so what favour is there to them from it? It is related that one of those who called themselves wise used to beat his father and say: "He is the one who brought me into the world of generation and corruption, and exposed me to death, poverty, blindness and affliction." It was said to Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri, who had no children: What shall we write on your grave? He said: Write upon it:

*This is the crime my father committed against me,*
*and I committed no crime against anyone.*

He also said, concerning abstaining from marriage and having no child:

*I left among them the blessing of non-existence, which preceded*
*and turned them away from the delights of the immediate.*
*Had they been born, they would have suffered a hardship*
*that would cast them into the destructive things of the hereafter.*

Ibn Rashiq said:

*May Allah disfigure a pleasure that the mothers and fathers obtained for our misery.*
*Had we not existed, we would not have suffered poverty; our coming into being is a calamity upon us.*

It was said to Alexander: Is your teacher greater in favour to you, or your father? He said: The teacher is greater in favour, because he bore various kinds of hardship and trials in teaching me, until he brought me to the light of knowledge. As for the father, he sought the pleasure of intercourse for himself, and brought me out into the world of generation and corruption.

We say: Suppose that at first the aim was the pleasure of intercourse. Still, the concern for bringing benefits and warding off afflictions from the moment the child enters existence until he reaches old age is greater than all that can be imagined of the aspects of good and kindness. It may be said: If bringing him into the world of generation and corruption, and exposing him to troubles and sorrows, were to cancel the right of the parents, it would follow that it cancels the right of Allah the Exalted, since He is the true Doer. Also, this exposure is counterbalanced by exposure to everlasting bliss and great reward, as is not hidden from one of sound intellect. By my life, denying their right is denying the most exalted of matters. And whoever Allah has not granted light, for him there is no light.

Your Lord knows best what is in your souls: the intention of righteousness toward them both and the formation of the reverence that is due to them. This, as has been said, is a warning against harboring aversion and resentment toward them. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that it serves as a reason (ta'lil) for what He emphasized upon them regarding kindness to the two parents: that God Most High knows what is in their hearts of this, and so He will recompense them according to it. The apparent meaning is that it is
صفحة 62
a promise to those who harbor righteousness and a threat to others, but that aspect was given precedence because the speech is primarily concerned with it. ﴿If you are righteous﴾, intending goodness and piety rather than disobedience and corruption, ﴿then indeed He﴾, exalted is His majesty, ﴿is ever forgiving to the oft-returning﴾, that is, those who turn back to Him in repentance from what has passed from them, which is something almost no human is free from, ﴿forgiving﴾ of whatever shortcoming or harm has occurred from them. This, as in al-Kashshaf, is facilitation after emphasis, and difficulty accompanied by restriction and warning.
