That is because He made a condition for the outburst that occurs rarely the intention of goodness, and He expressed it by the very word "righteousness" without explicitly stating that the outburst proceeds from them, but alluded to it by His saying: ﴿Indeed He is ever forgiving to the oft-returning﴾, since forgiveness indicates a sin, and "oft-returning" as well, for repentance from a sin is conditioned on the intention of goodness and on repenting from it with a complete repentance. This is a second resumptive statement required by the context of emphasis and stringency, as if it were said: "How can we fulfill their right when outbursts occasionally occur?" It is answered: "If you establish the matter on its foundation and that is your constant state, and then a sudden outburst occurs without intent to cause offense, God, in His kindness, will hold back His punishment from you, sustaining you in protection." That the verse concerns an outburst that proceeds from a man toward his parents is related from Ibn Jubayr, and it is also permitted that it be general for every penitent, so that one who has offended his parents and repented of his offense is included initially.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 26:**

﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾, that is, the one who is related to you, ﴿his right﴾ which is established for him. It has been said: Perhaps what is meant by "the near of kin" are the *mahram* relatives (those with whom marriage is forbidden), and by "their right" is the maintenance of them when they are poor and unable to earn, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the needy and the wayfarer﴾, for what is commanded regarding those two is financial equality; that is, give them their right, which was obligatory at Makkah in the manner of the zakat. Likewise [applies] the prohibition of squandering (*tabdhir*) and of excess in withholding and spending, for all of these are financial dealings. Some [scholars] have used this verse as evidence for the obligation of maintaining needy *mahram* relatives, even if they are neither ascendants such as parents nor descendants such as children. The statement is of the type of generalization after specification, for "the near of kin" includes the parents linguistically, even if it does not include them customarily. Hence they said in the chapter on bequests, which is based on custom: if one bequeaths to "his near of kin," the two (parents) are not included.

In *al-Mi'raj*, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever says to his father, 'My relative,' has indeed disowned him."

The purpose of this is to include other relatives besides them, and to enjoin concern for them.

In *al-Kashf* [it is stated]: The truth is that giving the right is general, and the context requires comprehensiveness, so it includes the financial right and other than it, such as kinship ties and good companionship. Therefore the verse does not stand as evidence for the obligation of maintaining *mahram* relatives. It has been objected: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿his right﴾ indicates entitlement due to need; moreover, if it is general, the financial and other [rights] enter into it, so how would the verse not stand as evidence? I am among those who hold to generality and that "the near of kin" is not restricted to blood relatives. The conjunction, and likewise what follows it, does not indicate specification with certainty, so reflect.

It has been said: What is meant by "the near of kin" is the relatives of the Messenger ﷺ, and this was related from al-Suddi.

Ibn Jarir related from Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said to a man from the people of Syria: "Have you recited the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Have you not recited in [surah] Bani Isra'il: ﴿So give the near of kin his right﴾?" He said: "And are you the near of kin whose right Allah, exalted is He, commanded to be given?" He said: "Yes."

The Shi'a narrated it from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and their right is honoring them and giving them the *khums*.

It has been weakened on the ground that there is no indication of specification. It has been answered that the address is itself an indication, but this is open to scrutiny.

As for what al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that "when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called Fatimah and gave her Fadak," it does not indicate that the address is restricted to him, peace and blessings be upon him, although the heart is somewhat inclined to doubt its soundness, on the basis that the surah is Meccan and this verse is not among the exceptions, and Fadak was not then under the control of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; rather, her request for it, may Allah be pleased with her, was as an inheritance after his death, peace and blessings be upon him, as is well known, which precludes the claim of soundness, as is not hidden.

﴿And do not squander with extravagance﴾: He forbade spending wealth on one who does not deserve it, for *tabdhir* is spending in a place other than its proper place, derived from scattering the seed and throwing it on the ground in any manner without attending to its places.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Tabdhir is spending wealth other than in its right." In *al-Mufradat* of al-Raghib and others [it is stated] that its origin is casting and throwing the seed, then it was borrowed for the squandering of wealth. Some counted among it the building of a house and the like. Al-Mawardi distinguished between it and *israf* (extravagance) by saying: *israf* is exceeding in quantity, being ignorant of the measures of rights, while *tabdhir* is exceeding in the place of the right, being ignorant of the manner and its places; both are blameworthy, and the second is more deserving of blame.

Al-Zamakhshari interpreted *tabdhir* here as scattering wealth on what is not fitting and spending it in the manner of extravagance, and he noted that there is in this an indication that *tabdhir*, in the usage of the language, includes *israf*, and is intended by it literally, even though he distinguished between them as he did. In *al-Kashf*, after citing the distinction and the statement that the second is more deserving of blame, [it is stated] that al-Zamakhshari was not unaware of this, because derivation points to it, but he meant that in the verse it includes *israf* as well by way of implication, since they do not differ in rulings, especially since He, glorified is He, followed it with the exhortation to moderation, which is appropriate to the consideration of quantity, pointing to its intention from the text. It has been objected: if *tabdhir* is more deserving of blame than *israf*, how can it include it by implication? And the prohibition of *israf* afterward makes its intention here remote, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils.﴾ This is a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition of squandering (tabdhir), by showing that it makes its practitioner bound together with the company of the devils (qarn al-shayatin). The word "brothers" (ikhwan) is the plural of "akh" (brother), and what is meant by it metaphorically is "those who resemble" (al-mumathil). That is, they resemble them in the evil qualities, of which squandering is one. Or it means "friends" and "followers," also metaphorically; that is, they are their friends and followers in what has been mentioned of squandering and spending on sins. For they used to slaughter camels and gamble over them, and they would squander their wealth for show and for every other thing that has no good in it, of forbidden and frivolous pursuits. Or it means "companions" (qarin), as mentioned earlier as well; that is, they are their companions in the Fire, by way of warning.

﴿And the Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ This is part of the reasoning: that is, exaggerating in ingratitude for the blessings of God, the Exalted, because his nature is to divert everything God, the Exalted, has given him of powers and capacities to other than that for which they were created, such as various kinds of sins, corruption on earth, misleading people, and leading them to disbelief in God, the Exalted, and ingratitude for His blessings bestowed upon them, and diverting them to other than what God, the Exalted, has commanded.

In singling out this attribute from among his ugly qualities, there is an indication that squandering, which is an expression for diverting the blessings of God, the Exalted, to other than their proper use, is a form of ingratitude (kufran), which is the opposite of gratitude (shukr), which is directing them to that for which they were created. In the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) there is an indication of the perfection of his rebelliousness, as is not hidden. And the words of some scholars suggest the permissibility of understanding "disbelief" (kufr) here as the opposite of faith (iman), but this is not the case.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 28:

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ means: from the near of kin, the needy, and the wayfarer, according to the apparent meaning. It was also said: from those who ask in general. Al-i'rad (turning away) originally means showing one's side (ʿarḍ, i.e. the side or direction), so the meaning of a'rada ʿanhu is: he turned away while displaying his side. What is intended here is its literal sense, according to what is said, based on what is narrated: that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked for something he did not have, he would turn his blessed face away and remain silent, so this verse was revealed: ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾.

The address is general, to him (ﷺ) and to others. The mercy is, according to what Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak, sustenance (rizq). The word ﴿seeking﴾ (ibtigha') is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

In al-Kashf it is said: the seeking of sustenance has been put in place of its absence, and there is subtlety in this. So that turning away is for the sake of striving on their behalf, and this is from placing the effect in the place of the cause, as clarified in al-Kashshaf. Ibtigha' may also be interpreted as waiting (intizar), and it is permissible to make it a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿you turn away﴾, meaning: seeking. Making it a circumstantial clause from the genitive pronoun is far-fetched.

It is also permitted that the turning away be a metaphor (kinaya) for not benefiting and not giving, because it customarily accompanies that, and that ibtigha' is a metaphor for not being able and being unable (al-ta'alluq) also with the condition. This is supported by what Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAta' al-Khurasani, who said: "Some people from Muzayna came asking the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to provide them with mounts, and he said: ﴿I cannot find anything to mount you on﴾, and they turned away, their eyes overflowing with tears from grief. They thought that this was from the anger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward them, so Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ the verse."

Some have interpreted the mercy as booty (fay'), but you know that this is not apparent, based on what you have heard, that this surah is Meccan, and the mentioned verse is not among the exceptions. Perhaps for this reason it was said: the meaning is: if it is established and confirmed in the future that you turned away from them in the past seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then say etc. What is intended is the causality of establishment for the command to speak, so reflect.

It is also permitted that ibtigha' be connected to the answer of the condition, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then say to them a gentle word﴾, meaning: if you turn away from them, then say that to them seeking mercy from your Lord. Al-Zamakhshari preferred this view over the rest, and it was objected that what follows the fa' does not govern what precedes it, except in the case of amma and what is attached to it. It was answered that he mentioned it according to the Kufan school, which permits governing absolutely, or he intended the semantic connection, in which case what governs it is implied and the mentioned clause is treated as an explanation. The turning away, according to this, is in its literal sense, and the possibility of it being a metaphor is specific to its connection with the condition, according to what al-Tibi claimed, but the truth is that it is not specific, as is not hidden.

The clause ﴿you hope for﴾, according to the other views, may be an attribute of mercy, or a circumstantial clause from the doer, with ﴿from your Lord﴾ connected to ﴿you hope for﴾.

It is also permitted that it be an attribute of mercy. Al-maysur is a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from yussira al-amr, in the passive voice, like sa'ida al-rajul, and its meaning is easy. That is: say to them a word that is easy and gentle, and promise them a good promise. Al-Hasan said: he was commanded to say to them "yes, and with honor, we do not have it today, but if something comes to us we will recognize your right." It was also said: al-maysur is a verbal noun (masdar) and was made an intensive adjective, or by supposing an omitted genitive; that is: a word possessing ease (dhu maysur), meaning ease. What is intended by it is the word containing a supplication for ease, such as: may Allah the Exalted enrich you and ease for you; and Ibn Zayd explained it as: may Allah the Exalted provide for us and for you, may Allah the Exalted bless you.

This was objected to, since maysur means "possessing ease," which is why it occurred as an attribute of qawl; so what necessity is there to make it a verbal noun and then interpret it as dhu maysur? It was answered that when the word containing supplication is intended, the word is then not easy but rather makes easy what they wanted.

That maysur is a verbal noun is among what is established in the language without strain, so making it an intensive adjective or by supposing a genitive has a sound basis, but there is room for reflection.

The truth is that considering it a verbal noun is contrary to the apparent meaning. In the verse, according to the last view, there is an indication that supplicating for the one who asks is not objectionable. It is reported from Imam Malik, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, that he did not consider it proper to say to the one who asks, when he is given nothing: "May Allah the Exalted provide for you" or the like, saying: this is something that weighs heavily on him and that he dislikes to hear; and the name of Allah the Exalted should not be mentioned to one who does not welcome it. By my life, this is a far-reaching point. Some have stated that the verse contains evidence for prohibiting turning away in the first sense, for the meaning is: if you intend to turn away from them, then say to them a gentle word and do not turn away. This has a sound aspect that is not hidden from one who has a keen sight.

Al-Izz ibn ʿAbd al-Salam raised an objection to making ibtigha' among the connections of the condition, because we are commanded to give a fair response whether we await something that will come to us or do not await it. He answered that what is intended by the gentle word is the promise of giving, so the meaning of the verse is: do not promise except when you are hopeful of obtaining what you promise, so the restriction by seeking is most fitting to the condition, because it is not good to promise when there is no hope, since that leads to breaking the promise. And this, as you see, is far-fetched.

These two examples depict the miser's withholding and the spendthrift's extravagance, as a warning against both and an exhortation to the moderation and balance that lie between excess and neglect. That is the praiseworthy generosity, for "the best of matters is their middle course."

Ahmad and others related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "He who is moderate never becomes impoverished."

al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Moderation in spending is half of livelihood."

In another report from Anas, traced to the Prophet: "Good management is half of livelihood, affection is half of intellect, worry is half of old age, and having few dependants is one of the two forms of ease."

It was said: Good management together with chastity is better than wealth together with extravagance.

﴿فَتَقْعُدَ مَلُومًا﴾ means: "so that you will become blameworthy" before Allah the Exalted and before people. ﴿مَحْسُورًا﴾ means regretful and distressed, or left stranded with nothing in hand. From ḥasara al-safar, meaning the journey wearied him and halted him until he was cut off from his companions. al-Raghib said: "The one who is worn out is called ḥāsir and maḥsūr. The ḥāsir is conceived as one whose own strength has been exhausted, while the maḥsūr is conceived as one whom fatigue has exhausted." This explains the ugliness of extravagance, which is understood from the final prohibition, and it is spelled out in its consequence, because the harm of extravagance lies at its end. Since the ugliness of miserliness, understood from the first prohibition, accompanies it and is known from the outset, the depiction was framed in the most hideous images, and it did not follow the same course as what comes after it. So it has been said. There is also a report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, transmitted by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, that supports this. Some verifiers said: "It is better that this be an explanation of the ugliness of both matters, and that the distribution be considered." Here, ﴿فَتَقْعُدَ﴾ is in the accusative as the answer to the two prohibitions. The word ﴿مَلُومًا﴾ refers back to the words ﴿ولا تَجْعَلْ يَدَكَ مَغْلُولَةً إلى عُنُقِكَ﴾, just as it has been said: "The miser is blameworthy wherever he is." And ﴿مَحْسُورًا﴾ refers back to His words, glorified is He, ﴿ولا تَبْسُطْها﴾. This is not far-fetched.

In al-Kashshaf, from Jabir: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting, a boy came to him and said: 'My mother asks you for a shirt.' He said: 'Come back to us in a while.' So he went to his mother, who said: 'Tell him: My mother asks you for the shirt you are wearing.' The Prophet (ﷺ) entered his house, took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat naked. Bilal called the adhan, and he waited, but the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, did not come out to the prayer. So this verse was revealed."

You know that this account is contradicted by the surah being Meccan, and the verse is not among the exceptions. Perhaps the report is not established. Wali al-Din al-Iraqi said that he did not find it in any of the books of ḥadīth, that is, with this wording. Otherwise, Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "A boy came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'My mother asks you for such and such.' He said: 'We have nothing today.' He said: 'She says to you: Clothe me with your shirt.' So the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat in the house uncovered. Then this was revealed." Ibn Abi Hatim related something similar from al-Munhal ibn 'Amr.

Neither of these two reports contains the story of Bilal's adhan and what follows it.

It was also said: The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, gave al-Aqra' ibn Habis one hundred camels, and 'Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari likewise. Then 'Abbas ibn Mirdas came and began to recite:

"Do you place my share and the share of the 'Ubayd (slaves) between 'Uyayna and al-Aqra'?
Hisn and Habis did not surpass Mirdas in gathering (in status),
I was not beneath either of them, and whoever is lowered today will not be raised."

The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "O Abu Bakr, cut off his tongue from me; give him one hundred camels." All of them were among those "whose hearts are being reconciled" (mu'allafat al-qulub, those whose hearts were inclined toward Islam). So this verse was revealed.

In this account the same objection stands, as is clear. Likewise is what Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Sayyar Abu al-Hakam, who said: "A Zamani (a type of cloth from Iraq) was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was generous and bountiful, so he distributed it among the people. This reached a group of Arabs, who said: 'Let us go to the Prophet and ask him.' They found that he had finished distributing it, so Allah the Exalted revealed the verse."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) for His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ and so on. It is as if it were said: If you turn away from them due to the lack of provision, then speak to them a gentle word and do not be concerned about that; for that is not because of any contempt from you in His sight, may He be exalted, but because the keys of provision are in the hand of Him, majestic and exalted, and He, glory be to Him, widens it for some and restricts it for others, according to what His will, which follows wisdom (hikmah), is connected to. So the narrow circumstances that befall you at times, which compel you to turn away, are only for your benefit. Thus His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿And do not make your hand [chained] to your neck﴾ and so on, is an interjected clause (i'tiradan) serving as an emphasis on the meaning of what His wisdom, mighty and majestic, requires of withholding and extending.

His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿Indeed He is ever﴾ (kana), He has always been and still is, ﴿of His servants﴾ all of them, ﴿Acquainted﴾ (khabiran), knowing their inner secrets, ﴿Seeing﴾ (basiran), knowing their outward matters, so He knows of their interests what is hidden from them. This is a justification for what precedes it. It has also been permitted that this be a justification for the command to moderation derived from the two prohibitions: either in the sense that extending and withholding are two matters specific to God, exalted be He, while as for you, be moderate and leave what is specific to Him, majestic and exalted; or in the sense that when you realize His majestic affair, that He extends and withholds, and you reflect deeply on that, you will find Him, exalted be He, moderate, so be moderate yourselves and follow His example. Some have made it a justification for everything that has passed, and in it there is obscurity, as is not hidden. It has also been permitted that it be a justification for the final prohibition, in the sense that He, exalted be He, extends and withholds according to His will, so do not extend to one whose provision He has restricted; but this is nothing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 31:

It is also permitted that this be a preparation (tamhid) for His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾. It has been deemed unlikely, since the apparent sense then would be "so no."

Al-imlaq (imlaq) is poverty, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and he cited the verse of the poet:

"And I, O people, am generous even in poverty, preparing roasted meat, reddened, for my guests."

The apparent meaning of the wording is a prohibition of all kinds of killing of children, male or female, out of fear of poverty and destitution. However, it is narrated that among the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) there were those who would bury daughters alive (wa'd) out of fear of being unable to provide for them, so the verse forbade this. Accordingly, the meaning of "children" is daughters, and "killing" is burying alive. Al-khashyah (fear) in origin is a fear mixed with reverence. Al-Raghib said: "Most often this occurs from knowledge of what is feared."

It is also read with a kasra on the kha'. The apparent view is that this prohibition is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the similar prohibition mentioned earlier. Al-Tabarsi permitted that it be coordinated with His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿That you worship none but Him﴾; in that case, the verb may be in the subjunctive governed by "an" (that), as in the preceding verb.

﴿We provide for them and for you﴾: a guarantee of their sustenance and a justification for the aforementioned prohibition by negating its supposed cause in their view; that is: We provide for them, not you, so do not fear poverty, relying on your knowledge of their inability to obtain their own provision. The placing of the pronoun for the children before the pronoun for the addressees, in contrast to what occurs in Surat al-An'am, is to indicate their being the origin in the bestowal of provision. The factor behind this nuance there is that what preceded there called for attention to the matter of the addressees in the verses; so it is said. Shaykh al-Islam al-Mawla permitted that this be the reason: because the motive for killing there is immediate poverty; hence it was said "from poverty" (min imlaq), whereas here the poverty is anticipated; hence it was said "for fear of poverty" (khashyata imlaq). It is as if it were said: We provide for them without your provision being diminished by anything, so that what you fear befalls you; and [We provide] for you too, as provision added to your provision.

Page 67
﴿Indeed, their killing is a great sin﴾: another justification, explaining that the thing prohibited is in itself a grave wrong, because of what it entails of cutting off procreation and cutting off the species. Al-khata' (sin) is like al-ithm (sin) in wording and meaning, and the verbs of both are of the pattern 'alima. Abu Ja'far and Ibn Dhakwan, from Amir, read khata'an with a fatha on the kha' and the ta', without an elongation. Al-Zajjaj explained this reading in two ways. The first is that it is an infinitive form (ism masdar) of akhta'a, yukhti'u, when one does not hit the mark; that is: their killing was not correct. The second is that it is a dialectal form for khata' in the sense of sin, like mathal and mithl, and hadhir and hadhur. As for one who objects to this reading on the grounds that khata' is what is not done deliberately, and that this is not its place, he has merely exposed his own lack of familiarity.

Ibn Kathir read khita'an with a kasra on the kha', a fatha on the ta', and an elongation. This too was explained in two ways: the first is that it is a dialectal form of al-khit' in the sense of sin, like daba' and dibagh, and libs and libas; the second is that it is the verbal noun of khata'a, yukhati'u, khita'an, like qatala, yuqatilu, qitalan. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Although we have not found khata'a, what is found is takhatta'a, its reflexive form, which guides us to it, as in the saying of people: 'the arrows missed his insides (takhatta'at al-nubl ahshaa'ahu)'." Muhammad ibn al-Sawi recited, in describing a wild cow, as in Majma' al-Bayan:

"A shaggy one whose hair was coarse on the hide, I handed it to him; I turned upon it the rain-bearing clouds that pour continuously.
The hunter missed it (takhatta'ahu) until I found it, and its snout was sunk in the water of a pool."

The meaning on this basis is: their killing was a deviation from the truth and what is correct. Hence Abu Hatim's statement that this reading is an error, an error, is [itself in error]. Al-Hasan read khata'an with a fatha on the kha' and the ta' with an elongation, and it is the ism masdar of akhta', like 'ata', the ism masdar of a'ta'. Al-Zuhri and Abu Raja' read khija' with a kasra on the kha', a fatha on the ta', and an alif at its end, replacing the hamza; and it is not a shortening of the elongated form, since that would be an unnecessary poetic license. In a narration from Ibn 'Amir, he read khata, like 'asa.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 32:

﴿Do not approach fornication﴾, by engaging in its near or distant beginnings, let alone engaging in it itself. The prohibition against approaching it, rather than against committing it, deviates from the pattern of what preceded and what follows, for the sake of emphasizing the prohibition against it itself, and because approaching it leads to engaging in it. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) defined it as intercourse with a woman outside a valid legal contract. The word (al-zina, fornication) appears in both the madd form (al-zina, with a long vowel) and the qasr form (al-zina, with a short vowel). When it is read with the madd, it may be the verbal noun of the form *mufa'alah* (an interaction between two parties). Placing the prohibition against it between the prohibition against killing children and the prohibition against killing a soul whose killing is forbidden, in absolute terms, is, as Shaykh al-Islam (the Shaykh of Islam, a title for a senior scholar) said, because it is a form of killing children, in that it destroys lineages, for whoever's lineage is not established is, legally, as one dead.

﴿Indeed, it is an abomination﴾, an act of conspicuous ugliness, exceeding its kind, ﴿and evil is the way﴾, meaning: and how evil is the way, as a way, because it disrupts the matter of lineages and kindles strife.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "A fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer."

It has been reported in another narration: "When a man commits fornication, faith departs from him and becomes like a canopy above his head. If he repents and gives it up, it returns to him." And it is among the major sins, and an abomination absolutely, according to what the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun, the rigorous scholars) have agreed upon. Indeed, in a sound hadith, [it is stated] that it, with the wife of a neighbor, is among the greatest of the major sins. Al-Halimi claimed that it is an abomination if it is with the wife of a neighbor, or with a blood-relative, or with a non-related woman during the month of Ramadan, or in the Sacred City, and a major sin, but if it is with the wife of one's father, or the wife of one's son, or with a non-related woman by way of coercion and compulsion. And if it does not necessitate a prescribed penalty (hadd), it is a minor sin. His view is not to be overlooked, and the weakness of its foundation is evident. The verse is clear that it is an abomination absolutely. Yes, the most abominable of its types is fornication with the wife of a neighbor. Some of them said: The greatest fornication in absolute terms is fornication with those within the forbidden degrees of kinship (al-mahārim).

Al-Hakim authenticated [the report] that he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has intercourse with a woman within the forbidden degrees, then kill him."

The fornication of a married person (thayyib) is more reprehensible than that of a virgin (bikr), as evidenced by the difference in their prescribed penalties. The fornication of an elderly man is more reprehensible than that of a young man, due to the completeness of his intellect. The fornication of a free person and of a scholar is more reprehensible than that of a slave (qinn) and of an ignorant person, due to the completeness of these two. Is it greater than sodomy (al-liwat) or not? There is a difference of opinion on this. In *al-Ihya'* [by al-Ghazali], it is stated that it is greater than sodomy, because desire drives to it from both sides, so it occurs frequently and its harm is great, and among its harms is the confusion of lineages through its frequency. It may be objected that its prescribed penalty is more severe, as evidenced by the statement of Malik and others that the active partner in sodomy is to be stoned even if he is not married, unlike the fornicator. It may be answered that the lesser may have a distinction. And there is much more to say on this.

Some exaggerated and said: It is, absolutely, next to polytheism in greatness. The more correct view is that what comes next to polytheism is murder, then fornication. As for the report that backbiting is worse than thirty acts of fornication in Islam, it has no basis, as Ibn Hajar al-Haytami said, apparently.

Yes, al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi and others narrated: "Backbiting is worse than fornication."

However, there is another report that clarifies its meaning, narrated by Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Abu al-Shaykh from Jabir and Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Beware of backbiting, for backbiting is worse than fornication. A man may commit fornication and Allah accepts his repentance, but the one who backbites is not forgiven until the person he backbit forgives him."

From this it is known that the greater severity of backbiting over fornication is not absolute, but rather from the perspective that inner repentance, fulfilling all its conditions, namely regret for the act of disobedience, ceasing it, and the resolve not to return to it, while not yet at the death rattle and before the sun rises from the west, expiates the sin of fornication by itself alone. Unlike backbiting, for even if repentance from it fulfills these conditions, it does not expiate it, but rather it is necessary that the seeking of the one backbit's pardon be added to it, along with his forgiveness. Thus backbiting is more severe in this respect, not absolutely. So the hadith is not contradicted, according to the more correct view. From this it is also known that fornication does not require, for repentance from it, seeking pardon from the one wronged, which is what many of the verifiers have explicitly stated. Yet it is still among the rights connected with a human being (*huquq al-adami*), for how could it not be, since it is a crime against honor and lineages. The meaning of their statement that fornication does not involve a human right is that it does not involve a right of property or the like, and the non-requirement of seeking pardon does not indicate that it is not among the rights connected with a human being absolutely. Seeking pardon is not required only because of the additional shame that results from mentioning it, and the strong likelihood that a husband or a relative, if told of it, would hasten to kill the fornicator or the one with whom the fornication was committed, or to kill both of them together. Given what has been mentioned, how is it possible to maintain that seeking pardon is a requirement? Hujjat al-Islam (Proof of Islam, a title of al-Ghazali) al-Ghazali explicitly stated something similar in *Minhaj al-Abidin*, saying, within a detailed discussion, as al-Adhra'i said: it is in the utmost of beauty and verification. As for sin committed in the sanctuary (*haram*), if you betrayed [someone] regarding his family and his child, there is no basis for seeking pardon, nor for disclosure, because that generates strife and rage. Rather, you should plead to Allah, glorified is He, that He may satisfy him with you and grant him much good in exchange. If strife and agitation are safe from occurring, which is rare, then seek his pardon. Al-Adhra'i said in several places, regarding envy and repentance from it:

It seems likely that informing him of it is prohibited if one's assumption dominates that he will not pardon him, and that it will produce enmity, resentment, and harm for the one informed. Then he said: It is permissible to look at the one envied. If he has such good character that one thinks he will pardon him, informing him becomes required, so that he may be freed from his injustice with certainty. If one's assumption dominates that informing him will bring evil and enmity, informing him is definitely prohibited. If one is in doubt, the apparent ruling is what al-Nawawi mentioned: that it is neither obligatory nor recommended, for a pure soul is rare, and it may often bring evil and enmity. And if he pardons him verbally, [the matter is settled]. End of quote. If this is the case with envy, despite its ease for most people and their indifference to it, which is why al-Nawawi absolutely stated the non-disclosure [of envy], saying: The preferred view, rather the correct one, is that informing the envied person is not obligatory, nor even recommended. Even if it were said to be disliked, it would not be far-fetched. Then what about fornication, which entails that a husband and a relative would be killed over it merely upon suspicion, let alone upon certainty? It is known from the reports that the fruits of fornication are ugly. Among them: it leads to the Fire and severe punishment; it brings poverty, loss of splendor, and shortness of life; and its like is exacted from the offspring of the fornicator. When this was said to one of the kings, he wished to test it with a daughter of his, who was extremely beautiful. He placed her with a woman and ordered her not to prevent anyone who wished to approach her, by any means he chose, and ordered her to uncover her face. She walked with her through the markets, and whenever she passed by anyone, that person would lower his gaze out of modesty and shame before her. When she had walked with her through the whole city and no one had lifted his gaze to her, she returned with her to the king's house. As she was about to enter, a man seized her and kissed her, then left her. She brought her in to the king and told him the story.

[Page 69]

He prostrated in gratitude and said:

"Praise be to Allah, the Exalted. In my whole life, I have committed nothing but a kiss, and I have been requited for it. We ask Allah, glorified is He, to protect us, our offspring, and those who are attributed to us from abominations, whether apparent or hidden, by the sanctity of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited, as Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him: "Do not approach fornication, for it is an abomination and a hateful thing, and evil is the way, except for one who repents, for indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." This was mentioned to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, so he came to him and asked him. [Ubayy] said: "I took it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and you have no work except slapping hands at al-Naqi'." And this, if it is authentic, was before the final recitation (al-'ardah al-akhirah, the final review of the Qur'an with the Angel Gabriel).

﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾, i.e., which Allah Most High has forbidden. What is meant is that He has forbidden its killing by granting it protection through Islam or through a covenant. ﴿except by right﴾ is connected to "do not kill." The *ba'* (بِ) indicates causation (*sababiyyah*), and the exception is *mufarragh* (an "emptied" exception, where the excepted element is left unspecified and the sense is supplied by context). That is: do not kill it for any cause except a cause of right. It is also permissible for it to be a *hal* (circumstantial clause) of either the subject or the object: do not kill except while being bound up with right, or do not kill it except as one bound up with right. It has also been allowed that it be an adjectival qualifier (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun: do not kill it any killing except a killing bound up with right. The first is the most apparent. As for its connection to "forbade," that is far-fetched, even if it is valid. "Right" has been explained by what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "The blood of a person who testifies that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah is not lawful, except in one of three cases: a life for a life, a married person who commits adultery, and one who abandons his religion and separates from the community."

It may be objected that this restriction is broken by repelling an aggressor (*al-sa'il*), since that may lead to killing. This is answered by saying that what is meant is that which is itself intended to kill, and what was mentioned is that whose intended purpose is repelling, though it may in general lead to killing. The truth is that the right is not limited to what was mentioned, and the restriction in the report is not literal. The Shafi'is have held that abandoning prayer out of laziness justifies killing, and likewise sodomy according to a group of the eminent scholars.

﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, without a right that requires his killing or permits it to the killer, so much so that his permission is not considered valid for anyone other than the killer. Our scholars have stated explicitly that if one who is owed retaliation (*qisas*) is killed by someone other than the one entitled to retaliation, the killer is subjected to retaliation on his behalf, and the guardian's saying "I ordered him to do it" does not benefit the killer, unless the order is evident. ﴿We have given his guardian﴾, i.e., to the one who has charge of his affair from among the heirs, or the ruler if there are no heirs. Some restricted the meaning to the first, out of consideration for what is most common. ﴿authority﴾, i.e., a power and control over the killer by holding him accountable through one of two matters: retaliation or blood money (*diyah*). Blood money may be specifically required, as in unintentional killing. The one killed by error is killed unjustly in the sense indicated, even if we say there is no sin in error, based on the hadith: "Error has been lifted from my nation."

Expiation (*kaffarah*) was prescribed in it for lack of verification and for avoiding what leads to it, so let this be reflected upon.

It has been argued from interpreting "guardian" as "heir" that women have a share in retaliation. But al-Qadi Isma'il said: they do not enter into it, because its wording is masculine. ﴿So let him not exceed bounds﴾, i.e., the guardian, ﴿in killing﴾, i.e., let him not transgress the limit prescribed in it, such as by killing two people when there is only one killer, as was the custom of the Jahiliyyah. When one of them was killed, they would kill his killer and kill others along with him. From this, Muhalhil said:

*Every slain man of Kulayb is a debt, until death reaches the family of Murrah.*

This was the view of Ibn Jubayr. Al-Mundhir narrated it through Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Or (the exceeding bounds means) killing someone other than the killer and leaving the killer alone. This was also related from Zayd ibn Aslam: al-Bayhaqi narrated in his *Sunan* from him that in the Jahiliyyah, if someone of non-noble status killed a noble, they would not kill him in return, but would kill a noble from his tribe. So this was forbidden. Or (exceeding bounds means) adding mutilation (*muthlah*) to the killing, as has been said.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Talq ibn Habib that he said: "He should not kill other than his killer, nor mutilate him." It was also said: the killer himself is to be killed, but the prescribed (ruling) is blood money.

Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from Qatadah that he said regarding the verse: whoever kills with an iron implement is killed with an iron implement; whoever kills with a piece of wood is killed with a piece of wood; whoever kills with a stone is killed with a stone; and no one other than the killer is killed. In this is the view that killing by a blunt instrument requires retaliation, and this contradicts our school.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *fa-la tusrif* (فَلا تُسْرِفْ) with the second person addressed to the guardian, as an *iltifat* (a shift from third person to second person). Abu Muslim, the companion of al-Dawlah, read *fa-la yusrifu* (فَلا يُسْرِفُ) with a *damma* (رفع), as a declarative statement with the sense of a command, and in it there is an emphasis not found in the imperative. ﴿Indeed, he was supported﴾ is a reason for the prohibition. The pronoun refers to the guardian also, in the sense that Allah Most High supported him by making retaliation or blood money obligatory and by commanding the rulers to assist him in obtaining his right. So let him not seek beyond his right, and let him not go outside the sphere of the supporter's authority.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid that the pronoun refers to the one killed, in the sense that Allah Most High supported him in this world by the exacting of retaliation or blood money, and in the Hereafter by reward. So let his guardian not exceed in his affair. It is also permissible that it refer to the one whom the guardian exceeded in regard to; that is, Allah Most High supported him by making retaliation obligatory, and the punishment (*ta'zir*) and the burden fall on the one who exceeded in his affair. It was also said that the pronoun in *yusrif* refers to the killer, i.e., the one who intends killing and initiates it directly. Al-Zamakhshari attributed this to Mujahid in *al-Kashshaf*. The two pronouns in the causal clause refer to the guardian or the one killed. It is supported by the reading of Ubayy: *fa-la tusrifu* (فَلا تُسْرِفُوا), since the killers are plural in the wording in His saying "do not kill" (*wa-la taqtulu*). The original principle is the agreement of the two readings. Yet it is not determined, because the guardian is general in the verse, so it carries the meaning of guardians, and thus the pronoun may be plural on this basis, and that would be an *iltifat*. The agreement of the two readings is not necessary. The meaning is: let him not exceed against himself in the matter of killing by exposing himself to immediate and deferred destruction. In *al-Kashf* it is said that it is a deterrent to the killer, in the style of His saying "And there is life for you in retaliation." The prohibition of exceeding is to depict that killing without right, however it is estimated, is excess. Its meaning is: let him not kill without right, while you know that this interpretation is not sound, so one should not rely upon it.

This verse, as several narrators related from al-Dahhak, is the first verse revealed concerning killing. You have learned that the more correct view is that it is the greatest of the major sins after polytheism. That deliberate, aggressive killing is among the major sins is agreed upon. Quasi-deliberate killing (*shibh al-'amd*) has been counted among them, as stated by al-Harawi and Shurayh al-Ruwayani. As for accidental killing, the correct view is that it is not a sin at all, let alone a major sin, so let this be noted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 34:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. He forbade approaching it, because of what was mentioned earlier of the emphasis in prohibiting any interference with it, and as a means to the exception stated in His words, ﴿except in the way that is best﴾. That is: except by the manner and method that is the best of manners and methods, which is to preserve it and make it grow. ﴿Until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾: this is a limit (ghayah) for permitting the handling of the property in the best manner indicated by the exception, not only for the manner mentioned alone. As for al-ashudd, it has been said to be the plural of shadd, like al-adurr being the plural of darr. Al-shadd means strength, and it is the consolidation of the strength of youth and age, just as shadd al-nahar (the shadd of the day) means its height. 'Antarah said:

"I knew him at the height of the day, as if his fingertips and his head had been dyed with al-'izlam."

It has also been said that it is the plural of shiddah, like ni'mah and an'um. Some of the Basrans said it is a singular, like al-anuk. The meaning of reaching his ashudd is reaching the point where, by virtue of his intellect and sound judgment, he is able to attend to the interests of his property. Then, dealing with the orphan's property in ways such as eating it in a manner other than that which is permitted is one of the major sins (al-kaba'ir). Ibn 'Abd al-Salam hesitated to restrict this to the threshold of theft (nisab al-sariqah), so he said in al-Qawa'id: The Law has explicitly stated that false testimony and consuming the property of an orphan are major sins. If they occur with a substantial amount of property, this is clear. If they occur with a trifling amount,
[Page 71]
such as a raisin or a date, it is permissible to regard them as major sins, as a deterrent against this kind of corruption, like a single drop of wine, even if the corruption is not actually realised. It is also permissible to define this by the threshold of theft. End of quote.

It has been said that they may be distinguished in that false testimony involves boldness in violating the sanctity of protected property, together with boldness in lying in testimony, whereas a small amount of an orphan's property does not involve this, so restricting it to that amount is not unlikely. Thus it has been said.

The truth is that the verses and reports concerning the threat for consuming an orphan's property are unrestricted, so they cover both little and much. It is not permissible to specify them except by a textual proof (dalil sam'i). Where there is no such proof, specification is not acceptable. The correct view is that there is no difference between consuming a little and consuming a lot in being a major sin, for which the doer deserves a severe threat. Yes, a trivial thing for which custom tolerates leniency is not far from being something whose consumption is not among the major sins. And God Most High knows best. Today the judges have arrived at consuming an orphan's property under the guise of safeguarding it. May God Most High deal with them by His justice and let the treacherous among them taste, in both abodes, the recompense of their deed.

﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾: that is, what you have covenanted with God Most High regarding undertaking His obligations, and what you have covenanted with others among the servants. This includes contracts (al-'uqud).

It is also permitted that what is meant is what God Most High has covenanted with you and imposed upon you. Fulfilment of the covenant (al-iifa' bi-l-'ahd) and fidelity to it (al-wafa' bihi) mean carrying out its requirements, safeguarding it, and not breaking it. Its opposite, treachery (al-ghadr), derived from it, indicates this, and it means abandonment (al-tark). It is hardly ever used except with the preposition bi, to distinguish it from the physical fulfilment (al-iifa' al-hissi), such as fulfilling the measure and the weight.

﴿Indeed the covenant﴾: it is stated explicitly in place of a pronoun, to show full concern for its matter. It has been said that this is to prevent the assumption that the pronoun returns to the fulfilment (al-iifa') understood from (awfu, "fulfil"). ﴿was (kana) answerable﴾: that is, it was answerable for, with the preposition elided and the pronoun, after being changed, becoming a nominative concealed within the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul). This is called al-hadhf wa-l-iisal (elision and conveyance), and it is common.

It is also permitted that the speech is by elision of a modifier: that is, the possessor of the covenant was answerable. It has been said that there is no elision at all, and the speech is figurative (takhyil), as if it were said to the covenant: "Why did you break? Why did it not fulfil you?", as a rebuke to the one who breaks it, just as it is said to the buried infant girl: ﴿for what sin was she killed?﴾ (81:9). It may also be considered that there is a metaphor, both implicit (makniyyah) and figurative (takhyiliyyah). Some have claimed that the covenant may be made to take the form of one to whom a question is directed, just as good deeds and bad deeds are given bodies in order to be weighed.

It is also permitted that ﴿answerable (mas'ulan)﴾ means "sought (matlub)", from "I asked for such-and-such" when you request it. Attributing being sought to it is a metaphor, and what is meant is that it is sought that it not be neglected. It is also permitted that the speech contains an elided modifier, the pronoun being raised and concealed after its elision. The original is what we have pointed to. You have just heard that such a thing is common. In this there is no giving a cause of a thing by itself, for the ultimate meaning is that it is said: "Fulfil the covenant, for not neglecting it has always been sought from everyone, so it is sought from you too." Then, regarding breaking the covenant, according to what the sound reports indicate, it has been said that it is a major sin.

It has come from 'Ali, may God honour his face, that he counted among the major sins the breaking of a transaction (nukth al-saf-qah), that is, treachery toward a treaty partner. Indeed, Shaykh al-Islam al-'Ala'i explicitly stated that there came in a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that he called it a major sin. Some verifiers said: In the unrestricted claim that the aforementioned breach is a major sin there is room for examination, based on the view that the covenant is the legal obligations (al-taklifat al-shar'iyyah), for among breaches some are major sins and some are minor, and one looks in this to the state of the one charged with the obligation. Perhaps those who said that breaching the covenant is a major sin meant by the covenant the pledge of allegiance to the imam (mubayi'at al-imam), and by breaching it the annulment of his pledge and rebellion against him without a valid reason. There is no doubt or interpretation or doubt that this is a major sin, so let this be considered.

**(Page 72)**

﴿And give full measure﴾: complete it and do not diminish it, ﴿when you measure﴾, that is, at the time of your measuring for the buyers. The restriction of the command to this time is because cheating (*tatfif*, giving short measure) occurs then. As for when one takes measure from people, there is no need to command equity, as God the Exalted says: ﴿when they take a measure from people, they take it in full﴾, and the verse.

﴿And weigh with the *qistas*﴾. It is the steelyard (*qabban*), according to what is related from al-Dahhak, and it is called *qarastun* in the language of the people of the Levant, as al-Azhari said. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the balance, whether small or large, of dirhams or other things. Al-Layth said: it is the most upright of balances. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada that it means justice, and from al-Hasan that it means iron. It is a Byzantine (Rumi) word that has been Arabized, as Ibn Durayd said, because its root is absent in Arabic. It has also been said that it is Arabic. It is related that its Arabization is affirmed, and that it means "balance" in the Byzantine language, from Ibn Jubayr and a group. It has also been said that it is compounded of two words: *qist*, which is justice, and *tas*, which is the pan of the balance, but one of the two *ta*'s was dropped because compounds are a place for lightening. This is as you see. On the view that it is a Byzantine word Arabized, which is the sound view, its use in the Qur'an does not conflict with its being in the Arabic language stated in His words: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾, because after being Arabized and heard in eloquent speech it becomes Arabic. There is thus no need to deny its Arabization, or to claim predominance (*taghlib*), or to say that what is meant is Arabic in style.

The Kufans read it with a *kasra* on the *qaf*, and the rest with a *damma*. The first *sin* may be replaced by a *sad*, as the *sad* was replaced by *sin* in *al-sirat* ﴿the straight﴾. That is, the just, upright (balance). This interpretation of *qistas* as justice is weak. Perhaps the reason for relying on its uprightness rather than commanding the completion of weighing is, as Shaykh al-Islam said, that when it is upright, injustice is generally inconceivable, unlike measuring, where cheating often occurs even when the instrument is upright. Likewise, relying on the completion of measuring rather than a command to calibrate the measure is because its completion is inconceivable without calibrating the measuring vessel. He also commanded its adjustment in His words: ﴿Give full measure and balance with justice﴾.

﴿That﴾, that is, the full giving of measure and weight with the upright *qistas*, ﴿is better﴾ in this world, because it causes people to desire dealing with its doer and brings him a good reputation. ﴿And better in outcome﴾, that is, better in consequence, for the reward in the Hereafter that results from it. *Ta'wil* is from the form *taf'il* of *aala*, meaning he returned. Its origin is the return of a thing to the goal intended from it, whether in knowledge, as in His words: ﴿and none knows its interpretation except God﴾, or in action, as in His words: ﴿the day its interpretation comes﴾, and the words of the poet:

*And for separation, before the day of parting, there is an interpretation.*

It has been said that what is meant is: that is better in itself, because it is trustworthiness, which is a quality of perfection, and better in outcome in this world, because it causes hearts to incline and people to desire dealing with him and to remember him well, which leads to wealth; and in the Hereafter, because it is a cause of deliverance from punishment and success in reward. It has also been said: ﴿better in outcome﴾, that is, better in meaning and rendering.

Furthermore, full giving of measure and weight is obligatory by consensus (*ijma'*), and diminishing them is among the major sins (*kaba'ir*) absolutely, as the severe threat against its doer requires, which is found in the verses and in the authentic hadiths. There is no difference between a little and a lot. Indeed, some of them said: cheating with a trifling thing that most people tolerate should be a minor sin (*saghira*). If you say: they mentioned regarding usurpation (*ghasb*) that usurping less than a quarter of a dinar is not a major sin, and the implication of this is that cheating should be likewise, I say: that is said to be problematic, so it should not be analogized to it. Rather, consensus has been reported against it.

Al-Adhra'i said: it is a limit without any basis. End. On the assumption of that ruling, one may distinguish that usurpation is not of the kind whose little leads to much, because it occurs only by compulsion and domination, unlike cheating. So it is required to warn against it by holding that each of its little and much is a major sin, following what they said about drinking a drop of wine being a major sin, even if the harm of wine is not present in it, because its little leads to its much. Similar to cheating in measure and weight is shortage in measuring cloth (*dhar'*), and in these times almost no measurer, weigher, or cloth-measurer is safe from shortage except whom God the Exalted protects.

[Page 73]

﴿And do not pursue﴾, that is, do not follow. The original meaning of *qafa* is to follow someone's back (*qafa*), and then the word was used for following in general until it became its ordinary meaning.

It has been read as *"wa-la taqfuwa"* (with the weak letter retained after the jussive particle), which is anomalous (*shadh*). It has also been read as *"wa-la taquf"* with a *dammah* on the *qaf* and a *sukun* on the *fa*, like *taqul*, on the basis that it is a hollow verb (*ajwaf*) in the jussive, whose perfect is *qaafa*. One says *qaafa atharahu yaqufuhu* when one traces and follows its trail, and from this comes *al-qiyafah* (tracking by traces), whose origin is knowledge gained from a person's footprints and their trace. It is reported from Abu Ubayda that *qaafa* is a metathesis of *qafa*, like *jadhaba* and *jabadha*. This has been criticized on the grounds that the correct view is the opposite.

﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾, that is: do not follow what you have no knowledge of, whether in speech or in action. Its essence returns to a prohibition against judging on the basis of what is not known, and a number of matters fall under this. Each of the exegetes restricted it to one thing. It has been said that the intended meaning is the prohibition of the polytheists from speaking about matters of divinity and prophethood by blind imitation of their forefathers and following of their whims. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah that the intended meaning is the prohibition of false testimony. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the prohibition of slander and the accusation of chaste men and women. From this is the verse of al-Kumayt:

*"I do not shoot the innocent without fault,*
*nor do I pursue the chaste women when we are accused."*

Al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* narrated from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Anas: "Whoever accuses a believer of what is not in him, intending to disgrace him by it, Allah, exalted is He, will detain him on the bridge of Hell until he comes out of what he said." It has also been said that the intended meaning is the prohibition of lying. Ibn Jarir and others reported from Qatadah that he said regarding the verse: Do not say "I heard" when you did not hear, or "I saw" when you did not see.

The Imam (al-Razi) chose generality, saying: the wording is general, encompassing everything, so there is no sense in restriction. The deniers of qiyas (analogical reasoning) used the verse as evidence, because qiyas is pursuing conjecture and judging by it. It has been answered that they agreed upon judging by conjecture and acting upon it in many cases, among them: the funeral prayer over the deceased and his burial in the cemetery of the Muslims, and inheriting from a Muslim on the basis that he is a Muslim, which is conjectural; facing the qiblah in prayer, which is based on ijtihad by indicators that yield only conjecture; eating a slaughtered animal on the basis that it was a valid slaughter, which is conjectural; testimony, which is conjectural; the values of destroyed property and the blood-money (*arsh*) for injuries, for which there is no way except conjecture. Whoever considers, even with the corner of the eye, sees that all the actions regarded as valid in this world, such as travel, seeking profit, transactions, the fixing of specified terms, reliance on the friendship of friends and the enmity of enemies, are all conjectural.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We judge by the outward, and Allah, exalted is He, takes care of the hidden matters."

So the prohibition of following what is not definite knowledge is specific to beliefs, and also to the fact that conjecture may be called knowledge, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When believing women come to you as emigrants, test them; Allah knows best their faith. If you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers﴾. For knowledge of their faith comes only through their profession, and this yields only conjecture. Also: when a decisive proof has indicated the obligation to act upon qiyas, that proof is evidence that whenever a conjecture arises that God's ruling in this case is equivalent to His ruling in the original text, you are obligated to act in accordance with that conjecture. Here, then, conjecture occurs in the path to the ruling, while the ruling itself is known and certain.

The deniers answered the first point by saying that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿do not pursue...﴾ is a general statement, to which specification has been applied in the cases they mention regarding acting upon conjecture, so generality remains in what lies beyond them. Moreover, there is a difference between the cases they mention and the point of dispute: the rulings connected to the first are specific to particular persons at particular times, so explicit stipulation of them is impossible, and conjecture was therefore accepted out of necessity. By contrast, the rulings established by analogies are universal, applicable to universal cases, and are governed by rules; explicit stipulation of them is possible, so it was not permissible to rely on conjecture for them.

They answered the second point by saying that the difference between knowledge and conjecture is beyond doubt, and it is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out to us? You only follow conjecture﴾. The believer is one who professes, and that profession is knowledge; so the verse does not name conjecture as knowledge.

They answered the third point by saying that it holds only if the authority of qiyas were established by a decisive proof, and it is not so.

The best that can be said in reply, according to what the Imam stated, is that the argument from the verse is an argument from a general text that has been specified, and this yields only conjecture. So if it indicated that relying on conjecture is impermissible, it would indicate that relying on it (the verse) is impermissible, and therefore affirming its authority leads to its negation, which is void. The respondent may say: we know by the manifest mass-transmission (*tawatur*) from the religion of the Prophet (ﷺ) that relying on the verses of the Qur'an is a proof in the Law. It may be answered to this that whether a general text that has been specified is a proof is not known by mass-transmission. So reflect.

﴿Indeed the hearing, the sight, and the heart, all of those﴾, that is: all of these organs. They are referred to by *ulaʾika* (those), on the view that this word is specific to rational beings, treating them as if they were such, since they are questioned about their states and bear witness against their owners.

Some have said: this word is predominantly used for rational beings but has come for non-rational ones because it is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*), which covers both categories. From this is the verse of Jarir, as transmitted by more than one narrator:

*"He blamed the abodes after the dwelling of al-Lawa,*
*and life after those days."*

On this view there is no need for treating them as rational beings or for resorting to metaphor in what preceded. ﴿was questioned about it﴾: all the pronouns are pronouns of *kull* (each), meaning: each of these was questioned about itself. So it is said to him: Did your companion employ you in what you were created for, or not? This is after making him fit to be addressed and questioned.

It is also permitted that the pronoun in *ʿanhu* refers to *kull*, while the rest refers to the subject of the verb (*al-qafi*), so there is a shift of person, since the expected form would be: "you were questioned about it" (*kunta ʿanhu masʾūlan*).

Al-Zamakhshari said: *ʿanhu* is the deputy subject of *masʾūlan*, so it is attributed to it, and there is no pronoun in it, like the example ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾.

Abu al-Baqa' and others refuted this, saying that the deputy of the subject has the same rule as the subject in that it cannot be placed before its governing element, as is the case with the original. It has been mentioned that Ibn al-Nahhas reported a consensus on the impermissibility of placing the deputy of the subject before it when it is a prepositional phrase. So it is not like the example ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾. One cannot say that it is according to the view of the Kufans, who permit placing the subject before its verb, unless the reporting of this is disputed. It is reported from the author of *al-Taqrib* that *ʿanhu* was permitted to be placed first, although it is the subject, out of regard for its original nature as an adverbial complement (*zarf*), not for the accidental status of being a subject; and because the subject does not precede (its verb) lest it be confused with the topic, and there is no confusion here; and because it is not truly a subject. Yet, in fairness, even with this, one may not say that the view of the master of Arabic (al-Zamakhshari) is an error.

It is mentioned in the commentary on the *Miftah* (of al-Sakkaki) that it is raised by an implied verb which the apparent word explains. It has been permitted that the explainer may be free of a subject when it is not a verb, since the principle of the verb is to raise the subject; so it is not permitted for it to be free of one, unlike the active and passive participles, which are treated as analogous to nouns.

Al-Tibi, in *al-Kashf*, criticized this, saying that there is a problem with it, both by transmission and by analogy. As for the first, it is because the claim is unique to him. As for the second, the need for it arises from the fact that when a word is predicated of something, it must have a pronoun returning to that thing so that it is connected to it, and that thing is the essence in which the attribute subsists, if it is an agent, or is associated with that essence. It is not like nouns, which are linked to what precedes them by the predication itself, because they do not signify a meaning attached to an essence. So the correct view is to say: the preposition has been deleted, and the pronoun after it is concealed in the attribute. I have recently heard that this falls under the category of deletion and connection (*al-hadhf wal-iṣal*), and that it is common.

It is also permitted that the deputy subject of *masʾūlan* is the verbal noun, which is *al-suʾāl* (the questioning), and that *ʿanhu* is in the accusative position. Ibn Jinni asked Abu ʿAli (al-Farisi) about the saying "fīka yarghab" (in you he desires), and said: it is not raised by what follows it, so where is the raised element? He said: it is the verbal noun, i.e., "in you desires the desire," with the meaning of "the desire is done," as in the saying "yuʿṭī yamnaʿ" (he gives, he withholds), i.e., he performs giving and withholding.

It is also permitted that the subject of *kāna* or its agent is the pronoun of *kull* with the genitive construction omitted, i.e., "its owner was questioned about it" or "its owner was questioned about it." Then it is said to him: Why did you use the hearing in what is not lawful, and why did you turn the sight to such-and-such, and the heart to such-and-such?

Al-Jarrah al-ʿUqayli read *"wal-fūād"* with a *fatha* on the *fa* and the replacement of the *hamza* with a *waw*. Its justification is that the *hamza* was replaced by a *waw* because it occurred with a *dammah*, according to the well-known usage, then the *fa* was given a *fatha* for lightness; this is a dialect for this word. The denial of Abu Hatim of it is not to be considered.

From the verse it is deduced that the servant is held accountable for acts of the heart, such as resolving to disobey, and for spiritual diseases such as rancor, envy, and self-admiration, and other things. Yes, they have stated explicitly that merely intending to sin without resolving upon it is not a ground for accountability, on account of the sound hadith to that effect.

Then, following conjecture may be a major sin and may be a minor sin, according to its types and categories, and among it is what is the greatest of the major sins, as is not hidden. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to protect us from all of that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 37:

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. That is, with pride and arrogance; this is what Qatadah said. al-Raghib said: *al-maraḥ* (exultation) is the intensity of joy and the expansion in it. The first (meaning) is more appropriate. It is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that has taken the place of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), and speech of this kind, when it occurs as a circumstantial state, a predicate, or a qualifier, is common. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative as an absolute object (*maṣdar*) of an omitted verb, meaning: "you exult with exultation," and that it be an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), meaning: "for the sake of exultation." It is also recited (as a *qirāʾa*, recitation) *marihan* with a kasra on the *rāʾ*, as an adjective of quality (*ṣifa mushabbaha*), and its accusative is in the circumstantial sense only. It has been said: this recitation, in terms of the ruling, is more eloquent than the recitation with the verbal noun, which conveys emphasis, by making it the very essence of the exultant, similar to what is said in "Zayd is just" (*zaydun ʿadlun*). This is because the attribute falls within the scope of the prohibition, which is in the sense of negation, and the negation of the very essence of the attribute is more eloquent than the negation of its increase and intensity, since the latter may suggest that its root remains to some extent. Taking the emphasis as returning to the negation rather than to the negated thing, as is said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾, is far-fetched here. And the claim that the adjective of quality indicates permanence, so that negating it does not entail negating its root, as is said regarding the verbal noun, is a sophistry that arises from not knowing the meaning of permanence in the attribute; for what is meant by it is that it does not indicate renewal and occurrence, not that it indicates perpetuity. al-Akhfash preferred the recitation with the verbal noun because of the emphasis in it, and did not consider that this (emphasis) applies to affirmation, not to negation or what is in its ruling. It has been raised against what was said that this involves preferring an irregular recitation (*shādhdha*) over a mass-transmitted one (*mutawātira*), and this, as you see, is (unacceptable).

For this reason some scholars preferred the recitation with the verbal noun, as al-Akhfash did, and made the emphasis derived from it return to the prohibition, and they rejected the claim that this is far-fetched. It has been said: if the estimate in the mass-transmitted recitation is taken as *dhā maraḥin* (possessor of exultation), it coincides with the irregular one. This was objected to on the grounds that *dhā maraḥin* is more eloquent than *marihan* as an adjective, because it indicates that he is one who possesses exultation and is constantly attached to it, as if he owns it. In this there is hesitation, as is not hidden.

The restriction to "the earth" cannot be said to be for the purpose of excluding walking in the air or on the water, because that is an extraordinary (*khāriq*) matter, and one is not warned against it. Rather, (the restriction) serves to remind (one) of the origin and the return, and this is more deterrent from walking the walk of the proud and arrogant, and more conducive to accepting admonition. It is as if it were said: do not walk in that which is your dominant element, from which you were created and to which you return, and which has gathered many of your kind, the walk of the proud and arrogant. It has also been said: (the restriction is) to specify that the prohibition against walking with exultation applies in all places and locations, and is not specific to one land over another. The first (explanation) is subtler.

﴿Indeed, you will never tear the earth apart﴾. This is a reason for the prohibition, and in it there is mockery of the arrogant; that is, you will never be able to make a rent in it by your treading and the heaviness of your stepping. ﴿Nor will you ever reach the mountains in height﴾, which are upon it, by your greatness and the stretching of your stature. So where are you, and haughtiness toward them? For haughtiness only occurs through abundance of strength and magnitude of body, and both of these are absent in you. Or (it means): you will never be able to do that, so you are weaker than each of these two inanimate things, and how then does haughtiness befit you? Some of the verifiers (*muḥaqqiqīn*) said: the upshot of the prohibition and the reason is: do not do that, for there is no benefit in it, and this is a good explanation. "In height" (*ṭūlan*) is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*). It is also permitted that it be an object of purpose. It has been said: the statement of some of them indicates that it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (*naẓʿ al-khāfiḍ*), and it has the meaning of extension, meaning: you will never reach the mountains by your extension. Its remoteness is not hidden. The choice of the explicit noun over a pronoun, where it does not say "you will never tear it," is for the increase of awakening and rebuke.

Furthermore, swaggering in walking is a major sin, as the sound hadiths indicate. This applies to (walking) other than between the two rows (in battle). As for walking between the two rows, it is permitted, due to a sound report concerning it. What is in the verse of mockery and rebuke suffices as a deterrent for whoever is accustomed to it where it is not permitted, as with many people today.

In al-Intisaf: God, exalted is He, has protected the common people of our time from this gait, but our reciters and jurists have fallen into it. One of them, if he has learned two issues, or has seated students before him, or has attained some share of worldly leadership, walks with conceit, and does not see that he is stretching toward the mountains, but sees that he is scraping the vault of heaven with the crown of his head, as though, regarding this verse, they do not pass by it, or they pass by it while turning away from it. End.

And if this is the condition of the reciters and jurists of his time, then what should I say about the reciters and jurists of my time, other than: may God not multiply their like, nor test us with any of their actions, and may He make them a bane for themselves.

﴿All that﴾ mentioned within the commands and prohibitions preceding it, from the qualities that amount to more than twenty, ﴿its evil﴾, namely what He forbade of them: setting up another god alongside Allah, may He be glorified, and worshipping other than Him, exalted is He; saying "uff" (to parents), wronging them, squandering; ﴿keeping your hand chained to your neck﴾ and ﴿extending it fully outstretched﴾; killing children for fear of poverty; killing the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right; the guardian's excess in killing; pursuing what one has no knowledge of; and walking on the earth exultantly. The genitive is of the lam type (lamiyya), an idafa of part to whole.

﴿with your Lord is hateful﴾, i.e. detestable, even though it is willed by Him, exalted is He, with the will of creation (al-iradah al-takwiniyya), for otherwise it would not occur, as indicated by his (ﷺ) saying: «What Allah, exalted is He, wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be», and other than that. This will is not synonymous with, nor necessarily accompanied by, approval, so that there is no entailing of the joining of two opposites, the aforementioned will and aversion, as the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) claim. This is a completion of the reason for all the matters forbidden. He described that with absolute aversion, although most of it is among the major sins, to indicate that mere aversion on His part suffices to make abstaining from it obligatory. Directing the reference to the whole and then specifying a part, rather than directing it to the part from the outset, is for what has been said: that the part mentioned is not mentioned as a whole but in a mixed manner, for a reason that required it. In this there is an indication that what is other than it is pleasing to Him, may He be glorified; and He did not state that explicitly, signifying that this is not needed.
