It has also been said: it is out of concern for the matter of deterring from the prohibitions, because they said that clearing away (al-takhliyah) takes precedence over adorning (al-tahliyah), and averting harms is more important than securing benefits. It is also permitted that the idafa be explanatory (bayaniyya).

"Dhalika" is either a reference to all that has preceded, and their opposites are taken from the commanded matters, which are then forbidden, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Do not associate anything with Him, and be good to your parents﴾, after His words, may He be glorified: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾; or it is a reference only to what He explicitly forbade.

The two Hijazis and the Basrans read «sayyi'ah» with a fatha on the hamza and the feminine ta' and in the accusative, as the predicate of kana, and the reference is to what He forbade explicitly and implicitly, or explicitly only. ﴿Hateful﴾ has been said to be a substitute (badal) for ﴿its evil﴾, and the agreement between the substitute and what it substitutes is not considered. It has been criticised on the ground that substitution with a derived noun (mushtaqq) is rare. It has been said: the description of ﴿its evil﴾ is taken according to meaning, since it carries the sense of "evil" (sayyi'an), and it has indeed been read thus; or that the word "sayyi'ah" has lost the sense of being a descriptive and is treated like the non-derived nouns, since it means "sin"; or the description applies to a masculine noun, i.e. "a hateful matter" (amran makruhan). It has also been said that it is a predicate of kana as well, and it is permissible to have multiple predicates for it according to the correct view. It has been said that it is a circumstantial (hal) of the pronoun concealed in kana or in the adverbial phrase, on the basis of making it a description.

﴿its evil﴾ not connected to "hateful", so that its pronoun is concealed in it; and the circumstantial in this case is emphatic. You know that the concealed pronoun of "sayyi'ah" is feminine, so making "hateful" a circumstantial of it is like making it a description of ﴿its evil﴾, both requiring interpretation. Using a masculine pronoun for it in the line: "nor a land whose greenery has sprouted like its sprouting (ibqal)," is not without its problems. And from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, it is reported that he read: «sha'nuhu» ("its matter").

[p. 77]

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned earlier of the detailed injunctions, ﴿is part of what your Lord has revealed to you﴾, meaning: some of it, or of its kind, ﴿of wisdom﴾, which is either the knowledge of the sharia (sacred law), or the knowledge of God, exalted is He, for His own essence and of the good for acting upon it, or the firm rulings (muhkamat) which are not subject to abrogation (naskh) or corruption. In al-Kashshaf, from Ibn 'Abbas: "These eighteen verses, meaning from ﴿Do not set up with God another god﴾ up to ﴿blameworthy and rejected﴾ in what has passed, were in the tablets of Moses, peace be upon him, and they are ten verses in the Torah." In ad-Durr al-Manthur: Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the whole Torah is in fifteen verses from the Children of Israel, then he recited: ﴿And do not set up with God another god﴾. This is a greater praise of the Noble Qur'an than what is in al-Kashshaf.

"Min" is either related to "awha" (revealed), as partitive or initial, or it is related to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) of the relative pronoun or its omitted resumptive pronoun, meaning: "of what your Lord revealed to you, being of wisdom." It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be an apposition (badal) for "ma." ﴿Do not set up with God another god﴾: the address is similar to the preceding address, repeated to draw attention to the fact that monotheism is the beginning and end of the matter, and that it is the head of all wisdom and its foundation. Initially, the consequence of it was ordered, which is its result in this world, which is shirk (association of partners with God) — where He said: ﴿so you will sit reproached and forsaken﴾. Here He ordered its result in the Hereafter, so it was said: ﴿you will be thrown into Hell, blameworthy﴾ from your own side and from the side of others, ﴿rejected﴾, removed from the mercy of God, exalted is He.

In al-Tafsir al-Kabir, the difference between "madhmum" (reproached) and "malum" (blamed) is that "madhmum" is one whom it is stated that the act he undertook is ugly and abominable, while "malum" is one to whom it is said: "Why did you do this act, what moved you to it, and what did you gain from it except inflicting harm upon yourself?" From this it is known that reproach (dhamm) comes first and blame (lawm) last. The difference between "makhdhul" (forsaken) and "madhur" (rejected): "makhdhul" is an expression for the weak, as it is said: "his limbs became slack", meaning: became weak; and what is meant by it is one whose help is withdrawn and who is left to himself. "Madhur" means the expelled, and what is meant by it is the humiliated and the one held in contempt. End.

In the use of "ilqa'" (being thrown) in the passive form, it follows the manner of majesty and of disdain for the polytheist, and he is made like a piece of wood that one takes and throws into the oven. Now, the address has been singular in some of these commands and prohibitions and plural in others. The secret of choosing singular or plural in each case, in a way that is free from dispute and pleasing to the perfect men, has not become clear to me. I mentioned this to some of my beloved friends among the great verifiers and chief teachers, and I asked him to write down what appears to him, since I know his perfection and excellence. He wrote the following text: "I say, acknowledging deficiency, guarding against conceit, excusing myself with the transmitted and commanded saying: an excuse that occurs to the mind of the poor one for changing the style of address has nine aspects which do not enter into reckoning.

First: the indication of the division of these obligations into three categories. One category concerns all, and the community was addressed with it twice: once explicitly by addressing themselves, and once allusively by addressing their Messenger ﷺ. This is the most important, namely monotheism. A second category is very important but below the first, and they were addressed with it once explicitly; it consists of seven matters. The first is general kindness to parents, for its absence, by not being good to them at all, is among the most severe degrees of disobedience ('uquq). The second: abstaining from killing children. The third: adultery. The fourth: abstaining from killing a forbidden soul except by right. The fifth: abstaining from dealing with the property of an orphan except in the best manner. The sixth: fulfilling the covenant. The seventh: weighing with the straight balance.

A third category, below the first two in importance, they were addressed with once allusively, and it also consists of eleven matters. The first: not saying 'uff' to parents. The second: not rebuking; for saying 'uff' and rebuking are among the lightest degrees of disobedience, unlike abandoning kindness entirely. The third: speaking a noble word to them. The fourth: lowering the wing of mercy. The fifth: supplicating for them with God's mercy, and these three, abandoning them is not like abandoning general kindness, for example. The sixth: abstaining from giving the due rights of the near kin, the needy and the wayfarer; and it is evident that failing to give the whole of these three rights is lighter than abandoning the matters mentioned in the second category. The seventh: abstaining from squandering. The eighth: speaking a gentle word. The ninth: justice in withholding and giving. The tenth: abstaining from pursuing what one has no knowledge of, such as judging by mere conjecture. The eleventh: abstaining from walking in arrogance. And abandoning any one of these five, whichever it is, does not reach the abandonment of any one of the matters charged and mentioned in the second category, as is not hidden.

The second of these aspects is the allusion, through the conjoining of the address to the community in the prohibition of grave major sins, for example, with his address ﷺ concerning what is not as dangerous, indicating that sins increase in gravity with the gravity of the one who commits them, supposing it, as the verse indicates: ﴿And had We not made you firm, you might have almost inclined to them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double [punishment] in death﴾, and the noble verse: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality, the punishment will be doubled for her two times﴾. As is well known, the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near, and those brought near are in great danger. But this subtlety was not observed in the prohibition of shirk, as an indication that it is at the utmost greatness, such that it is not fitting to imagine in its greatness any increase or variation among individuals. Or we say: when this subtlety conflicted with another subtlety that was given preference because it is more deserving of observance, namely the indication that shirk was great in the sight of God, exalted is He, so the address was repeated with the prohibition against it, both specifically and generally. Likewise we say about the non-observance of the subtlety of the following aspects in the obligation of monotheism, and we do not repeat it.

The third of these aspects is the alert through generalizing the address in the prohibition of some sins and the command of some acts of obedience, indicating that the trial of doing those sins and abandoning those acts of obedience does not afflict only those who did wrong.

The fourth of them is the indication, through generalizing the address in what was generalized of prohibitions and commands, that just as it is obligatory on every responsible person to refrain from those prohibited things, it is also obligatory on him to prevent others, such that if he left it he would be like the doer of them in having committed a major sin, which he forbade in the manner of those prohibitions; and that just as those commanded acts are obligatory on everyone to perform, it is obligatory to compel the one who abandons them to perform them, such that if he were not compelled he would be like the one who abandons them in having neglected an obligation that he was commanded, in the manner of those commanded acts. And by specifying the address in what was specified, it indicates that it is not of that status; for although it is obligatory to compel others to some of one's obligations, perhaps its abandonment is not a major sin.

The fifth is the symbol through making the address singular in what was made singular: that this act of obedience is not performed except by individuals, because only the scrupulous righteous fulfill its right, and they are few, unlike other things, for it is regulated.

The sixth: the indication that the obligations addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, while the community is intended, are not fulfilled rightly except by him or by one who follows his lights, traces his footsteps, strives to follow his upright way, and endeavors to be adorned with his noble character, unlike the others to whom they were addressed explicitly, for they are fulfilled by most of them.

The seventh: that He turned the address away from him ﷺ in the prohibition of killing children, adultery, killing a forbidden soul except by right, and dealing with the property of an orphan except in the best manner, indicating that the Prophet, prayers and peace be upon him, does not commit those abominations, even if he were not forbidden from them; for his natural disposition, his intelligence, the soundness of his subtle temperament and the uprightness of his noble constitution were sufficient to restrain him from them. Likewise, the address was turned away from him in the command of kindness to parents, fulfilling covenants, and weighing with the straight balance, indicating that he ﷺ would perform these matters even if he were not commanded to them, because abandoning general kindness to parents, were they to reach old age with him, for example, would entail harshness, coarseness of heart and roughness of disposition, which his nature ﷺ would refuse. Likewise treachery and cheating, his noble character would refuse them. But he was addressed with the prohibition of shirk, because natural disposition and character have no role in monotheism and shirk.

The eighth: that He, exalted is He, out of honor for His beloved ﷺ, did not address him with the prohibition of the grave sins of killing a child, adultery, and killing a soul without right, lest it be implied that he had been — and far be it from him — committing them before the prohibition. Likewise He did not address him with the command to fulfill the covenant and weigh with the straight balance, lest it be implied that he had been — and far be it from him — abandoning them before this. This implication is more deserving of being warded off than the implication in what he was addressed with alone. He was addressed with the prohibition of shirk because the known character of his call to the elite and the common folk throughout the nights and days sufficed him against this implication.

The ninth: perhaps the obligations with which the Prophet ﷺ was addressed, such as abstaining from pursuing what one has no knowledge of and abstaining from walking in the earth arrogantly, were not in any religion other than his among all other religions, or were not explicitly stated and specified in the heavenly books other than the Qur'an. So the address to him alone is a hint that these are among the particularities of his religion, or that the explicit statement and specification of them is among the particularities of his book. This aspect is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He, after the prohibition against pursuing without knowledge and walking arrogantly: ﴿That is part of the wisdom your Lord has revealed to you﴾.

Then I do not claim certainty or decisiveness in this, nor in all the other aspects, and I do not pursue what I have no knowledge of. Rather I say: this occurred to my broken mind, and knowledge is with the Subtle, the All-Aware." End.

It is objected to his statement in the first point: "its absence, by not being good to them at all, is among the most severe degrees of disobedience," that disobedience, which is a major sin, is doing that which causes a harm to the parents that is not light by custom, as you have heard; and the absence of kindness altogether may not be of that kind. The great scholar Ibn Hajar said in the course of discussing the difference between disobedience and severing kinship: "If it were supposed that his relative never received from him any kindness or harm, he would not be a sinner for that; for if this is supposed regarding his two parents, without him doing with them what entails great harm, for their being wealthy, for example, it would not be a major sin, so the rest of the relatives are more so." End. It seems that God, exalted is He, be gracious to him, thought that when the absence of kindness is realized, harm is realized, and he is far from the truth.

It is also objected to his statement: "It is evident that failing to give the whole of these three rights is lighter than abandoning the matters mentioned in the second category," that if he means it is lighter than abandoning all of those matters together, there is no doubt that some of what he counted in the third category, such as weighing with the straight balance, abandoning its performance is lighter than abandoning all the obligations; so what is the meaning of this specification? And if he means it is lighter than abandoning each one of the matters mentioned, then it is disputed. How not, when in it there is severing of kinship, and the one who severs kinship is cursed in three places in the Book of God, exalted is He. Ahmad reported with a sound chain that: "Among the usury of usury is seeking superiority without right, and this kinship is a branch of the Merciful, so whoever severs it, God forbids him Paradise." And also withholding zakah (obligatory alms).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 39 (part 2 of 2):

And Allah the Exalted has said in Ha Mim al-Sajdah (Surah Fussilat), which is Meccan like this surah: ﴿Woe to the polytheists who do not give zakat (obligatory almsgiving), and who are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾ [41:6-7]. And if one objects regarding what has been mentioned, we say: failing to give what has been mentioned applies to withholding the rights of three categories of people. There is no doubt that withholding a rightful person's right is an injustice toward him, so injustice is multiplied in what we are discussing. I do not think that this is less grave than tatfif (cheating in measure and weight), even though it is also an injustice:

*And the wronging of close kin is more painful to the heart
than the strike of a polished Indian sword.*

From what we have mentioned, it is known that his statement, "apparent but not apparent," is problematic. It also applies to his statement: "And abandoning one of these five... etc." That is, the statement of the Exalted: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [17:36] is, according to what the Imam chose, a prohibition against major sins (kaba'ir), there being no doubt that some of them are far greater than some of what is in the second category, such as speaking about divine matters and prophethood in the manner that the polytheists say, out of blind imitation of their forefathers and following their desires. And if you insist on restricting it to some of what the exegetes have said and the Imam transmitted, namely the least of its instances, such as lying, it is said to you:

Page 80

Indeed, that it is less grave than the absence of ihsan (kindness) in general, while it may not be a major sin, is a clear denial, as is not hidden. Likewise, regarding the walking in arrogance (maraha) being less than each of the matters previously mentioned, there is room for discussion.

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) have related: "While a man was walking in a garment that pleased him, admiring himself, with his hair combed, strutting in his gait, Allah the Exalted caused the earth to swallow him, and he will keep sinking into the earth until the Day of Resurrection."

Ahmad, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim related: "No man exalts himself within himself and struts in his gait except that he will meet Allah the Exalted while He is angry with him."

And it is authentically reported: "No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of arrogance will enter Paradise."

Besides these, there are other hadiths, and no similar ones have come concerning one who does not do good to his parents. Yes, such has come concerning one who disobeys his parents (uquq). Between disobeying them and not doing good to them there is a general and specific relationship, absolutely. Based on this, the matter is not hidden, as is not hidden.

And the second aspect, despite what it contains, is that it does not fully achieve the purpose. As for the third, it is merely a claim that the narrations do not support. Yes, something has come in some of what was mentioned, that its trial does not afflict only the wrongdoer, which supports it. Among that is what al-Bayhaqi and others related: "O company of the Muhajirun (emigrants), there are five traits; if you are tested with them, and they befall you, I seek refuge in Allah the Exalted that you reach them: Immorality never appears among a people to the point that they openly commit it, except that the diseases spread among them that were not present among their predecessors. They do not diminish the measure and the balance except that they are seized with years (of drought), harshness of livelihood, and the tyranny of the ruler. They do not withhold the zakat of their wealth except that they are denied rain from the sky, and were it not for the animals, they would not be given rain. They do not break the covenant of Allah the Exalted and the covenant of His Messenger ﷺ except that Allah the Exalted sends upon them an enemy from outside them, who takes some of what is in their hands. And whenever their leaders do not rule by the Book of Allah the Exalted, Allah the Exalted makes their violence (ba's) among themselves."

And if not giving to the needy (miskin) and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) their rights is considered withholding zakat, then the matter of the indication mentioned, and its status is not hidden, for the reports have converged on the general evil consequence of that.

It is authentically reported: "No people withhold zakat except that Allah the Exalted withholds the rain from them."

And in an authentic narration: "Except that Allah the Exalted tests them with years (of drought)."

And besides that. The fourth aspect is refuted by the fact that some have absolutely said that abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil is a major sin.

The author of al-'Uddah explicitly stated that backbiting itself is a minor sin, and abandoning forbidding it is a major sin. Some later scholars said, and al-Jalal al-Bulqini transmitted it: "It should be distinguished regarding forbidding evil: if it is a major sin, then remaining silent about it while being able to prevent it is a major sin; and if it is a minor sin, then remaining silent about it is a minor sin. The abandonment of what is commanded is measured by this, if we say that obligations vary in degree, and this is the apparent view." End of quote.

You know that among the commands in which the address is in the singular there are those whose abandonment is a major sin, and among the prohibitions there are those whose commission is likewise. So what was hoped for has not been realized, may Allah grant us safety. Moreover, in his expression "compulsion" (ijbar) in what he expressed, there is what is not hidden. The fifth aspect is refuted by the claim that the acts of obedience in which the address is in the singular are only performed by individuals, because only the scrupulous (mutawarri'un) fulfill their due. This is a clear denial, for most people, both righteous and wicked, do not walk on the earth in arrogance. Similarly, invoking mercy upon the two parents, for we hear it done most perfectly by many who do not know what piety (wara') is. Likewise, regarding his statement: "Unlike the others, for it is restricted," for abstaining from disposing of an orphan's property except in the way that is best, for one who has guardianship over it, is a hard matter that only individuals can accomplish. Ibn 'Abidin said in Radd al-Muhtar, the supercommentary on al-Durr al-Mukhtar: "It is not appropriate for the appointed executor (al-musa ilayhi) to accept, due to the extreme difficulty of justice." Hence Abu Yusuf said: "Entering into executorship the first time is an error, the second time is betrayal, and the third time is theft." From this it is known what is in the sixth aspect.

The seventh aspect is also refuted by the fact that walking on the earth in arrogance is like the matters whose prohibition was addressed to him ﷺ, in that his natural disposition, his intelligence, the soundness of his gentle nature, and the uprightness of his noble temperament are sufficient to restrain him from it. For arrogance among humans arises only from ignorance and dullness, while he, peace and blessings be upon him, was created with the most perfect humility, and indeed all the qualities that are perfection in the human species.

Page 81

This is supported by the statement of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed you are of a great character﴾ [68:4], even though the address was not directed to him in it. And since he considered intelligence as sufficient for abstention, the excuse for the singular address in the prohibition against polytheism does not benefit him, for intelligence has a complete role in monotheism, as is not hidden to the discerning.

Regarding his statement in the eighth aspect: "And this suggestion, etc." is a clear denial, so its status is not hidden, as is not hidden.

The ninth aspect is that it is supported neither by transmission nor by reason; rather, transmission has come with what contradicts it, as you have heard from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. And if the prohibition against polytheism is considered among those obligations, then it suffices to refute this aspect, because the prohibition against polytheism was brought by every Messenger, and every Book has spoken of it. What he cited supporting his purpose is far from being supportive.

This is what there is, and other objections remain against these aspects, which we have set aside and left for the intelligent and discerning, to avoid prolixity. So reflect on that, and may Allah take charge of your guidance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 40:

﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from the angels?﴾ This is addressed to those who claim that the angels are the daughters of God, glory be to Him. *Al-isfa'* (singling out, choosing) means making a thing pure and exclusive. The *hamzah* (the interrogative hamzah, used for rebuke) here enters upon an implied element, according to one of the two opinions, and the *fa'* (the *fa'* of conjunction) connects to that implied element. The meaning is: "Has He preferred you over Himself, singling you out with the most excellent of children in purity, while choosing for Himself the basest and lowest?" The mention of the title of Lordship (*al-Rububiyyah*) serves to intensify and emphasize the denunciation. The use of "females" (*al-inath*) expresses lowliness.

Shaykh al-Islam said: By mentioning the angels, peace be upon them, and using "females" instead of "daughters," it is pointed to another disbelief of theirs, namely their describing the angels, peace be upon them, with femaleness, which is the basest attribute of animals, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [43:19]. In *al-Kashshaf*: When He, exalted is He, forbade association (*shirk*) and indicated its corruption, He brought the connecting *fa'* and denounced them for this, as an indication of the place of inversion (*al-ta'kis*), and that after they had come to know, through evidence of reason and revelation, that He, glory be to Him, is free from partners, they attributed to Him, exalted is He, what is association and deficiency, and contempt toward those of His servants whom He chose. How monstrous is such a grave disbelief! And for this it was said:

﴿Indeed, you utter﴾ according to the requirement of your false doctrine ﴿a monstrous saying﴾ whose magnitude cannot be measured in what it entails of sin and in its violation of the axioms of reason, such that no person of intellect would dare to utter it, since you make Him, glory be to Him, of the kind of bodies that are swiftly perishing and need the continuation of the species through procreation, whereas "there is nothing like unto Him" [42:11], and He is the One, the Subduer, the Everlasting in His own essence. Then you attribute to Him, exalted is He, what you dislike, the basest of offspring, and you prefer yourselves over Him, glory be to Him, with sons. Then you describe the angels, peace be upon them, with what you describe.

﴿And We have certainly diversified﴾ from *tasrif* (variation), which is the frequent turning of a thing from one state to another. Its object is omitted here because it is understood. That is, We have diversified it, meaning this meaning. The intended sense is that We expressed it in various phrasings and established it through many modes of demonstration. ﴿in this Qur'an﴾, the great one, that is, in various places within it. So the word "Qur'an" refers to the whole of the revelation. It is also permissible that it refers to a part of it that contains the refutation of attributing daughters to Him, glory be to Him. The object of ﴿We have diversified﴾ is also omitted, so that the sense is: We have diversified the speech containing the refutation of the aforementioned attribution in this meaning. Placing the Qur'an upon the meaning and making it a container for the speech is either by applying the name of the locus to what is located in it, since it is well known that words are the moulds of meanings, or the reverse, as one says: "the such-and-such chapter is about such-and-such," and "this verse is about the prohibition of such-and-such," meaning, in its explanation. It is also permissible to treat the verb as intransitive and to make it transitive by means of *fi* (in), as in the saying of the poet: "He wounds with my sword in their hamstrings."

That is, We have caused the diversification to occur in it.

It is also read *sarafna* with the light form. *Al-sarf* is like *al-tasrif* except that the latter denotes intensification.

﴿that they may take heed﴾, that is, that they may remember, be admonished, and be reassured by it, for repetition necessitates acceptance and tranquillity of the soul.

﴿But it increases them﴾, that diversification, ﴿only in aversion﴾ from the truth and turning away from it, and this is a reversal. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read here, and in ﴿that they may take heed﴾, from *al-dhikr*, which has the sense of *al-tadhakkur* (recollection), the opposite of forgetfulness and heedlessness. According to the first reading, *al-tadhakkur* means admonition, as has been indicated. The shift to the third person is to signal that the situation requires that He turn away from them and relate their follies to the listeners.

[Page 82]

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on Surah 17, verses 42–43:

﴿Say﴾, to demonstrate the falsity of that in another way: ﴿If there were with Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He, gods, as they claim﴾, that is, the polytheists all together. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the verb with the ta' as the third letter (*ta'*, *al-huruf al-thalith*), addressing them directly. Both readings are common in this kind of context. When someone is commanded to convey a statement to another person, the one conveying it is, at the time the commander speaks, in the third person (*ghaybah*, absent), and becomes the addressee (*khitab*) at the time of delivery. If one considers the first aspect, the verb should take the third person; if one considers the second, it should take the second person. They read the subsequent verbs in the same way. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with the ta' here and with the ya' (third-person prefix) there, on the basis that it is an act of glorification (*tanzih*) by Him, glory be to Him, for Himself, beginning without the Messenger (ﷺ) being commanded, peace and blessings be upon him, to say it to them. The *kaf* (in *kama*) is in the accusative position, functioning as a qualifier (*na't*) for an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: "a state resembling what they say." By "resemblance" is meant, as has been said, agreement and conformity.

﴿Then they would have sought﴾ is the answer to their statement that there are gods with Allah, glory be to Him, and it is the consequent (*jaza'*) of *law* (if). That is: the gods would have sought ﴿a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, that is, to the One who possesses dominion and lordship absolutely, ﴿a way﴾ by contention and resistance, as is customary among kings. This points to the proof of mutual exclusion (*burhan al-tamanu'*), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, both would have been corrupted﴾. This is expressed through a conditional syllogism (*qiyas istithna'i*), in which the contradictory of the consequent is affirmed in order to produce the contradictory of the antecedent, which is the desired conclusion. Its exposition will come, Allah willing, in its proper place. Sa'id ibn Jubayr took this view, as Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him. From Mujahid and Qatadah, the meaning is that they would have sought closeness to Him, exalted is He, and nearness through obedience, since they would know His exaltedness over them and His greatness. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek a means of access to their Lord﴾. This points to a categorical syllogism (*qiyas iqtirani*) of this form: if they were gods, as you claim, they would have drawn near to Him, exalted is He; and whoever is like that is not a god; therefore they are not gods. It has been said that *law* in the first interpretation is for impossibility (*imtina'iyyah*), and in this one it is conditional (*shart*). The syllogism is composed of two premises: a conditional premise of conjunction (*ittifaqiyyah*) and a categorical premise (*hamliyyah*).

The verifying scholars (*al-muhaqqiqun*) preferred the first aspect, because it is clearer and more appropriate to His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, for it clearly indicates that the purpose is to show that what they say entails a great impossibility from a direction they do not reckon.

As for seeking a way to Him, exalted is He, by drawing near, this is not specific to this supposition, nor is it something that would follow for them from a direction they are unaware of. Rather, it is a matter they believe outright. That is: He is declared free of every imperfection, in a manner truly fitting to Him, glory be to Him, ﴿and exalted is He﴾, far removed ﴿from what they say﴾, of the monstrous claims, namely that there are gods with Him, exalted is He, and that He has daughters, ﴿high exaltation﴾, that is, exaltedness. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) not from its own verb, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and caused you to grow from the earth a [gradual] growth﴾. ﴿Great﴾, far-reaching in its extent, indeed without any limit beyond it. How could it not be so, when He, exalted is He, is at the furthest reach of existence, which is necessary existence in Himself (*al-wujub al-dhati*), whereas what they claim, that there are gods with Him and that He has offspring, lies at the lowest level of nonexistence, which is impossibility in itself (*al-imtina' al-dhati*). It has also been said: because He, exalted is He, is at the highest level of existence, which is that He is necessarily existent and subsists by His own essence, whereas taking a son is among the lowest of its levels, since it is among the properties of what cannot subsist.

It has been objected that what they claim is not merely taking a son, but taking it together with what you have heard. There is no doubt that this does not fall within the bounds of possibility, let alone within existence. Its being among the lowest levels of existence applies only relative to one who is capable of it. It has been answered that this is by way of drawing attention to the state of the lower in order to indicate the state of the higher. Yet it is not hidden that mentioning exaltedness after the title "Lord of the Throne" is among the highest levels of eloquence.

[p. 83]

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on Surah 17, verses 42–43:

﴿Say﴾, to demonstrate the falsity of that in another way: ﴿If there were with Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He, gods, as they claim﴾, that is, the polytheists all together. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the verb with the ta' as the third letter (*ta'*, *al-huruf al-thalith*), addressing them directly. Both readings are common in this kind of context. When someone is commanded to convey a statement to another person, the one conveying it is, at the time the commander speaks, in the third person (*ghaybah*, absent), and becomes the addressee (*khitab*) at the time of delivery. If one considers the first aspect, the verb should take the third person; if one considers the second, it should take the second person. They read the subsequent verbs in the same way. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with the ta' here and with the ya' (third-person prefix) there, on the basis that it is an act of glorification (*tanzih*) by Him, glory be to Him, for Himself, beginning without the Messenger (ﷺ) being commanded, peace and blessings be upon him, to say it to them. The *kaf* (in *kama*) is in the accusative position, functioning as a qualifier (*na't*) for an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: "a state resembling what they say." By "resemblance" is meant, as has been said, agreement and conformity.

﴿Then they would have sought﴾ is the answer to their statement that there are gods with Allah, glory be to Him, and it is the consequent (*jaza'*) of *law* (if). That is: the gods would have sought ﴿a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾, that is, to the One who possesses dominion and lordship absolutely, ﴿a way﴾ by contention and resistance, as is customary among kings. This points to the proof of mutual exclusion (*burhan al-tamanu'*), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, both would have been corrupted﴾. This is expressed through a conditional syllogism (*qiyas istithna'i*), in which the contradictory of the consequent is affirmed in order to produce the contradictory of the antecedent, which is the desired conclusion. Its exposition will come, Allah willing, in its proper place. Sa'id ibn Jubayr took this view, as Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him. From Mujahid and Qatadah, the meaning is that they would have sought closeness to Him, exalted is He, and nearness through obedience, since they would know His exaltedness over them and His greatness. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek a means of access to their Lord﴾. This points to a categorical syllogism (*qiyas iqtirani*) of this form: if they were gods, as you claim, they would have drawn near to Him, exalted is He; and whoever is like that is not a god; therefore they are not gods. It has been said that *law* in the first interpretation is for impossibility (*imtina'iyyah*), and in this one it is conditional (*shart*). The syllogism is composed of two premises: a conditional premise of conjunction (*ittifaqiyyah*) and a categorical premise (*hamliyyah*).

The verifying scholars (*al-muhaqqiqun*) preferred the first aspect, because it is clearer and more appropriate to His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, for it clearly indicates that the purpose is to show that what they say entails a great impossibility from a direction they do not reckon.

As for seeking a way to Him, exalted is He, by drawing near, this is not specific to this supposition, nor is it something that would follow for them from a direction they are unaware of. Rather, it is a matter they believe outright. That is: He is declared free of every imperfection, in a manner truly fitting to Him, glory be to Him, ﴿and exalted is He﴾, far removed ﴿from what they say﴾, of the monstrous claims, namely that there are gods with Him, exalted is He, and that He has daughters, ﴿high exaltation﴾, that is, exaltedness. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) not from its own verb, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and caused you to grow from the earth a [gradual] growth﴾. ﴿Great﴾, far-reaching in its extent, indeed without any limit beyond it. How could it not be so, when He, exalted is He, is at the furthest reach of existence, which is necessary existence in Himself (*al-wujub al-dhati*), whereas what they claim, that there are gods with Him and that He has offspring, lies at the lowest level of nonexistence, which is impossibility in itself (*al-imtina' al-dhati*). It has also been said: because He, exalted is He, is at the highest level of existence, which is that He is necessarily existent and subsists by His own essence, whereas taking a son is among the lowest of its levels, since it is among the properties of what cannot subsist.

It has been objected that what they claim is not merely taking a son, but taking it together with what you have heard. There is no doubt that this does not fall within the bounds of possibility, let alone within existence. Its being among the lowest levels of existence applies only relative to one who is capable of it. It has been answered that this is by way of drawing attention to the state of the lower in order to indicate the state of the higher. Yet it is not hidden that mentioning exaltedness after the title "Lord of the Throne" is among the highest levels of eloquence.

[p. 83]

[Page 83 of the commentary]

**﴿تُسَبِّحُ﴾** (tusabbihu) with the feminine prefix *fawqaniyyah* (تَاء الفوقانية, the "upper" ta, i.e. the feminine form). This is the reading of Abu 'Amr, the two Akhawayn (al-Kisa'i and Hamzah) and Hafs. The rest read it with the masculine prefix *tahtaniyyah* (يَاء التحتانية, the "lower" ya), because the feminine marking of the subject is metaphorical (*majazi*) and separated from the verb. There is also a reading: «سَبَّحَتْ» (sabbahat, in the past tense).

**﴿لَهُ السَّماواتُ السَّبْعُ والأرْضُ ومَن فِيهِنَّ﴾** ("The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him"), that is, of the angels and the two species (*al-thaqalan*, humans and jinn).

**﴿وإنْ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾** ("And there is not a thing") among things, whether animal, plant or inanimate,

**﴿إلا يُسَبِّحُ﴾** ("but glorifies") while **﴿بِحَمْدِهِ﴾** ("with His praise") — that is, praising Him, exalted is He. The meaning of glorification here is indication by the tongue of the state (*lisan al-hal*): it indicates, by its possibility and its origination, a clear indication of the necessary existence of Him, exalted is He, of His oneness, His power and His transcendence above what are the necessary consequences of contingency and the attendant features of origination, just as an effect indicates its agent. Thus in the statement there is a *isti'arah* (metaphor, specifically a *tab'iyyah*, a metaphor in a verb/derived sense), as in the phrase "the state spoke" (نَطَقَتِ الحالُ).

It is also permitted to consider here a *isti'arah tamthiliyyah* (an extended, pictorial metaphor). The statement of Allah, exalted is He, does not preclude taking glorification in this sense: **﴿ولَكِنْ لا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهُمْ﴾** ("but you do not understand their glorification"), based on the view that many of the rational beings understood that indication. This is because the address is to the polytheists and disbelievers, not to people in general, since the mention of their ugly deeds has preceded — their attributing to Him, exalted is His majesty, what is not fitting to His grandeur. Allah, glorified is He, described His essence as free of that and emphasised it as much as He did, then followed it with what He mentioned, indicating that all existents bear witness to that transcendence, emphasis upon emphasis. So if the address were to other than these deniers and their like, the statement would not fit together and would fall out of order.

And His statement, exalted is He: **﴿إنَّهُ كانَ حَلِيمًا غَفُورًا﴾** ("Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving") is a *tadhyil* (a concluding summary phrase), part of the denunciation, in the most eloquent manner; that is: indeed He, glorified is He, is Forbearing, and for that reason He did not hasten to punish you for your neglect of the correct reflection that leads to tawhid. If you repented and reflected, He would forgive you what came from you of shortcoming, for He is Forgiving to whoever repents.

Ibn al-Munayyir (ابن المُنَيِّر) thought that this *tadhyil* rules out that the address is to the polytheists, saying: "For He, glorified is He, does not forgive them, nor does He overlook their ignorance and their association [of partners]." He said: "The apparent meaning is that those addressed are the believers, and their not understanding the glorification issuing from inanimate things is an allusion (*kinayah*) to their not acting upon what that requires. For if a person awakened to the fullest awakening to the fact that the ant, the gnat and every particle of existence glorify Allah, exalted is He, and declare Him free of imperfection, and bear witness to His majesty, greatness and dominance, and filled his heart with this understanding, it would occupy him from food, let alone superfluous acts and speech. And the one absorbed in backbiting, which is our fruit in our time, if he sensed, while indulging in it, that every particle of his tongue, which he wags, is under the wrath of Allah, exalted is He, occupied and filled with the sanctification of Allah, His glorification, the fear of His punishment and the warning of His might, and he awoke to that to the fullest awakening, he would nearly be struck dumb for the rest of his life. So the apparent meaning is that the verse came as an address according to the most common states of the heedless, even if they are believers." End of his words. But this is not sound, because the statement would fall out of order by this. The reason for the *tadhyil* is what you have heard, so there is no objection, as will not be hidden from people of understanding.

It is also permitted that by glorification is meant the indication of the transcendence of the Creator, glorified is He, above the necessary consequences of contingency and the attendant features of origination, absolutely, whether they are indicated by the state or by speech. This is either on the basis that it falls under general metaphor (*'umum al-majaz*), or by combining the literal and metaphorical meanings according to the opinion of those who permit that. Thus the glorification of some is verbal, and the glorification of others is by state. But this was criticised, on the grounds that it does not suit the context.

**﴿لا تَفْقَهُونَ﴾** ("you do not understand") — because among that glorification is what the polytheists and others understand, namely the verbal glorification. It has been answered that the polytheists, because of their not reflecting upon it and not benefiting from it, their understanding was as if nonexistent; or that because they did not understand some of what is meant by glorification, they were placed among those who do not understand all of it, by way of *taghlib* (giving precedence to the majority/predominant element).

Some of the Zahiriyyah (literalists) went the way of holding that, and al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) approved of it, and in the tafsir of al-Khazin he said: "It is the most correct, on the basis that glorification is in its literal meaning, so everything glorifies by verbal speech, even inanimate things."

[Page 84]

But al-Imam (al-Razi) did not approve of that, because this glorification does not occur except with knowledge, and that is not conceivable in an inanimate thing, since it lacks its rational condition, which is life. And if that were not a rational condition, the door of knowing that He, glorified and exalted is He, is living would be closed. Also, the preceding *tadhyil* rules that out, since it indicates that the non-understanding of the aforementioned glorification is a sin, and there is no doubt that not understanding the glorification of inanimate things through their words is not a sin; rather the sin is not understanding their indication, through heedlessness and deficiency of reflection.

Whoever traces the hadiths and reports will see in them what bears witness to what this faction went to, a witness that hardly admits of interpretation. For the hearing of the glorification of pebbles in the palm of the Prophet (ﷺ) is authentically established.

Abu al-Shaykh (أبو الشيخ) transmitted from Anas, who said: "A dish of thareed (a stew of bread and broth) was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'This food is glorifying.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you understand its glorification?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he said to a man: 'Bring this bowl near this man.' So he brought it near him, and he said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, this food is glorifying.' He said: 'Bring it near another.' So he brought it near him, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this food is glorifying.' Then he said: 'Take it away.' A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if you were to command it for the whole people?' He said: 'No, for if it were silent in front of a man they would say: it was rejected because of a sin.' So he took it away."

Ibn Mardawayh (ابن مردويه) transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "We were the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), counting the signs as a blessing, while you count them as a warning. While we were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with no water among us, he said to us: 'Seek whoever has surplus water.' So water was brought, and he put it in a vessel, then he put his hand in it, and the water began to flow from between his fingers. Then he said: 'Come to the blessed purification, and the blessing is from Allah, exalted is He.' So we drank from it." Abdullah said: "We used to hear the sound of the water and its glorification while it was being drunk."

Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Noah, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he said to his two sons: 'I command you with *subhan Allah wa bihamdih* (Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him), for it is the prayer of everything, and by it everything is provided for.'"

Ahmad transmitted from Mu'adh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he passed by a people who were standing upon their animals and riding beasts, and he said to them: "Ride them safely, and leave them safely, and do not take them as seats for your conversations in the roads and markets, for many a mount is better than its rider, and make much mention of Allah, exalted is He, upon them."

An-Nasa'i, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade killing the frog, and said: 'Its croaking is glorification.'"

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* transmitted from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "Dawud (David), peace be upon him, thought within himself that no one had praised his Creator with what he had praised Him with. Then an angel descended while he was sitting in the mihrab, and the pond was beside him, and he said: 'O Dawud, pay attention to what the frog is vocalising.' So Dawud listened, and behold, the frog was praising Him with a praise He had not been praised with. The angel said to him: 'How do you see it, O Dawud? Did you understand what it said?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What did it say?' He said: 'It said: Glory be to You and praise be to You, the extent of Your knowledge, O Lord.' Dawud said: 'No, by the One who made me His prophet, I will not praise Him except with this.'"

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Shahr ibn Hawshab, in a long hadith, that Dawud, peace be upon him, came to the sea at a certain hour and prayed, and a frog called out to him: "O Dawud, you have told yourself that you have glorified in an hour in which no one other than you mentions Allah, exalted is He. Indeed I am among seventy thousand frogs, all of them standing on one leg, glorifying Allah, exalted is He, and sanctifying Him."

Al-Khatib transmitted from Abu Damrah, who said: "We were with 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, and sparrows passed by us chirping. He said: 'Do you know what these sparrows are saying?' We said: 'No.' He said: 'Indeed I do not say that we know the unseen, but I heard my father say: I heard the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, when birds rise in the morning, they glorify their Lord and ask Him for the provision of their day, and these are glorifying their Lord and asking Him for the provision of their day."'"

[Page 85]

Ibn Rahawayh in his *Musnad* transmitted through al-Zuhri, who said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, was brought a crow with full wings, and he said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No game is hunted, no thorny tree is cut down, and no tree trunk is felled, except through a lack of glorification."'" Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No game is hunted, and no tree is cut, except through its neglect of glorification."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu al-Darda', and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn Mas'ud, a similar report, raised (*marfu'*) to the Prophet (ﷺ) as well.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Hasan: "Were it not for what is concealed from you of the glorification of the houses that are with you, you would not be able to settle [in them]." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Lut ibn Abi Lut, who said: "It has reached me that the glorification of the lowest heaven is: 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High'; of the second: 'Glory be to Him, exalted is He'; of the third: 'Glory be to Him and praise be to Him'; of the fourth: 'Glory be to Him; there is no power nor strength except by Him'; of the fifth: 'Glory be to the One who gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Powerful'; of the sixth: 'Glory be to the King, the Holy'; and of the seventh: 'Glory be to the One who filled the seven heavens and the seven earths with might and dignity.'" And there are countless other reports and traditions, which together support one another in indicating that glorification is verbal, as is not hidden. This is the view of the Sufis, and they mention that the seeker, upon reaching some of the stations, hears the glorification of things in various languages.

It has been related from some of the early generation (*salaf*) that they heard the glorification of some inanimate things. Those who hold this glorification have differed. Some of them said it is established for things absolutely. It has been said that the dust glorifies as long as it is not moistened, and when it is moistened it stops glorifying; that the pebble glorifies as long as it is not lifted from its place, and when it is lifted it stops; that the leaf glorifies as long as it is on the tree, and when it falls it stops; that the garment glorifies as long as it is not soiled, and when it is soiled it stops; and that wild animals and birds glorify when they cry out, and when they fall silent they stop. In accordance with this is what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Shawdhab, who said: "Al-Hasan sat with his companions at a table, and some of them said: 'This table is glorifying now.' Al-Hasan said: 'No indeed, that is only: each thing according to its origin.'"

It is related from al-Suddi that he said: "Nothing that remains on its original state and has not died except that it glorifies with His praise, exalted is He." Perhaps by "death" he meant its departure from its original state.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Qatadah that he said regarding the verse: "Everything that has a spirit glorifies, of a tree and of an animal." That a tree has a spirit is based on the view of people that when it dries it dies. Some scholars excepted certain animals from the generality of "everything," because of what Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Everything glorifies except the donkey and the dog."

I do not see a basis for the exception of what has been mentioned, and there is some doubt concerning the soundness of the report from the rabbi (Ibn 'Abbas, as the 'Ḥibr'). Likewise for the restriction, since inanimacy was not preventing glorification, and the reports indicating non-restriction are more numerous, and I do not think that what contradicts them has any superiority over them in soundness.

Against this view stands what was previously mentioned from al-Imam (al-Razi), concerning the *tadhyil* ruling it out and the absence of the knowledge which verbal glorification requires in inanimate things. Some have tried to escape this by committing to the view that everything has a life and a knowledge appropriate to it, and that the reality of that is known only to Allah, the Subtle, the All-Aware. Thus, according to this position, everything in the world is living and knowing, but its degrees in knowledge and life vary.

Al-Sha'rani related from al-Khawwas that he said: "Every inanimate object understands address and feels pain just as an animal does." Al-Shaykh al-Akbar (may God sanctify his secret) said: "Whatever is called inanimate or vegetative has, in our view, spirits that remain hidden from perception in the ordinary way, apart from unveiling (kashf) of them. Everything, in our view, is alive and speaking, except that this particular temperament is called 'human' by form alone. Differences among created beings lie in temperament, and everything glorifies God Most High, as the verse has stated. Only a living being who is rational, knowing, and aware of the one he glorifies can glorify."

It is reported that the muezzin is witnessed by everything, moist and dry, within the reach of his voice.

The revealed laws and prophetic traditions are full of what belongs to this category. We have added to faith in the reports the unveiling (kashf), and so on to the end of what he said.

Some scholars, in this context, cited what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said in his supplication against fever: "O Umm Muldam, if you have believed in God Most High, do not eat flesh, do not drink blood, do not disperse from the mouth, and move on to one who claims that there are other gods besides God Most High. Indeed I testify that there is no god but God alone, without partner, and I testify that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger ﷺ."

And there came from al-Sajjad, may God Most High be pleased with him, in the Sahifa, in addressing the moon, what is apparent in showing that it has awareness. It is widely reported from Umar, may God Most High be pleased with him, that he wrote a document to the Nile addressing it with what he addressed it with, and that he struck the earth with his whip when it quaked and said to it: "I am being just to you." How many similar reports there are in the traditions. It was said: there is no need to interpret them, since no one claims that the awareness of inanimate things is like the awareness of animals in a manifest way, such that everyone perceives it, so that acting on the apparent wording would contradict the perception of the sensible; therefore interpretation and metaphorical usage are required. Whoever knows the greatness of God's power, the Mighty and Majestic, that nothing can overcome Him, and that created beings, with their varying ranks, especially those immersed in the states of worldly ties and obstacles and imprisoned in the prison of base nature, have not grasped a tenth of a tenth of what has been deposited in the world of possibility and inscribed by the hand of wisdom upon the cold forms of entities, will accept what the Truthful one ﷺ brought, and if it contradicts what he has, he will attribute the deficiency to himself. Such is a proximate thought that a person supposes to be true while it is among illusions, as will not be hidden from one who is fair and does not strain.

On the basis of what they have mentioned, there is no need to return the pronoun of the rational ones in ﴿تَسْبِيحَهُمْ﴾ [their glorification] to what preceded, as an alternative explanation and another way out, namely that His words ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ حَلِيمًا غَفُورًا﴾ [Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving] are connected to His words ﴿سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى عَمّا يَقُولُونَ﴾ [Glory be to Him, and exalted far above what they say]. The weakness of this escape is not hidden. Perhaps the better course is to adopt that the glorification is taken in its more general sense, encompassing both the state-based and the verbal, and that both kinds are affirmed for every thing. The closing phrase is in terms of the deficiency in the understanding of the other.

It is also problematic that among those to whom glorification is attributed are the deniers, let alone the silent ones, so the interpretation as metaphor is necessary. It was answered that the exception of those is known from the context of what precedes and what follows. Someone claimed that the denier is also sanctifying, and they recited for al-Hallaj:

"My denial of You is a form of sanctification, and my intellect concerning You is bewildered;
So there is no Adam but You, and in existence there is no Iblis."

You know that such excess and ecstatic expression became the cause of what he encountered of death. So what then shall I say, other than: God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.

It was also read: "لا يَفْقَهُونَ" [they do not understand], in the passive form from the verbal pattern of taf'il.

﴿And when you recite the Qur'an﴾, the Qur'an that speaks of glorifying God and declaring Him free of imperfection, and you call them to act upon what is in it, ﴿We place﴾ by Our power and Our will, which are founded on hidden wisdoms.

﴿between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, namely the polytheists mentioned earlier. The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl, "those who") is used in place of a pronoun in order to disparage them through the content of its relative clause (al-ṣilah, the clause that follows the relative pronoun). This, together with what preceded, completes the indication of their disbelief in the Originator and the Return.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim: "They are singled out for mention in their disbelief in the Hereafter from among the rest of what they disbelieved in, such as tawhid and the like, to show that it is the greatest of what they were commanded to believe in the Qur'an, and as a preparation for what will be reported of them regarding their denial of the resurrection, their urging its coming, and similar matters." (End of quotation.)

Regarding whether the Hereafter is the greatest of what they were commanded to believe in the Qur'an, there is hesitation. It may be argued that this is tawhid. The better course is to limit it to the view that it serves as a preparation. [page 87]

﴿a veil﴾ that prevents them from perceiving you as you are, in your prophethood and your exalted rank. For this reason they became bold enough to utter the monstrous statement: ﴿You follow only a man under enchantment﴾. The basic meaning of ḥijāb (veil) is like ḥajb, meaning prevention from reaching, so it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), but it has been used to mean the descriptive adjective, i.e., "a barrier."

﴿concealed﴾, meaning possessing a covering. It is then of the type of nisbah (attribution of the quality to something possessing it), like the Arabic phrases rajulun marṭūb (a man who is moist), makānun mahūl (a place that is terrifying), and jāriyatun maghnūjah (a girl who is shapely). From the same type is the verse ﴿His promise is ever fulfilled﴾ (mā'tiyyan, "coming"). Likewise, sayl mufʿam (a torrent that is full), with the vowel of the ʿayn being a fatḥah, and the most common usage for this type is the form fāʿil, as in lābin (possessing milk) and tāmir (possessing dates).

It is also permitted that the attribution be figurative (majāzī), as is well known in the last example. On the authority of al-Akhfash, the form maf'ūl may come with the meaning of fā'il, as in maymūn (blessed) and mash'ūm (ill-omened), meaning yāmin (auspicious) and shā'im (ill-omening). Just as fā'il may come with the meaning of maf'ūl, as in mā' dāfiq (gushing water). So mastūr would mean sātir (covering). Or mastūran may mean concealed from the senses, in which case it is on its apparent meaning, and it serves as an explanation, since it is a non-sensory, spiritual veil. Or mastūran may mean concealed in itself by another veil, in which case it indicates multiple veils. Or mastūran may mean that its being a veil is concealed, since they do not realize that they do not realize. It has also been said that it is an elliptical construction (ḥadhf) with the transitive form (īṣāl), meaning: concealed by it is the Messenger ﷺ.

[p. 87]

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings (akinnah)﴾, plural of kinan, meaning coverings. From the context, the intended sense is multiplicity: many coverings.

﴿Lest they understand it (an yafqahuhu)﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), with an omitted genitive noun (mudaf) before it, meaning: out of aversion to their coming to grasp its reality and recognising that it is from Allah, the Exalted. It may also be an object (maf'ul bihi) of a verb that is omitted but understood from the sentence, or from ﴿akinnah﴾, not that ﴿ja'alna﴾ or something else mentioned has been made to include it, as is imagined. The meaning is: We prevented them from understanding it and from grasping its reality. ﴿And in their ears is a heaviness (waqran)﴾, meaning deafness and a great weight that prevents them from hearing it in the proper manner, for they used to hear it without reflection. These are, as some of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) said, figurative expressions (tamthilat) indicating the full extent of their ignorance of the affairs of the Prophet (ﷺ), the extreme remoteness of their hearts from understanding the noble Qur'an, and the rejection of their ears by it. They were brought in as a clarification of their lack of understanding, an eloquent statement following the clarification of their lack of understanding by the indication of the situation (dalalat al-hal). In this there is a notice that what the Qur'an contains of guidance is in the utmost clarity, such that its non-understanding is conceivable only due to a strong obstacle that afflicts the faculties and nullifies them. It is also a warning that their present state is more ugly than their previous state. Whoever takes the verse as referring to what has been mentioned, and does not take the glorification (tasbih) mentioned earlier as merely verbal, is in agreement; but for one who makes it verbal, it is not fitting to interpret the verse that way, as is not hidden.

Some have said: the intended sense of the veil is that which screens them from understanding what the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him recites. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah that he said: "The concealed veil is the coverings over their hearts, lest they understand it and benefit from it." This view was taken by al-Zajjaj, and it has been criticised on the grounds that it does not fit ﴿between you and those who﴾ etc., except by supposing two omitted genitive nouns, meaning: We placed between the understanding of your recitation [and them]. Also, it entails repetition without new benefit. It has been answered that the apparent meaning is that nothing is to be supposed there, and that this would be required only if it were literal; this is a figurative depiction of their not hearing the truth, like one who is behind a wall and a screen, just as the coverings are likewise. As for the objection of repetition without benefit, it is refuted by the fact that the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We have placed﴾ etc., is an explicit statement of what the negation of eloquent speech after the negation of understanding the indication of the situation required, namely that they were sealed upon error. And the superiority of what was mentioned earlier is not hidden from the fair-minded.

It is related from al-Jubba'i that the intended sense of the veil is that which keeps them from harming the Messenger (ﷺ). That is because they used to target him when he recited in order to harm him, so Allah, the Exalted, made him secure and told him, Prayer and Peace be upon him, that He, may His majesty be exalted, had placed between him and them a veil during recitation, so they could not reach him. In my view this is not objectionable. Its mention in the context of escaping the argument of our companions from the verse, that Allah, the Exalted, prevents from faith whom He wills just as He guides whom He wills, is acceptable; yes, it is inferior to the first view according to one who reflects.

[p. 88]
It has been said: the intended sense is the veil that prevented them from seeing the person of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his noble self.

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il together narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ was revealed, al-'Awra' Umm Jamil came, with a wail, and in her hand was a stone, and she was saying:

We reject Mudhammam, we despise his religion, we disobey his command.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting, and Abu Bakr was beside him. Abu Bakr said: 'This woman has come, and I fear she will see you.' He said: 'She will not see me.' And he recited a Qur'an by which he sought protection, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed veil﴾. She came until she stood over Abu Bakr, but she did not see the Prophet, Prayer and Peace be upon him. She said: 'O Abu Bakr, it has reached me that your companion has satirised me.' Abu Bakr said: 'No, by the Lord of this House, he did not satirise you.' She departed, saying: 'Quraysh already knows that I am the daughter of its chief.' It is reported in another narration that when she turned away going, Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, she did not see you.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Jibril, peace be upon him, stood between me and her.'"

The Imam (al-Razi) mentioned that when he (ﷺ) intended to recite the Qur'an, he would first recite three verses: His saying, the Exalted, in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿Indeed We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears a heaviness﴾; His saying, glorified is He, in al-Nahl: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has sealed﴾; and His saying, exalted is He, in Surat Ha Mim al-Jathiyah: ﴿Have you seen one who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ etc. So Allah, the Exalted, would veil him by the blessings of these verses from the eyes of the polytheists, and this is what is meant by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place﴾ etc. Our companions argued by this that it is permissible for the sense faculty to be sound and the object of perception to be present, yet one does not see because Allah, the Exalted, creates in the eye an obstacle that prevents sight. They said: the Prophet, Prayer and Peace be upon him, was present, or the senses of the disbelievers were sound, and they did not see him; and Allah, glorified is He, has informed that this was due to His placing between him, Prayer and Peace be upon him, and them a concealed veil, and there is no meaning to a concealed veil except the meaning that He creates in their eyes and which prevents them from seeing. End.

Some verifying scholars said: that the veil be taken as what is related in the hadith of Asma' is something that sound taste does not accept, nor does the noble wording support it. It seems he intended that to take it in the verse as the veil preventing sight is likewise, and it applies to what is related from the Imam also. From this one knows the status of the argument of the companions, along with what is objected to in their view; and "there is no meaning to the veil" etc. — that it contradicts the earlier narration in which Jibril, peace be upon him, is mentioned as interposing.

And the report which al-Daraqutni and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There was between me and her an angel who shielded me with his two wings whenever she went."

Both reports clearly show that the obstacle was not in their eyes; rather it was either Jibril, peace be upon him, or another angel, who came between him (ﷺ) and them, so they did not see him. But there remains the discussion of whether preventing a subtle object from being seen is also contrary to custom; that is another matter, so let it be considered. Furthermore, what is related from Asma' is not explicit that the veil in the verse is the veil preventing sight, as is not hidden from one who considers carefully. This view is only needed if one takes into account the authentication by al-Hakim, or if one of the hadith scholars who is considered to have authenticated it explicitly stated its soundness. If not, the matter is easy.

al-Zamakhshari made what preceded a narration of what they said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is a deafness, and between us and you is a veil﴾, in the sense: We placed, according to their claim. Shaykh al-Islam did not accept this, because their aim in saying that was only to inform of what they believed concerning the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ), out of ignorance and disbelief, by attributing to them qualities that prevent belief and acceptance, such as the Qur'an being sorcery, poetry, and fables; and the state of the Prophet, Prayer and Peace be upon him, is to be judged by analogy with this; not an informing that there is something beyond what they perceived, [when] an obstacle from their side has come between them and its perception. There is no doubt that this meaning hardly suits the context. End.

It may be said: since the discourse is directed at enumerating their ugly deeds and rebuking them, suitability is beyond doubt. Yes, al-Zamakhshari's choice of this interpretation is not free from a Mu'tazili (i'tizali) subtlety, and I do not think it is hidden from you.

﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, meaning: not accompanied by the mention of any of their deities which they claim, as they used to say: "by Allah, and al-Lat" for example. This is true of mentioning Him, glorified is He, with the negation of the deities. ﴿Alone (wahdahu)﴾, according to al-Zamakhshari, is a verbal noun (masdar) of the triliteral root: one says waḥadahu yaḥiduhu waḥdan wa-ḥidah, like wa'adahu ya'iduhu wa'dan wa-'idah; it fills the place of a状 (hal, circumstantial accusative) meaning "singly". It was said: it is a masdar of awḥada with the augments dropped, and its original form is iyḥad. Sibawayh's view is that it is not a masdar but a noun placed in the position of a masdar, namely iyḥad placed in the position of the circumstantial accusative, and it is muwahhad (singled out).

The view of Yunus is that it is in the accusative of place (zarfiyyah), and the detailed discussion of the sayings on it is in al-Rif'dah, as we mentioned earlier. He mentioned that it is in the circumstantial sense (hal) when it occurs after a subject and object, as here, so it may be a circumstantial accusative of each of them, meaning: when you mention your Lord, unifying Him, or unifying Him in the mention.

﴿They turned away upon their backs (wallaw 'ala adbarihim)﴾, meaning they fled or recoiled. ﴿With aversion (nufuran)﴾: it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) governed by ﴿wallaw﴾ because their meanings are close. It is also permitted that it be an object of purpose, meaning: they turned away out of aversion and agitation; and that it be a circumstantial accusative, taking it as the plural of nafir, meaning: they turned away averse from that. The pronoun refers to the polytheists who do not believe in the Hereafter. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas something whose apparent meaning is that it refers to the devils, and this can hardly be correct from al-Hibr except with an interpretation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 47:

﴿We are most knowing of what they listen to when they listen to you﴾. That is, [they are] engaged in it, from idle talk, mockery and ridicule of you and of the Qur'an.

It is related that when he (ﷺ) would stand, there were two men from the clan of ʿAbd al-Dar on his right and two men from among them on his left, and they would clap, whistle, and mix their poetry in with his recitation.

It is also permissible for the bāʾ (bāʾ, the particle "with/by") to be causal (sababiyya) or to carry the meaning of lām (lām, the particle "for"), so that the meaning is: We are most knowing of what they listen to because of it, or for its sake, namely the mockery; and it is connected to yastamiʿūna ("they listen"). To keep it on its literal sense, [the meaning would be]: "Do they listen with their hearts or with the outward ears?" – [a question whose answer is] not apparent. The first bāʾ is connected to aʿlam ("most knowing"). The superlative form (afʿal al-tafḍīl) in matters of knowledge and ignorance takes bāʾ, while in other matters it takes lām, so one says: "He is most generous to the poor," for example. What is meant by God's being most knowing of that is the threat against them.

﴿when they listen to you﴾: this is an adverbial clause (ẓarf) governed by aʿlam, not an object (mafʿūl bihi). Its benefit, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is to emphasise the threat by informing that just as the aforementioned listening takes place on their part, knowledge is attached to it; not that the knowledge gained there comes from anyone. The intention is not to restrict God's knowledge to that time, and likewise His saying: ﴿when they are in secret conference﴾, but rather in terms of its connection to that which the secret conference is about, as indicated by the context of the verse.

The meaning: We are most knowing of what they listen to of what contains no good, of what you have heard, and of what they confer about among themselves. It is also permitted that the first [idhʾ] be an adverb for yastamiʿūna and the second an adverb for yatanājawna, and the meaning: We are most knowing of that by which listening occurs at the time of their listening, without delay, and of that by which conferring occurs at the time of their conferring. The first is more apparent. "Najwā" is a verbal noun in the nominative, functioning as a predicate, with what is found in "Zayd is just." It is also permissible to regard it as the plural of najiyy, like qatlā and qatīl, i.e.: when they are conferring privately.

﴿when the wrongdoers say﴾: this is a substitute (badal) for the second "idh" and an explanation of what they confer about; so it is other than what they listen to, not an object of a suppressed "udhkur" (remember), as has been said.

"The wrongdoers" (al-ẓālimūn) is an apparent noun placed in the position of a pronoun, to indicate that their conferring is a kind of wrongdoing. That is, each of them says to the others during their conferring: ﴿You follow only﴾, i.e., what you follow, if following occurs from you, supposing it: and it is permitted that the meaning be: what you follow with idle talk and mockery; ﴿but a man bewitched﴾, i.e., he has been bewitched and so has become mad, and this is like their saying: "He is only a madman." It was also said: he has been given magic by which he reaches, through its subtlety and fineness, what he brings and claims, so it has the meaning of their saying: "a sorcerer." Some have taken ﴿bewitched﴾ to mean "sorcerer," like mastūr meaning "one who conceals." It is related from Abu ʿUbayda that masḥūr means: he has been given magic, or one who has magic, i.e., a windpipe (ri'a). From this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

We find ourselves made to wait for an unseen matter, and we are nourished (nuskhar) with food and drink.

He meant: we are nourished. And the verse of Labid, or Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

So if you ask us what we are about, indeed we are sparrows from this bewitched (al-musahhar) human kind.
