They used this as a metaphor for his being a human who breathes, eats and drinks, and who does not differ from them in anything that would require following him, according to their corrupt opinion. What is contained in this of remoteness is not hidden, until Ibn Qutayba said: "I do not know what moved Abu ʿUbayda to this objectionable interpretation, when the predecessors explained it with clear meanings." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it does not fit His saying, the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 48:

﴿Look how they strike similitudes for you﴾ That is: they liken you (to things), saying at one time "a poet," at another "a sorcerer," and at another "a madman," while they know the opposite of this, ﴿so they have gone astray﴾ in all of that from the clear path of reason, ﴿and they cannot find a way﴾, that is, any path to a criticism that anyone could accept, so they stumble about, flounder, and bring forth what no one who hears it doubts to be false, or (they cannot find) the way of truth and right guidance. In this there is, of warning and of consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), what is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 49:

﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled particles, will we truly be resurrected as a new creation?"﴾ It is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to ﴿they struck﴾, and since he marvelled at their striking of comparisons, he conjoined to it another matter at which he also marvels. In al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, by al-Zamakhshari): "The more evident view is that this, up to the end of the three statements, is an explanation (tafsir) of ﴿they struck for you the comparisons﴾. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and strike for them an example﴾? Explaining it as ﴿mathalukà﴾ (they made you a comparison) is not apparent; rather the apparent reading is ﴿mathalū laka﴾ (they made a comparison for you). There is no doubt that the coherence of the discourse according to what we have mentioned is more complete, for when He mentioned their mockery of him, peace and blessings be upon him, and of the Qur'an, He marvelled at their mockery of its content, namely the resurrection, indicating that it is more deserving of marvel, because the intellect also points to it, but in a general way. As for explaining ﴿they struck for you the comparisons﴾ as ﴿mathalukà﴾, its rationale is that it is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they went astray﴾, since it is a door of going astray; or it is conjoined to an implied element indicated by: ﴿how they struck﴾, because its meaning is ﴿they made you a comparison﴾, and they said: 'a poet, a sorcerer, a madman,' and they said: ﴿When we are...﴾ etc." End of quotation.

It is not hidden that according to the explanation he has chosen, ﴿they said﴾ is also conjoined to ﴿they struck﴾ as an explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf tafsiri), but the evident particle in this case is then the فاء (fa', the particle of consequence), and according to what we have mentioned it does not need the forced conjunction to an implied element; the connection to it is no weaker than the connection he mentioned. Its conjunction to ﴿so they went astray﴾ is not good, because it does not appear to be included with it within the scope of the فاء. The objection to the explanation as ﴿mathalukà﴾, that they did not make a comparison of him, peace be upon him, with a poet or a sorcer for instance, but rather said at times one thing and at other times another, and also that the apparent wording should have been ﴿fīka﴾ (about you) instead of ﴿laka﴾ (for you), is nothing of substance; because what they mentioned was by way of comparison, to rebuke him, peace and blessings be upon him, and to show their inability to oppose him, and ﴿laka﴾ is more apparent than ﴿fīka﴾, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, is the one to whom the comparison is made. I say: Consider whether there is any obstacle to conjoining ﴿they say﴾ to ﴿the wrongdoers say﴾, and making this saying also one of the things they confide in one another and sometimes announce openly; this does not prevent this construction, and likewise the difference between the two conjoined elements, one in the past tense and one in the present tense, does not prevent the conjunction. Yes, it needs a subtle point, and I do not think it is hidden, so reflect upon it.

Al-Rufat (الرفات, crumbled particles) is what has broken and decayed of anything. The pattern fuʿal is common for everything that has been shattered and scattered, such as duqaq (fine powder) and futat (crumbs).

Ibn Jarir and others related from Mujahid that it is dust, and this is the view of al-Farra'. Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is dust (ghubar), and al-Mubarrad said: it is every thing that is pounded, with much emphasis on its pounding. These are close views. The hamza is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari), conveying the utmost remoteness and rejection of resurrection after the state has come to this condition, as if they said: "That will never happen at all."

Its source is that between the freshness and suppleness of the living, which requires connection, and which requires life, and between the dryness of the decayed (al-rami), which requires dispersal, and which requires the absence of life, there is a contradiction. "Idha" (إذا, when) here, as in al-Durr al-Masun (Durr al-Masun, by al-Samin al-Halabi), is purely a temporal adverb, and the element governing it is what is indicated by what precedes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will we truly be resurrected?﴾ The word إنّا (inna, "truly") is not the governor of the adverb; because إنّ (inna) takes precedence at the beginning, so what follows it does not govern what precedes it, and likewise the interrogative, even if it is an emphasis; with the interrogative being on the verb, which is preferable, namely نُبْعَث (nubʿath, "we are resurrected") or نُعاد (nuʿād, "we are returned"), and this is the focus of the denial. Restricting it to the stated time is to strengthen the denial of resurrection by directing it at a state contrary to it; otherwise the apparent state of them is that they deny revival after death, even if the body remains in its condition.

It is permitted that the إذا be conditional (شرطية), with an implied answer, meaning: "we are resurrected" or something similar, and that is what governs it. It was said: the conditional is the protasis, and the meaning is: "Will we be resurrected when we had been crumbled particles at a time?" This is a view of some grammarians, not well-known and not relied upon. The sentence being embellished with إنّ and the lam is for emphasizing the denial, not for denying the emphasis as might be suspected from the apparent wording. The basis of their denial is not that they are firmly established in being resurrected in actuality while in the state of being bones and crumbled particles, as might appear from the apparent nominal sentence; rather it is that they are in a state of potential for that and in readiness for it, and its return is to denial of resurrection after that state. In this there is an indication of their extreme excess in disbelief and their persistence in error beyond which there is no further degree, as stated by some of the verifying scholars (muḥaqqiqīn).

﴿A new creation﴾ is in the accusative governed by مبعوثين (mabʿūthīn, "resurrected"), either as an absolute object (مفعول مطلق) from a verb not of the same verbal form, or as a circumstantial state (حال), on the basis that الخلق (khalq, "creation") here means the created thing (al-makhlūq). It is singular because the singular is equal to the plural in the verbal noun, even if what is meant by it is the form of the passive participle, meaning "created ones."

[صفحة 91]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 50:

﴿Say﴾: as a reply to them and to bring closer what they found unlikely.

﴿Be stones or iron﴾: He, glorified is He, returned His saying ﴿be﴾ to their saying "we are" (kunna), so it is of the kind of mushakalah (correspondence in form) and muqabalah (opposition) by genus. The meaning of the imperative, as has been said, is contempt (al-istihanah, belittling), as in the words of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Throw down what you are throwing down﴾. The author of al-Idah (Sharh al-Talkhis by al-Qazwini, i.e., al-Idah fi 'Ulum al-Balaghah) made it an imperative of humiliation (amr ihanah), and al-Fadil al-Tibi made it an imperative of subjugation (amr taskhir), as in His, exalted is He, words: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾. However, he said: it is on the supposition (ala al-farad). In al-Kashf it is said that this is not apparent. And if it were taken as of the kind of "be so-and-so" (kun fulanan) in the sense of "you are so-and-so", using the imperative in the sense of a declarative statement, i.e., "you are stones and not bones, and yet you will certainly be resurrected," it would have been a sound view. Al-Shihab discussed it, saying: how can it be said "you are stones" as a declarative statement when it does not correspond to reality? So there must be an intention of humiliation and indifference, and the imperative must be considered a metaphor for the declarative, and the declarative is a hypothetical declarative, and there is nothing in it that indicates the supposition, even with the two conditional forms. So it is of what is not hidden in its remoteness, and it is no closer than what they found unlikely. Therefore the correct view is that it is for humiliation, as al-Idah's author inclined to, so reflect.

The hijarah (stones) is the plural of hajar, like ahjar, and it is well known. Likewise al-hadid (iron), which is a singular noun whose plural is hada'id and hadidat.

The apparent meaning is that what is intended is: "be of these two kinds."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 51:

﴿Or a creation﴾, i.e., another created thing, ﴿of what seems great in your breasts﴾, i.e., of what you consider far-fetched that it could receive life, since it is the furthest thing from life. Its specification is left to you, for Allah the Exalted is not incapable of reviving you, since bodies are equal in receiving accidents (a'rad). So how much more so when you are decayed bones, and they were previously described as being alive; and a thing is more acceptable to what is familiar in it than to what is not. Mujahid said: "What seems great" refers to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains.

Ibn Jarir and a group related from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jubayr that they said: "What seems great in their breasts" is death, for there is nothing greater in the self of the son of Adam than death. The meaning is: even if you were embodied from the very substance of death, He would restore you, let alone a origin that does not oppose life if it does not necessitate it. In this there is a fine hyperbole, though the wording is not apparent in it. ﴿So they will say﴾ to you: ﴿"Who will restore us?"﴾ despite the distance and remoteness between us and restoration. ﴿Say﴾ to them, to establish the truth, remove the sense of far-fetchedness, and guide them to the method of reasoning: ﴿"He who originated you"﴾, i.e., the Mighty, Powerful One who brought you into being ﴿the first time﴾ without any model to follow or pattern to imitate, when you were dust that had not smelled the fragrance of life. Is not He who is capable of that also capable of bestowing life upon decayed bones and returning them to their familiar state? Indeed, He, glory be to Him, is over all things Powerful. The relative pronoun is the subject, whose predicate is the omitted "will restore you," indicated by the question; or it is the agent of a verb implied; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, according to the differing views on the first, as detailed in its proper place.

﴿First time﴾ is an adverbial complement of "originated you." ﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾, i.e., they will move them toward you mockingly, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, and he cited the poet's verse:

"Do you shake your head at me on the day of boasting, while you see horses upon which are lions, fierce?"

And similar is the saying of another:

"He raised his head toward me and looked up, as if he sought something he hoped for."

In the Qamus: "Nagha" (nagh'a) in the forms of nasara and daraba: nagdan, nugudan, naghadanan, and naghdan (with both vowels) means: he moved and was agitated, like anghada; and "harraka" like anghada. Al-Farra' explained inghad as moving the head up and down. Abu al-Haytham said: whoever is informed of something and shakes his head in denial of it has shaken his head; so it is as if they will shake their heads in denial. ﴿And they will say﴾ mockingly: ﴿"When is it?"﴾, i.e., what you have mentioned of restoration. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the return or the resurrection understood from the discourse. ﴿Say﴾ to them: ﴿"It may be that it is near"﴾, for what is certain to come is near. He did not specify its time, because it is among the unseen matters that none knows except Allah the Exalted, and He does not inform anyone of them. It was also said: its nearness is because what remains of the life of this world is less than what has passed of it. The accusative of ﴿near﴾ is as the predicate of the defective kana, whose subject is a pronoun referring to what has been indicated. It is also permissible that it be accusative as an adverb of time, the original being "a near time," so the modified noun was omitted and its adjective placed in its stead, taking its accusative case; and on this view, kana is complete with that pronoun as its agent, i.e., "it may be that this occurs at a near time." And it is permissible that "that" be in the position of an accusative verbal noun that serves as the predicate of 'asa, with its subject a pronoun referring to what the subject of yakun refers to. It is also permissible that it be nominative with 'asa, which is then complete with no predicate; i.e., "it may be its occurrence, or at a near time."

It was objected that 'asa indicates proximity, so it would be as if it were said: "It has come near to being near," which has no benefit. It was answered that Najm al-A'immah did not establish the meaning of proximity in 'asa, neither by its lexical form nor by usage; and the mention of "near" after it in the verse supports this, so there is no need to say it has been stripped of that meaning. The meaning is: its occurrence is hoped for and expected to be near.

[p. 93]

﴿Yawma yad'ukum﴾ (on the Day He calls you) is in the accusative, governed by a suppressed verb, meaning "remember," or it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿qariban﴾ (soon), taking it as an adverb of time (zarf), or it is dependent on ﴿tastajibuna﴾ (you will respond), or on ﴿tub'athuna﴾ (you will be raised), which is suppressed, or on the implicit pronoun of the verbal noun in ﴿yakunu﴾ (it may be) or ʿasā (perhaps), referring to "the return," for example. This follows the view of the Kufan grammarians, who permit the verbal noun's pronoun to govern, as in the line of poetry:

"And war is nothing but what you have known and tasted, and he is not about it a talk that is concealed."

Making it a substitute for the implicit pronoun as a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion) is possible, and it is not put in the nominative, because when it is attached to a clause of this kind it may be built on the fatha. Claiming that its being built is apparent is a stubborn assertion (mukabara). It has been said that the calling (du'a') is a metaphor (majaz) for the resurrection (al-ba'th), and likewise the responding (istijaba) in His words, ﴿fa-tastajibuna﴾ (then you will respond), is a metaphor for rising up (al-inbi'ath), meaning: on the day He raises you up, you will rise. So there is no calling and no responding. This is similar to His words, (Be, and it is), in that there is no address and no one addressed, according to the well-known view. The calling and responding are used figuratively for that, to draw attention to speed and ease, because saying "Stand up, O so-and-so" is a command that involves no delay, and mere summoning is not like the act of bringing into existence, as far as we are concerned. Also, the intended meaning is bringing them to the reckoning and the recompense, for a master's calling of his slave is only for his service, or for examining his affair. The first is ruled out, since the Hereafter contains no obligation, so the second is determined.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) and Abu Hayyan said: "He calls you" with the call that makes you hear it, which is the last blast, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿On the Day when the caller calls from a near place﴾ (50:41), and so on. It is said that Israfil, peace be upon him, (and in another report Jibril, peace be upon him) calls upon the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis: "O bodies that have decayed, O bones that have crumbled, O scattered parts, return as you were."

Abu Dawud and Ibn Hibban narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed you will be called on the Day of Resurrection by your names and the names of your fathers, so beautify your names."

Perhaps this is at the time of calling to the reckoning, which is after the resurrection from the graves. Many have limited themselves to the earlier figurative usage, and it was said that in it there is an indication of the impossibility of taking the words literally, because taking them literally would require addressing inanimate matter, namely the scattered parts. And if it were not impossible to intend the literal meaning, that would be a metonymy (kinayah) for the resurrection and rising, not a metaphor. The one who permits the literal intention says: the calling is by the creative command (al-amr al-takwini), which may be directed at the non-existent. A group has said this about the word "Be," and they did not use figurative language in that. As for the claim that if the literal meaning were not impossible it would be a metonymy and not a metaphor, that is a minor matter, as is not hidden. So reflect.

﴿Bi-hamdihi﴾ (with His praise) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the addressees, who are the disbelievers, as is apparent. The ba' is for accompaniment (mulabasa). That is: "you will respond, being accompanied by His praise," i.e., praising Him, exalted is He, for the perfection of His power. It was also said: the meaning is acknowledging that praise belongs to Him for the blessings, and you do not deny that, because the knowledge there is necessary.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others narrated from Ibn Jarir that he said: They will come out of their graves saying: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You." There is no distance in such a statement coming from the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection, even if it does not benefit him. Al-Zamakhshari took that in a figurative sense, the intended meaning being exaggeration of their submission to the resurrection, like your saying to someone you command to ride something that is hard on him, so he hesitates and refuses: "You will ride it while you are praising and thankful." He means: you are compelled to it and forced by force, until you become gentle, like one who is willing and desires it and praises it. So it is as if it were said: "Submitting to His raising as those who praise Him submit." The attachment of the prepositional phrase to ﴿yad'ukum﴾ (calls you) is nothing. It is narrated from al-Tabari that ﴿bi-hamdihi﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the two coordinated items, like its insertion between the particle inna and its predicate in the line of poetry:

"Indeed, by the praise of Allah, I have not worn a garment of wickedness, nor do I veil myself with treachery."

The statement would be in the manner of your saying to a man whom you have defeated in a matter: "You have erred, praise be to Allah, exalted is He."

So it is as if the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "It may be that the resurrection is near, on the day you are called, and you will rise, contrary to what you believe today, and that is by the praise of Allah, glorified is He, for the truthfulness of my report."

Its summary: it will be contrary to your belief, and praise belongs to Allah, exalted is He. And it is not hidden that this is a far-fetched meaning that is hardly understood from the speech, and we are in no need of committing to it, and praise belongs to Allah. It was said: the address is to the believers, and the address to the disbelievers ends at His words, ﴿qariban﴾ (soon), so they respond praising Him, glorified is He, for His kindness to them and His granting them success in believing in the resurrection.

[p. 94]

al-Tirmidhi, al-Tabarani and others narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no fear for the people of 'There is no god but Allah' in their graves, nor at their gathering. As if I see the people of 'There is no god but Allah' shaking the dust from their heads and saying: 'Praise belongs to Allah, who has removed grief from us.'"

In another report from Anas, traced to the Prophet: "There is no fear for the people of 'There is no god but Allah' at death, nor in the graves, nor at the assembly. As if I see the people of 'There is no god but Allah' having come out of their graves, shaking the dust from their heads, saying: 'Praise belongs to Allah, who has removed grief from us.'"

It was said: the address is to both groups, and all of them say what was narrated from Ibn Jubayr.

﴿Wa-tazunnuna﴾ (and you will think): the apparent view is that it is coordinated with (tastajibuna, you will respond), and al-Hufi and others took this view. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is with a suppressed subject, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: "and you think" ﴿in labithtum﴾ (that you remained) — i.e., that you did not remain in the graves — ﴿illa qalilan﴾ (except a little), like the one who passed by a village, or that you did not remain in the world, as many narrated from Qatadah. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "they regard as little their remaining between the two blasts," for the punishment is lifted from them during that interval; therefore they say: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ (36:52). It was said: they regard as little their remaining in the place of gathering on the Day of Resurrection, since the outcome of their affair is entry into the Fire. This is extremely far-fetched, as is not hidden. The verb "to think" (zann) may be understood in its ordinary sense, and it may be taken to mean certainty (yaqin). It is then suspended from operating because of the negating "in" (in), and few who mention the particles of suspension have mentioned it, as Abu Hayyan said. The accusative of ﴿qalilan﴾ (a little) is taken as an adjective of a suppressed noun of time, meaning: "except a little time." It was also permitted that it be an adjective of a suppressed verbal noun, meaning: "a little remaining." The verb's indication of its verbal noun is a strong indication.

﴿And say to My servants﴾, meaning the believers. The idafah (possessive construction) here is for the honouring of the one who is added to. ﴿They should say﴾ when they engage in dialogue with the polytheists ﴿that which﴾, meaning the word or expression ﴿which is best﴾, and they should not be harsh with them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best﴾ (29:46). The object of the imperative verb (fi'l al-amr, the command form) is omitted; the meaning is: "Say to them: Speak what is best, and they will say that." So yaqulu is jussive because it is the response to the command. This is the view of al-Akhfash. Since those addressed are the believers, who hasten to carry out the command of God and the command of His Messenger ﷺ as soon as they are told, there is no doubt about this jussive form.

Al-Zajjaj said: yaqulu is the object of the speech, and it is jussive by means of an omitted lam of command, meaning: "Say to them: let them say what is best," and so on. Al-Mazini said: it is also the object of the speech, except that it is a mudari' (imperfect verb) that is mabni (indeclinable), because it occupies the position of the indeclinable form, which is the imperative verb. The meaning is: "Say to My servants: Speak what is best." This, as you see, is [weak]. The object of yaqulu is "allati" (that which). If it is intended as a word, it is taken in its general meaning, which includes speech.

﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾, meaning he corrupts and stirs up evil between the believers and the polytheists through harshness. So perhaps that leads to the hardening of enmity and the growth of corruption. Thus the sentence gives the reason for the preceding command. Talha recited yanzigh with a kasra on the zay. Abu Hatim said: it may be a dialect form, and the recitation is with a fatha. The author of al-Lawami' said: the fatha and the kasra are two dialectal forms, like yamnahu and yamnihu.

﴿Indeed, Satan has always been﴾ from of old ﴿to man an open enemy﴾, clearly hostile. So it is from abana, which is intransitive, and the sentence gives the reason for what was mentioned before: that Satan incites discord among them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 54:

﴿Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you﴾ by granting you success in faith, ﴿or if He wills, He will punish you﴾ by causing you to die in disbelief. This is the explanation of "[say] that which is best" (ahsan, the most excellent manner of speech). The two clauses are a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between them, and the address in it is to the polytheists. It is as if it were said: Say to them this statement and what resembles it, and make their affair dependent upon the will of God, the Exalted, and do not declare outright that they are among the people of the Fire; for that would incite them to evil, and moreover the final outcome is unknown and none knows it but Him, the Exalted, so perhaps He will guide them to faith. The apparent meaning is that "aw" (or) here is for real separation (al-infisal al-haqiqi).

Page 95

Al-Kirmani said: it is for transition (al-idrab); for this reason "in" (if) was repeated with it. Ibn al-Anbari said: "aw" entered here to indicate the breadth of both options with God, the Exalted. It is also called the permissive (al-mubihah), like the one in their saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," for they mean: "We have granted you latitude in the matter." And this, as you see, is [far-fetched].

﴿And We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾, i.e., one entrusted with and delegated with their affair, compelling them to Islam and forcing them to it. ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾. So be gentle with them, command your companions to be gentle with them, bear their harm, and abandon confrontation with them. This was before the revelation of the verse of the sword.

Your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth, and their apparent and hidden states. So He chooses from among them, for His prophethood and guardianship (wilayah), whomever He wills, of those whom His wisdom sees as fit for that. This is a rebuttal of them when they said: "It is far-fetched that the orphan of Ibn Abi Talib should be a prophet, and that the destitute and hungry ones, such as Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab and others, should be his companions, rather than that this should be [granted] to the great and the chieftains."

He mentioned "whoever is in the heavens" to refute their saying, "Why were the angels not sent down to us?" and He mentioned "whoever is on the earth" to refute their saying: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?" So the specifying of these two groups by mention, and their connection to "knows best" (a'lam), does not indicate that His knowledge is restricted to what has been mentioned. What Abu 'Ali said, that the prepositional phrase is connected to a verb "knows" (ʿalima) understood and omitted, and that it cannot be connected to a'lam because that would imply that He, glorified is He, is not most knowing of other than that, arises from lack of knowledge of what we have mentioned. Moreover, Abu Hayyan denied that ʿalima takes a complement with the particle bi (in), and it only takes a single object directly in a context like this.

"And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others" [Qur'an 17:55], by the psychological virtues, the holy qualities, and the sending down of the heavenly books, not by abundance of wealth and followers. "And We gave David the Psalms" [Qur'an 17:55] is an explanation of the aspect in which he was preferred, peace be upon him: that it is by his being given the Psalms, not by his being given kingship and rule. In it is also an indication of the preference of our Prophet (ﷺ). For his being the seal of the prophets, and his community being the best of communities, is among what the Psalms contained. Allah, glorified is He, has informed of this in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: "And We have certainly written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants" [Qur'an 21:105]. He means Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community.

Some have stated that this is from the category of allusion (talmih), like the story of al-Mansur, who had promised al-Hudhali a sum of money but forgot it. When they performed the pilgrimage and came to Medina, one day while he was walking beside him, [al-Hudhali] said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is the house of 'Atika, about which al-Ahwas says: 'O house of 'Atika, the one I court in love-verse.'" [Al-Mansur] understood his purpose from what he said, and did not ask him, and knew that he was pointing to his saying in this qasida:

"I see you do what you say, while some of them are smooth-tongued, saying what they do not do."

So [al-Mansur] fulfilled his promise. The word Zabur (Psalms), originally, is a descriptive form in the sense of the object (maf'ul), like halub (milked), or a verbal noun like qabul (acceptance). Indeed this pattern is rare among verbal nouns, and the more common is with the first letter damma (fa' with a damma), and Hamza recited it so. Some have made it, on this reading, a plural of zibr (with a kasra on the zay), in the sense of maznur (written), then it was made a proper name for the particular book, and there is nothing of rulings in it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "The Zabur is praise of Allah, mighty and majestic, supplication and glorification." Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir also related from Qatada, who said: "We used to be told that the Zabur is supplication taught to David, peace be upon him, and praise and glorification of Allah, mighty and majestic; in it there is no lawful nor unlawful, no obligations nor prescribed punishments." What some narrations indicate, however, is that it includes some prohibitions and commands.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated that it is written in it: "Indeed I am Allah; there is no god but I, the King of kings. The hearts of kings are in My hand. Whenever a people are upon obedience, I make the kings a mercy upon them; and whenever a people are upon disobedience, I make the kings a punishment upon them. So do not occupy yourselves with cursing the kings, but turn to Me in repentance, and I will incline their hearts toward you."

The psalms (mazamir) from which commands and prohibitions can be understood are numerous in it, as will not be hidden from one who has seen it. Along with this, the difference between it and the Torah is evident. The entry of the definite article (al) on it in some verses is to indicate the origin, and that does not contradict its being a proper name, as in al-Abbas and al-Fadl.

It has also been permitted that it be an indefinite common noun, not a proper name, and it was made indefinite to convey that it is a part of the divine books or of books in general. There is also no difficulty in the entry of al on it, that is: "We gave him a zabur from among the zubur (scriptures)." It is also permitted that it be specific to the book of David, peace be upon him, and not a proper name, but rather from the dominance of a generic noun. It is like the Qur'an, which is applied to the whole and to its parts. The indication of indefiniteness for partiality was already mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: (laylan, "by night") [Qur'an 17:1]. So it is permitted that what is meant here is: "We gave him a part of the Zabur in which is mention of him (ﷺ)."

This is the connection of the verses with what preceded, according to this interpretation, as in al-Kashshaf: when He, exalted is He, guided His Prophet (ﷺ) to respond to the disbelievers, with seriousness in face of their mockery and composure in face of their levity, so that it would be more enraging to them and more choking to their throats, He guided him to have his companions also act accordingly and to follow his example. He gave as the reason for this what has been objected to, that Satan, through his incitement, drives to harshness. So it is incumbent upon the wise and prudent person not to be deceived by his whisperings, how so, when it has become clear to him that he is a manifest enemy.

His saying, exalted is He: "And We did not send you as a guardian over them" [Qur'an 17:54] is connected to all that preceded from His saying: "Say: Be [stones or iron]" [Qur'an 17:50], which includes disputing with them in the manner that is best, and "And say to My servants" [Qur'an 17:53], which includes urging them to it, up to His saying, glorified is He: "Or if He wills, He will punish you" [Qur'an 17:54], and His saying, mighty and majestic is He: "And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth" [Qur'an 17:55] is a continuation of "If you follow none but a man bewitched" [Qur'an 17:47]. For they attacked him, and may he be far above it, at times by saying he is a poet, a sorcerer, and a madman, and at other times by such things as "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?" [Qur'an 43:31] and "If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it" [Qur'an 46:11]. The first was answered with what was answered, and the second was answered by His saying, glorified is He: "Your Lord knows best."

It is also permitted that the address in His saying, exalted is He: "Your Lord knows best [about you]" and so on, is to the believers. This is related from al-Kalbi. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related the first from Ibn Jurayj. The meaning is that if He, exalted is He, wills, He will have mercy on you, O believers, in this world, by saving you from the disbelievers and granting you victory over them; or if He wills, He will punish you by giving them power over you. By "that which is best" is meant good disputation. So it is as if He, exalted is He, when He mentioned the certain argument regarding the truth of the Return, commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to say to the believers: "When you want to present the argument to those who oppose you, mention the proofs in the best way, which is that it should not be mixed with insult and abuse, for if it were mixed with it, it is not unlikely that it would be met with its like, so anger would increase and evil would be stirred up, and the purpose would not be achieved." He, glorified is He, indicated this by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: "Indeed, Satan..." etc. The pronoun in "between them" refers either to the disbelievers, or to both groups. It is related that the polytheists were excessive in harming the believers, so they complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this was revealed. It has also been said: a man cursed 'Umar, and he (may Allah be pleased with him) intended to retaliate, so Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to pardon. In al-Kashshaf it is said: on these two statements, "the word which is best" is like: "Allah guides you," and it is not interpreted as "Your Lord knows best about you."

His saying, glorified is He: "Indeed, Satan incites [discord] among them" [Qur'an 17:53] is a justification for the command to speak in the best manner, on the ground that harshness is an act of Satan. The address in His saying, exalted is He: "Your Lord knows best about you" is to the believers. In it is an exhortation to tolerance, meaning: "So be tolerant with them, for your Lord knows best about you and what is suitable for you of commands. If He wills, He will have mercy on you by your acceptance of His commands and prohibitions; or if He wills, He will punish you by your refusal; or if He wills, He will have mercy on you through gentleness and mutual compassion, for that is the cause of safety from the harm of the disbelievers; or if He wills, He will punish you by your harshness at an inappropriate time." And "We did not send you as a guardian over them" means: these believers, who are your followers, are more deserving, and more fitting, not to be a guardian over them. Then he said: "The first is more consistent with the composition of the verse. Yet the implication of 'Your Lord knows best about you' for the exhortation to what has been established is a forced reading, and so on."

It has also been said: the intended "My servants" are the disbelievers. Since the purpose of the verses is invitation (da'wah), it is not unlikely that they are referred to thus, so that this becomes a cause of attracting their hearts and inclining their natures toward accepting the true religion. So it is as if it were said: "Say, O Muhammad, to My servants who have acknowledged that they are My servants: let them say that which is best, which is the true word that indicates monotheism and the affirmation of the power to resurrect. Inform them that it does not befit them to persist in the false doctrine out of zealous attachment to their forefathers, for that is from Satan, who is a manifest enemy to man, so one should not heed his words." By the command to speak is meant the command to believe that, and speech is mentioned because it is the evident indication of belief. Then He, glorified is He, said to them: "Your Lord knows best about you. If He wills, He will have mercy on you" by guidance, "or if He wills, He will punish you" by causing you to die in disbelief. Except that this will is hidden from you, so strive yourselves in seeking the true religion, and do not persist in falsehood, lest you become deprived of eternal felicities and everlasting goods. Then He, glorified is He, said: "And We did not send you as a guardian over them," that is: do not make the matter hard for them, nor be severe to them in speech. The aim of all this is to show gentleness and kindness toward them when calling them, for that is closer to achieving the aim. Then He, exalted is He, generalized His knowledge by His saying: "Your Lord knows best," and so on. On this interpretation, what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and what Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Sirin, regarding the explanation of "that which is best" as "there is no god but Allah," is fitting. Ibn 'Atiyya related this from a group of scholars, then said: "It follows from this that by 'My servants' is meant all of creation, for all of them are called to the saying 'there is no god but Allah.' Then His saying, glorified is He: 'Indeed, Satan incites among them' would not fit, except in the sense that he incites within them and in their midst, and the incitement is explained as whispering and causing weariness." It is not hidden that this is objectionable. And the evidence mentioned does not hold unless there is no point to the specification, and here the point is evident, and his saying, exalted is He:

[Page 98]

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 17, verse 56:

﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides Him﴾, etc. This is like an argument for the truth of what he (the Prophet) called them to, namely tawhid (the oneness of God), and it connects with what came before, according to what we mentioned at first, which I do not think is hidden. *Al-zaʿm* (claim), with the letter *zay* having three vowel options, is close to *al-zann* (supposition). It is said that it is a statement whose truth is doubtful, and it is used in the sense of lying, to the extent that Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Every occurrence of *zaʿama* (claimed) in the Qur'an means a lie." It is also sometimes used for a firmly established statement and a truth about which there is no doubt.

Muslim transmitted from the hadith of Anas that "a man from the desert dwellers, whose name was Dimam ibn Thaʿlaba, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, your messenger came to us and claimed (*fa-zaʿama*) that you claim (*tazʿumu*) that Allah the Exalted sent you.' He said: 'He spoke the truth...' the hadith."

The Prophet's (ﷺ) confirmation of him, together with his use of *zaʿama* and *tazʿumu*, is evidence for what we have said.

It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Jibril (peace be upon him) claimed (*zaʿama*) such-and-such." Sibawayh, the imam of the Arabic language, used the expression very often in his book, saying: "Al-Khalil claimed (*zaʿama al-Khalil*), Abu al-Khattab claimed (*zaʿama Abu al-Khattab*)," meaning by this a firmly established statement. Groups of the people of lexicography and others have transmitted this. Abu ʿUmar al-Zahid, in his commentary on *al-Fasih*, transmitted it from his teacher Abu al-ʿAbbas Thaʿlab, from the scholars of language among the Kufans and the Basrans.

It is a verb that takes two objects. Both objects (or what stands in their place) are omitted here, and omission is permissible. The disagreement concerns the omission of one of them. The apparent meaning is that the relative pronoun (*alladhina*, "those") refers to everyone who was worshipped besides Allah, the Glorified, among rational beings.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani, and a group transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "There was a group of humans who worshipped a group of jinn. Then the group of jinn accepted Islam, while the humans held fast to their worship. So this verse was revealed." These humans were Arabs, as stated explicitly in the narration of al-Bayhaqi and others from him. In another narration, it is explicitly stated that they were from Khuza'a. In the narration of Ibn Jarir, he said:

"Some Arab tribes worshipped a category of angels called the jinn, and they said they were the daughters of Allah, the Glorified. Then the verse was revealed."

From Ibn ʿAbbas: it was revealed concerning those who associated partners with Allah the Exalted, who worshipped ʿIsa (Jesus), his mother, ʿUzayr (Ezra), the sun, the moon, and the stars.

According to this, there is, as al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) states, *taghlib* (the dominance of the rational over the non-rational in expression). If it is valid to include the sun, the moon, and the stars by way of *taghlib*, on the basis that they are not of those endowed with knowledge, then all that was worshipped falsely, the idols, should also be included, and the *taghlib* employed. It has been objected that what will come shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills, concerning seeking the means (*al-wasila*), hoping for mercy, and fearing punishment, supports the intention of rational beings such as ʿIsa and ʿUzayr (peace be upon them both), on the basis that idols cannot be described with these qualities. Employing *taghlib* there too is very much contrary to the apparent meaning.

*Al-du'a'* (calling/supplication) is like *al-nida'* (calling out), but *al-nida'* may be said when one says "ya" or "aya" or similar, without the name being added to it, whereas *al-du'a'* is hardly said except when the name accompanies it, as in "ya Fulan" (O so-and-so). Each of them may be used in the place of the other.

The meaning is: call upon them to remove the harm, which is more important and more significant than bringing benefit, and directing the heart toward the one who removes it is more perfect and complete.

﴿So they have no power﴾, meaning they are not able by themselves ﴿to remove the harm from you﴾, such as sickness, poverty, drought, and other things, ﴿nor to transfer it﴾, meaning nor to move it from you to others who did not worship them, or nor to change it into another kind. Whoever does not have power over these things does not deserve worship, since the condition for deserving worship is complete and perfect power to repel harm and bring benefit. This is not the case when that power is bestowed by another.

It seems that the intention of negating their possession of these things is the negation of their complete and perfect power over them. That the power of the false deities is bestowed by Allah the Exalted is accepted by the unbelievers, because they do not deny that it is created by Allah the Exalted with all its attributes, and that Allah the Glorified is more powerful and more perfect in attributes than they are. By this the argument is completed and the opponents are silenced. Otherwise, the negation of the power of such beings as jinn and angels, who were worshipped besides Allah the Exalted, absolutely, to remove harm, is not something whose proof is evident. For if it is said that the proof is that we see the unbelievers humbling themselves before them and their request is not granted, it is countered that we also see Muslims humbling themselves before Allah the Exalted and their request is not granted. It may also be said that the intention is the negation of their power over that at all, and it is argued for by the proof of al-Ashʿari concerning the ultimate attribution of all possible things to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, from the beginning.

Some have interpreted *al-darr* (harm) here as drought, on the basis of what is reported: that the polytheists were struck by a severe drought, in which they ate dogs and carrion, and so they sought help from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he might pray for them, and then this was revealed. You know that this does not necessitate restricting the verse to that. This narration has been used as evidence that the negation of capability entirely from their deities was then accepted by them; otherwise they would not have abandoned them and sought help from the Prophet (ﷺ) to pray for them. But there is consideration in this, so reflect and ponder.

[Page 99]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 57:

﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ means: those deities whom they call upon and name as gods, or whom they call upon and invoke to remove harm from them. ﴿seek﴾ means they strive earnestly to seek for themselves ﴿the means of access﴾ to ﴿their Lord﴾, the Lord and Owner of their affairs, namely nearness through obedience and worship. So the pronoun in ﴿call upon﴾ refers to the polytheists, and the pronoun in ﴿seek﴾ refers to those who are indicated (by the demonstrative). Ibn Fawrak said: both pronouns refer to those who are indicated, and what is meant by them is the prophets who were worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted. The object of ﴿call upon﴾ is omitted, meaning: they call people to the truth, or they call upon Allah, glorified is He, and humble themselves before Him, may He be exalted. On this view, it is not necessary that what is meant by them be the prophets, peace be upon them, as is not hidden. And this is, as you see, (weak).

Ibn Mas'ud and Qatada read ﴿tad'una﴾ with the letter ta' (second person), Zayd ibn Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) read ﴿yad'una﴾ with the letter ya' (third person) in the passive form, and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read ﴿ila Rabbika﴾ with the second person kaf (addressing the Prophet). The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) is a subject (mubtada'), the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is an attribute (na't) or an explanatory apposition (bayan), and the predicate (khabar) is the clause ﴿yabtaghuna﴾. Alternatively, the relative pronoun itself is the predicate, and ﴿yabtaghuna﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) or a substitute (badal) for the relative clause (sila).

As for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾, there are several grammatical possibilities. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned two. The first is that ﴿ayyu﴾ is a relative pronoun serving as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in ﴿yabtaghuna﴾, a partial substitute (badal ba'd min kull), and it is either declinable (mu'rab) or indeclinable (mabni) according to the two opinions. The meaning is: those deities, whoever is closer to them seeks the means of access to Allah, the Exalted, through obedience to Him, so how much more so the one who is more distant. There is nothing in this except the omission of the beginning of the relative clause (sadr al-sila), and the estimated form is: "whichever of them is closer." This is not objectionable. And this does not contradict the plural of (yarjuna wa yakhafuna) that follows, because what was mentioned is not restricted to the closest, or because the closest is more than one. The second is that ﴿ayyu﴾ is interrogative, and it is the subject, and ﴿aqrabu﴾ is its predicate, and the clause is in the position of a accusative (nasb) after ﴿yabtaghuna﴾, and it has been made to include the meaning of ﴿yahrisuna﴾ (they eagerly strive). It is as if it were said: they eagerly strive which of them will be closer to Allah, the Exalted, by obedience and increase in good and righteousness. It was said: the implicit meaning (tadmin) was taken into account so that the suspension (ta'liq) would be valid, for it is specific to verbs of the heart, contrary to the view of Yunus. Al-Tibi said: it is necessary to estimate a preposition, because ﴿harasa﴾ takes ﴿ala﴾, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿if you are eager for their guidance﴾, and it is necessary to interpret the interrogative construction (inshā') by saying: they eagerly strive for that about which it is said "which of them is closer to Allah, the Exalted, by means of it, by obedience," and then the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿to their Lord﴾ would be connected to ﴿aqrabu﴾, and this, as you see, (is weak).

The author of al-Kashshaf, in verifying this view, said: when the objectives are shared, they naturally require hastening towards them, and this is itself eagerness or what is not separate from it. So it is appropriate that the seeking be implicitly understood to carry the meaning of eagerness, especially since after it there is an interrogative which does not fit its place without this implicit meaning. For your saying: "which of them is closer to so-and-so by such-and-such" is a question about distinguishing one of them from the rest by that through which he draws near, with an extra excellence, while they are equal in the basic nearness. So when it comes as a new independent clause (isti'naf) after a verb that is suitable to be its cause, it is necessary to estimate that. For when you say: "these people eagerly strive for guidance," it is a statement that runs on its apparent meaning, but when you say: "these people eagerly strive which of them will be more guided," it informs that their eagerness for that guidance is with each of them contending with the others in it, so it is more complete in describing them with eagerness for it.

The way this conveys meaning is that it follows it as a cause-clause (ta'lil), and as if each one asks himself: is he more guided, or is another? That is: is he more eager for it, or is another? For there is no meaning to this question about oneself except urging and finding out whether there is any shortcoming in that or not. On this basis, if you were to say: "they eagerly strive for guidance, which of you will be more guided," it would be considered objectionable, because the new independent clause has taken the place of its relative clause, as in: "I commanded him, so he stood," "if your Lord had willed, He would have believed," "he wished that he had done well," and "how many, how many." On this basis, the seeking applies to the means of access, which is obedience, and the eagerness for being closer through it and the increase from it. And it is not possible to dispense with ﴿yahrisuna﴾ by treating ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ as an explanation for ﴿yabtaghuna﴾ in the way indicated, because ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ is not suitable as a distinguishing answer between the seekers and others. Rather it distinguishes between the seekers themselves, meaning those who draw near to one another, and this suits eagerness and ardor. Also, the complement of the seeking, namely the means of access, is mentioned, and you have known that the new independent clause suffices for that, and the combination is objectionable. End of quotation.

By my life, he has left no room for an archer's shot in verifying it. Yet this view, despite all this, is forced (mutakallaf). Al-Hufi and al-Zajjaj permitted that ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ be a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate of the clause is in the position of an accusative after ﴿yanzurun﴾, meaning: they reflect, and the meaning is: they consider which of them is closer, so they seek a means through him. It seems that what is intended is that they seek a means through his supplication, since otherwise there is a problem with seeking a means through the persons themselves.

This was criticized in al-Bahr: in the suppression of the suspended verb there is a problem, and despite that it is a view that is not evident. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿ayyuhum aqrabu﴾ be an interrogative clause in the position of an accusative after ﴿yad'una﴾, and that ﴿ayyu﴾ be a relative pronoun serving as a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿yad'una﴾. The first was criticized on the ground that it involves suspending something that is not a verb of the heart, and the majority hold that it is prohibited. As for the second, Abu Hayyan said: in it there is a separation between the relative clause and its complement by a circumstantial clause (jumla hāliyya), but this does not harm, because it is itself governed by the relative clause. And if you consider the meaning on this basis, you would not be satisfied that the verse be interpreted in this way.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and they hope﴾ are coordinated with ﴿they seek﴾; that is: they seek nearness through worship, and they expect ﴿His mercy﴾, the Exalted, ﴿and they fear His punishment﴾, just as all other servants do. So where are they from a King who removed harm, let alone being gods? ﴿Indeed the punishment of your Lord is ever something to be feared﴾, deserving that everyone, from the angels, the messengers, peace be upon them, and others, should beware of it and guard against it. The clause is a reason for the words of the Glorified: ﴿and they fear His punishment﴾. In specifying it with the causal clause there is an added warning to the disbelievers about the punishment. And the mention of hope before fear is because its object is prior to the object of fear.

In the sacred hadith: "My mercy has preceded My wrath."

In the uniformity of the style of the two clauses there is an indication of the equality of the hope of those seekers of the means of access to Him through obedience and worship, and their fear. The scholars have mentioned that this is what the believer should have, so long as death has not come upon him. When death comes, he should prefer his hope over his fear. And in the verse there is evidence that hope for mercy and fear of punishment do not diminish the perfection of the worshipper. It has spread from some of the worshippers that he said: "I do not worship Allah, the Exalted, out of hope for His Paradise, nor out of fear of His Fire." People are divided between one who criticizes whoever says this and one who praises him. The truth is a distinction: whoever says it to display independence from the grace and mercy of Allah, the Exalted, is mistaken and a disbeliever. Whoever says it because he believes that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is worthy of worship in His very essence, so that even if there were no Paradise and no Fire, He would still be worthy of being worshipped, then he is a realizer and a knower, as is not hidden.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 58]

﴿There is not a town but We shall destroy it before the Day of Resurrection﴾. The apparent meaning is generality, because *in* is a negation and *min* is an emphatic particle, which covers the whole class: there is no town among the towns but that. ﴿...by causing its people to die a natural death﴾, ﴿or punish it with a severe punishment﴾ by killing and various kinds of affliction. This was narrated from Muqatil, and it is the apparent meaning of what was narrated from Mujahid. Al-Jubba'i and a group of scholars also held this view. It was narrated from the first (Muqatil) that he said: "Destruction is for the righteous towns, and punishment is for the wicked towns." He also said: "I found in the book of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, in his tafsir of this verse: As for Makkah, Abyssinia will ruin it; Madinah will perish by hunger; Basra by drowning; Kufa by the Turks; the mountains by thunderbolts and quakings; and as for Khurasan, its destruction takes many forms." Then he mentioned city after city.

It was narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that the Jazira will be safe from ruin until Armenia is ruined; Armenia will be safe until Egypt (Misr) is ruined; Egypt will be safe until Kufa is ruined; and the Great Battle (al-Malhamah al-Kubra) will not occur until Kufa is ruined. When the Great Battle occurs, Constantinople will be conquered at the hand of a man from the Banu Hashim. The ruin of al-Andalus will come from the Zanj; the ruin of Ifriqiya from al-Andalus; the ruin of Egypt from the cutting off of the Nile and the disagreement of armies within it; the ruin of Iraq from hunger; the ruin of Kufa from an enemy who will besiege them and prevent them from drinking from the Euphrates; the ruin of Basra from Iraq; the ruin of al-Ubulla from an enemy who will besiege them by land and sea; the ruin of al-Rayy from the Daylam; the ruin of Khurasan from the Nabat; the ruin of the Nabat from China; the ruin of India and Yemen from locusts and the ruler; the ruin of Makkah from Abyssinia; and the ruin of Madinah from hunger.

And it is related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The last town of Islam to be ruined will be Madinah."

Thus Abu al-Su'ud, the Allamah, transmitted it. What is in the book of al-Dahhak, and likewise what was narrated from Wahb, is hardly to be relied upon. What was narrated from Abu Hurayrah is acceptable. al-Nasa'i narrated it from him with this wording, and al-Tirmidhi also narrated it in similar wording, and said: "Hasan gharib" (a grade of hadith: good, but unusual in its chain).

Abu Hayyan narrated it with the wording: "The last town in Islam to be ruined will be Madinah."

In al-Buhur al-Zakhirah it is stated that the cause of its ruin is that some of its people will go out with the Mahdi to jihad, then it will shake with its hypocrites and cast them out to the Dajjal; and some of the sincere ones will migrate to Bayt al-Maqdis to their imam; and whoever remains of them will have his soul taken by a pleasant wind, and the city will remain desolate. It rejects the idea that its ruin is caused by hunger, as you have heard from al-Dahhak and Ibn Munabbih. The apparent meaning of what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated is: "Madinah will be left in the best state it was in, its fruits abundant, visited only by the wild beasts and birds of prey, and the last to be gathered (on the Day of Resurrection) will be two shepherds from Muzayna." The hadith continues.

Imam Ahmad narrated, with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy: "The people will leave Madinah while it is still fresh and fertile." They said: "Who will eat it?" He said: "The beasts and birds of prey."

What is mentioned that Makkah will be ruined by Abyssinia is established in the Two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others, but with the wording: "The one with the two small legs from Abyssinia will destroy the Ka'bah."

In the hadith of Hudhayfah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is as if I see an Abyssinian, red-legged, blue-eyed, flat-nosed, big-bellied, who has placed his two feet on the Ka'bah, he and his companions, tearing it down stone by stone and passing it among themselves until they throw it into the sea."

In the hadith of Ahmad from Abu Hurayrah: the Abyssinians will come and ruin it, meaning the House will be ruined so that it is never rebuilt after that.

Yes, it has been disputed when that will be. It was said: in the time of Jesus, peace be upon him. It was also said: when there will remain on the earth no one who says "Allah." This is the last of the signs. al-Saffarini inclined to this view. The apparent meaning of the reports already mentioned about Madinah, that it is the last town of Islam to be ruined, indicates that the ruin of Makkah comes before it. And Allah knows best.

As for what is mentioned in the report of Ibn Munabbih, that Egypt will be safe until Kufa is ruined: if it is authentic, it indicates that Kufa will first be rebuilt and then ruined. Otherwise, it has been in ruins for hundreds of years and remains a ruin until now. Egypt is safe and flourishing today in the best condition. Numerous reports have come about its prosperity, as the report implies, as will not be hidden from anyone who has consulted the books compiled on the signs of the Hour and the reports of the Mahdi and al-Sufyani, although in most of them there is room for the critical scholar to object. Al-Buni and his kind claimed that it will be rebuilt at the end of the thirteenth century (AH). They took this from the words of Shaykh Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified. You know that his words resemble Hindi (obscure) and can hardly be counted as Arabic language. As for what is mentioned, that the ruin of Iraq is from hunger, it encompasses Baghdad, for it is its capital.

Al-Qadi Iyad said in al-Shifa': It has been narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "A city will be built between the Tigris, Dujayl, Qutrubbull and al-Sarat, to which treasures will be transported, and it will be swallowed up by the earth."

He means Baghdad. This is explicit that its destruction will be by being swallowed up, not by hunger. However, the scholars of hadith have mentioned that there is an unknown narrator in the chain of this report. Furthermore, the apparent meaning according to this interpretation is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿or punish it﴾ and so on, is restricted in the same way as the preceding clause it is joined to, so that both the destruction and the punishment will be before the Day of Resurrection, that is, in the period close to it. The use of this expression in this sense is widespread, and you will hear it shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills, in the hadith. To deny it is obstinate and not to be heeded. It seems that after He, glorified is He, mentioned matters concerning the Resurrection and the Oneness of Allah, He mentioned some of what will occur before the Day of Resurrection, which points to His greatness, glorified is He, and this supports what was mentioned before. It is established that after the death of Jesus, peace be upon him, a cold wind will come from the direction of Syria and will leave no one on the face of the earth in whose heart there is an atom's weight of faith without taking his soul. Then the wicked of mankind will remain, and the Hour will be established upon them. In other reports, it is mentioned what will befall people before the Hour of punishment. Among that is what al-Tabarani and Ibn Asakir narrated from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, may Allah be pleased with him: "A fire which today is extinguished in a valley called Barahut will certainly overtake you. Painful torment will cover the people through it. It will consume souls and wealth. The whole world will revolve in eight days, flying like the wind and the clouds. Its heat at night will be more intense than its heat by day. Between heaven and earth it will have a roar like the roar of the crashing thunder." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, will there be safety that day for the believing men and women?" He said: "And where are the believing men and women? The people that day will be worse than donkeys, copulating like beasts, and among them there will be no man saying: 'Mah, mah' (enough)." And other reports to this effect.

It is not far-fetched, after taking the generality of "town" into account, to interpret the destruction and punishment as what those reports include, namely the killing of the believers by the wind and the punishment of the remaining wicked people by the aforementioned fire. It is established that the wind will drive them to the gathering place (al-Mahshar). It is reported that they will shield their faces from every thorn and thicket, and that a plague will fall upon the back until no one with a back remains, so that a man will be given a pleasant garden in exchange for a she-camel with a saddle so that he may flee on it.

That this will be before the Day of Resurrection is the view relied upon. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar adopted it, al-Qadi Iyad corrected it, al-Qurtubi and al-Khattabi held it, and it has been stated explicitly in some hadith.

Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi narrated, and al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan sahih" (a grade of hadith), from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "A fire will come out of Hadramawt, or from the sea of Hadramawt, before the Day of Resurrection, gathering the people." The hadith continues.

It is not far-fetched that they will also be punished in other ways. Indeed, there are reports that support what is meant by ﴿That was﴾, that is, what has been mentioned of destruction and punishment, ﴿written in the Book﴾, that is, in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the tablet on which all decrees are recorded), as narrated from Ibrahim al-Taymi and others, ﴿inscribed﴾, written down. Many have mentioned that there is nothing except that it is made clear in it: its modes, its causes that necessitate it, and its appointed time. The generality has been questioned on the grounds that it requires the non-finitude of dimensions, whereas the textual and rational proofs establish otherwise. Therefore one must say that it is restricted, by taking "thing" to refer to what relates to this world or something similar. Some have held the generality while maintaining that the clarifying is of a kind compatible with finitude. Thus the Preserved Tablet, in its clarifying, contains all worldly and otherworldly things, what has been and what will be, like the Jafr al-Jami' (a book of esoteric knowledge) in what it clarifies. I have myself seen a scroll of the Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, from which he claimed to know what will happen in the place of gathering on the Day of Resurrection. Another he claimed to know from it the names of the people of Paradise and Hell and the names of their fathers. Another he claimed to know from it the events that will occur in Paradise. The acceptance or rejection of these claims is left to you. Some have interpreted the Book as the prior decree (al-qada' al-sabiq), so there is a figurative usage in the statement that will not be hidden.

Furthermore, Abu Muslim held that what is meant is: there is no town among the towns of the disbelievers but that We shall certainly ruin it, either by sinking it into the earth or by destroying its people entirely, because of the great sins they committed that necessitate this; or We shall punish its people with a severe punishment whose reality cannot be comprehended. What is meant by this includes worldly afflictions such as killing and captivity and the like, and otherworldly punishments known only to Allah, the Exalted, as is suggested by the unrestricted use of "punish," unlike "destroy," which is restricted by being before the Day of Resurrection. It is not to be restricted to worldly afflictions. How could it be, when many arrogant and rebellious towns have had their punishment postponed until the Day of Resurrection? Then it may be said, in explaining the connection on the assumption of restriction, that after He indicated that the disbelievers addressed were in affliction and harm, and that their gods could neither remove this from them nor alter it, He indicated that the like of this must befall the disbelievers, and no one could remove it or alter it from them. This is clear on the basis of what was mentioned earlier from some on the occasion of revelation, by which "harm" was interpreted as drought. So reflect.

As for the choice of the active participle form in both places, although it has the sense of the future, it carries what it carries of indicating certainty and firmness. And the restriction by the Day of Resurrection is because destruction on that day is not specific to disbelieving towns, nor is it by way of punishment; rather it is for the ending of the life of this world. Then he said: "The generalization of 'town' is supported neither by the preceding context (al-sibaq) nor by the following context (al-siyaq)." This is his statement, and there is room for reflection in it.

Among the people is one who preferred it
[Page 103]
over what preceded, on the ground that it involves taking destruction in the sense it usually conveys, namely what results from punishment, and this is not the case in what preceded.

It was answered that this is easily managed, for it has been used in the context of warning for what did not result from punishment, such as His saying, exalted is He:

[p. 103]

﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs﴾, that is, the signs which the Quraysh proposed.

Al-Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), al-Tabarani and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The people of Makkah asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to turn Safa into gold for them and to remove the mountains from them so that they could farm. It was said to him: 'If you wish, we will give you time with them; and if you wish, we will give them what they asked for. But if they disbelieve, they will be destroyed as I destroyed the nations before them.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'No, rather I will give them time.' So Allah revealed this verse."

The phrase that follows it (*anna* with what comes after) is, in its interpretation, a verbal noun in the accusative, functioning as the second object of *mana'a* (prevented), as al-Tabarsi explicitly stated. Or it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, as has been said, because the verb reaches its second object by means of a particle, as in His words: ﴿Did We not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?﴾ (4:141). The sense is: "And nothing prevented Us from the sending [of the signs]," or "from sending the signs." ﴿Except that the former [peoples] denied them﴾, that is, denied their kind, ﴿the first ones﴾ among the earlier nations who had made such proposals. The exception is a "disjunctive" (*mufarragh*) exception from the most general class of things, and *anna* with what follows is the subject of *mana'a*. That is: nothing among things prevented Us except the denial of the earlier people.

Abu al-Baqa' claimed that this is on the assumption of an omitted noun, meaning: "except the destruction [resulting from] the denial of the former people." But according to the others there is no need for this.

Linguistically, *al-man'* means to hold a person back and compel him away from an act he wishes to do. Since that is impossible for Him (glorified is He), because it would imply an impossible incapacity that contradicts lordship, they said: here it is used metaphorically (*musta'ar*) for "turning away." The meaning is: "What turned Us away from sending the proposed signs was only the denial of the former people who had proposed them, which entails their annihilation. For it leads to the denial of the latter proposers, by virtue of their sharing in arrogance and obstinacy, and that leads to the same fate befalling them, by virtue of their partnership in the crime and corruption, and the continuation of the divine custom and Lordly practice in this regard. And doing this to them would contradict what was written on the Preserved Tablet with the ink of wisdom concerning delaying their punishment. The summary of this is: We abstained from sending the signs because Our will had already preceded delaying the punishment from them for wisdoms that We know."

Some of them sensed a kind of objection in the "turning away" reading, so they made *al-man'* a figurative use (*majaz*) for "abandonment." It was objected that this is not valid when the agent is the denial, because the one who abandons is Allah, the Exalted.

It was answered that the claim that the agent must be the same in the literal and the metaphorical meanings is not supported by any proof; rather the apparent meaning is the opposite. One of the verifiers (may Allah be his father's guardian) mentioned, though it was challenged, that the denial of the former people, which entails annihilation and implies the denial of the latter people that leads to the descent of calamity, is incompatible with sending the proposed signs. Therefore the denial that calls for what contradicts wisdom in delaying the punishment of this nation is determined. So He expressed that incompatibility by "preventing," as a metaphor, to indicate the reciprocal support of the principles of sending. This is not as they claimed, that Allah does not will it, in order to support His Messenger (ﷺ) with miracles. And this is the secret of choosing *al-irsal* (sending) over *al-iytaʾ* (giving), because it implies that the signs are poised to descend, were it not for the grip of divine decree holding them back. Attributing the prevention to the denial of the former people, rather than to His knowledge of what the latter proposers would do, is as in His words: ﴿Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear; and had He made them hear, they would have turned away while refusing﴾ (8:23), in order to establish proof against them by presenting the model, and to indicate that the cause for not granting their proposal is nothing but their own conduct.

Then, as to the wisdom of the delay: it has been said that it is to show the greater nobility of the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said: it is out of concern for those among them who will be born as believers, and for those among them who will believe. More can be added to each of these, and so on, as examples; otherwise the list is not restricted. It has also been said: the meaning of the verse is: "We do not send the proposed signs because We know that they will not believe when they come, just as those who proposed them before them did not believe. So sending them would be pointless, and the Wise does not do what is pointless." You know that if sending the proposed sign when its proposers will not believe is pointless and the Wise does not do it, then its very doing becomes problematic from the first time. Moreover, what is related about the occasion of revelation requires the first interpretation, as is clear.

The signs were interpreted as "the proposed ones" because what they contain, establishing the claim of prophethood, is among the requirements of sending; and what goes beyond that, which was not in response to a proposal, is a kindness from the King, the Exalted.

[p. 104]

﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel﴾ is a conjunction with what the noble wording makes clear, as if it had been said: "Nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former people denied them, when We gave them what they proposed to their prophets, peace be upon them, of striking signs, and they denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel, in response to their proposal to their prophet Salih (peace be upon him), and We brought it forth for them from the rock as a ﴿visible sign﴾." The word *mubṣiratan* is in the form of the active participle and is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "the she-camel." The intended meaning is "possessing sight," or "possessing insight," which others see and by which they gain insight. So the form indicates a relation, or it makes the people possessors of insight, taking it as an active participle from *abṣarahu*, where the hamzah is for transitivity, meaning "he made him possessor of insight and perception." It is also possible that attributing sight to it is figurative, and that in reality it is the state of the one who observes it. A group read *mubṣaratan* in the form of the passive participle, meaning "which people see," and there is no obscurity in that.

Qatadah read *mubaṣaratan* with a fatha on the *mim* and the *ṣad*, meaning "a place of sight," by treating what causes the thing as if it were its place, as in the expression "the child is a cause of stinginess, a cause of cowardice." Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with both of them) read *mubṣiratan* in the form of the active participle, with nominative case by supposing an omitted subject: "it is a visible sign."

The majority read *Thamuda* as not taking tanwin (diptote). Harun said: the people of Kufa read it with tanwin in every case. Abu Hatim said: the common readers do not put tanwin on it, and the scholars of the Qur'an, in one of its forms and in four places, write an *alif*, but we read it without an *alif*, end quote.

[The author notes] this is as al-Raghib said, a non-Arabic word. It has also been said it is Arabic, and its non-declension is because it is the name of a tribe. It is on the pattern *faʿūl* from *al-thamd*, which is a little water with no source. From it comes the saying: "So-and-so is *mathmud*, the women have drained him," meaning they cut off the source of his water through frequent intercourse with them. And *mathmud* also means one on whom questions have multiplied until the source of his wealth is exhausted. Many have affirmed its Arabic origin. That is, Allah gave that tribe the she-camel. ﴿But they wronged themselves through it﴾, that is, they disbelieved in it and denied that it was from Allah, the Exalted, as confirmation of His Messenger; or they disbelieved in it while being wrongdoers. That is, they were not content with mere disbelief in it but did to it what they did, namely slaughtering it; or they wronged themselves and exposed themselves to destruction through its slaughter.

Perhaps the specific mention of its being given is because Thamud were Arabs like the Makkan proposers, and they have as much knowledge of their situation as one could want, since they see the traces of their destruction, their dwellings being close to them, by coming and going. It has also been permitted that this is because the she-camel, as an animal brought forth from a rock, is the clearest proof for the realization of the content of His words: ﴿Say: Be stones or iron﴾ (17:50), etc. The first is closer.

﴿We send the signs only as a warning﴾, that is, to those to whom they were sent. What is meant by them is either the proposed ones, so the warning is of annihilation, since Allah, the Exalted, in His custom, warns of it by them. That is: We send them only as a warning of the destroying punishment, like a vanguard for it. If they do not fear, what was done to them will be done. Or the signs are others, such as the verses of the Qur'an and the miracles, so the warning is of the punishment of the Hereafter, not the worldly punishment by annihilation. That is: We send them only as a warning and admonition of the punishment of the Hereafter.
