Abu Hayyan preferred that what is meant by them is the signs accompanied by a respite, such as eclipses, the intense thunder and lightning, winds, earthquakes, the drying up of the water of springs, and their overflowing beyond the limit so that some lands are drowned. al-Hasan counted among these the devastating plague. That is: We send them only as a warning of what is far greater than them.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, who said: "Indeed Allah frightens people with whatever signs of His He wills, so that they may repent, or be mindful, and return." Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned that the signs of Allah by which one takes lesson are of three kinds: one kind is general in everything, for in everything there is a sign showing that He is One, and there the reflection of scholars applies. Another kind is customary, like thunder and eclipses, and there the reflection of the ignorant applies. And a third kind is what breaks custom, which ended with the ending of prophethood; today it is only taken as a lesson by imagining its like and conceiving of it. End quote.

In this there is an oversight regarding *karamah* (a wonder granted to a saint), for the People of the Sunnah affirm it for the saint in every age.

The sentence is resumptive (*isti'naf*) and has no place in the grammatical analysis. It has been permitted, on the first reading, that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fazalamu* (they wronged), meaning: "they wronged themselves through it and did not fear the consequence, while the case is that We send the signs, which are among them, only as a warning of the punishment that follows them, so there befell them what befell them." *Takhwifan* (as a warning) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*).

It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause, meaning "frightened." The *ba'* in both places is the "sword of the orator," meaning a superfluous particle used for emphasis. *Al-ayat* (the signs) is the object of *nursilu*, or it is for association, and the object is omitted, meaning: "We send no prophet associated with them." It has been said that the *ba'* is for transitivity and that *ursila* is transitive by itself and by the *ba'*. It was rejected that this was not transmitted from any trustworthy authority. Al-Khafaji said: there is no proof in the verse of Kuthayyir:

"The slanderers have lied: I did not reveal to them any secret, nor did I send them with a messenger,"

because the *ba'* there may also be a superfluous addition. Moreover, the *rasul* there carries the sense of *risalah* (message), so it is an absolute object, and the discussion concerns its use with a direct object. It is not hidden that making *rasul* a direct object and adding the *ba'* to it is something no scholar of standing would undertake.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 60 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿And when We told you﴾, i.e., remember the time when We spoke to you through revelation, ﴿O Muhammad, that your Lord surrounds the people﴾, i.e., in knowledge, as related by more than one narrator from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. Nothing about their conditions or actions, past or future, including their disbelief and denial, is hidden from Him, glorified is He.

And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾, through to the end of the verse, is an indication of its reality, by way of argument from what proceeded from them when some of the signs came, since all of them share in being extraordinary matters that go beyond customary norms, sent down from the presence of the Lord of Might, may His majesty be exalted, to confirm His Messenger (ﷺ). So their denial of some of them indicates their denial of the rest, just as the denial of the earlier peoples of signs that were not requested indicates their denial of those that were requested.

By "the vision" is meant what he (ﷺ) witnessed on the night of the Night Journey (al-Isra') of the heavenly and earthly wonders, as recorded by al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and a group from Ibn 'Abbas. According to many, the word (ru'ya) has the general meaning of "seeing," and both (ru'ya and ru'yah) are verbal nouns of (ra'a), like (qurba) and (qarabah).

Some have said: it is literally used for both dream-vision and waking vision at night. The well-known view is that it is specifically used for dream-vision in the linguistic sense. Those who claimed that the Night Journey was a dream held to this well-known view, and the verse itself refutes them. Those who hold the well-known view and maintain that it was a waking experience, as is the correct position, said: the use of the term here is either a case of (mushakalah), i.e., conformity in wording to their own naming of it as a "vision," or it follows their assumption, like calling idols "gods." It is narrated that when he (ﷺ) recounted the Night Journey to them, some of them said to him: "Perhaps it was something you saw in your dream." Or the term is used by way of comparison to vision because of its wonders, or because it took place at night, or because of its swiftness. That is: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you as a manifest sight﴾, despite it being a great sign, and what a sign it was, and you had already established the proof of its truth, ﴿except as a trial for the people﴾, by which many of them were tested, to the point that some who had embraced Islam among them apostatized.

﴿And the tree﴾ is conjoined to ﴿the vision﴾, i.e., ﴿And We did not make the tree cursed in the Qur'an﴾ except as a trial for them as well.

By it is meant, as al-Bukhari and a great many others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, the tree of zaqqum. Its being cursed means the cursing of those among the disbelievers who eat it, as also narrated from him. Describing it thus is a metaphor in attribution (majaz fi al-isnad), and it contains exaggeration to the extent that it does.

Or its own self is what is cursed, and "cursing" is meant in its linguistic sense, which is distance. So it is, because of being in the most distant place from mercy, which is the root of Hell in which it grows, truly cursed.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from al-Habr (Ibn 'Abbas) that it was described as "cursed" because its fruit resembles the heads of devils, and devils are accursed. It has also been said: the Arabs say of every disagreeable, harmful food: "cursed."

It was also narrated, regarding its being a trial for them, that when what was revealed about it in al-Saffat and elsewhere was sent down, Abu Jahl and others said: "This Muhammad (ﷺ) threatens you with a fire that burns stones, then says that trees grow in it. We know zaqqum only as dates with butter." Abu Jahl then ordered a slave-girl of his to bring dates and butter and said to his companions: "Eat zaqqum!" (tazaqqamu).

Some of the weak-minded were also tested by this statement, and they erred greatly in this, to the point that they contradicted the evidence of their own reason. For they see the ostrich swallowing embers and red-hot pieces of iron, yet it is not harmed. And the salamander (al-samandal), a creature that lives in fire, has its wool made into napkins which are thrown into the fire when they become soiled, so the dirt goes away and they remain intact. And among their proverbs: "In every tree there is fire," and "al-Markh and al-'Afar have been kindled" (i.e., they rub together to produce fire).

And from Ibn 'Abbas, it is said that it is the dodder (al-kashuth) mentioned in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability﴾. Its being cursed in the Qur'an means describing it in the manner you have heard in this verse. What the Arabs said has passed just now. The trial regarding it was that they said, upon hearing the verse: "What is with the grasses that they are mentioned in the Qur'an?" The reliable narration from al-Habr is the one relied upon by the majority (jumhur).

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read: "and the tree" in the nominative (al-shajaratu), as a subject with the predicate omitted; that is, "and the cursed tree in the Qur'an" is likewise.

﴿And We warn them﴾ by this and similar signs, for all of them are for warning. The choice of the imperfect form indicates continuity of renewal.

Al-A'mash read: "and He warns them" with the letter ya' (yu-khawwifuhum). ﴿But it only increases them in transgression﴾ from the warning, ﴿a great one﴾, exceeding the limit, whose measure cannot be estimated. So if We had sent down what they requested of the signs, they would have done with them what they did with their counterparts, and what was done to those like them would have been done to them. Our word had already preceded regarding delaying the general punishment until the Greatest Catastrophe. This, in my view, is the most fitting to the noble arrangement of the verse, and it was chosen by (Abu al-Sa'ud) in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim.

From al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and most of the exegetes is the interpretation of "surrounding" as "power." The statement is directed at consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for whatever grief might afflict him from their not responding to the sending down of requested signs, since those signs contradict wisdom. Some of the disbelievers used to say: "If you were truly a messenger, you would bring this miracle just as the prophets before you brought theirs (peace be upon them)." It is as if it were said: remember the time when We said to you: "Indeed your Lord, the Gentle with you, has surrounded the people, so they are in the grip of His power and cannot escape the noose of His will. He protects you from them, so do not be concerned about them, and proceed with what I commanded you of conveying the message. Do you not see that the vision which We showed you earlier, We made a trial for the people, causing doubt, yet it did not weaken your cause nor cause slackness in your state?"

Some have understood "surrounding" as surrounding by knowledge, but he mentioned in the summary of the meaning what approaches what has been stated, saying: that is, He, glorified is He, is knowing of the people in the most complete manner, so He knows their intent to harm you if you do not bring them what they requested, and He will protect you from them. So proceed in what you are engaged in of conveying and warning. Do you not see, etc.

It is not hidden that mentioning the Lord with the pronoun referring to him (ﷺ), and commanding him, peace and blessings be upon him, to mention that statement, is more fitting to the verse being directed toward consoling him in the manner that was reported. And the mention of warning, and that it only increases them in great transgression, is more fitting with how the verse was interpreted at first. Some have claimed that it is not free of a kind of consolation.

It has also been said: "surrounding" here means destruction, as in His statement: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed [by destruction]﴾. "The people" are the Quraysh, and the time of that destruction is the Day of Badr. It is expressed in the past tense even though it was awaited, as indicated by His statement: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾, and His statement: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered into Hell"﴾, and other verses, because of the certainty of its occurrence. And the vision was interpreted as what he (ﷺ) saw in a dream of their being struck down, as stated explicitly in some narrations.

It is authentically reported that when he (ﷺ) arrived at the water of Badr, he said: "By Allah, it is as if I am looking at the places where the people will fall," and he placed his noble hand on the ground here and there, saying: "This is the place where so-and-so will fall, this is the place where so-and-so will fall."

This is clear that it was a dream.

It is narrated that the Quraysh heard what had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning Badr, and what he had been shown in his dream of their deaths, so they laughed and mocked. This is what is meant by the trial. And by what he (ﷺ) saw, peace and blessings be upon him, that he would enter Mecca, and he informed his companions, so he set out toward it, but the polytheists prevented him in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. Abu Muslim and al-Jubba'i held this view. He excused the fact that what was mentioned is Medinan by saying that it is possible the revelation about their destruction, and likewise the vision, occurred in Mecca, and the mention of the vision and the specification of the places of death happened after the Hijrah. This would entail that the trial with it occurred after the Hijrah, and that their increase in transgression was something anticipated and not yet occurring at the time of the revelation of the verse. All of this is contrary to what is apparent.

Ibn Jarir recorded from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw the Banu Umayyah leaping on his minbar like monkeys, and that distressed him, and he was never seen laughing until he died, peace and blessings be upon him. And Allah the Exalted sent down this verse: ﴿And We did not make the vision...﴾, etc."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and Ibn 'Asakir recorded from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw the Banu Umayyah on the pulpits, and that distressed him, so Allah the Exalted revealed to him: 'It is only a worldly matter, given to them.' So his eye was comforted. And that is His statement: ﴿And We did not make...﴾, etc."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ya'la ibn Murrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I saw the Banu Umayyah on the pulpits of the earth, and they will rule over you, and you will find them to be masters of evil.'" He (ﷺ) was concerned about that, so Allah the Glorified sent down: ﴿And We did not make...﴾, the verse."

It is recorded from Ibn 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw the sons of al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As on the pulpits as if they were monkeys." And Allah the Exalted sent down concerning that: ﴿And We did not make...﴾, etc. "And the cursed tree" is al-Hakam and his offspring.

In the wording of some exegetes, it is the Banu Umayyah.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said to Marwan ibn al-Hakam: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say to your father and your grandfather: 'You are the cursed tree in the Qur'an.'"

Based on this, the meaning of His surrounding the people is the surrounding of His decrees over them. The statement, as has been said, has an omitted modifier: that is, "We did not make the interpretation of the vision...", or "the vision" is a metaphor for its interpretation. The meaning of making that a trial for the people is making it a test and a means of examination for them. Ibn al-Musayyab explained it this way. This applied to their caliphs who did what they did and deviated from the paths of truth, and what follows applies to those other than their caliphs among them who acted as agents of corruption, or among their helpers, in whatever form. It is possible that the meaning is: We did not make their caliphate, nor did We make them themselves, except as a trial, and this contains as much exaggeration in condemning them as it does. The pronoun in (We warn them) according to this is either referring to what was mentioned earlier, or to the tree, with the understanding that by it is meant the Banu Umayyah. And [He curses them] because of what proceeded from them of permitting forbidden blood, violating protected chastity, taking wealth unlawfully, withholding rights from their people, altering the rulings and judging by other than what Allah sent down upon His Prophet, peace be upon him, and other great abominations and grave disgraces that will not easily be forgotten as long as the nights and days endure. Their being cursed in the Qur'an is either specifically, as the Shi'a claim, or generally, as we say. For the Exalted has said: ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾, and the Mighty and Majestic has said: ﴿So would you, if you were to turn away, cause corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship? Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He has deafened them and blinded their vision﴾, and other verses. Their entering into the generality of that is almost a primary entrance. However, it should not be overlooked that this does not, according to most of the Ahl al-Sunnah (Sunni scholars), permit cursing any one of them specifically. They have stated that it is not permissible to curse a particular disbeliever unless his death upon disbelief has been established, like Pharaoh and Nimrod. How then could one curse someone who is not a disbeliever? Al-Siraj al-Bulqini claimed that it is permissible to curse a specific sinner, and he supported his claim with the hadith of the two Sahihs: "When a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses to come, and he spends the night angry, the angels curse her until morning."

His son, al-Jalal, said: "I discussed this with my father, with the possibility that the cursing of the angels against her is general, so that it is said: 'May God Most High curse whoever spends the night forsaking her husband's bed.' This would be more apparent if one were to cite in support the report of Muslim: 'He (ﷺ) passed by a donkey that had been branded on its face, and said: "May God Most High curse whoever did this."'"

"For the demonstrative 'this' is explicit in cursing a specific person, unless it is interpreted to mean the doer of this kind of act, not the doer of this particular act. And there is much to be said about that." Some who agree with him also cited, for this, what is soundly reported: that he (ﷺ) said: "O God, curse Ri'l, Dhakwan and 'Usayyah, who disobeyed God and His Messenger."

In this there is the cursing of specific groups of people by name. It was answered that it is possible that he (ﷺ) knew their death, or the death of most of them, to be in disbelief, so he cursed only those whom he knew would die upon it. This, as you see, is far-fetched. It should not be overlooked that interpreting the verse in the manner mentioned is not clearly suited to the context (siyaq). God Most High knows best the soundness of the hadiths.

It was also said: "the cursed tree" is a metaphor for Abu Jahl, who was a trial and a affliction upon the Muslims; may God Most High curse him. It was said: it is a metaphor for the Jews who conspired against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and their cursing is evident in the Qur'an. Their trial was that they used to await his mission (ﷺ), but when he was sent, they disbelieved in him and said: "He is not the one we were waiting for," and so they discouraged many people from Islam by their words.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 61:

﴿And when We said to the angels﴾ is a reminder of what had already taken place from Him, exalted is He, of the command, and from the angels, of their compliance and obedience without hesitation, and a confirmation of the content of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek means of access to their Lord﴾, and so on. As for whether the relative term refers to the angels, the point is clear. If it refers to others, the comparison is by analogy. This also hints at the fate of those who opposed the truth, demanded signs, and denied the Messenger (ﷺ), for they are included among the offspring whom Iblis, may the curse of God be upon him, led astray, and they followed him as a shadow follows its owner, entering into that path first and sharing his obstinacy to the fullest degree, until they said: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is therefore clear. It has also been said that the point of resemblance is between the Quraysh who denied the Prophet (ﷺ) and Iblis, in that each of them was driven by envy and arrogance to what proceeded from him. That is: remember the time when We said to the angels: ﴿Prostrate yourselves before Adam﴾, honouring him and showing him reverence, peace be upon him. It has also been said that the meaning is: make him the direction (qibla) of your prostration to God, exalted is He.

﴿So they prostrated﴾ without any hesitation, in compliance with the command of God, exalted is He. ﴿Except Iblis﴾: he was not among those who prostrated, though he was counted among them and was included under the command to prostrate. ﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani, a resumption that answers an implied question), as if it were said: what did he do after holding back? So it is answered that he said, that is, after being rebuked with what he was rebuked for, as God, glorified is He, related in another place, in the form of denial and astonishment: ﴿Shall I prostrate myself before one whom You created from clay?﴾ Here the words ﴿Since You created me from fire﴾ are added. The word ﴿clay﴾ (ṭīnan) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naz‘ al-khāfid, the omission of the governing particle), that is, ﴿from clay﴾, as stated explicitly in another verse. Al-Zajjaj permitted it to be a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the omitted returning pronoun, with the governing verb being ﴿You created﴾, so the meaning would be: shall I prostrate to one who, at the time of his creation, was clay? Although clayness precedes his creation as a human being, it is nonetheless concurrent with the beginning of that creation. Al-Zamakhshari also permitted it to be a state of the relative term itself, with the governing word then being ﴿Shall I prostrate﴾, in the sense: shall I prostrate to him while he is clay, that is, his origin is clay. In al-Kashf he said: this is more emphatic, because it reinforces the meaning of denial, and it contains a belittling of him, peace be upon him, which is far from him, by making him the very thing he was made of, from which that lowliness was never removed. Making it a state of the returning pronoun does not carry this emphasis. You know that taking it as a state in any case goes against the apparent sense, since clay is a solid substance, and for this reason some have interpreted it as ﴿rooted﴾. Al-Zajjaj also permitted it to be a specifying term of clarification (tamyīz), and Ibn ‘Atiyya followed him, but this does not appear evident. Mentioning creation (khalq), although the purpose would be served by saying: ﴿to one who was of clay﴾, is more pointed to the purpose, and it is said to contain an allusion to another cause, namely that he is a creature, and prostration is only due to the Creator, exalted is His majesty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 62:

﴿He said﴾: that is, Iblis. The repetition of the verb ﴿said﴾ between the two speeches of the accursed one signals that the second speech is not connected to the first and is not built upon it, but rather upon something else. He has mentioned this in other places. The meaning is: he said, after being expelled from the exalted station, cursed, and granted respite and delay: ﴿Have You considered this one whom You have honored above me?﴾

The kaf (ﻙ, the particle of address) is a particle of address that reinforces the meaning of the ta' (ﺕ) before it. It is of the linguistic kind of emphasis, so it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The verb ra'a (ﺭﺃﻯ) is used in the sense of knowledge (ʿilmiyyah), so it takes two objects. Hadha (ﻫﺬﺍ, "this") is its first object, the relative clause is its description, and the second object is omitted, because the relative clause indicates it. This form of speech is a metaphor for another form of speech. From here you will hear them say: the meaning is, "Inform me about this one whom You have honored above me: why have You honored him above me, when I am more honorable than him?" The connection between knowing and informing is one of causality and effect, and of concomitance and implication. The clause "why have You honored him" stands, as Abu Hayyan explicitly stated, in the position of the second object. Some grammarians held that ra'a is visual (basariyyah) and so takes one object. Al-Radi chose this view, and they make the interrogative clause mentioned above a resumed clause (mustaʾnafah, a new sentence).

Al-Farra' said: the kaf is a pronoun in the accusative position, meaning "Have you considered yourself?" It is like when you say: "Have you reflected on the end of your affair, for I am doing such-and-such?" And ﴿this one whom You have honored above me﴾ is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar), and the interrogative has been omitted from it, meaning: "Is this...?" Some scholars said this too, except that they made the kaf a particle of emphatic address, meaning: "Inform me, is this the one whom You have honored ﴿above me﴾?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the kaf is a particle, as has been said, but the meaning of "Have you considered yourself?" is "Have you reflected?" It is as if the speaker alerts the addressee to bring to mind what he is about to say to him right after. That it means "inform me" is the view of Sibawayh, al-Zajjaj, and those who followed them, al-Hufi, al-Zamakhshari, and others. Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that this applies where there is an interrogative, and there is no interrogative in the verse.

You know that what is established regarding arayta (ﺃﺭﺃﻳﺖ) in the sense of "inform me" is that it enters upon an initial nominal clause whose predicate is an interrogative, either stated or implied. So the mere absence of it does not preclude this.

In any case, the demonstrative ﻫﺬﺍ (this) is for belittling, and what is meant by honoring is preferring.

The clause ﴿If You respite me until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a resumption and the beginning of a new speech. The lam is a preparatory lam for an oath, and its answer is ﴿I will surely seize control of his descendants﴾.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): "Someone might go so far as to say that this is the first object of arayta(ka) in the sense of 'inform me,' and the second object is the oath clause mentioned, because the two form a subject and predicate before arayta(ka) enters. That would be a fine way of putting it, since on this view there is no need to posit an omission in the speech, and it is as you see." And what is meant by ﴿respite me﴾ is: let me live, or delay my death. The meaning of ﴿I will surely seize control of his descendants﴾ is: I will certainly gain strong control over them, from the expression "he bridled the animal" (ḥannaka al-dabbata wa-ḥtanakahā), when one places a rope under its lower jaw to lead it by it.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Farra' also held it. Or the meaning is: I will utterly uproot them and destroy them through misguidance, from the expression "the locust stripped the land" (ihtanaka al-jarad al-ard) when it destroys its vegetation and strips what is upon it, and "so-and-so stripped the wealth of so-and-so" when he takes it and consumes it. Upon this is the saying of the poet:

*We complain to You of a year that has ruined us,*
*hardship upon hardship has weakened us,*
*and has stripped our wealth and left us bare.*

It seems to be derived from the ḥanak (ﺣﻨﻚ), which is the inner upper part of the mouth from inside the beak. So it is a derivation from the name of a physical thing. Al-Tabari, al-Jubba'i, and a group chose this. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd that he said: he means: "I will mislead them," and this is an explanation of the essential meaning. This is like the words of the accursed one: ﴿I will certainly make [evil] seem fair to them on earth and I will mislead them all﴾.

﴿Except a few﴾ of them, who are the sincere servants (al-'ibad al-mukhlasun), whose exception is mentioned in another verse. May God Most High make us and you among them.

The accursed one knew that this request would be granted to him, so much so that he mentioned it with emphasis. This was either through receiving it from the angels by hearing, though God Most High had informed them of it, or they saw it in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), or by deducing it from their words ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾ together with God Most High's affirmation of this to him, or by insight (firasah) into what he saw in them of the strength of imagination (wahm), desire, and anger that necessitate this.

It is not far-fetched that the exception of the few was also by insight. As if, when he saw that the one preventing him from gaining control over the few was shared between him and Adam, peace be upon him, he mentioned it from the very beginning. It is reported from al-Hasan that he thought this because he whispered to Adam and deceived him until what happened happened. So he analogized the branch to the root. But this is problematic, because this statement was before the whispering through which what happened happened. Whoever claims that there were two whisperings, the burden of proof is on him. And he will not bring it (i.e., the proof) until the two evening-pickers return, or Satan prostrates to Adam, peace be upon him.

The Exalted said: ﴿Go﴾. It does not mean the literal command to go, the opposite of coming. Rather, it means leaving him to what his self has beautified for him, as a humiliation of him, just as you say to someone who opposes you: "Do what you want." It was also said: it may be from going (*dhahab*), the opposite of coming, and its meaning would then be like the meaning of His words: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed﴾. It was also said: it is a driving away and a leaving alone. Taking it literally would require combining the literal and the metaphorical (*jam' bayn al-haqiqa wal-majaz*), and the one who says so is among those who permit that. What shows that it does not mean the opposite of coming is that it is followed by the threat in His words: ﴿As for whoever of them follows you﴾ and goes astray from the truth, ﴿then indeed Hell is your recompense﴾, that is, the recompense of you and of them. The addressee is given precedence over the absent party out of regard for the right of the one who is followed (*al-matbu'iyya*). Al-Zamakhshari, and many after him, permitted that the address is to the followers, as an *iltifat* (shift) from the third person of the explicit noun to the second person. Ibn Hisham criticised this in his *Tadhkira*, saying: "In my view it is invalid, because the response or the predicate is devoid of a connecting pronoun, since the pronoun of address cannot serve as a connector." It was answered that it is to be interpreted with an implied element, so it is said to them: "Indeed Hell is your recompense." It was rejected on the grounds that this then falls outside the *iltifat*. Some of the researchers said: "If it is granted that the pronoun of address does not refer back, we do not grant that when it is intended to refer to the absent party as an *iltifat*, it is not connected to it, for it is no more remote from connection than an explicit noun is. So keep this in mind."

﴿a full recompense﴾, that is, complete, with nothing withheld from it, as Ibn Jubayr said: from *farra* (to complete), as in "*farra 'irdahu li-sahibika fira*", meaning: complete the honour of your companion. Upon this is the poet's saying:

"Whoever makes kindness at the expense of his honour, it will be completed for him; and whoever does not guard against insult will be insulted."

*Wafara* also occurs intransitively, as in: "*wafara al-mal yafiru wufuran*", meaning: it became complete and abundant. The word *jaza'an* (recompense) is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), by implying *tujzawn* or *tujazawn*, since both have the same meaning, and this verbal noun belongs to both of them.

Page 111

Abu Hayyan and others permitted that the governing element for it is "*jaza'ukum*" (your recompense), based on the view that the verbal noun governs the absolute object. It was also permitted that it is a preparatory circumstantial qualifier (*hal muwatti'a*) for its adjective, which is itself a circumstantial qualifier in reality; for this reason it came in an uninflected form, as in His words: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. There is then no need to estimate *dhawi* (possessors of) in it. The possessor of the circumstance is the implied object of *tujzawnahu*, and the governing element is the verb. It was also said: it is a circumstantial qualifier of its subject, with the implied *dhawi jaza'in* (possessors of recompense). Al-Tibi said: "It was said: the meaning is *dhawi jaza'in*, so that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun of the addressees, and the verbal noun is the governing element; otherwise there is no governing element." Then he said: "The most apparent view is that it is an emphatic circumstantial qualifier for the content of the sentence, like: *Zayd hatimun jawadan* (Zayd is a Hatim in generosity)." In *al-Kashf* it is stated that this is the definite view, and the first is not the correct one. Similar to it is making it a circumstantial qualifier of the subject. It was also said: it is a specification (*tamyiz*), but this is not accepted by its proponents.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 64:

﴿And incite﴾, i.e., and provoke (*istakhiffa*). It is said: *istafazzahu* means that he made him light-headed (*istakhaffahu*), so he deceived him and led him into what he wanted from him. The original meaning of *al-fazz* is cutting, and from it comes *tafazzaza al-thawb*, meaning the garment tore. It is also said that *fazz* means "light," and for this reason the young of the wild cow was named by it, as in the words of Zuhayr:

*When he seeks help from something, the fazz of a gheytala (a wild cow's young), he fears the eyes, and is not looked at by the Hashak.*

The *waw* (and), according to *al-Bahr* (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), is for conjunction with *idhhab* (go). The meaning of the command is a threat, and so is the case with the commands that follow. What prevents taking it literally is that God, exalted is He, does not command indecency.

﴿whomever you can﴾, i.e., those whom you are able to incite ﴿from among them﴾. Here *man* is a relative pronoun serving as the object of *istafziz*, and the object of *istatta'ta* is omitted, which is what we have indicated. Abu al-Baqa' chose that *min* is an interrogative in the accusative position after *istata'ta*, but this is very contrary to the apparent meaning, and there is no reason to resort to it. ﴿with your voice﴾, i.e., with your calling to disobedience of God, exalted is He, and your whispering. He expressed the calling by "voice" to belittle it, to the point that it is as if it had no meaning, like the voice of a donkey.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir, and others related from Mujahid that it means singing, flutes, play, and falsehood. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned that Adam, peace be upon him, settled the children of Habil on the top of a mountain and the children of Qabil at its base, and among them were beautiful daughters, so Satan played the flute, and they could not restrain themselves from descending and mixing together.

﴿And cry out against them﴾, i.e., shout against them, from *al-jalabah*, which is shouting. This was said by al-Farra' and Abu Ubaydah, who also mentioned that *jalaba* and *ajlaba* have the same meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: *ajlaba 'ala al-'aduww* means he gathered horses against the enemy.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: *jalaba 'alayhi* means he helped against him. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *ajlaba 'ala al-rajul* means when he threatened him with evil and gathered the people against him. Some interpreters explained *ajlib* here as *ajma'* (gather). Accordingly, the *ba'* in His words, ﴿with your horse and your foot soldiers﴾, is extra (*mazidah*), as in *la yaqra'na bi al-suwar* (they do not recite the surahs). Al-Hasan read *wa-ijlub* with a connecting alif and a *damma* on the lam, from *jalaba* as a triliteral verb. The word *khayl* (horses) is applied to horses literally, and it has no singular from its own form. It was said that its singular is *khaʼil*, because of its strutting (*ikhtiyal*) in its walk. It is applied to horsemen figuratively, and this is what is meant here. From this is his saying, ﷺ, in some of his campaigns to his companions, may God be pleased with them: "O cavalry of God, mount up!" (*Ya khayl Allah irkabi*).

*Al-rajil*, with a kasra on the jim, is the form *fa'il* with the meaning of *fa'il* (active participle). Thus it is an adjective, like *hadhir* meaning *hadhir* (cautious). One says: "So-and-so walks *rajilan*," that is, not riding.

The author of *al-Lawami'* said: it has the meaning of *al-rijal* (men). That is, it is a singular used to mean the plural, because it is the appropriate form for the context and for what is coordinated with it. This is how Hafs and Abu Amr (in one narration) and al-Hasan read it. The apparent meaning of the verse requires that the Devil has horses and foot soldiers, and a group held this view. It was said: they are from the jinn. It was said: they are from the jinn and the humans, and this is what is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and from Mujahid and Qatadah. They said: he has horses and foot soldiers from the jinn and the humans. So whoever rides and fights in disobedience to God, exalted is He, is from the horses of Iblis, and whoever goes on foot and fights in disobedience to God, exalted is He, is from the foot soldiers of Iblis. Others said: Satan has no horses and no infantry, and they are only a metaphor for helpers and followers, without considering that some of them ride and some walk.

[Page 112]

Some allowed that his inciting is by his voice, and his gathering against them with his horse and foot soldiers is an image of his dominance over those whom he leads astray. It is as if a raider fell upon a people, shouted at them with a shout that drives them from their places, and gathered against them his troops of horsemen and foot soldiers until he uprooted them. What is meant is that there is a figurative metaphor (*istiʻarah tamthiliyyah*) in the speech, and considering a figurative or metonymic usage in the individual words does not harm it, so do not be heedless.

The majority read *rajlika* with a fatha on the ra' and sukun on the jim, and it is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) of *rajil*, like *rakb* and *rakib*, not a plural, because this pattern is dominant among singular nouns. It was read *rajulika* with a fatha on the ra' and damma on the jim, and it is singular, as in the reading of Hafs. Words of the adjective pattern (*al-sifah al-mushabbahah*) have come in the forms *fa'il* and *fa'ul*, with kasra and damma, such as *hadith* and *nadus* and others.

Ikrimah and Qatadah read *rijalika*, like *nibalika*. It was also read *rujjalika*, like *kuffarika*. Both are plurals of *rujlan* and *rajil*, as in *al-Kashf*. In some copies of *al-Kashshaf* it is read *rajjalika* with a fatha on the ra' and shadda on the jim, on the basis that its origin is *rajjalah*, and its *ta'* was dropped for lightness. That is a weak copy. ﴿And share with them in the wealth﴾, by urging them to acquire it by what is not befitting and to spend it on what is not befitting.

It was said: by urging them to spend it on fornication. It is related from al-Dahhak: by urging them to slaughter for the idols. It is related from Qatadah: by urging them to make the sawa'ib (free-roaming camels) and bahira (slit-eared camels) into a practice. Generality is more preferable.

﴿and the children﴾, by urging them to seek them through forbidden means and to commit what does not please God, exalted is He, regarding them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: sharing in the children is urging them to name them *Abd al-Harith* and *Abd Shams*. In another narration: urging them to make them desire false religions and to dye them with other than the dye of Islam. In another: urging them to obtain them through fornication. And another: adorning for them the killing of their children out of fear of poverty or shame. It was said: urging them to make them desire fighting and memorizing poetry that contains obscenity and vile, wicked trades. From Mujahid: when a man does not mention the name of God at intercourse, the jinn coils around his penis and has intercourse with him. That is what is meant by sharing in the children. The preferable view is what we have mentioned.

﴿And promise them﴾, false promises, such as the intercession of the gods and the benefit of noble lineages for one who has not obeyed God, exalted is He, at all, and that no one will abide in the Fire, because that contradicts the greatness of mercy and the long hope of remaining in this world. Among the false promises is his promise to them that when they die they will not be resurrected, and other things that are too numerous to count. This is of the type of sharing in the self, as in *al-Bahr*.

﴿Satan promises them nothing but delusion﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) between what Satan was addressed with, to explain the state of his promises. The shift to the third person (*iltifat ila al-ghaybah*) strengthens the meaning of the insertion, along with diverting the speech from addressing him and explaining his state to the people. It also hints at the causality of his devilry for delusion, which is making error appear as correct by what makes it seem to be right. It is said: *gharra fulanan* when one catches him unaware, i.e., in his heedlessness, and obtains from him what he wants. The origin of this, as al-Raghib said, is from *al-gharr*, which is the visible trace of a thing. Its accusative form is because it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, that is: a promise of delusion, in the same ways as in *rajulun 'adlun* (a just man).

It is permitted that it be an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), that is, "and he promises them and gives them hope in what will not be fulfilled and will not happen except in order to deceive them." The first is more apparent.

The Imam mentioned, regarding the reason why Satan's promise is only delusion, that it only calls to one of three matters: fulfilling desire, executing anger, and seeking leadership and elevation. It never calls at all to knowledge of God, exalted is He, or to serving Him. And those three things are not pleasures in reality, but rather the removal of pains. Even if it is granted that they are pleasures, they are base ones, in which the deficient and the perfect share, rather, man and the dog share them. And along with that, they are quickly passing, and are not obtained except through many hardships and great difficulties, and they are followed by death and old age, and the preoccupation of the mind with fear of their loss and greed to keep them. The pleasures of the belly and the groin are not complete except by engaging in putrid, filthy moistures. So adorning these things is hardly possible except with what is more false than the claim of the combination of two contradictories, and that is delusion.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 65:

﴿Indeed, My servants﴾: The idafa (the construct form, "My servants") is for honour, and so it indicates that the servants are restricted to the sincere (al-mukhlisin), as was stated explicitly in another verse. It is also indicated by the context that God, exalted is He, is their Guardian (wakil), protecting them from the evil of Satan. Whoever is like this can only be a noble servant, specially devoted to Him, exalted is He. It is frequently said of one whose love for something has come to dominate him, so that he submits to it, that he is a slave of that thing, such as "slave of the dinar and the dirham," "slave of the khamisa" (the fine garment), and "slave of his belly." From this it is said of one who follows Satan, "a slave of Satan." So there is no need to say that the sentence contains an omitted qualifier, i.e., "Indeed, My sincere servants."

Al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) claimed that "My servants" is general, applying to all those charged with religious obligation (mukallafun), and that there is no omitted qualifier, but the exception was omitted, relying on its explicit mention in another place. This is not correct. In this idafa there is also an indication of the reason for the ruling in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿You have no authority over them﴾: that is, no power or ability to mislead them. The emphasis on the ruling, even though the opponent acknowledges it, is for greater attention to it.

﴿And your Lord suffices as a Guardian﴾ for them. They rely upon Him, exalted is He, and seek His help to be freed from your misguidance, so He, glorified is He, protects them from him. The address in this sentence is said to be to Satan, as in the preceding sentence. In the mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which indicates absolute ownership and complete disposal, together with its attribution to His pronoun, there is a hint of the manner of His sufficiency for them and His protection of them from him, namely the removal of his power to mislead them.

It is also said that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to the human being. It is as if, when He, glorified is He, had explained the condition of Satan to the extent that He did, fear arose in the hearts, so He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And your Lord suffices﴾, O Prophet, or O human being, as a Guardian. He, majestic is His majesty, repels the plot of Satan and protects from him. The heart inclines to the view that it is not an address to Satan, even though in the preceding sentence it was addressed to him.

The verse has been used as evidence that the one protected (ma'sum) is the one whom God protects, and that a human being cannot guard himself by his own effort against the places of misguidance; otherwise it would have said: "And a human being suffices as a guardian for himself."

Here there are two questions, which the Imam raised together with their two answers.

The first: Did Iblis know that the one who spoke with him with these threats was the God of the worlds, or did he not know? If he did, how could he persist in the severe warning, given His saying, glorified is He:

﴿Indeed, Hell is your recompense, a full recompense﴾, which did not prevent him from disobedience, although he heard it from God, exalted is His majesty, without any intermediary? And if he did not know, how did he say: ﴿Have you seen this one whom You have honoured above me?﴾

The answer: Perhaps he was doubtful about everything, and he would say in each case whatever came to his mind as a matter of conjecture. I say: The weakness of this answer is not hidden.

The truth in this matter is that he was certain that the one who spoke with him in that manner was the God of the worlds, exalted is He, but his wretchedness overcame him, the wretchedness for which his essence had been prepared, so the warning did not prevent him. This is why, when the snares are set for his destruction at the appointed time, and he sees the punishment he sees, and the earth becomes too narrow for him despite its vastness, it will be said to him: "Prostrate today to Adam, peace be upon him, so that you may be saved." He will not prostrate and will say: "I did not prostrate to him while he was alive, so how would I prostrate to him when he is dead?" as is related in some reports.

This is no more astonishing than the condition of the disbelievers who are tormented on the Day of Resurrection with the most severe torment for their disbelief, and who seek to return so that they may believe, whereas God, exalted is He, has informed us that if they were returned they would revert to what they were forbidden.

It may be said: The accursed one, despite this warning, has a hope of salvation. It is related that our master Abdullah al-Tustari (Abdullah al-Tustari) asked God, exalted is He, to show him Iblis, and he saw him. He asked him: "Do you hope for the mercy of God, exalted is He?" He said: "How could I not hope for it, when God, glorified is He, says: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾, and I am one of the things?" Al-Tustari said: "Woe to you! Indeed God, exalted is He, restricted it at the end of the verse." Iblis said to him: "Woe to you! How ignorant you are! The restriction is for you, not for him." Perhaps he thinks that the verses of warning are absolutely restricted by the Will (mashi'a) even if it is not mentioned, as some of the Ash'arites say concerning the verses of warning for sinful believers.

The second question: What is the wisdom in God, exalted is He, granting him respite until the Day of Resurrection and empowering him to whisper? A wise one, when He wills a matter and knows that there is an obstacle that prevents its occurrence, does not strive to bring about the removal of that obstacle. The answer, according to our school, is evident. As for the Mu'tazila, al-Jubba'i among them said: God, exalted is He, knew that those who disbelieve at the whispering of Iblis would disbelieve even if he did not exist, and at that time there would be no further corruption from his existence. Abu Hashim said: It is not far-fetched that there could result from his existence further corruption, but God, exalted is He, kept him in existence to intensify the obligation upon creation, so that they might deserve through it greater reward.

I say: Iblis is not an obstacle to what God, glorified is His glory and exalted is His majesty, wills. Whatever God, glorified is He, wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. God, blessed and exalted, created creation in accordance with His knowledge, and He knew it in accordance with what it is in itself. So understand. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 66:

﴿Your Lord is He who drives for you the ship in the sea﴾ is a mubtada' and khabar (subject and predicate). It has been said: the relative clause (al-mawsul) is an attributive (sifah) of ﴿your Lord﴾, and it is itself an attributive of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who created you﴾, or a substitute (badal) for it, and that is permissible even if the distance between them is great. End of quote, and there is much to consider in it. The root of izja' (driving) is leading along step by step, and what is intended by it is making things run (ijza'). It seems that He chose it over other terms because it indicates compulsion (al-qasr) more clearly, and it is more fitting to the context and greater in bestowal. That is: He, glorified and exalted, is the Capable, the Wise, who causes the ships to run for your benefit in the sea, by the gentle wind and by means of the instruments, as His custom, exalted is He, has been. ﴿So that you may seek of His bounty﴾ is an explicit statement of the benefit; that is, that you may seek of His provision, which is a bounty from Him, glorified is He, or of the profit, of which He, majestic is His affair, is the Giver. Min here is partitive (tab'idiyyah). Interpreting fadl (bounty) as the pilgrimage (hajj) or the military raid (ghazw) is not appropriate. This is a reminder of some of the blessings which are signs of the Oneness of God, which is the primary aim of the mission (ba'thah), and a preparation for mentioning their affirmation of Oneness when harm touches them, as a completion of what passed in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿then they do not possess﴾, and the verse.

﴿Indeed He has always been﴾, eternally and everlastingly, ﴿Merciful to you﴾, in that He has prepared for you what you need and made easy for you what would otherwise be difficult from its beginnings. This is a concluding clause (tadhyil) containing a reason (ta'lil) for what preceded regarding the driving and the seeking of bounty. The form al-Rahim, as in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, serves to indicate that what is meant by mercy is worldly mercy and immediate blessing, divided into the great and the small. This is based on the view that al-Rahim is specific to this world, as is well known, and upon it [is the supplication] "O Compassionate of this world and the next, and Merciful of this world." It has been said that it is not specific, and upon that view [the supplication is] "O Compassionate of this world and the next, and Merciful of both."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 67:

﴿And when harm touches you at sea, the ones you call upon vanish from you, except Him﴾: that is, out of fear of drowning, by the violence of the wind and the tossing of the waves. "Vanish" (ḍalla) means: every one you call upon and hope for benefit from departs from your thoughts, so you do not remember them, ﴿except Him﴾, may He be exalted, for you remember Him alone, glorified is He; you remember none other, and no one other than Him, exalted is He, occurs to your minds, for the removal of the harm that has befallen you, whether independently or in partnership. So the meaning of their "going astray" is their absence from thought, not from sight and sense, because this is a known matter from their saying: "Such-and-such went astray from him" (ḍalla 'anhu kadha) when he forgot it. In al-Kashshaf it is said: it is the one who is lost to him (ḍalla 'anhu kadha) when it is lost; there is no need for an implied meaning. Or from "ḍallahu fulan" (so-and-so lost him), meaning it departed from him so that he could no longer control it; al-Azhari mentioned this and recited:
Page 115

"And the seeker who pursues its noblest qualities knows that my excuses lose me (tuḍillunī 'ilalī)"
That is: they part from me and leave me, so I no longer make excuses with any pretext. This is more evident. Yes, the "going astray" refers to the remembrance, not in the sense of its being concealed, for that is weak. One says: "Such-and-such went astray from my mind" when you do not recall it; it is a going astray of it for him, not a going astray of its remembrance. You do not say: "its remembrance went astray from my mind." Likewise: "the matter lost me" (ḍallanī al-amr). End quote. The supplication here is on its apparent sense, and the exception is continuous (muttaṣil), on the basis that "mā" refers to those called upon in general, and that they used to call upon God, exalted is He, and others in calamities. If "mā" refers only to their false deities, and they used to call upon these alone in times of ease, as the apparent sense of what follows indicates, then the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), and the supplication is interpreted on this basis as the supplication of worship and seeking refuge.

Abu Hayyan said: the apparent reading is disjunction, because He, exalted is He, is not included among "those you call upon," since the meaning is: their gods went astray, that is, their worshipped objects, while they do not worship God, exalted is He. It was objected that the implication of their being polytheists is that they also worship Him, glorified is He, but in the manner of association. Rather, their saying, ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾, as He related about them, indicates that He, may His majesty be glorified, is the true object of worship in their view. It may be said that the Lawgiver has removed such worship from the level of consideration, so they are not worshippers of God, exalted is He, in the sense of the law. Indeed it has been said that they are not worshippers even linguistically, because worship linguistically is the utmost submission and humbling, and this is not realized with association, even in the form they claimed. So reflect.

Many have permitted that the meaning is: those you call upon went astray from aiding you, except Him, exalted is He, and the going astray in it is either in the sense of absence or in the sense of not being guided to it, as if it were said: they strayed from the path of right in rescuing you and were unable to do so. The matter of the exception, whether continuous or disjunctive, rests on its own basis for each. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the meaning is: those of the gods you call upon went astray from aiding you, but God, exalted is He, is the One you hope in, and he made the exception upon Him disjunctive. It was said: this is for singling out the ones called upon as the gods.

In al-Kashshaf: perhaps the point in it is that they did not call upon Him, that is, the call of worship and seeking refuge, except in that state; as for in a state of ease, they single out their gods with the call. The verification is that the going astray in this sense did not encompass the Truth, glorified is He, because its meaning is: the ones called upon went astray and were absent from aiding them, and it is not meant that they were absent while God, exalted is He, was present; rather, it means that they hoped He would aid them and not forsake them, the act of the ones called upon according to their supposition. This is the point, God willing, end quote. The basis of this verification is not hidden from one trained in the science of grammar.

Among the subtleties: some people said to one of the imams: "Prove to me the existence of God, and do not mention to me substance and accident." He said to him: "Have you ever boarded a ship?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Has the wind raged?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did the ship come close to sinking?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did you despair of the benefit of those in the ship and others of the created beings for you, and of their rescuing you from what you were in?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did your heart remain attached to anything other than them?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is God, mighty and majestic." He admired that.

﴿Then when He rescued you﴾ from the harm and brought you ﴿to the land, you turned away﴾ from His remembrance, after you had been remembering none but Him, glorified is He; or you turned away from His oneness, exalted is He; or from thanking Him, mighty and majestic, by His oneness and obedience, glorified is He; or you went to extremes in excessive ingratitude for the blessing. This is from "ʿarḍ" (breadth) as opposed to "ṭūl" (length), and it was made a metonymy for that, as in the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"The gift of a youth who has established himself in lofty deeds, so he turned away in generosities and grew haughty."

It is as if it was intended: you turned away and grew haughty in ingratitude, except that he dispensed with mentioning the length (istaṭāla) by the mention of the breadth (ʿarḍ), because it entails it.

﴿And man is ever ungrateful﴾: this is as a cause for the turning away, and it is an explanation of the ruling on the species, and from it is known the ruling on those addressed. And there is subtlety in that He, glorified is He, turned away from addressing them specifically and mentioned that the species of man is disposed to ingratitude; so when they turned away, God, glorified is He, turned away from them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 68:

﴿Do you then feel secure﴾: The hamza (interrogative particle) here expresses denial, meaning that feeling secure is not appropriate. The fa' (the conjunctive fa') coordinates with an elided element placed between it and the hamza, meaning: "Were you saved, and then you felt secure?" This is the view of some grammarians (nuhah). Others chose that the hamza is placed before its position through a deferment, because of its original priority at the head of the sentence and its coordination with what precedes it. The clause "the human being was..." (kana al-insan) and so on is a parenthetical insertion between the two coordinated elements, and there is no elision in such a case. This is the view of most scholars. However, it does not clearly appear that the denial of security is caused by what precedes it, as this view requires; rather, it appears to follow only from the deliverance (from drowning). Turning away has no bearing on the causation of the denial. In my view, the correct approach in such cases is whichever reading yields sound meaning without strain. One is not obliged to adopt either of the two views, and if one of them leads to strained interpretation, that is pure partisanship (ta'assub).

The address is to those mentioned earlier: "Do you then feel secure, you who turned away when you were saved, ﴿that He will cause the side of the land﴾ which is your place of refuge to swallow you up?" That is, that God will cause it to conceal you, and carry you down into the depths of the earth, while you are with it. That is, "while you are upon it," with the ba' meaning accompaniment, and the prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). It is also permitted that the ba' is causal (sababiyyah), and the prepositional phrase is connected to what follows it, meaning: that He, glorified is He, will conceal it because of you. This is objected to on the grounds that it does not follow from the overturning of the land because of them that they would be destroyed and swallowed. It is answered that, since the intended meaning of "the side of the land" is the side where they are, its swallowing entails their destruction; otherwise there would be no benefit in the threat. The word "side" (janib) is in the accusative in both readings, as the direct object of "to swallow" (yakhsifa).

In al-Durr al-Masun (a grammatical commentary by al-Samin al-Halabi) it is stated that it is in the accusative as an adverb of place (zarfiyyah). In that case, the ba' may be transitive, meaning: "Do you feel secure that He will conceal you therein?"

In al-Qamus (the dictionary of al-Fayruzabadi): "God caused the earth to swallow so-and-so," meaning He concealed him in it. The apparent meaning is that this explains the lexical sense of the word. Mentioning the side contains an indication that when they reached the shore they turned away. Alternatively, the meaning is that all sides and directions are equal in relation to His power, dominion and subjugation, so for Him, in every side, whether land or sea, there are causes of destruction lying in wait. The side of the sea alone is not specifically associated with this. Rather, if drowning occurs on the side of the sea, then on the side of the land there is something of its like, namely swallowing, since it is concealment beneath the dust, just as drowning is concealment beneath the water. So the sensible person must fear God in all directions.

The first reading is according to the supposition that by "the side of the land" is meant its edge adjoining the sea, which is the shore. This second reading is on the supposition that it means all of its sides together. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read "nakhsifa" (with the first-person plural "we") with the royal plural nun, and likewise in the four that follow it.

﴿Or He will send against you﴾ from above you ﴿a hasiban (a violent wind laden with pebbles)﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas that he said: it is a rain of stones, that is, a rain that pelts you, meaning that it strikes you with pebbles (hasba'), which are small stones. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada that he explained "hasib" as the stones themselves, and perhaps in that case it is a form of attribution, meaning: possessing pebbles, and what is intended is the act of throwing. Al-Farra' said: the hasib is the wind that throws pebbles. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the dust in which there are pebbles, and the form is also of attribution. It also comes to mean scattered fine snow and hail, and from it is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Facing the north of al-Sham, it strikes them
with a hasib like scattered cotton tufts.

It also comes to mean the cloud that throws both of them. Al-Zamakhshari and those who followed him chose the explanation of al-Farra'. The apparent meaning is that the statement is taken in its literal sense. So the meaning is: or if He does not strike you with destruction from beneath through the swallowing of the earth, He strikes you with it from above by a wind that He sends against you, in which there are pebbles, which pelt you with them, so that it is more severe for you than drowning in the sea. The same may be said of all the other interpretations of "hasib." Al-Khafaji said, describing the wind as pelting with pebbles: it is an expression for its intensity. Mentioning it is an indication that they feared the wind destroying them at sea, so it was said: if He wills, He may destroy you with wind on land as well. I do not know what prevents taking the apparent meaning, and intensity necessarily entails the aforementioned pelting in the usual course. The indication is the same indication.

﴿Then you will not find for yourselves any disposer of affairs (wakil)﴾ to whom you may entrust your affairs, so that he may protect you from that, or turn it away from you, other than Him, exalted is He, for there is no one who can repel His decisive command, exalted is His majesty.

[Page 117]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 69:**

﴿Or do you feel secure﴾, meaning: rather, do you feel secure ﴿that He will return you to it﴾, meaning: to the sea from which He delivered you, so that you turned away, by boarding ships, ﴿and not into the ship﴾, because the ship is feminine. The preposition *fi* ("in") was chosen over *ila* ("to"), which indicates mere arrival, to show that they would remain in it. ﴿Another time﴾, meaning: a time other than the first. It is in the accusative as a *zarfiyya* (adverbial accusative of time or place). It may be pluralized as *tarat* and *tiyar*, as in the saying: "He stands *taratin* and walks *tiyaran*." Sometimes they drop the *ha'* from it, as in his saying:

*"With woe, once, and with perdition, once."*

The attribution of the return to Him, exalted is He, although the return is by their own choice, is because it is among the things attributed to them. Though it is created by Him, glory be to Him, like all their actions, this is by way of the creation of the motives within them that compel them to that. There is in this an allusion to the extreme intensity of the terror of what has no strength against it in the first time, such that, were it not for the return, they would not have returned.

﴿Then He sends upon you﴾ while you are in the sea ﴿a violent wind﴾, which is the strong wind that shatters whatever it passes over of trees and the like, or the wind that has a *qaṣīf*, which is a loud sound, as if it were *tataqaṣṣafu*, meaning it breaks apart.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: *al-qāṣif min al-rīḥ* is the wind that drowns. It was also said: the wind that destroys on land is *ḥāṣib*, and the wind that destroys at sea is *qāṣif*. The *ʿāṣif* is like the *qāṣif*, as was related from Abdullah ibn Amr. In another narration from Ibn Abbas, *qāṣif* is explained as *ʿāṣif*. Abu Ja'far read *min al-riyāḥ* in the plural.

﴿So that He drowns you﴾, Allah, glory be to Him, through the means of what strikes your ship from the *qāṣif*. Abu Ja'far read *fa-tughriqakum* with the *tā'* of the third person, so that the verb is attributed to the wind. Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read *fa-yughriqakum* with the *yā'* of the third person, the *ghayn* with a *fatḥa*, and the *rā'* doubled. In a narration from Abu Ja'far it is the same, except with *tā'* rather than *yā'*. Humayd read it with *nūn*, the *ghayn* with a *sukūn*, and the *qāf* assimilated into the *kāf*. It was also narrated from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Muhaysin.

﴿Because you disbelieved﴾, meaning: because of your previous disbelief, which is their turning away at the time of deliverance the first time. It was also said: because of your disbelief, which is your constant habit.

﴿Then you will not find for yourselves against Us any avenger for it﴾, meaning: any helper, as was related from Ibn Abbas, or one who pursues us for what We did, seeking vengeance from us, or one who exacts retribution from our side. This is like His exalted saying: ﴿So He leveled it﴾ and ﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾, as was related from Mujahid. The pronoun in *bihi* ("for it") has been said to refer to the sending, and it has been said to refer to the drowning, and it has been said to refer to both, in view of what has occurred and the like, as has been indicated. It seems that when Allah, glory be to Him, made the drowning, which lies between the return to the sea, a retribution in response to disbelief, He followed it with the negation of finding an avenger. It is as if it were said: We will take vengeance without anyone standing up to help you. This is a threat upon a threat. And the placing of what came before, which is the torment of hardship, like the touch of harm at sea, is followed by the negation of finding a guardian, so it is as if it were said: you will not find anyone upon whom you rely to repel it except Him, exalted is He, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Those whom you call upon will be lost, except Him﴾. This is the view of the author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari), so do not be heedless of it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 70:

﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾. That is: We made them all, the righteous and the wicked alike, possessors of honor (karam), meaning nobility and many excellent qualities that no limit can encompass. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that He honored them with the intellect ('aql). In another report, He honored them by their taking food with their hands, not with their mouths like the rest of the animals.

It is related from al-Dahhak that the honor is speech (nutq). From 'Ata' it is related that it is the balance and extension of stature. From Zayd ibn Aslam it is related that it is food and pleasures. From Yaman it is related that it is beauty of form. From Ibn Jarir it is related that it is their dominion over other creatures and the subjugation of those creatures to them. From Muhammad ibn Ka'b it is related that it is the making of Muhammad ﷺ one of them.

It has been said: it is by Allah's creating their father Adam with His own hands. It has been said: it is by managing their livelihood and their return. It has been said: it is by writing (al-khatt). It has been said: it is by the beard for men and the forelock for women. It has been said, and it has been said, and all of these, in reality, are by way of illustration (tamthil). As for one who claims that the honor is restricted to one thing, like Ibn 'Atiyya, when he said:

"The honor is only by the intellect and nothing else,"

he has asserted something erroneous, aimed at something excessive, and opposed both clear reason and sound transmission. For this reason, the Imam al-Shafi'i used the verse as evidence that the human being is not rendered impure by death.

﴿And We carried them on the land and the sea﴾: on moist livers and dry sticks, meaning on animals and ships. It is derived from "hamaltuhu 'ala kadha," when you give him what he rides and carries, so the object of carrying (al-mahmul 'alayhi) is understood by the context (qarina al-maqam).

It has been said: the meaning of carrying them on land and sea is making them stationary in them, in that He did not cause the earth to swallow them and did not drown them in water. The first is more fitting to the honor, since none of the animals other than them is established as having this, unlike the second.

﴿And We provided them with good things﴾: that is, kinds of blessings and types of delightful things, of what is obtained by their own making and by other than their making, of foods, clothing, furnishings, possessions and other things.

﴿And We preferred them﴾. It has been said: that is, by the honor mentioned, ﴿over many of those We have created, with a [marked] preference﴾, a great preference. The meaning is that this is specific to them in relation to the many, so the many were not honored as they were honored. The Imam [al-Razi] raised a question on this point: He, the Exalted, said first, ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾, and then said here, ﴿And We preferred them﴾. So there must be a difference between honor (takrim) and preference (tafdil), lest there be repetition.

The closer view on this is that He preferred the human being over the rest of the animals by innate, natural, essential matters, such as the intellect, speech, writing, beautiful form and tall stature. Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, exposed him, through the intellect and understanding, to acquiring the true beliefs and the virtuous morals. The first is the honor, and the second is the preference. It is as if it were said: We preferred them by exposing them to acquiring that in which there is salvation and nearness, through what We honored them with of the beginnings of that. So it is incumbent upon them to be thankful, and to direct what was created for them toward what they were created for: that they should affirm the oneness of Allah, the Exalted, not associate anything with Him, and abandon what they are upon of worshipping other than Him, the Mighty and Majestic. Something similar is said, as previously mentioned, with slight variation.

Al-Tibi said: In the verse there is a repetition of what indicates the utmost praise, by mentioning honor, preference, and the subjugation of things, in an ascending order. It is as if it were said: And We certainly honored the children of Adam through the honor of their father, peace be upon him; then We subjected things to them, and provided them with good things; then We preferred them with a preference of what a preference! Therefore, He followed these with His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, etc. This is to explain the honor of their father. What lies between the two of them of verses is like a digression (istitrad) and an interjection (i'tiraD), and so on to the end of what he said. From this it is known that the repetition is removed, even if the passage was not directed to that purpose. In it is also the restriction of the honor. Likewise in what has been said: the honor is by the blessings through which the obligation (taklif) is valid, and the preference is by the obligation through which He exposed them to a lofty rank. The "many" means those other than the angels, peace be upon them, according to the majority, and among them is al-Zamakhshari, who claimed that the verse is explicit in the preference of the angel over the human, and he vilified the People of the Sunna with a vilification of the most foul kind.

The truth is that it is not suitable as evidence for the disputed preference. In al-Kashf it is said that the apparent context of the verse is that it urges the human to gratitude and to not associate anything with Him, since it mentions what is on land and sea of His good guardianship (husn kila'ihi) toward him. It also includes that He, the Exalted, guided them to the ship and its construction and what follows from it of benefits, in His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿Your Lord is He who drives for you the ships﴾, and so on. Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾, that is, this type from among the other types, with favors by which We singled them out. He mentioned from them carrying them on land and sea, providing for them of good things, and preferring them over many of the created beings. This preference is not meant to indicate the greatness of rank and the increase of nearness to Allah, the Exalted, which is the disputed matter, because the ruling is for the type as such. Allah mentioned for this reasons that encompass the righteous and the wicked alike. Therefore, whether the angels entered into this "many" or did not enter, it does not indicate superiority in the sense mentioned, and so it is not suitable as evidence for either of the two parties. End.

Furthermore, even on the assumption that the preference is in the disputed sense, the verse does not indicate that the angel is superior to the human except by way of implication (mafhum), and there is disagreement about its authority (hujjiyya). Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, does not hold this view. Moreover, it indicates that they were preferred over the many, but were not preferred over their counterpart, and that counterpart allows for equality as well as the preference of the counterpart. So it is not explicit in the position of al-Zamakhshari.

Al-Tibi took "min" (from) as explicative (bayaniyya), as in your saying: "I spent for him the broad [part] of my dignity." That is: We preferred them over the many whom We created among those possessing intellects, as is apparent from "min." They are confined to the angel, the jinn and the human. Since the human is excluded, because a thing is not preferred over itself, the angel and the jinn remain. So the meaning is the explanation of the preference of the human over all of them, and this is what the context of praise requires, since the verse is directed to it. If it is taken as partitive (tab'id), then ﴿those whom We have created﴾ is a substitute: that is, We preferred them over some of the created beings.

Mentioning "some" in this context indicates the magnification of the one preferred over, as was established in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And He raised some of them in degrees﴾. And what a praise for the children of Adam and an affirmation of excellence and honor in general, by the oath-form sentence, if they are made preferred over the jinn and the devils. Moreover, if the attribute of multitude is made restrictive to exclude some, then the angels are more deserving than the jinn and the devils, since they are the ones described with multitude, as the many reports indicate, such as the report of the creaking of the heaven, the report of the descent of raindrops, and the report of the angels who enter the Inhabited House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur) every day, and so on. To this the statement of the author of al-Taqrib refers: that it is possible that by "many of those We have created" is meant the angels, since they are a multitude of the created rational beings. End.

It has been objected that what he mentioned of taking "whom We have created" to generalize to those possessing intellects is acceptable, since the preference over those who do not possess intellects comes in this case by way of the implication of agreement (mafhum al-muwafaqa), so there is no need to commit a departure from the apparent meaning and to consider the predominance (taghlib) of them to include them and others. But taking "min" as explicative is not acceptable, since it is very far-fetched, because the restriction of multitude is lost under it. Taking "min" to generalize by predominance or by convention is also not acceptable, and because its use in partition is common wherever it occurs in the revelation and in the usages of the eloquent. And it is more forced than taking it to mean the limit in His saying, Exalted is He: "wipe your heads and your feet from it," according to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned about it, and that when it is compared with something else, it indicates a fewness in the counterpart, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So among them is one guided, and many of them are defiant﴾. For he explicitly said that it indicates that the predominance is for the defiant, because of the comparison.
