Indeed, al-Bayhaqi did not relate that the shafaq is the redness except from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

As for what al-Daraqutni related from him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The shafaq is the redness; when it sets, the prayer becomes obligatory," al-Bayhaqi and al-Nawawi said that the sound view regarding it is that it is a statement (mawquf) of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

A similar disagreement exists regarding the beginning of the time of 'Asr. The Imam said: it begins when the shadow of every object becomes twice its length, after the shadow of noon (zawal). His two companions said: when the shadow of every object becomes equal to its length, after the shadow of noon. The verdict of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqin) follows his view, may Allah have mercy on him. Indeed, Ibn Nujaym said that issuing a fatwa according to other than his view is not permissible. He discussed this at length in his treatise: Raf' al-Ghisha' 'an Waqtay al-'Asr wa-al-'Isha' (Lifting the Veil from the Times of 'Asr and 'Isha').

﴿And the recitation of dawn﴾ is in coordination with the object of "establish" (aqim), or it is in the accusative as an incitement (al-ighra'), as al-Zajjaj and Abu al-Baqa' said, but the majority follow the first. What is meant by the recitation of dawn is the prayer of dawn, as related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It was called a recitation (qur'an), that is, a recitation (qira'a), because recitation is its pillar (rukn), just as it was called bowing (ruku') and prostration (sujud). This is an argument against Ibn 'Ulayya. The position of al-Asamm and Ibn 'Ulayya is that recitation is not a pillar of the prayer, as stated in the Kashshaf, and this was refuted on the grounds that this does not indicate pillarhood, since the metaphor may be based on recitation being recommended within the prayer. In the Kashf it was said that this is answered by the fact that the relationship ('alaqa) that is valid when a non-prayer term is used to mean the prayer is the relationship of whole and part, according to the parallel examples. Here, since it is used metaphorically, it is necessary to interpret it according to the known parallel from induction. Recommendation (nadbiyya) is not suitable as a valid relationship except with forced effort. Sabbaḥa is taken to mean "prayed," because glorification (tasbih) means the thorough declaration of God's transcendence, and the one who prays glorifies Him verbally by reciting al-Fatiha, and indeed by the obligatory takbir, which is agreed upon, and also physically by bowing and prostration, for example, which indicate the perfection of exaltation and reverence. So it is the whole pillar, not because tasbih means the words "subhan Allah," such that it would be a metaphor for the prayer by something recommended within it. It was objected that relying on the relationship of recommendation, which al-Asamm and Ibn 'Ulayya hold, involves no forced effort, since the Qur'an is a part of the complete prayer, so it is like the parallel examples, without harm or detriment. Also, their position on takbir is not known, so the claim of agreement is not accepted from them. If it were as he mentioned, then obligation would be sufficient as another relationship, namely necessity. There is discussion on this point.

Al-Jassas kept the Qur'an in its literal sense and said: The verse indicates that recitation is obligatory in the dawn prayer, because the implied meaning is "establish the recitation of dawn," and the command is for obligation. No recitation at that time is obligatory except in the prayer. He claimed that the meaning "pray the dawn prayer" is an error in two respects. The first is that it diverts the word from its literal sense without evidence. The second is that ﴿so pray the tahajjud with it﴾ afterward contradicts it, since there is no sense in tahajjud with the dawn prayer. In reply: the evidence is established, namely ﴿establish﴾, because ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ is well known, whereas "establish the recitation" is not. The pronoun in "with it" later may refer to the Qur'an in its literal meaning, by a figure of speech (istikhdam), and this occurs more often than can be counted. Furthermore, if the verse indicates the obligation of recitation in the dawn prayer explicitly, then the obligation of recitation in the other prayers is established by analogy (qiyas).

Some have mentioned that the specification of the dawn prayer by name in this way indicates that longer recitation is required in it than in other prayers. This is good. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: The verse indicates that it is recommended to pray the dawn prayer in darkness (taghlis), because the Qur'an is attributed to dawn in it, in the sense of "establish the recitation of dawn." The command is for obligation. Dawn is the first appearance of morning light, from the breaking of the darkness of night by the light of morning at that time, and for this reason it is called fajr (dawn). This requires that establishing the dawn prayer at the very first appearance of dawn be obligatory. Since it is agreed that this is not obligatory, the recommendation remains, because obligation is the preponderance of preventing omission. When a barrier prevents the realization of obligation, as the consensus (ijma') does here, the barrier against omission must be removed, and the basic preponderance must remain, so that opposition to the evidence is minimized.

You know what the scholars have said about what remains after the lifting of obligation. What was mentioned is one opinion on the matter, but it does not establish what is sought, because the name "dawn prayer" refers to the specific prayer whether it is performed in darkness or in brightness. The sound reports indicate the recommendation of performing it in brightness (isfar), such as the hadith of al-Tirmidhi, who said it is hasan sahih: "Perform the dawn prayer in brightness, for it is greater in reward."

To interpret this as meaning the clear appearance of dawn, so that there is no doubt about its breaking, is nothing; for until it is clearly appearing, the prayer is not judged permissible, let alone obtaining the reward indicated at the end of the hadith. And even if "greater" (a'zam) in it were taken as "great," it is refuted, because the appropriate reason in the explanation is that the prayer is not valid without it. Moreover, even in its own terms, the narration of al-Tahawi negates this: "Perform the dawn prayer in brightness; whenever you make it brighter, it is greater in reward," or "for your rewards," or as he said. It was also related with a sound chain from Ibrahim, who said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never agreed on anything as they agreed on lighting (tanwir) [the dawn prayer]. It is impossible, given their high status, that they would agree against what their beloved Messenger of Allah, upon whom be prayers and peace, left them upon.

In the Sahihayn, from Ibn Mas'ud: "I did not see the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pray a prayer at its appointed time except two: the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers at Jam', and he prayed the dawn prayer that day before its appointed time, even though it was after dawn," as the wording of al-Bukhari indicates.

So the meaning is "before its appointed time," which is the time at which he was accustomed to performing it. Apparently the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, did not habitually perform it in darkness, but he did it that day in order to prolong the standing (wuquf). We say it is recommended to perform it in the dawn of Muzdalifah on the basis of this hadith.

The report of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray the morning prayer in darkness (ghalas), and women would attend with him wrapped in their cloaks, then return to their houses, and no one could recognize them because of the darkness."

Some of our companions interpreted the darkness (ghalas) in it as the darkness inside the mosque. But this is contradicted by her words: "then they return to their houses, and no one could recognize them because of the darkness," since it is not possible to interpret this darkness, which prevented their being recognized on their way back to their houses, as the darkness inside the mosque. And that the meaning is "no one could recognize them inside the mosque because of the darkness" is contrary to the apparent sense, on the assumption that the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "they return." The apparent sense is what we have pointed to. Likewise, making the clause a circumstantial clause from "women" or an attribute of it, as if it were said: "women attend with him wrapped in their cloaks, no one recognizing them because of the darkness, then they return to their houses," is also possible.

It was said that this occurred on a cloudy day. This is distant, because of the word "used to" (kana), which is commonly used for what the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, was constant in doing. It was also said that it has been abrogated (mansukh), as the consensus of the Companions on lighting indicates. This is also distant, because abrogation requires that the abrogated ruling existed earlier, whereas Ibn Mas'ud's words "I did not see..." etc. indicate that it had no earlier existence.

Some have said: Among the conflicting reports here, the narration of men is preferred, especially someone like Ibn Mas'ud, because the situation is more evident to them in congregational prayer. So reflect carefully.

Al-Tahawi mentioned that what is appropriate is to enter the dawn prayer at the time of darkness and to exit at the time of brightness. This is the view of Imam Abu Hanifa and his two companions. It differs from what the later scholars (ashab) report from them about starting and finishing in brightness. This latter view is indicated by the hadith of al-Tirmidhi and others. And Allah knows best.

Furthermore, although the dawn prayer is one of the five prayers that were enjoined on the night of the Isra' upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community, and this verse indicates the obligation of establishing it in this way, nevertheless the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, did not perform it on the morning of that night, because he did not know its manner at that time. He learned the manner only afterward.

Earlier we mentioned that the beginning of the prayer fell at the time of the noon prayer (ẓuhr), as a sign that his religion (ﷺ) would prevail over the other religions just as it prevails over the other prayers. Here, Allah, glorified and exalted, honoured the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-fajr) by saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾, and He did not say: "Indeed, it was witnessed."

Aḥmad, al-Nasā'ī, Ibn Mājah, al-Tirmidhī, and al-Ḥākim, who declared it authentic (ṣaḥḥaḥahu), together with a group of scholars, related from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said in explaining this: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it."

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim), also from him (may Allah be pleased with him), he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer." Then Abū Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾."

By these angels is meant the recording angels (al-katabah) and the guarding angels (al-ḥafaẓah). The angels of the day descend and the angels of the night ascend, and the two groups meet at that time. Likewise the two groups meet [at the time of the evening prayer], and the matter of descending and ascending is reversed at the time of the afternoon prayer (ʿaṣr), as has been reported in the narrations. This is something that undermines the Imam in his claim that this is also strong evidence that performing the prayer in the dark (taghlīs) is better than performing it in the light (tanwīr). For when a person begins the prayer at the very start of dawn, the angels of the night are present because the darkness remains; but if the prayer is prolonged because of reciting slowly and at length, the darkness departs, the light appears, and the angels of the day arrive. Based on this argument, which only passes with children, it would follow that delaying the afternoon prayer until the light disappears and darkness appears is permissible. He does not say that, and indeed no one says that.

Is the group that witnesses today, for example, the same group that witnesses tomorrow, or does each day a different group witness it, one that did not witness before and will not witness after? There is a difference of opinion on this, and discussion of it will come, Allah willing, in what relates to that matter.

It has been said: most of the worshippers customarily witness it. It has been said: it is proper that a large congregation witness it. It has been said: it is witnessed, and there appear in it signs of power, such as the change of light into darkness and the awakening from sleep, which is the brother of death. This is a possibility the Imam raised and discussed at length. Then he said: "This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn was ever witnessed﴾." Then he mentioned the possibility that what is meant is that it is witnessed by a large congregation, and he also discussed its verification at length. You know that there is no basis for the restriction implied by his saying "This is what is meant," and that, after the Prophet's (ﷺ) explanation of it as you have heard had been authenticated, it is not fitting to say about anything else "This is what is meant." 

Nor is hidden what this sentence contains of encouragement and exhortation to give attention to the matter of the dawn prayer, because at that time the servant is accompanied by noble angels who see him off and noble angels who receive him. So he should be in the best of states, such that the departing traveller speaks well of him and the one who arrives is pleased with him.

[Page 138]

﴿And during part of the night﴾. It has been said: meaning, "and keep vigil during part of the night." Its apparent sense is that it is of the type of *al-ighra'* (urging someone toward an action by a command), as transmitted from al-Zajjaj and Abu al-Baqa' regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that the one being urged toward something cannot be a particle, and that the claim that *min* is for partitive meaning does not help, because that does not make it a noun. Do you not see the consensus of the grammarians (*nuhat*) that *waw* in *ma'a* is a particle, even if it is construed as *ma'a*? It was answered that it is possible that the one who says this holds the view that *min* is a noun in such a usage, just as they said that the *kaf* is a noun in such expressions as ﴿so He made them like chewed-up stalks﴾, and *'an* in such expressions as "*min 'an yamini* (from the right of me) at times and *shimali* (and the left)," and in the manner of "*min 'alayhi*." Likewise, the one who says that it is in the accusative by way of adverbial sense (*zarfiyyah*) with an implied verb, i.e., "and stand during part of the night."

[Page 139]

Al-Hufi preferred that *min* is related to a verb indicated by the meaning of the utterance, i.e., "and stay awake during part of the night." Then the *fa'* in His words, ﴿so keep vigil with it﴾, is either conjunctive to that implied verb or explanatory, based on it being from the style of ﴿and fear Me alone﴾. In *al-Kashf* it is said that the incitement (*ighra'*) is the apparent meaning here, unlike what preceded it, because the accusative by way of explanation (*tafsir*) and the relative clauses are different and do not become entirely clear, whereas the meaning of incitement from what precedes and what follows is supported by evidence; yet there is a clear objection to this.

*Tahajjud*, according to what is transmitted from al-Layth, is waking from sleep for prayer, and it is also applied to the prayer itself after rising from sleep at night. It is said *tahajjada*, meaning he prayed during the night after waking; similarly *hajada*. This implies that sleep must precede the realization of *tahajjud*, so if one does not sleep and prays as much as he wishes, it is not said of him that he performed *tahajjud*. This is what is narrated from Mujahid, al-Aswad, 'Alqamah, and others. Al-Mubarrad said: it is staying awake for prayer or for the remembrance of God, Exalted is He. It was also said: staying awake for obedience. Its apparent meaning is that preceding sleep is not a condition for its realization. The well-known view is that this is called *qiyam* (standing in prayer), while what comes after sleep is called *tahajjud*.

Al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr al-Mazini stated something strange, for it is narrated from him that he said: "Does one of you think that when he rises at night, prays until morning, that he has performed *tahajjud*? *Tahajjud* is only prayer after sleep. Then another prayer after another sleep, then another prayer after another sleep. This is how the prayer of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was." I say: the intervening of sleep between the prayers appears in Sahih Muslim through the narration of Husayn from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, and it is among what al-Daraqutni criticized Muslim for, due to its irregularity (*idtirab*). For he said: "It was narrated from him in seven ways, and the majority differed about it," meaning the report in which there is intervening sleep; and most of the narrations do not contain this, so let it be memorized.

It is stipulated that the prayer is not one of the five obligatory prayers. So if one slept through the night prayer (*'isha*) then rose and prayed it, he is not called one who performs *tahajjud*. There is no harm in its being obligatory, as when one slept through the *witr* and then rose to it.

In *al-Qamus*: *al-hujud* is sleep, like *tahajjud*, and *tahajjada* is "he woke up," like *hajada*, which is an antonym. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *hajada al-rajul* means he prayed during the night, and *hajada* means he slept at night. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-hajid* is the sleeper and the one who prays. In *Majma' al-Bayan* it is said that one says *hajadtuhu* meaning "I made him sleep," and upon this is the verse of Labid:

"I said, 'We have slept,' and he said, 'The night journey has been long.'"

It is narrated from Ibn Barzakh that one says *hajadtuhu* meaning "I woke him," and the verbal noun of this is *al-tahjid*. *Al-Qamus* explicitly states that it is also among the antonyms.

Some have mentioned that the well-known usage in the speech of the Arabs is that *al-hujud* means sleep, and *tahajjud* is explained as abandoning *hujud*, i.e., sleep, with the *tafa'ul* form signifying negation, like *ta'ththum* (avoiding sin) and *tahannuth* (abstaining from idolatry). This is the basis of those who interpreted it as waking. It is also possible to say that the *tafa'ul* form signifies effort, i.e., the exertion of *hujud* in the sense of wakefulness. This was preferred on the ground that the *tafa'ul* form coming for effort is more common than its coming for negation.

[Page 140]

It was objected that the usage of *hujud* for wakefulness is disputed as to its establishment, and even if it is established, it is less common than its usage for sleep. The pronoun in *bihi* (with it) refers to the Qur'an as such, not restricted by its being attached to dawn. This was used as evidence for lengthening the recitation in the *tahajjud* prayer, and the scholars have explicitly stated that this is recommended.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Hudhayfah: "I prayed behind the Prophet (ﷺ) one night, and he began Al-Baqarah. I said: he will bow at the hundredth verse. Then he continued, and I said: he will pray it in one rak'ah. He continued, and I said: he will bow with it. Then he began An-Nisa', and recited it. Then he began Al-'Imran, and recited it. He recited deliberately, and when he passed a verse of glorification, he glorified God." The report continues.

It is possible that it refers to the part understood from His words, ﴿and during part of the night﴾, with the *ba'* being for the adverbial sense, i.e., "keep vigil in that part." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it refers to the time implied in the noble wording, i.e., "Rise at a time of the night and keep vigil in it," ﴿as an extra gift for you﴾, meaning an additional obligation beyond the five obligatory prayers, specific to you alone and not the community (*ummah*). Perhaps this is the reason for mentioning it after the mention of the dawn prayer, despite its time preceding the time of that prayer. It was used as evidence that what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to do, his community is also commanded to do, unless a proof indicates specificity, as here. What indicates that the intended meaning is what has been mentioned is what Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said regarding it: meaning specifically for the Prophet (ﷺ): "He was commanded to stand in prayer at night, and it was prescribed for him, but the correct view is that the obligation of *tahajjud* was abrogated for him," and Abu Hamid of the Shafi'is transmitted it and said: "It is the sound view."

It was also said: the address in "for you" is to him (ﷺ), and what is meant is him and his community, in the manner of the address in ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ earlier; i.e., an additional obligation beyond the five prayers for your benefit. So in this there is evidence for the obligation of *tahajjud* upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, and upon his community; but this was abrogated for the community and remained for him, peace and blessings be upon him, based on what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "The standing in prayer at night was abrogated except for the Prophet (ﷺ)." Or it was abrogated for him (ﷺ) as well, based on the sound view; and this is very contrary to the apparent meaning.

It is possible that *nafilah* means excellence: either because he, peace and blessings be upon him, was favored over his community by its being obligatory for him, though it was later abrogated; or because it is an excellence for him (ﷺ) and an increase in his ranks, and it is not, in relation to him, an expiation for sins or a filler for the deficiency found in the obligatory acts, just as it and the rest of the supererogatory acts are in relation to the community in that way. Because he, peace and blessings be upon him, has been forgiven what preceded of his sin and what followed, and his obligatory acts and all his acts of worship were done in the most perfect manner.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and Ibn Jarir and others transmitted this last view from Mujahid; Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted it from Qatadah; and Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Hasan. The Imam (al-Razi) found it good, while al-Tabari considered it weak. Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed the generality of the address, as you have just heard, except that he took *nafilah* to mean *tatawwu'* (voluntary), and this too is nothing.

Perhaps it occurs to some minds, based on what was mentioned earlier from Abu al-Baqa' regarding His words, ﴿the practice of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾, that it is by way of implicit: "Follow the practice of," as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿so follow their guidance﴾. The possibility is that His words, ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ and so on, are an explanation of the following that is commanded, and it includes the command to the five obligatory prayers. The prophets, peace be upon them, used to pray them, as indicated by the words of Gabriel, peace be upon him, in the report of his teaching the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, the manner of prayer after his prayer of the five: "This is the time of the prophets before you." For this is clear that they, peace be upon them, used to pray them. The most that can be said is that on the view that they were not combined for anyone other than our Prophet (ﷺ), which is the sound view, it is possible that what is meant is that it is their time in general, even if some of them were specified with a particular time. It is reported that the dawn prayer belonged to Adam, the noon prayer to David, and in another narration to Abraham; the afternoon prayer to Solomon, and in another narration to Jonah; the sunset prayer to Jacob, and in another narration to Jesus; and the night prayer to Jonah, and in another narration to Moses, peace be upon them all. However, this does not harm; rather, it is more fitting to the command to follow the practice of all of them.

The Imam (al-Razi) argued that he (ﷺ) is superior to the rest of the prophets, peace be upon them, by His words, ﴿so follow their guidance﴾, from the aspect that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded to follow the guidance of all of them, and he complied with that. So he possessed the guidance that all of them possessed, and thus he is superior to each one of them. Then it may be said: the meaning of this being an extra gift for him, peace and blessings be upon him, is that it is beyond the five prayers and specific to him (ﷺ), not to the rest of the prophets, peace be upon them, who were commanded to follow their practice. This is something that should not be turned to or relied upon; rather, what is fitting is that it be considered as one of the imaginings of the soul, a sea of musk whose waves are gold, for its corruption, in its roots and branches, is not hidden from anyone who has the least understanding and the least knowledge. And God, Exalted is He, is the Protector from error and the Guardian from mistake and confusion.

The accusative of *nafilah* is either as a verbal noun (*masdar*) with an implied *tanaffal* (perform a supererogatory act). Al-Hufi estimated *naffalnaka* (We have granted you a supererogatory gift); or by making *tahajjad* mean *tanaffal*; or by making *nafilah* mean *tahajjudan* (as a form of *tahajjud*), since that is an additional act of worship. Or it is in the state (*hal*) of the pronoun referring to the Qur'an, i.e., in the state of being a supererogatory prayer, as Abu al-Baqa' said. Or it is as the object of *tahajjad*, as al-Hufi allowed if it means *salli* (pray). Or the genitive pronoun is referring to the implied part, or to the implied time; i.e., "pray in it as a supererogatory prayer for you."

﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you﴾, who brings you to your fitting perfection, after the greatest death, since you were raised from the lesser death through prayer and worship. The meaning is by way of causation and of easing the hardship of standing in prayer at night. Some even claimed that *'asa* means *kay* (in order that), but this is a mistake; rather, as the scholars of rhetoric (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said, it is for raising hope. Since it is the way of a generous person to raise a person's hope in something and then deny him it, which would be deception, and God, Exalted and Glorified is He, is far too majestic and generous to deceive anyone, raising his hope for something and then not giving it to him, they said: it is for obligation from Him, may His majesty be exalted, in the sense that what raises hope is certainly going to happen, as a promise. It was also said: it remains on its original meaning, of hoping, but it is turned toward the one addressed, i.e., "Let there be hope in you that your Lord will raise you ﴿to a praised station﴾." It is complete (*tamma*), and ﴿that your Lord will raise you﴾ is its subject, and "your Lord" is the agent of it, and ﴿a station﴾, as a group said, is in the accusative as an adverb of place, either by implying the verb of establishing, or by including that meaning in the verb mentioned: "It may be that He will raise you and establish you in a station," or "He will establish you in a praised station," raising you. For it is not valid for such an adverb of place to be governed except by a verb carrying the meaning of settling, unlike al-Kisa'i's view. Al-Bahr favored that it is the object of *yab'athaka* (raise you), and it is a verbal noun from a root other than the verb itself, because *nab'athu* means *nuqimu* (we establish); you say: "He was raised (*uqima*) from his grave," and "He was raised (*bu'itha*) from his grave."

Abu al-Baqa' and others allowed that it is in the state of an implied genitive: i.e., "We raise you as one possessing a station." It was also said: it may be the direct object of *yab'athaka*, by including in it the meaning of "give you," as in "He gives you a station." Abu Hayyan allowed that *'asa* is defective (*naqisah*), and "your Lord" is the agent, with ﴿a station﴾ governed by an implied verb other than *yab'athu*, to avoid separating the governing word from what it governs by a foreign element. The indefiniteness of "a station" is for magnification. The intended station is the station of the Great Intercession (*al-shafa'ah al-'uzma*) in the judgment, where no one is except under his banner (ﷺ).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 79 (part 2 of 3):**

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The sun will draw near until the sweat reaches the middle of the ear. While they are in that state, they will seek help from Adam. He will say: I am not the one for that. Then Musa (Moses), and he will say the same. Then Muhammad, and he will intercede. Allah will then judge among the creation, and he will walk until he takes hold of the ring of the Gate of Paradise. On that day Allah will raise him to a praiseworthy station (maqam mahmud), which all the people of the gathering will praise.'"

Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and graded it as hasan (sound-good), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, and I say this without boasting. In my hand is the banner of praise, and I say this without boasting. There is no prophet on that day, from Adam onward, who is not under my banner. I am the first whom the earth will split open for, and I say this without boasting. The people will be struck with terror three times. They will come to Adam and say: 'You are our father, so intercede for us with your Lord.' He will say: 'I committed a sin for which I was sent down to the earth. Rather, go to Nuh (Noah).' They will come to Nuh, and he will say: 'I invoked a supplication against the people of the earth, and they were destroyed. Rather, go to Ibrahim (Abraham).' They will come to Ibrahim, and he will say: 'Go to Musa.' He will say: 'I killed a soul. Rather, go to Isa (Jesus).' He will say: 'I was worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted. Rather, go to Muhammad.' They will come to me, and I will set out with them. I will take hold of the ring of the Gate of Paradise and knock on it, and it will be said: 'Who is this?' I will say: 'Muhammad.' They will open for me and say: 'Welcome.' I will fall down in prostration, and Allah, the Exalted, will inspire me with praise, thanks and glory. It will be said: 'Raise your head. Ask, and you will be given. Intercede, and your intercession will be accepted. Speak, and your speech will be heard.' This is the praiseworthy station of which Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [17:79]."

[p. 141]

In some narrations it is mentioned that he (peace and blessings be upon him) prostrates four times, i.e., like the prostration of prayer, as is apparent, beneath the Throne, and so his plea is answered for what they sought from him. Al-Ghazali, in al-Durra al-Fakhira, mentioned that the interval between their coming to one prophet and their coming to the next was a thousand years, but this has no basis, as the hafiz Ibn Hajar said. It has also been said that this is the station of intercession for his community (ﷺ), based on what Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the praiseworthy station in the verse, and he said: "It is the station in which I will intercede for my community."

Those who held the first view answered that it is possible that what is meant is the station in which he first intercedes for his community.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from Abu Hurayra as well, in a long hadith about intercession, in which the people went to Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa (peace be upon them), and each of them excused himself for a sin, except Isa (peace be upon him). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They will come to me, meaning the people, after those prophets (peace be upon them) whom I have mentioned, and they will say: 'O Muhammad, you are the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets. Allah has forgiven you your earlier and later sins. Intercede for us with your Lord. Do you not see what we are in?' So I will set out and come beneath the Throne, and I will fall down in prostration to my Lord. Then Allah will open for me of His praises and of the excellence of His praise something He has not opened for anyone before me. Then it will be said: 'O Muhammad, raise your head. Ask, and you will be given. Intercede, and your intercession will be accepted.' So I will raise my head and say: 'My community, O Lord!' It will be said: 'O Muhammad, admit from your community those who have no reckoning, through the right-hand door of the gates of Paradise, and they will share with the people in the other doors.'"

Some people interpreted it as the station of intercession at the place of gathering, where all acknowledge their inability. This is more general, whether it is a general intercession for the judgment to be decided, or a specific intercession for some of the sinners of his community (ﷺ) to be pardoned. Restricting the account to one of the two in some reports is for a reason required by the situation, and for every situation there is a suitable statement. The carrying of this intercession for the community in the report of Abu Hurayra mentioned above to the intercession for some of its sinners at the place of gathering, before they enter the Fire, is the only way. Otherwise, if what is meant is intercession for them after the reckoning, and after the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire the Fire, as is narrated from Abu Sa'id, then the reports cannot be reconciled except by saying: the praiseworthy station is the station of intercession, in the general sense, whether it occurs at the place of gathering, whether it is general or specific, and whether it occurs after that. The restriction is for a reason. Indeed, its interpretation as the station of intercession has come in an unqualified form.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the praiseworthy station, and he said: 'It is the intercession.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Wahb, from Abu Hurayra, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The praiseworthy station is the intercession.'"

Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated by various chains from Ibn Abbas that he interpreted it in this way. Then, intercession in itself, although the Prophet (ﷺ) shares it with others, such as the angels, the prophets (peace be upon them), and some believers, the complete intercession and its excellent types are not established for anyone other than him (peace and blessings be upon him). Some have counted the intercession specific to him (ﷺ) as ten, and some commentators on al-Bukhari mentioned it, so let it be referred to. The station is described as praiseworthy according to what has been mentioned, on the basis that the Prophet (ﷺ) will be praised in it for his bounty that reaches the particular and the general among the kinds of mankind.

Al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and a group narrated from Hudhayfa (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The people will be gathered in one plain. The caller will make them hear him, and the sight will reach them. Barefoot, naked, as they were created, standing, no soul will speak except by His permission. Then he will call: 'O Muhammad!' He will say: 'Here I am at Your service, and I am at Your pleasure. The good is in Your hands, and evil is not attributed to You. The one guided is the one You have guided. Your servant is before You. By You and to You, there is no refuge and no escape from You except to You. You are blessed and exalted. Glory be to You, Lord of the House.'" This is the praiseworthy station.

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said about the verse: "He will seat him between Himself and Jibril (peace be upon him), and he will intercede for his community, and that is the praiseworthy station."

[p. 142]

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid that he said: "The praiseworthy station is that He will seat him with Himself on His Throne." You know that the praise in most of these reports is figurative according to those who say that it is specific to praise for bounty. As for those who say that it is not specific, there is no figurative sense.

Al-Wahidi criticized the view that the praiseworthy station is seating him (ﷺ) by the Mighty and Majestic on the Throne, after mentioning its narration from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), saying that it is a vile, repugnant, dreadful statement, and such a thing cannot be authentically attributed to Ibn Abbas. The text of the Book cries out against its corruption in several respects:

First: "Ba'th" (raising) is the opposite of seating. One says: Allah raised the dead when He brought him up from his grave, and I raised the one who kneels or sits, and he rose. So interpreting it this way is interpreting an opposite by its opposite.

Second: If He, glorified and exalted, were seated on the Throne, He would be bounded and finite, and therefore created, exalted far above that.

Third: He, glorified, said: ﴿maqaman﴾ (a station), and did not say: "maq'adan" (a seat). A maqam is the place of standing, not sitting.

Fourth: Foolish and ignorant people say that all the people of Paradise sit with Him, the Exalted, and He asks them about their worldly affairs, so there is no distinction for him (ﷺ) in His seating him with Himself, the Mighty and Majestic.

Fifth: When it is said that the sultan sent so-and-so, it is understood that he sent him to a people to set right their affairs, and it is not understood that he seated him with himself. End of quote.

Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) had only found the narration of this from Mujahid, so he said: "Mujahid, although he is one of the imams in interpreting the Qur'an, to the extent that it was said: 'If an interpretation comes to you from Mujahid, that is sufficient for you,' nevertheless he has two views that are abandoned among the scholars. One is the interpretation of the praiseworthy station as this seating, and the second is the interpretation of ﴿looking at its Lord﴾ [75:23] as waiting for the reward."

Al-Naqqash narrated from Abu Dawud al-Sijistani that he said: "Whoever denies this hadith, we consider him accused." The people of knowledge continued to narrate it. Ibn Atiyya said: "He meant: whoever denies it on its interpretation, he is accused." It may be interpreted that his (ﷺ) saying: "He will seat me with Him" refers to the elevation of his rank and his honor over creation, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [7:206], and His saying, quoting another: ﴿Build for me a house with You﴾ [66:11], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾ [16:128], and other such things which are metaphors for station, not place.

You know that it is not appropriate for Mujahid or anyone else to interpret the praiseworthy station as seating on the Throne, as you have heard, without it being established to him that this seating is true.

As for a report like that of al-Daylami from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His saying, glorified be He: ﴿It may be that He will raise you﴾, etc.: 'He will seat me with Him on the throne.'"

If the commentator holds to this or something similar, he is answered only by criticizing its authenticity, and once authenticity is established, there is no room for anything but acceptance. What al-Wahidi mentioned does not require that it be unauthentic, for how many a hadith whose authenticity they have affirmed also implies something impossible, like the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, which includes the believers seeing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, then His coming to them in the lowest form of the form in which they saw Him, and His saying to them: ﴿I am your Lord﴾, and their saying: "We seek refuge in Allah from You," until He uncovers a shin for them, so they prostrate, then raise their heads, and He has changed into the form in which they saw Him the first time. This is in the two Sahihs.

And the hadith of Laqit ibn Amir, which includes the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "You will remain as long as you remain, then your Prophet will die, then you will remain as long as you remain, then the Screamer will be sent, by the life of your God, and it will leave no one on its back alive, and the angels who are with your Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and your Lord will turn about the earth, and the lands will be emptied for Him..." until the end of the hadith.

The imams of the Sunnah have narrated this in their books, and they received it with acceptance and submitted to it and yielded to what is beyond counting of this kind. The views of the hadith scholars and the people of thought among the scholars on the discussion of this are not hidden. Whatever you apply there, apply here, for all of it is close to what is close. The Sufis say: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has manifestation in whatever He wills, in whatever form He wills, and He, glorified be He, while manifesting, remains upon His absoluteness, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness, for He is the Mighty, the Wise. And when He, exalted and high, manifested in

[p. 143]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 79 (part 3 of 3):

…a form upon which His rulings (Exalted is He) are applied in terms of manifestation. Thus His glorious majesty is described, according to them, as sitting and the like, in that respect, and by this many matters are resolved. However, it is built upon something whose affirmation is (as difficult as) "plucking the thorny qatad (plant)." And what al-Wahidi mentioned in the third aspect is refuted, that the maqam (station), although originally meaning the place of standing, has become widespread in the sense of any place, and it is also used for rank and nobility. As for what he mentioned in the first aspect, there is nothing there except the explanation of al-maqam al-mahmud (the praiseworthy station) as "seating," not the explanation of al-ba'th (the raising/sending) as "seating." Yes, there is some looseness in it. The meaning is that His placing him in the praiseworthy station is His seating him upon the Throne, and this meaning can be achieved by keeping ba'th in its own meaning, and by estimating "fa-yuqimaka" to mean "fa-yuhilluka" (He will settle you), and by explaining it with iqamah in the sense of ihlal. It may be said: there is no looseness, and what is meant by maqam is rank, and ba'th contains the meaning of giving; i.e., "perhaps your Lord will give you a praiseworthy rank, which is His seating you upon His Throne, raising you up." What he mentioned in the second aspect is correct if by sitting upon the Throne its apparent meaning is intended. If another meaning is intended, we do not accept the implication. The door of interpretation is wide. Sitting with Him has been interpreted as raising of the station and honor, and it is a term applied by gradation. So whenever it is established that all the people of Paradise sit with Him, we believe in it, along with affirming the distinction for the Messenger ﷺ. Thus what he mentioned in the fourth aspect is dispelled. And what he mentioned in the fifth aspect is objected to: sitting with Him was not understood from mere ba'th, and no one claimed that. The statement "the sultan sent so-and-so" is understood from it as sending him to a people to fix their affairs, and it is not understood from it that he seated him with himself. This does not harm us, as is not hidden from a fair-minded person.

In sum: whatever has been said or may be said is not to be heeded, if the interpretation is authentically transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. But then it would still result in a conflict between the apparent meanings of the narrations. From here some of them said: what is meant by al-maqam al-mahmud is whatever encompasses every station that includes honor for him ﷺ, and the restriction in some narrations to one of them is for a particular wisdom, like what has passed. Describing it as "praiseworthy" is either in regard to his ﷺ praising Allah Most High for it with the most eloquent praise, or in regard to every one who witnesses it praising him. It is not required that the praise be in return for a blessing. And included in this is every station of his ﷺ that is praiseworthy in Paradise.

Likewise included in it is what the mufti of the Sufis, my master Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi, permitted: that the praiseworthy station, which is his ﷺ being given a rank of knowledge not given to any other creature at all, is (the meaning). For he mentioned in a treatise of his on creed that the knowledge of the common believers on the Day of Resurrection will be like the knowledge of their scholars in this world, and the knowledge of the scholars at that time will be like the knowledge of the prophets (peace be upon them), and the knowledge of the prophets will be like the knowledge of our Prophet ﷺ, and our Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) will be given knowledge that no one among the worlds has been given. Perhaps this is the praiseworthy station, though I have not seen this attributed to anyone else, may God have mercy on him. And Allah Most High knows best.

Then this disagreement about the praiseworthy station here did not arise concerning it in the adhan supplication, rather the scholar Ibn Hajar al-Haytami claimed that in it is the station of the Great Intercession for the judgment to be decided, by consensus. So reflect upon this station. And Allah Most High is the Bestower of favors and of understanding.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 80:**

﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance"﴾. That is: an entrance that is pleasing and good, in which nothing disliked is seen. The idafah (genitive construction) here is for emphasis (mubalaghah).

﴿And cause me to exit a sound exit﴾ is similar to the first. Scholars differ on determining what is meant by this. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar related from Zayd ibn Aslam that what is meant is entering Madinah and exiting Makkah. What supports this is what has been said regarding the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed they were about to unsettle you﴾, and so on.

This is reinforced by what Ahmad, al-Tabarani, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and a group of others related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was in Makkah, then he was commanded to emigrate, so God, Exalted is He, revealed to him: ﴿And say, 'My Lord...'﴾ [the verse]." He began with entering because it is the more important.

Page 144

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that it means entering the grave and exiting from it, and this is reinforced by its mention after resurrection (al-ba'th). It has also been said: entering Makkah openly by conquest, and his exit from it (ﷺ) safe from the polytheists. It has been said: his exit from Madinah and his entry into Makkah by conquest. Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said: his entering the cave and his exit from it. It has been said: entering Paradise and exiting Makkah. It has been said: entering prayer and exiting from it. It has been said: entering into the commanded acts and exiting from the forbidden ones. It has been said: entering into what the Prophet (ﷺ) was charged with of the burdens of prophethood and the conveying of the Law, and his exit from it having discharged what he was charged with without neglect. It has been said: entering into the seas of tawhid (oneness of God) and tanzih (transcendence), and exiting from preoccupation with the proof to knowledge of what is proven, and from contemplation of the signs to total absorption in knowledge of the One, the Subduer. It has been said and said, but the most evident view is that what is meant is his (ﷺ) entering into everything he enters into and engages with, whether a place or a matter, and his exit from it. Thus it is general over all the places of entry and departure. Abu Hayyan favoured this view. In al-Kashf it is stated that this is the view that agrees with the apparent sense of the wording and conforms to the requirement of the composition (nazm), for what precedes and what follows it are not restricted to one place rather than another. And it suffices as evidence for it the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And grant me from You a supporting authority﴾, and so on, as a witness of sincerity regarding His preference for him.

Qatadah, Abu Haywah, Humayd, and Ibrahim ibn Abi Ablah read "madkhala" and "makhraja" with a fatha on the meem in both. The author of al-Lawami' said: both are verbal nouns (masadir) from "dakhala" and "kharaja", but they came from the meaning of the preceding imperatives, "adkhilni" and "akhrijni", rather than from their own wording. Similar to this is the saying: ﴿And God caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾. It is also permissible that they be nouns of place, their accusative being adverbial of place (zarf). Other verifiers said: they are verbal nouns in the accusative, under the assumption of two triliteral verbs, since the verbal noun of the derived forms has a dammah on the meem, as in the widely transmitted reading. That is: "Cause me to enter, so that I enter a sound entrance, and cause me to exit, so that I exit a sound exit."

﴿And grant me from Yourself a supporting authority﴾: that is, a proof that gives me victory over whoever opposes me. This is what Mujahid meant by his saying "a clear proof". In another report from him, it is a book containing the hudud (prescribed punishments) and the rulings. From al-Hasan: it is meant to have dominion over the disbelievers by the sword and over the hypocrites by establishing the hudud. Close to this is what has been said: that what is meant is power and might by which you support Islam over others.

Some claimed that it is the conquest of Makkah. It has been said: "sultan" is one of the rulers and kings, so the intended meaning seems to be a supplication that in every era there be a king who supports the religion of God, Exalted is He. It has been said: this is the apparent meaning of what al-Bayhaqi related in al-Dala'il and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, from Qatadah, who said: "God, Exalted is He, brought him out of Makkah with a sound exit and caused him to enter Madinah with a sound entrance. The Prophet of God knew that he had no capacity for this matter except with an authority, so he asked for a supporting authority for the Book of God, Exalted is He, and His hudud and obligations, for authority is a might from God, Mighty and Majestic, which He placed among His servants. Were it not so, some of them would raid others and the strong would devour the weak." There is something to examine in this. The form fa'il (nasir) in all its other aspects is an intensive form (mubalagha) of the active participle.

It is allowed that in some aspects it carries the sense of the passive participle. The truth is that what is meant by "sultan" is everything that conveys dominance over the enemies of God, Exalted is He, and the manifestation of His religion, glorified is His majesty. He described it as "nasir" (supporting) for emphasis.

﴿And say, "The truth has come"﴾: that is, Islam and the religion that is firm and established.

The clause is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical coordination) with the earlier clause "say" (*qul*). The possibility that it is part of the content of the first speech (*maqul al-qawl*, what is said) is very remote, because it implies a response, which is highly unlikely.

﴿And falsehood has vanished﴾: that is, it passed away and was annihilated, and did not establish polytheism, disbelief, and the whisperings of Satan. The verb is from "zahaqat nafsuhu," meaning his soul departed from him in distress. It is related from Qatadah that the truth is the Qur'an and the falsehood is Satan. It is related from Ibn Jurayj that the first (the truth) is jihad and the second (falsehood) is polytheism. It is related from Muqatil: the truth is the worship of God Most High, and the falsehood is the worship of Satan. This is close to what we have mentioned.

Page 145

﴿Indeed, falsehood﴾, whatever it may be, ﴿was bound to vanish﴾: annihilated, not established now or hereafter, or absolutely, because it is as if it had never existed. The form *fa'ul* (فَعُولٌ) is used for intensive emphasis (*mubalagha*).

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and a group related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah while around the House there were three hundred and sixty idols. He began striking them with a stick in his hand, saying: ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed, falsehood was bound to vanish﴾, and ﴿The truth has come, and falsehood neither originates nor restores﴾."

In the narration of al-Tabarani in *al-Saghir* and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il*, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) came with a staff, and he began pointing it at each idol among them, and it would fall on its face, while he said: ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed, falsehood was bound to vanish﴾, until he had passed by all of them.

[p. 146] ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers﴾. That is, it is, in the preparation of their religion and the reform of their souls, like the healing medicine for the sick. The *min* here is for specification (*li-al-bayan*), and it is placed first out of concern for its importance. Abu Hayyan denied the permissibility of this fronting and chose here that *min* is for the beginning of the limit (*li-ibtida' al-ghayah*). This denial is not accepted, and it implies that the whole Qur'an is so.

In a report: "Whoever does not seek healing through the Qur'an, may Allah the Exalted not heal him."

Or *min* is partitive (*li-al-tab'id*), and its meaning, according to what is in *al-Kashshaf*, is: "We send down that which is a healing," i.e., it descends gradually, healing by healing. It does not mean that it is divided into what is a healing and what is not a healing. The first "sent down" thing, as al-Huwfi mistakenly thought, led him to deny the permissibility of the partitive sense. Rather, the meaning is that what has not yet been sent down is not a healing for the believers, due to their not having knowledge of it, and that everything that is sent down is a healing for a particular disease, the healing renewing its descent in proportion to the renewal of the disease. In this there is also the point that this view is more suitable to the requirement of the context. Its remoteness is not hidden from you. For this reason, in the explanation of the partitive sense, it has been chosen that it is with regard to physical healing, which is a property of some portions and not others. Among the first portion is al-Fatihah, which has well-known effects. The verses of healing are six: ﴿And He will heal the breasts of a believing people﴾; ﴿and healing for what is in the breasts﴾; ﴿In it is healing for mankind﴾; ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers﴾; ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾; ﴿Say, "It is for those who believe a guidance and healing"﴾.

Al-Subki said: "I have tried it much." It is related from al-Qushayri that a son of his fell ill and he despaired of his life. He saw Allah the Exalted in a dream and complained to Him of that. He (glorified is He) said to him: "Gather the verses of healing and recite them over him, or write them in a vessel and give him to drink what has been wiped off with it." He did so, and Allah the Exalted healed him. The physicians acknowledge that among things and incantations there is that which heals by a spiritual property, as al-Andalusi detailed in his *Mufradat*, and likewise Dawud in the second volume of his *Tadhkirah*. Whoever denies this is not to be heeded.

Yes, the scholars differed on the permissibility of things like what al-Qushayri did, by way of visions, and it is a kind of *nashrah* (the unbinding of spells). They defined it as: that some of the names of Allah the Exalted or of the Qur'an be written, then washed with water, and then the patient is wiped with it or is given it to drink. Al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and Mujahid forbade this.

Abu Dawud related from the hadith of Jabir that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about *nashrah* and said: 'It is from the work of Satan.'"

Ibn al-Musayyib permitted this. The *nashrah* about which the Prophet (ﷺ) said what he said is the *nashrah* that was practiced in the Jahiliyyah, and it is of various kinds. Among them is what the practitioners of *ta'zim* (formulaic incantation) do in most eras: reciting things whose meaning is unknown and which are not established in the Sunnah, or writing them and hanging them, or giving them to drink. Malik said: "There is no harm in hanging books in which are the names of Allah the Exalted on the necks of the sick, seeking blessing through them, provided the one who hangs them does not intend by it to repel the evil eye." He meant by this that there is no harm in hanging them after the affliction has come, hoping for relief and goodness, like the incantations (*ruqa*) for the evil eye which the Sunnah has reported. As for before the affliction descends, there is harm in it, and this is an unusual view. According to Ibn al-Musayyib, it is permissible to hang an amulet (*'awdhah*) from the Book of Allah the Exalted on a reed or the like, and it is placed during intercourse and when relieving oneself, and he did not restrict it to before or after. Al-Baqir permitted an amulet hung on children absolutely. Ibn Sirin did not see any harm in any portion of the Qur'an that a person hangs, whether adult or child, absolutely, and this is what people have followed, past and present, in all the regions. But the explanation of the partitive sense with what has been mentioned is not supported by His saying (glorified is He): ﴿and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾. That is: the entire Qur'an, or each portion of it, does not increase the disbelievers, those who deny it, who place things in other than their proper places, while it is in itself a healing for what is in the breasts of the diseases of doubt and the maladies of illusions.

﴿except in loss﴾: that is, destruction, by their disbelief and denial, and an increase from the standpoint that whenever they renew disbelief and denial toward the verse sent down gradually, they increase in destruction thereby. Some interpreted *khasar* as deficiency. Abu al-Su'ud preferred the first, on the basis that the disease of disbelief and misguidance they have is worthy of being expressed as destruction, not as deficiency, which would indicate the attainment of some principles of Islam in them. In this there is, as he said, an allusion. However, what is in believers of doubts and suspicions that befall them during guidance and seeking direction is in the position of illnesses, and what is in the disbelievers of ignorance and obstinacy is in the position of death and destruction. The attribution of the mentioned increase to the Qur'an, although it is they who increase in it due to their evil conduct, is by consideration of its being the cause of it. In this there is a marvel at its matter, in that it is the locus of both healing and destruction:

"Like water that became pearls in the oyster shells,
and in the mouths of vipers became poison."

Having said this, it may be said: the division of the Qur'an into what is a healing from the diseases of doubt and the maladies of illusion, and into what is not so, of that which should not contain doubt, is because the healing of the diseases of doubt is only through proofs, such as the verses indicating the invalidity of polytheism and the establishment of His oneness, and such as the verses indicating the possibility of bodily resurrection. Not every verse of the Qur'an is like this, for among it is what is a command to prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, and among it is what is a prohibition against killing, fornication, theft, and the like, and these are not cured by it from the diseases of doubt and the maladies of illusion. Likewise the verses of narratives. Yes, in what has been mentioned there is a benefit other than the healing of those diseases, and that is a mercy. Then it may be said: there is an ellipsis in the verse; that is: "We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and that which is a mercy," in the sense of "We send down of the Qur'an verses which are a healing and verses which are a mercy."

In this there is that doubt is not specific to what concerns Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the possibility of resurrection, but it also occurs regarding the prophethood and his truthfulness (ﷺ) in claiming it. And there is no verse in the Qur'an except that it is either independently or has a share in healing from that disease, due to what it contains of inimitability (*i'jaz*). Likewise, there is no verse except that it contains benefit from another aspect. So every verse is a mercy, just as all of it is a healing. But its being a mercy in relation to each individual believer is because each believer benefits from it in some kind of benefit, while its being a healing in actuality is in relation to the one who has been afflicted by some of the diseases of doubt and maladies of illusion, and not all the believers are like that. The claim that all are like that at the beginning of faith is not accepted, nor is it needed, as is not hidden.

The Imam (al-Razi) generalized its healing-ness, and he did well when he said: "It is a healing for spiritual diseases, and these are of two kinds: false beliefs and blameworthy character traits. Because it includes the true proofs that uncover false doctrines regarding theology, prophethood, the afterlife, and divine decree and predestination, clarifying their invalidity, it heals the first kind of disease. And because it includes the details of blameworthy character traits, and the definition of the corruptions in them, and guidance to praiseworthy character traits and commendable deeds, it heals the other kind." Healing is an allusion to *takhliyah* (emptying of vices), and mercy is an allusion to *tahliyah* (adorning with virtues). And because the first is more important than the second, healing is placed before mercy. So reflect. And Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success.

The two Basrans read *nunzilu* with *nun* and without doubling. Mujahid read it with *ya'* and without doubling, and al-Marwazi related it from Hafs.

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with both of them, read *shifa'an wa rahmatan* with the accusative on both. Abu Hayyan said: "This can be construed as both being circumstantial accusatives (*hal*), and the predicate is *lil-mu'minin*, and the governing element of the circumstantial clause is the verb contained in the prepositional phrase. A parallel to this is *wa-al-samawatu matwiyyatun bi-yaminihi* in the reading with the accusative of *matwiyyatin*, and the poet's saying:

"The clan of Ibn Kawz, having tied their shields behind them, are among them, and the clan of Rabi'ah ibn Hadhar."

Then he said: "Placing the circumstantial element before its governing element, when it is an adverbial phrase, is not permitted except according to al-Akhfash. Whoever forbids it makes it accusative by an implied *a'ni* (I mean)." And you know that whoever permits the circumstantial element to come from the subject does not need that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 83:

﴿And when We bestow favor﴾ with health, abundance and the like, ﴿upon man﴾, meaning mankind. The existence of the judgment in some individuals suffices for its truth, and the existence of its opposite in others does no harm. It was said: what is meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. ﴿He turns away﴾ from remembering Us, as if he were independent of Us, let alone fulfilling the duties of thanking Us. ﴿And turns aside with his side﴾: he bends his flank away from obedience to Us and turns his back to it. The basic meaning of *nā'a* (to turn away, to be distant) is distance. This is an emphasis on *al-i'rāḍ* (turning away), by depicting its form, so it is more complete in conveying the intended meaning. Its conjunction (with the preceding phrase) is permissible for the sake of implying a difference between the two, and it is more eloquent than omitting the conjunction, as explained in its proper place. Moreover, what the rhetoricians (*ahl al-ma'ānī*) mention, that emphasis necessarily requires omitting the conjunction because of complete connection, is not accepted. The word *janib* (side) is in its apparent sense, and what is meant is the abandonment of that. It is also permissible that it be a metaphor (*kināya*) for arrogance, for bending the flank is one of the actions of the arrogant. It is not far-fetched that *janib* means the self, as one says "such-and-such came from the side of so-and-so," meaning from him, and this is also a metaphor, just as *maqām* (station) and *majlis* (assembly) are used to refer to their owner. Ibn ʿĀmir, according to the transmission of Ibn Dhakwān, read *wa-nā'a* (with the hamza after the nūn) here and in Fuṣṣilat. It was said that this is by way of *qalb* (metathesis), placing the letter *ʿayn* in the position of the *lām*, as in *rāʾ* and *warāʾ*. It was also said: there is no metathesis; *nā'a* here means "rose up," as in the saying of the poet:

*Until, when his joints were knit, he rose up, and his shoulder-blade was raised on the left side.*

That is, he rose up, leaning on his left side. *Nahaḍa* (rose up) here was explained as "hastened," and the sentence is on the assumption of an elided *muḍāf* (a governed noun), that is: he hastened by turning his side away. It was also said: its meaning is that he was slow to render thanks, acting in the manner of one who turns away. ﴿And when evil touches him﴾ from illness, poverty, or any of the calamities. ﴿He is despairing﴾, exceedingly despairing of Our mercy, because he did not treat Us well in ease, so that he might hope for Our bounty in hardship. The attribution of touching to evil, after the attribution of bestowing to His own pronoun (exalted is He), is an indication that good is willed in itself, whereas evil is not so; for this is what the absolute generosity and the wide mercy require. To this the Prophet (ﷺ) alludes in his saying: "O Allah, the good is in Your hands, and evil is not attributed to You."

The philosophers and those who follow their path in this matter have a lengthy discussion, and there is no harm in becoming acquainted with it, so that what is clear may be taken from it and what is turbid may be left. They said: the First (*al-Awwal*), exalted is He, is perfect in power, wisdom and knowledge, complete in all His acts. His withholding the emanation of goods is inconceivable, and the only motive for Him to do so is His knowledge of the aspects of good and the interests of others, which is identical with His essence, as with all His attributes. As for the deficiencies and evils that occur in some of the possibles, and their failure to reach the perfection conceived for them, these are due to the deficiency of their receptivities (*qābiliyyāt*) and the lack of their preparedness (*istiʿdādāt*), not due to the stinginess of the Truth, exalted is His glory, above that.

The deficiency of receptivity ends, in the Hereafter, in the necessary attributes of the possible quiddities (*māhiyyāt*), and its source is contingency (*imkān*). The verification of this is that evil is used conventionally in two senses. The first is what is a privation (*ʿadam*), such as poverty and simple ignorance. This is of two kinds. The first is pure privation, which is not opposed to the existence that the nature of the thing seeks, nor to any perfections and goods that could be attained by it, such as the deficiency of the possible in relation to necessary existence and essential necessity, and the deficiency of some possibles in relation to others, such as the deficiency of bodies in relation to souls. The good that is opposed to this is confined to the Necessary Existent, exalted is He, for He possesses absolute perfection and true existence without any possible aspect in any respect. Everything other than Him, of the dispositions that are accidental to existence, does not escape some admixture of evil and some darkness, according to the variation of their possibilities in accordance with the variation of their ranks in distance from the fountainhead of existence and the rising-place of the light of goodness and generosity. This evil has its source in essential contingency. The second kind is the privation of what the thing seeks, or of the perfections that could be attained by it. This is not conceivable in non-material beings, for the originated intelligibles (*ibdāʿiyyāt*) have their existence in the most perfect form conceivable for them, so there is no evil in them in this sense. Whatever else is connected to matter does not escape some evil, according to the variation of their potential preparednesses, in accordance with the variation of their levels in attachment to *hayūlā* (prime matter). This evil has its source in prime matter, and the source of prime matter is contingency; for were it not for contingency, they would not have proceeded from their source. Thus evil ultimately returns to contingency, as you have heard at the beginning.

The second sense is what prevents a thing from reaching the good possible for it, whether existence or the perfection of existence, such as cold and heat that spoil fruits, and rain that prevents launderers from whitening clothes; and the blameworthy character traits that prevent the soul from reaching its intellectual perfection, such as stinginess, extravagance, compound ignorance, foolishness; and blameworthy actions such as fornication, theft, slander, and things similar to these; and pains and griefs, and other things among existent things, but which are followed by a non-existence. The application of the word "evil" by them to the first sense is literal, and to the second sense is metaphorical. For true evil has no essence of its own; rather it is either the non-existence of an essence or the non-existence of a perfection of an essence. The proof of this is that if it were an existential thing, it would either be evil in itself or evil for something else. The first is false, otherwise it would not exist, since a thing does not necessitate, by its essence, its non-existence or the non-existence of its perfection. How could that be, when all things seek their perfections and do not necessitate their non-existence? Moreover, if it did necessitate it, the evil would be that non-existence, not the thing itself. Likewise the second: its being evil for something else is either because it causes the non-existence of that other thing, or because it causes the non-existence of some of its perfections. For if it caused the privation of nothing at all, neither of its existence nor of the perfection of its existence, it would not be evil for that thing, by necessity; because whatever does not cause the non-existence of a thing or the non-existence of its perfection is not evil for it. Therefore evil is nothing but the non-existence of that thing or the non-existence of its perfection, not the existential matter that has been made non-existent. Rather, it is in itself among the psychic or bodily perfections, like injustice; for although it is evil in relation to the one wronged and to the rational soul whose perfection lies in subduing its powers and breaking them, it is good in relation to the irascible power, whose perfection lies in retaliation. Likewise burning is a perfection of fire and an evil for whoever is harmed by it. Thus it is known that evil is either the non-existence of an essence or the non-existence of a perfection of it. So existence, insofar as it is existence, is pure good, and non-existence, insofar as it is non-existence, is pure evil.

Then you have learned that evil, in the sense of privation, is of two kinds: some of it is among the necessary attributes of quiddities that have no cause, and some of it is not of this kind but rather befalls quiddities not from their essence, so it must have a cause. The discussion is not about the first, which has no *lamm* (quiddity-whence, i.e., no ground); for it has been established that quiddities have no cause for their being possible, nor for their need of a cause for their existence, nor for the deficiency of the possible in relation to the Necessary Existent by Himself, nor for the variation of the levels of this deficiency among quiddities. Rather, that is due to the difference of the quiddities in the limits of their essences, not due to something external to them. How could it be otherwise? For if the deficiency were similar in all of them, the quiddities would be one single quiddity. Rather, the discussion concerns the second, which is the non-existence of something that is among the additional matters beyond what the species requires,
[Page 149]
like ignorance of philosophy for a human, for example. That is not evil for him because he is a human, but because it is the absence of what a person prepared for it, longing for it, would demand, insofar as this readiness and longing exist in him; and it is not beneficial that this should be general.

This evil is found in things only in the manner of rarity. So everything that exists is either pure good, or its good is greater than its evil. As for what is pure evil, or whose evil dominates, or whose two sides are equal, such things have no existence at all, so as to require a source for them other than the Necessary Existent, who is pure good, from whom no evil at all proceeds, as the disbelieving Magians imagined. Then everything that is pure good, or whose good is greater, proceeds from the Necessary Existent, by virtue of the fact that it is in His nature to bestow goodness; for the abandonment of the first is pure evil, and the abandonment of the second is predominant evil. The world of the elements belongs to the second category. For His causing evils in a rare manner is not incompatible with the solicitude of the Originator and the mercy of the Generous; and if He neglected it, there would follow a great good forfeited for a small evil, which is itself a great evil. Moreover, these [evils] are for the benefit of things which, had they not been created, the garment of existence would not have been woven, the mantle of generosity would have been shortened, and many worlds and abundant, vast treasures would have remained in the veil of non-existence. From this aspect, that small evil is necessitated per se, though it exists under the sphere of the moon, in some parts of the earth, which are insignificant, indeed nothing in relation to what is with your Lord, glory be to Him. It occurs to some individuals at some times, and it is not even evil in relation to the order of the whole. So when you conceive the speck of evil within the oceans of the rays of the sun of good, it does not harm them, but rather increases them in splendour, beauty, radiance and perfection, like the black beauty mark upon a fair, lovely face, which increases its loveliness, charm, brightness and radiance.

It is not hidden that this holds only upon the view that He, exalted is He, cannot have His will equally related to a thing and its opposite without a motive or an interest, as is the doctrine of the Ash'arites (*al-Ashāʿira*). Otherwise, it may be said: the agent of all things, if He is free in choice, may choose whatever He wills of goods and evils. But the sages and the pillars of Islam (*asāṭīn al-Islām*) said: His choice, exalted is He, is higher than this type; the affairs of the world are bound to universal laws, and His acts, exalted is He, are tied to wisdoms and interests, both manifest and hidden.

As for the saying of the Imam: since the philosophers spoke of necessitation and compulsion in acts, their deliberation on this matter is among the superfluities and errors, because the question "why" about their emanation is not applicable, like the emanation of burning from fire, since it issues from it by its very essence. This arises from partisanship, for their verifiers affirm free choice. And the emanation of acts from God, exalted is He, according to them is not like the emanation of burning from fire. And after granting this supposition, their investigation of how evil occurs in this world is, for the reason that the Creator, blessed is His name, is according to them pure, simple good, and they do not allow the emanation of evil from what has no aspect of evil in it at all. It would then follow for them, at first glance, the affirmation of what the Dualists (*al-Thanawiyya*) fabricated, namely two principles, one good and one evil. So they escaped from that by means of this investigation. Thus it is a virtue, not a superfluity. In sum: what emanates from Him, exalted is He, is either something entirely free of evil, or something that entails a small evil whose abandonment would entail a great evil. He, exalted is He, does not emanate such a thing in relation to any person except after the quiddity of that person seeks it for itself, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿He gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾, and other verses to this effect.

In the *al-Ishārāt* and its commentaries there is a lengthy discussion related to this station, and perhaps what we have mentioned suffices for those of understanding.

(p. 150) ...This is what it is. Then, after He, glorified is He, mentioned the state of the Qur'an in relation to the believers and the disbelievers, and explained the condition of the disbeliever in the two states of bounty and its opposite, He mentioned what is suitable as an answer to the question: "Why is the matter so?" So He, mighty is His saying, said: ﴿Say: Each one acts according to his manner﴾. That is, each one, of the believer and the disbeliever, the one who turns away and the one who turns toward, the one who hopes and the one who despairs, ﴿acts﴾

(p. 150) his deed ﴿according to his manner﴾. That is, according to his way and his method, which accords with his state and with what he is in reality, and its resemblance in goodness and ugliness. From their saying: "a road with shawakil (branches)," meaning roads branching off from it. It is derived from the shakl (شكل), with a fatha on the shin, meaning the like and the equal. It is said: "You are not of my shakl (kind) nor my shakila (counterpart)." As for the shikl (شكل), with a kasra on the shin, it means the form or appearance.
