It is said: "a girl of good shikl," that is, good appearance. The apparent wording of the Qamus (the dictionary of al-Firuzabadi) is that each of shakl and shikl is used for both the like and the form.

This interpretation is narrated from al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, and al-Zamakhshari and others chose it, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way﴾, that is, the one who created you differing, ﴿who is best guided in the way﴾, the most direct path and the clearest course. Mujahid interpreted shakila as "nature," taking it from shakaltu al-dabba (I tied the animal) when you restrain it; that is, according to its nature, by which you have restrained him, because the dominion of nature over man is evident, and it governs him and overpowers him. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Similar in its source is the interpretation of some as "habit," and among their well-known sayings is: "Habits are compelling." Likewise, Ibn Zayd's interpretation of it as "religion." Both of these interpretations are less apt than the first two. Perhaps "religion" here carries the meaning of "state," which is one of its meanings.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) and others permitted that the intended meaning is that every person acts according to what accords with the essence of his self and the requirement of his spirit. If it is a self that is luminous, free, pure, and lofty, noble actions proceed from him, ﴿And the good land brings forth its plants by the permission of its Lord﴾. If it is a self that is turbid, base, wicked, dark, and low, vile and corrupt actions proceed from him, ﴿And that which is bad comes forth only with difficulty﴾. He chose that human rational souls differ in their quiddity (mahiyya, essential reality); therefore their effects differ. The discussion of this will come, God willing, shortly. It is not an objection that the baseness and nobility of actions, if they follow from the baseness and nobility of the soul, and these two are innate qualities in which choice has no part, then why is there praise and blame, reward and punishment? For they have said that this is due to an essential matter, namely the goodness of the soul's readiness in itself and the badness of its readiness also in itself, and the soul is not rewarded or punished except for its readiness in eternity and its seeking of that through the tongue of its state. The well-known position is an absolute statement that this is not made (by God), but rather what is made is its existence and its manifestation in accordance with what it is in itself. So act, for each is made easy for what he was created for. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame none but himself. Some said that it is made by simple making (al-ja'l al-basit, the simple causation of existence), meaning that it is the effect of the most holy overflow, which is the requirement of His essence, mighty and majestic is He, by way of necessity. What is similar to this applies to the first two aspects.

Some of the later philosophers of Islam, who undertook to combine the Shari'a and philosophy according to their opinion, said: The human essence, according to its original nature (fitra), requires only obedience. Its requirement of disobedience comes from extraneous accidents, which function like illness and departure from the natural state. Therefore its inclination toward disobedience is like the inclination of one whose original temperament is distorted toward eating clay. It has been established in philosophy that nature, through an extraneous accidental cause, produces in the body of the sick a particular temperament called illness. So illness comes from nature through the mediation of the extraneous accident, just as health comes from it.

In the sacred hadith: "I created My servants all as hunafa' (upright monotheists), and the devils came to them and led them astray from their religion."

And in a report: "Every child is born upon the fitra (innate nature) of Islam, then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian."

That is, through the mediation of the devils. Or the intended meaning is what includes the devils of mankind and jinn. Or "devils" is a metaphor for the extraneous accidents. So if no touch of the devil had reached them, they would not have disobeyed, or they would have remained upon their fitra. But the devil touched them, and so their original fitra was corrupted for them.

(p. 151) Thus they sought things that were contrary to them, opposed to their radiant divine essence, from the dark states, and forgot themselves and what they had been created upon:

Had it not been for the disturbing nights, the sandgrouse would not have abandoned the sweetness of sleep.

For this reason they needed messengers who would convey to them the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and establish for them what reminds them of the covenant of their essences, such as prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and maintaining ties of kinship, so that they might return to their original fitra and the requirement of their radiant essences, and their temperament would be balanced and their crookedness straightened. For this reason it is said: "The prophets are physicians," and they know best the disease and the remedy. Moreover, that illness which afflicted their essences and that contrary state which settled upon them would not have occurred or attached to them, had their essences not found in themselves an acceptance for their occurrence and a permission for their taking hold within them. So if it is among what their essences require that contrary, opposing matters should attach to them, then when those matters attach to them, two aspects are combined in them: agreeableness and contrariety. As for their being agreeable, it is because their essences required them. As for their being contrary, it is because they required them in a way that makes them contrary to them. For if they were not contrary, what was supposed to be required by them would not be required, but rather something else. Consider the nature that requires a dryness which holds any shape whatever, until it becomes retaining the forced shape that is contrary to its natural roundness, and is prevented from returning to it. The occurrence of that shape to earthiness is because it is constrained in one respect and natural in another. So the human being, upon the occurrence of such a contrary, is delighted and pained, happy and wretched, delighted. But his delight is his pain, and his happiness is his wretchedness. This, by your life, is a wonderful matter, but it is clarified in a strange pattern. Whoever reflects and is fair will see that many of the doubts in this chapter can only be resolved by going to the saying of eternal readiness, and that everything has a state in itself, apart from all other considerations, which is not bestowed upon it except that state, lest knowledge turn into ignorance, which is among the greatest impossibilities. Reward and punishment follow from that. Glory be to the Wise, the Owner. So be firm. How many feet have slipped in this station, feet of great scholars like the mountains. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to illuminate our understanding and make our feet firm, and there is no power nor might except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

Then know that it was narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I have not seen in the Qur'an a verse that gives more hope than this one: nothing matches the servant except disobedience, and nothing matches the Lord except forgiveness." He said this when they were discussing the Qur'an. Then 'Umar said: "I have not seen a verse more hopeful than the one in which is: ﴿Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance﴾, where He placed forgiveness before the acceptance of repentance." And 'Uthman said: "I have not seen a verse more hopeful than: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾."

And 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, said: "I have not seen a verse more hopeful than: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾," to the end of the verse.

Other things have been said about the most hopeful verse, and it will pass over you, God willing. But what al-Siddiq said is only possible on the assumption that what is intended is: everyone, absolutely, acts according to his manner. So understand.

**[Page 152]**

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 17, verse 85 (part 1 of 5):

﴿They ask you about the Spirit.﴾ To the impartial scholar, the apparent meaning is that the question concerned the reality of the Spirit (*al-ruh*), which is the sustainer of the human body and the source of its life. This is because it is among the most subtle matters, which no one can deny, toward which everyone yearns to know, toward which the intellects of the wise are strongly drawn, and before which minds fall short. It is hardly known except through revelation. Ibn al-Qayyim claimed that what was asked about is the Spirit
**[Page 153]**
about which God Almighty informed in His Book that it will stand on the Day of Resurrection together with the angels, peace be upon them. He said: "They were asking him, peace and blessings be upon him, about a matter that is not known except through revelation, and that is the Spirit which is with God Almighty and which people do not know. As for the spirits of the children of Adam, they are not among the unseen…" to the end of what he said, and he made it long.

In *al-Buhur al-Zakhira*: "This is the view held by most of the early scholars (*al-salaf*), indeed by all of them. The truth is what we have mentioned, and it is the view of the majority, as stated explicitly in *al-Bahr* and elsewhere."

Yes, what Ibn al-Qayyim claimed is related from some of the early scholars. Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The Spirit is a creation of God Almighty, and He fashioned them in the form of the children of Adam. No angel descends from the sky except that with him is one of the Spirits." Then he recited: ﴿The day the Spirit and the angels stand [in rows]﴾.

Abu al-Shaykh and others narrated through the chain of Ata from him, may God be pleased with him, that he said about the Spirit being asked about: "He is one angel who has ten thousand wings; two of them span from the east to the west. He has a thousand faces, and for each face a tongue, two eyes, and two lips. He glorifies God Almighty with them until the Day of Resurrection."

He and others also narrated from Ali, may God honour his face, that he said about it: "He is an angel among the angels who has seventy thousand faces, and for each face seventy thousand tongues, and for each tongue seventy thousand languages. He glorifies God Almighty with all those languages, and God creates from every glorification an angel who flies with the angels until the Day of Resurrection."

This has been criticised by saying that it is not authentically related from Ali, may God honour his face, and the Imam (al-Razi) criticised it with what he criticised.

Ibn al-Anbari narrated in *Kitab al-Adda*d from Mujahid that he said: "The Spirit is a creation from among the angels, peace be upon them, whom the angels do not see, just as you do not see the angels."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Salman that he said: "Humans and jinn are ten parts: humans are one part, and the jinn are nine parts. The angels and the jinn are ten parts: the jinn are one part of that, and the angels are nine. The angels and the Spirit are ten parts: the angels are one part of that, and the Spirit is nine. The Spirit and the Kerubiyyun are ten parts: the Spirit is one part of that, and the Kerubiyyun are nine."

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: "The Spirit is Jibril, peace be upon him, and he has been named a spirit in God's words: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ ﴿upon your heart﴾. The question was about how he descends and how he casts revelation to him, peace and blessings be upon him."

Some of them said: "It is the Qur'an, and it has been named a spirit in God's words: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Spirit from Our command﴾. And other things have been said."

Some of them claimed that the question concerned the origin (*huduth*) of the Spirit in the first sense and its eternity (*qidam*), but this is nothing, as you will hear, God willing.

The pronoun in "they ask" refers to the Jews. Al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, who said: "I was walking with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the ruins of Medina, and he was leaning on a palm-stalk. He passed by a group of Jews, and some of them said to others: 'Ask him about the Spirit.' Others said: 'Do not ask him.' But they asked him, saying: 'O Muhammad, what is the Spirit?' He kept leaning on the palm-stalk, and I thought he was being revealed to. When the revelation descended, he said: ﴿They ask you about the Spirit﴾ — the verse."

Some of them said that the Quraysh said to the Jews, based on what Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Hibban and a group narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Quraysh said to the Jews: 'Give us something to ask this man.' They said: 'Ask him about the Spirit.' So they asked him, and the verse ﴿They ask you…﴾ etc. was revealed."

In the biographies (*al-siyar*), it is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the rabbis of the Jews in Medina, saying to them: "Ask them Muhammad, for they are people of the Book who have knowledge that we do not have." So the two set out until they reached Medina, and they asked them. The Jews said: "Ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the Spirit. If he answers them or remains silent, he is not a prophet; but if he answers some and remains silent about others, then he is a prophet." So they came and asked him, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, explained to them two matters and left the matter of the Spirit unspecified, which is also unspecified in the Torah. According to this, the verse and what precedes it were Meccan; according to the report of the two Sahihs, it was Medinan. Some scholars reconciled this by saying that the verse was revealed twice. So reflect.

In any case, the connection of what precedes with this verse, if the Spirit is explained as the Qur'an, is clear and fitting with God's words: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy﴾, and with what follows of the favour bestowed upon him and upon his followers by preserving it in their hearts and its permanence. The same holds if it is explained as Jibril, peace be upon him. As for the view of the majority, it has come as a digression indicating the loss and misguidance of the wrongdoers, that they are preoccupied with avoiding reflection upon the Book and benefiting from it, and instead with seeking to provoke by asking about what wisdom has determined to block the path of knowing.

Something similar can be said on the view related from some of the early scholars: ﴿Say: the Spirit﴾ — here the term is stated explicitly in place of the pronoun, to show complete concern — ﴿is from the command of my Lord.﴾ The word "from" (*min*) is partitive, and it is said to be explicative. "Command" is the singular of "affairs," in the sense of matter or affair. The attribution (*idafa*) is for specific knowledge, not for origination, since there is nothing except that it is attributed to Him, Mighty and Majestic, in this sense. In it there is an honouring of the thing attributed that is not hidden, as in the second attribution there is an honouring of the one to whom it is attributed. That is: it is of the kind of what God Almighty has kept exclusively for His knowledge, among the hidden secrets which the eyes of human intellects can hardly perceive.

﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little.﴾ This cannot be connected to such things. This, as has been said, is an omission of explanation and a prohibition to them against asking.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ata ibn Yasar, who said: "This verse was revealed in Mecca. When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, migrated to Medina, the rabbis of the Jews came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, has it not reached us from you that you say: ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾? Do you mean us, or your people?' He said: 'Both of you I have meant.' They said: 'But you recite that we were given the Torah, and in it is the explanation of everything.' The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'It is, in God's knowledge, little. God has given you what, if you act upon it, you will benefit.' Then God Almighty revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens…﴾ until His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, God is Hearing and Seeing.﴾"

It seems that he, peace and blessings be upon him, pointed out that what is meant in the verse by "an explanation of everything" is of religious matters. There is no doubt that these are a very small fraction compared with the known things of God Almighty, which have no end. By this, the view of those who hold to real generality is refuted.

In the narration of al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, which they authenticated, the Jews said when the verse was revealed: "We have been given much knowledge; we have been given the Torah, and whoever has been given the Torah has been given much good." So God Almighty revealed: ﴿Say: if the sea were ink…﴾ — the verse.

It is not hidden that this also does not entail contradiction, because abundance and scarcity are relative matters. Something may be little in relation to what is above it and much in relation to what is below it. So what is in the Torah is little in relation to what is in the knowledge of God, exalted is His majesty, and much in relation to something else.

In a narration recorded by Ibn Mardawayh from Ikrima: "When he, peace and blessings be upon him, said that, the Jews said: 'We are specially addressed by this address.' He said: 'Rather, we and you.' They said: 'How wondrous is your affair: one moment you say: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾, and another moment you say this.' So God revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens…﴾ etc." Nor does this entail contradiction either, in the manner mentioned earlier, by saying: human wisdom is to know of good what human capacity can bear — or rather what organises the affairs of livelihood and the hereafter — and this is little in relation to His known things, exalted is He, yet much in relation to other things. And Ibn Jurayj, as Ibn Jarir narrated from him, and Ibn al-Mundhir, went to the view that the address is general so as to include all people. But against the view of generality there stands the apparent reading of Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash: ﴿and what they have been given﴾, since it requires restriction to the askers. As for the last hadith, which is explicit in this matter, al-Iraqi said it is not authentic. As for the first hadith, God Almighty knows its status best.

Others said: The meaning of the Spirit being "from His command" is that it is among the originated things brought into being by the command of creation (*al-amr al-takwini*), without being formed from matter or generated from a root, like the human body. So "command" here means the singular of commands, namely "Be!" The question was about the reality, and the answer is summary. Its outcome is that the Spirit is from the world of command, originated without matter, not from the world of creation. This is of the wise method, like Moses' answer, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh when Pharaoh asked him: ﴿What is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, indicating that the essence of its reality is something which the circle of human perception cannot encompass, and that what can be known is only this summary measure, falling under what was excepted in God's words: ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾ — that is, only a little knowledge which you acquire through the senses. For the conceiving of theoretical knowledge is mostly from sensing particulars. This is why it has been said: whoever loses a sense has lost a branch of knowledge. Probably most things are not perceived by the senses, either because they are not sensible, or because they are sensible but something prevents perceiving them, such as absence, for example. Likewise, one does not perceive any of its accidents with which one could define it, let alone move from them to the essential attributes so as to arrive at the reality. The apparent sense of some scholars' words is that reaching the reality of the Spirit is not possible, so there is no difference in their view between the two answers.

Al-Khafaji distinguished that explaining the reality of the Spirit is possible, unlike the reality of the Most Holy Essence. In the *Kashshaf* it is said that the way to knowing the Spirit is removing the veil from the eyes of hearts by beholding the collyrium of gems from the speech of the Knower of the Unseen; it is then most clear to those who use this collyrium, and most hidden to those who are preoccupied.

What contradicts this is what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abdullah ibn Buraydah, who said: "The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was taken (in death) while he did not know the Spirit." Perhaps this Abdullah holds that knowing it is impossible; otherwise the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, was not taken until he knew everything that can be known, as is shown by what Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi narrated, and al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a sound hadith." Al-Bukhari, when asked about it, said: "It is a good, sound hadith," from Mu'adh, may God be pleased with him, that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I rose at night and prayed what was decreed for me, then I dozed in my prayer until I became heavy with sleep. Suddenly I was with my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, in the best of forms. He said: 'O Muhammad, about what do the exalted assembly dispute?' He said: 'O Muhammad, about what do the exalted assembly dispute?' I said: 'I do not know, my Lord.' He said: 'O Muhammad, about what do the exalted assembly dispute?' I said: 'I do not know, my Lord.' I said: 'I do not know, my Lord.' Then I saw Him place His palm between my shoulders until I found the coolness of His fingertips between my chest, and everything was made manifest to me, and I knew.'" The hadith goes on.

The word "I saw" (*ra'aytu*) in the preceding report is found in some books vocalised in the passive voice (*ru'iya*), and "the Spirit" vocalised in the nominative (*al-ruhu*). The objection to that is weaker, but this reading is contrary to the apparent sense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 85 (part 2 of 5):

It is understood from the words of some of the later Sufis that it is impossible to comprehend the reality of the soul. Indeed, this group stated that the reality of all things cannot be comprehended. This is based on what is not hidden from you, and its rejection or acceptance is left to you. Furthermore, I have a reservation about this view. The apparent meaning is that applying the term "the world of command" to what exists without being formed from matter or generated from a source, and applying the term "the world of creation" to its opposite, is a purely technical convention that is not known to the Arabs and that they did not recognise. Using the verse ﴿Surely His is the creation and the command﴾ as evidence for this is something that is not hidden from any fair-minded person.

This is what the Imam mentioned. He also said that the question about the soul may be asked in many ways, and the verse ﴿They ask you about the soul﴾ does not indicate any one of these ways, except that the answer given is only suitable for two of them. The first is that it is a question about its quiddity (mahiyyah, the essential nature of a thing). The second is that it is a question about eternity (qidam) and origination (huduth).

The summary of the answer to the first is that the soul is a simple, immaterial substance, originated by the command of Allah, His bringing into being, and His influence in granting life to the body. Not knowing its particular reality does not necessarily mean that it is denied, since most realities of things, their quiddities, are unknown, and the fact that they are unknown does not entail their negation. Allah points to this with ﴿You have been given only a little knowledge﴾. The basis of this also lies in the distinction between the world of command and the world of creation, and you have heard what is in that.

The summary of the answer to the second is that it is a originated thing that came into existence by the act of Allah, His bringing into being, and His creation. The words of Allah ﴿You have been given only a little knowledge﴾ are taken as an argument for origination, in the sense that souls at the beginning of their natural state are empty of sciences and knowledge, and then these come to exist in them, so they continue to change from one state to another, and this is one of the signs of origination. You know that interpreting the question as referring to what was mentioned, and taking the answer as a report of origination, while it does not suit the condition of the questioners, is not supported by the mention of explaining their lack of knowledge. What they asked about is something their knowledge at that time could encompass, and it was reported about. Taking this as an argument for origination is one of the most astonishing of arguments, as is not hidden from any person of sense. And Allah knows best.

Here are some discussions that are worth presenting.

* * *

The first discussion concerns explaining the positions of people regarding the reality of the human being. The apparent meaning of the Imam's words is that the disagreement about the reality of the human being is the same as the disagreement about the reality of the soul, and there is something to be questioned about this. The majority of the theologians (mutakallimun) held that the human being is a designation for this sensible structure and this perceptible physical frame, which is what a person points to when he says "I." The Imam refuted this with seventeen arguments, both transmitted and rational, but there is room for discussion regarding some of them. Among them is what has been mentioned before, that the parts of the structure change through increase, decrease, withering and growth. Necessary knowledge attests that the human being, as such, is a single thing that remains from the beginning of life to its end, and what remains is not what does not remain.

Among them is that a human being may be affected by something that distracts him from attending to the parts of his structure, whether as a whole or in part, yet he does not lose sight of his specific self. The evidence is that, with that distraction, he says, for example, "I did" and "I left," and what is not known is not the same as what is not known.

Among them is that the particular structure may exist while the reality of the human being is not present. The Angel Gabriel, peace be upon him, was often seen in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi, and Iblis, may he be cursed, was seen in the form of a Najdi old man. And the structure may be absent while the reality of the human being remains. For example, a person who has been transformed into a monkey still has his reality while the particular structure is absent. Otherwise no transformation (maskh) would have taken place, but rather a death of that person and the creation of a monkey.

Among them is that it has been reported in a narration that when the deceased is carried on the bier, his soul hovers above the bier and says: "O my family! O my children! Let the world not play with you as it played with me. I gathered wealth from its lawful and unlawful sources, then I left it to others. Its pleasure is theirs and its consequence is upon me. So beware of what has befallen me." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) stated that there is something that calls out, other than the one carried, and that the family were the people it addressed, and that the one who gathered the wealth from lawful and unlawful sources was that very thing. And this is none other than the human being, along with other points which he mentioned in his tafsir.

It has been said that the human being is the soul that is in the heart. It has been said that he is an indivisible part in the brain. It has been said that he consists of fiery parts mixed with the heart-spirits and the brain-spirits, which are called the innate heat (al-hararah al-gharizziyyah). It has been said that he is the blood that dwells in the body. It has been said, and it has been said, up to about a thousand opinions. The reliable view among the scholars who verify matters (muhaqqiqun) is two opinions:

The first: the human being is a designation for a luminous, elevated, living, moving body, different in quiddity from this sensible body, which permeates it as water permeates a myrtle, oil permeates an olive, and fire permeates coal. It does not accept dissolution, change, separation or disintegration. It gives the sensible body life and its consequences as long as it is fit to receive the overflow, since nothing has occurred that prevents its permeation, such as thick humours. When that occurs, death takes place because permeation has been cut off. The soul is a designation for that body. The Imam praised this view and said: "It is a strong doctrine and a noble position that must be carefully considered, for it is very consistent with what has been mentioned in the divine books about the states of life and death." Ibn al-Qayyim said in his book al-Ruh: "It is the correct view and nothing else is valid. It is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus of the Companions, the evidence of reason and the natural disposition (fitrah)." He mentioned a hundred proofs and five proofs, so let it be consulted.

The second: the human being is not a body, nor corporeal. This is the soul. It is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither connected to it nor separate from it. Rather, it is attached to the body in the manner of management and disposal. This is the view of most of the divine philosophers (al-ilahiyyin min al-falasifah, the metaphysicians among the philosophers). A great group of Muslims also held it, including Shaykh Abu al-Qasim al-Raghib al-Isfahani, the Proof of Islam Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, Ma'mar ibn 'Abbad al-Sulami from the Mu'tazilah, al-Shaykh al-Mufid from the Shi'ah, a group from the Karramiyyah, and most of the people of unveiling (mukashafah) and spiritual discipline (riyadah). We have already presented the evidence for this to you. Whoever wishes to comprehensively understand this should refer to the books of the two Shaykhs, Abu 'Ali and Shihab al-Din al-Maqtul, and to the books of the Imam al-Razi, such as al-Mabahith al-Mashriqiyyah and others. The Shaykh al-Ra'is has a separate treatise on this, which he named al-Hujaj al-Ghurr. Its most decisive and firmest argument is based on the self's knowledge of its own essence. Ibn al-Qayyim refuted its arguments in his book, and that is a very beneficial book. It gives the soul a soul and bestows expansion upon the breast.

The Imam, in his tafsir, used the aforementioned verse as evidence for this, saying: "If the soul were a body that moved from one state to another and from one attribute to another, it would be equal to the body in being generated from bodies that had acquired particular attributes after having been characterised by other attributes. So if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been asked about it, he would have had to explain that it was a body that was such-and-such and then became such-and-such, until it became a soul, just as was mentioned about the manner in which the body is formed: that it was a drop, then a clot, then a lump of flesh. But when he did not say that and said, 'It is of the command of my Lord,' meaning that it does not come into being or enter existence except by Allah saying to it, 'Be,' and it is, this indicates that it is a substance that is not of the kind of bodies, but rather a holy, immaterial substance." It is not hidden that this is one of the persuasive rhetorical arguments (al-iqna'iyyat al-khitabiyyah), and there are many of them in this domain. Among them is the words of Allah ﴿And I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ and His words ﴿and His word which He cast to Mary﴾. This attribution indicates the nobility of the human substance and that it is free from sensible garments. Among them is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "I am the naked warner." This points to the spirit's detachment from the attachments of bodies.

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah Most High created Adam in the image of the All-Merciful." In another narration: "in His image."

And the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "I spend the night with my Lord; He feeds me and gives me drink." In this there is an announcement of the nobility of the spirit and its nearness to its Lord, a nearness in essence and attributes, free from the attachments of bodies and the obstacles of physical forms, and other things beyond counting. It goes along these lines, and there is much room for discussion in it.

Thabit ibn Qurrah used to say: "The soul is attached to luminous, subtle celestial bodies that are not subject to generation, corruption, separation or disintegration. These bodies permeate the body, and as long as they permeate it, the soul manages the body. When they separate from it, the attachment is severed." This is an eclectic view, and I do not find it improbable.

* * *

"The second discussion concerns the disagreement of people about whether the soul is originated or eternal." The Muslims agreed that it is originated in a temporal origination, like the rest of the parts of the world. However, they disagreed about whether it was originated before the body or after it. A group held that it was originated before. It has been said that among them was Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi, and Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm al-Zahiri, who reported it as a consensus, but he lied. He used as evidence for this what is in the two Sahihs from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Souls are gathered armies. Those among them that recognise one another become attuned, and those that disagree with one another become estranged."

Ibn al-Jawzi said in his Tabsirah: Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: "The meaning of this hadith is information that souls were created before bodies." Ibn Hazm claimed that they are in a barzakh, which is a place free of elements, and when a body is prepared to receive one of them, it descends to it, and that after death they return to that barzakh. There is no evidence for this from the Book or the Sunnah.

Some of them used as evidence the report that Allah created the souls two thousand years before the bodies. Ibn al-Qayyim criticised this by saying that its chain of transmission is not sound. Others, among them the Proof of Islam al-Ghazali, held that it was originated afterwards. Among the evidence for this, as Ibn al-Qayyim said, is the authentic hadith: "The creation of the son of Adam is gathered in his mother's womb for forty days as a drop, then it is a clot for a similar period, then it is a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then an angel is sent to him, and he breathes the spirit into him."

The point of the evidence is that if the soul had been created earlier, it would have been said: "Then an angel is sent to him with the spirit, and he enters it into him."

He also stated explicitly in Rawdat al-Muhibbin wa Nuzhat al-Mushtaqin his choice of this view. He said: "The claim that souls were created before bodies is a corrupt view and a clear error. The correct view, indicated by the Shari'ah and reason, is that they are created together with the bodies, and that the angel blows the spirit, that is, brings it into being by breathing it into the body when four months have passed over the drop and it enters the fifth. Whoever says that they were created earlier has erred, and more reprehensible than that is the view of whoever says that they are eternal." End of quote. There is room for reflection in this. The view of origination is supported by the words of Allah ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, so let it be understood.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 85 (part 3 of 5):

Plato and those philosophers before him held that the soul (*ruh*) is eternal (*qidam*). The First Teacher (*al-Mu'allim al-Awwal*, i.e., Aristotle) held that it is created (*hudūth*) together with the body that prepares for it (*al-badan al-musta'idd*), as some Muslim thinkers also held. The arguments of each side have already been discussed, both in criticism and in defense. It may be said here that the First Teacher, like other philosophers, held that the soul, called in their terminology the rational soul (*al-nafs al-nāṭiqa*), is immaterial (*mujarrad*) from matter (*māddah*). So how could he hold that it is created, given their principle that every temporal created thing requires matter? It has been answered that matter here is more general than the substrate (*maḥall*) and the thing dependent on it (*al-muta'alliq bihi*), and that the body is matter for the soul in this sense. You know that the preparedness (*isti'dād*) of one thing for another occurs only when that thing is connected to it, not separate from it. So it is better to say: when the human body, for its particular temperament (*mizāj*), required a governing form (*ṣūrah mudabbirah*) that acts upon it, that is, a thing described by this attribute insofar as it is such, then, according to the overflowing bounty of the Bestowing Giver, there had to exist a thing that would be the source of the human management (*tadābīr al-insiyya*) and human actions (*af'āl al-bashariyya*). Such a thing can only be an essence that perceives universals and is immaterial in its essence. So without doubt the soul was truly bestowed upon it, not because the body required it, but because it does not separate from what required it. The body, by its particular preparedness, required a material thing, and the existence of the overflowing Source bestowed a holy substance (*jawhar qudsī*). Just as one thing may, according to what they have established, be both a substance and an accident (*'araḍ*) under two aspects, so one thing may be both immaterial and material under two aspects. The human soul is therefore immaterial in its essence and material in its actuality (*fi'lan*). Insofar as its action is management and motion, it is preceded by the preparedness of the body and is connected to it. But insofar as its essence and reality are concerned, the origin of its existence is the existence of the Giving Source alone. Therefore the preparedness of the body does not precede it in that respect, its existence does not necessarily require connection to the body, and no defect of material things befalls it except accidentally.

It may be possible to interpret what is reported from Plato concerning the eternity of the soul in this subtle way, as some later scholars have said. So reflect on it.

* * *

**The Third Investigation:** People have differed over whether the spirit (*ruh*) and the soul (*nafs*) are one thing or two. Ibn Zayd reported from most scholars that they are one thing, for it is authentically established in the reports that each of them is applied to the other. And there is what al-Bazzar related with a sound chain from Abu Hurayrah, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The believer, when death comes upon him and he witnesses what he witnesses, wishes that his soul had departed, and God, exalted is He, loves to meet him. And the believer's spirit ascends to heaven, and the spirits of the believers come to him and ask him about his acquaintances from the people of the world." The hadith is clear on this.

Ibn Habib said: they are two things. The spirit is the breath that circulates in the human being, and the soul is something other than that. It has two hands, two feet, a head and two eyes. It is what feels pleasure, pain, joy and grief. It is what is taken in sleep, goes out and wanders, sees visions, while the body remains without it, with the spirit alone, not feeling pleasure or joy until it returns. He argued from the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death﴾, and the verse. Ibn Mandah related from some people that the soul is earthly and fiery, and the spirit is luminous and spiritual. And from another that the soul is human (*nāsūtiyya*) and the spirit is divine (*lāhūtiyya*). It is mentioned that the people of tradition (*ahl al-athar*) hold that they are distinct, and that the subsistence of the soul is through the spirit. The soul is the person's form (*ṣūrat al-'abd*), and desire, lust and affliction are kneaded into it. No enemy is more hostile to the son of Adam than his own soul: it wants only the world and loves only it, while the spirit calls to the Hereafter and prefers it.

The apparent statement of some of the verifying Sufi scholars (*muḥaqqiqī al-ṣufiyya*) also holds that they are distinct. In *Muntaha al-Madarik* by the verifier al-Farghani, it is stated that the soul attributed to the human being is an expression for a misty vapor (*bukhār ḍabābī*) emanating from the inner part of the pineal heart (*al-qalb al-ṣanawbarī*), carrying the power of life, assimilated by the influence of the spiritual spirit (*al-ruh al-ruhāniyya*), which is meant by God's words: ﴿And I breathed into him of My spirit﴾, whose designation is established in the world of spirits (*'ālam al-arwāḥ*), and whose influence reaches this life-carrying vapor. So the soul is a thing composed of vapor, with the attribute of life and the influence of the spiritual spirit. By virtue of its assimilation to the influence of the spiritual spirit, this soul is specified for managing the human body, and it is capable of lofty matters and base ones, as God, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿So He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾. The spiritual spirit is something that cannot be fully comprehended.

The truth is that they may be identical in general application, and they may be different. Ibn al-Qayyim relied on the view held by most scholars, that they are identical in essence. Many have mentioned that this is the view of the Sufis. However, they say that the soul is the origin of the human being, and when it is polished by discipline (*riyāḍa*) and various kinds of remembrance (*dhikr*) and reflection (*fikr*), it becomes a spirit. Then it may ascend further until it becomes one of the secrets (*asrār*) of God, exalted is He.

The detailed account in this context is that the soul has stages through which it ascends. The first is the refinement of the outward through the use of the divine laws (*nawāmīs ilāhiyya*), such as standing in prayer, fasting, and others. The second is the refinement of the inward from base dispositions (*malakāt radiyya*) and lowly characters. The third is the adornment of the soul with holy forms (*ṣuwar qudsiyya*). The fourth is its annihilation from its own essence and its contemplation of the majesty of the Lord of the worlds, may His majesty be exalted.

As for how one ascends through these stages, it is said that when a human being is first born, he is like the rest of the animals, knowing only eating and drinking. Then gradually there appear to him the other qualities of the soul: lust, anger, greed, envy, and other states which are the results of veiling and distance from the source of generosity and the perfect attributes. Then, when he awakens from the slumber of heedlessness and rises from the sleep of ignorance, and it becomes clear to him that behind these bestial pleasures are other pleasures, and above these stages are other perfect stages, he repents of his preoccupation with the forbidden matters of the Law and turns back to God, exalted is He, by turning towards Him. He begins to abandon worldly excess in pursuit of the perfections of the Hereafter. He resolves with complete determination and turns to travel to the King of kings from the station of his own soul. He emigrates from it and falls into strangeness (*ghurba*), and "Blessed are the strangers" (*ṭūbā lil-ghurabā'*). And if it is said: "Strangeness is only for the free," he is slaughtered. Then, when he enters the path, he renounces everything that hinders him from his goal and prevents him from his object of worship. He becomes characterized by scrupulousness (*wara'*), piety (*taqwā*), and true asceticism (*zuhd ḥaqīqī*). Then he constantly calls his soul to account in his words and deeds, and suspects it in everything it commands, even if it is an act of worship, for it is inclined to love of desires and disposed to hidden deceits. So he must not feel secure with it or be confident in it.

It is related of one of the great saints (*akābir*) that his soul never ceased to command him to struggle (*jihād*) and to urge him to it. He was surprised at this, then realized that it wanted to rest from the toil of standing in prayer and fasting through death. So he did not comply with it. When he freed himself from it, his time became clear and his life pleasant through what he found on the path of the Beloved. His inner self becomes illuminated, and the flashes of the lights of the Unseen (*anwār al-ghayb*) appear to him, and the gate of the Dominion (*malakūt*) opens for him, and its lights shine on him again and again. He witnesses unseen matters in imaginal forms (*ṣuwar mithāliyya*). When he tastes something of them, he desires seclusion, solitude, remembrance, constancy in purity and worship, vigilance and self-accounting. He turns away from all sensory pleasures, and his heart is emptied of love for them, so his inner self turns entirely to the Real, exalted is He. Then ecstasy (*wajd*), intoxication (*sukr*), longing (*shawq*), passionate love (*'ishq*) and bewilderment (*hayamān*) appear to him, and they make him annihilated (*fānī*) from himself, heedless of it. He then witnesses the secret realities and the unseen lights, and he is established in witnessing, direct observation (*mu'āyana*), and unveiling (*mukāshafa*). Lights appear to him sometimes and disappear at other times, until he becomes firm and is freed from fluctuation (*talwīn*). The tranquility of the spirit and the divine serenity descend upon him, and the arrival of these flashes and states becomes a settled disposition (*malaka*) for him. He enters the worlds of might (*jabarūt*) and witnesses the pure intellects and the overpowering lights of the angels brought near and the guardians, and he becomes established in their lights. Then the lights of the sovereignty of Oneness (*aḥadiyya*) appear to him, and the dazzling rays of divine greatness and majesty, which make him dust scattered (*habā'an manthūran*). Then the mountains of his selfhood (*injiyya*) crumble, and he falls down prostrate before God, exalted is He, in utter prostration. He vanishes into the essential determination (*ta'ayyun dhātī*), and his existence is effaced into the divine existence. This is the station of annihilation (*fanā'*) and effacement (*maḥw*), and it is the ultimate goal of the first journey of the wayfarers (*sālikīn*). If he remains in annihilation and effacement and does not come to subsistence (*baqā'*) and sobriety (*ṣaḥw*), he becomes absorbed in the very unity of the totality (*'ayn al-jam'*), veiled by the Real from creation, and his gaze never turns from contemplating His beauty, glorious is His majesty, and the lights of His essence and majesty. Multiplicity dissolves in his witnessing, and detail is hidden from his existence. That is the great triumph. Above that is a station in which he returns to sobriety after effacement, sees detail within the totality, and his breast embraces both the Real and creation. He witnesses the Real in everything and sees everything through the Real, in a manner that does not entail multiplicity or corporeality. This is a stage beyond the stage of reason.

It occurs in the expression of some that the knower may become characterized by the character traits of God, exalted is He, in reality, not in the sense that the divine attributes become an accident subsisting in the soul, for that is never conceivable, and to hold it is to depart from the Law, the Path, and the Reality. Rather, it is in the sense of another relation, more complete than its relation with the bodily worldly attributes and others, whose reality is not known. Perhaps what they intend by the station to which the soul ascends, so that it becomes one of the secrets of God, exalted is He, is this station. Knowledge of it requires following the way of the righteous (*abrār*), and it is not attained merely by speculation and thought. God, exalted is He, is the One who grants success in the journey and who bestows richness upon the pauper.

* * *

**The Fourth Investigation:** People have differed over whether the spirit dies or not. One group held that it dies, because it is a soul, and every soul shall taste death. The Book has established that nothing remains except God alone, and this requires the perishing of spirits like other created things. If the angels, peace be upon them, die, then human spirits are more deserving of it. Also, God, exalted is He, reported about the people of the Fire that they say: ﴿You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice﴾, and these two deaths are not realized unless the body dies once and the spirit dies another time.

Another group said: it dies, because of the hadiths indicating its bliss and punishment after separation from the body, until God returns it to the body. If we say it dies, then the bliss and punishment would cease. The correct position is to say: the death of the spirit is its separation from the body. If by its death this measure is meant, then it does taste death. If it is meant that it ceases to exist and perishes, then it does not die, but remains separated for as long as God wills, then returns to the body and remains with it in bliss or punishment forever and ever. It is excepted from those who swoon at the blast of the Trumpet. Moreover, swooning does not necessarily entail death and destruction, since it is not restricted to nonexistence, but is realized by a thing going beyond the limit of benefit from it, and similar. What has been mentioned in explaining the two deaths is not accepted, and God, exalted is He, willing, the discussion of it will come later.

Also held by the philosophers is that the soul does not die with the death of the body. The Shaykh (Ibn Sina) argued for this, saying: It has been established that the soul must come into being at the same time as the body. So either the two exist together, or one of them precedes the other. If they exist together, then either they are together in quiddity (essence) or they are not together in quiddity. The first is false, for otherwise the soul and the body would be correlatives (mutually dependent in definition), yet both are substances; this is an absurdity. If the togetherness is only in existence, with neither of them needing the other in that existence, then the non-existence of each of them entails the non-existence of that togetherness, but does not entail the non-existence of the other. If, however, one of them needs the other in existence, then either the prior is the soul or the body. If the prior in existence is the soul, that priority is either temporal or essential. The first is false, since it has been established that the soul does not exist before the body. The second is also false, because every existent whose existence is caused by something has its non-existence caused by the non-existence of that thing. For if that effect were to cease to exist while its cause remained, that cause would not be sufficient to bring it about, and so it would not be a cause but only a part of a cause; this is an absurdity. Therefore, if the body were caused (by the soul), the non-existence of the body could come about only through the non-existence of the soul. But the consequent is false: the body may cease to exist through other causes, such as poor temperament, poor composition, or the dissolution of its connection. Thus it is invalid that the soul be the cause of the body. It is also invalid that the body be the cause of the soul, because the causes, as is known, are four. It is impossible for the body to be an efficient cause of the soul, for it is either an efficient cause of the soul's existence merely by its corporeality, or by something additional to its corporeality. The first is false, for otherwise every body would be so. The second is also false. As for the first reason, it has been established that material forms act only by means of position, and whatever acts only by means of position cannot perform acts abstracted from space and position. As for the second reason, material forms are weaker than the abstract self-subsisting entity, and the weaker cannot be the cause of the stronger. It is impossible for the body to be a material cause of the soul, since it has been established that the soul is abstract and independent of matter. It is impossible for it to be a formal or final cause of the soul; rather the matter is more fitting to be the reverse. Hence there is no necessary connection at all between the body and the soul, so the non-existence of one is not a cause of the non-existence of the other.

If it is said: Did you not make the body a cause of the soul's coming into being? We say: It has been shown that when an agent is free of change and then the act proceeds from it after it had not proceeded, it must be because the condition of coming into being has been realized at that time and not before. Then, since that condition is a condition only for coming into being, and it is independent in its existence of that thing, it is impossible that the non-existence of that condition should affect the non-existence of that thing. Then, when it happened that this condition was disposed to become an instrument for the soul in attaining perfections, and the soul in its essence yearns for perfection, there arose in the soul a natural longing to manage that body and to direct it in the best manner. Such a thing cannot be such that its non-existence is the cause of the non-existence of that newly arisen thing. Rather, the philosophers went so far as to hold the impossibility of the soul's annihilation, and they demonstrated this with what they demonstrated. But for us, there is no impossibility in that.
* * *
"The Fifth Inquiry: On the differentiation of spirits after their separation from bodies." Ibn al-Qayyim affirmed that each spirit takes from its body a form by which it is distinguished from others, and that the differentiation of spirits is greater than the differentiation of bodies. However, he claimed that differentiation among them is impossible on the view that they are abstract substances free of matter. This is open to scrutiny, for those who hold this view also hold to differentiation, in terms of what they acquire from their attachment to the body or in some other manner of differentiation. Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani mentioned in some of his treatises that after separating from their particular bodies, spirits become attached to other, imaginal bodies suited to them. To this refers the mention of green birds in the hadith about the martyrs. In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, the spirits of the martyrs are in the bellies of green birds. Sa'id ibn Mansur reported from Makhul, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The spirits of the children of the believers are in sparrows in trees in Paradise."
That is, they are in bodies of those forms. This is supported by the narration of Ibn Majah from Ibn Mas'ud: "The spirits of the martyrs with Allah, the Exalted, are like green birds."
In another wording from Ka'b: "The spirits of the martyrs are green birds."
The wording from Ibn 'Umar: "In the form of white birds."
In the narration of 'Ali ibn 'Uthman al-Lahiqi from Makhul: "The spirits of the children of the believers are sparrows in Paradise."
On this basis, the denial by some theologians of the report about birds' bellies, and likewise the report about sparrows, is because it would entail two spirits attached to one body. They have held this to be impossible, arising from lack of reflection and careful consideration. For according to what we have established, the bird would have no spirit other than the spirit of the martyr. Moreover, if the report is left on its apparent meaning, no impossibility follows, since the spirit may be inside the bird's belly in the manner of a fetus in its mother's womb. So reflect.
* * *
"The Sixth Inquiry: On the abode of spirits after their separation from bodies." What the reports indicate is that the abode of spirits after separation differs. The abode of the spirits of the prophets, peace be upon them, is in the highest 'Illiyyin. It is authentically reported that the last words the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke were: "O Allah, the Highest Companion." This supports what has been mentioned. The abode of the spirits of the martyrs is in Paradise; they drink from its rivers, eat from its fruits, and take refuge in lamps suspended beneath the Throne. Something close to this has been reported regarding the spirits of the children of believers.

Ibn al-Mubarak reported from Ka'b, who said: The Garden of Refuge is a garden in which there are green birds; in it the spirits of the martyrs graze beside the glittering stream at the gate of Paradise, in a green dome, and their provision comes out to them from Paradise morning and evening.

Perhaps this, as Ibn Rajab said, refers to the common martyrs, while what preceded refers to their elite; or perhaps this refers to the martyrs of the Hereafter, such as the drowned and the one who dies of abdominal illness, and so on. As for the abode of the spirits of all other believers, it has been said that it too is in Paradise, and this is the explicit text of Imam al-Shafi'i.

Imam Malik reported from Ka'b ibn Malik, as a marfu' hadith: "The soul of the believer is only a bird hung in the trees of Paradise until Allah, the Exalted, returns it to its body on the day He resurrects it." It was narrated by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, extracted by al-Nasa'i through the chain of Malik, extracted by Ibn Majah, and narrated by a great many others.

Ibn Mandah reported from the hadith of Umm Bishr, as a marfu' report, something explicit that the abode of the spirits of believers is like the abode of the spirits of martyrs.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Allah, the Exalted, has in the seventh heaven a house called al-Bayda', in which the spirits of believers gather, and the abode of the spirits of disbelievers is in Sijjin.

In the hadith of Umm Bishr: "The spirits of the disbelievers are in the crops of black birds that eat from the Fire, drink from the Fire, and take refuge in a hole in the Fire. They say: 'Our Lord, do not bring our brothers to us, and do not give us what You promised us.'"

It has been said: the abode of the spirits of the dead is the courtyards of their graves. Ibn Hazm related this from the general body of the people of hadith, and some of them cited as evidence the hadith of Ibn 'Umar from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When one of you dies, his seat is displayed to him morning and evening: if he is among the people of Paradise, then from the people of Paradise; and if he is among the people of the Fire, then from the people of the Fire. It is said to him: 'This is your seat until Allah, the Exalted, resurrects you.'"

And that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he visited the dead, said: "Peace be upon you, abode of a believing people."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr preferred that the abode of the spirits other than those of martyrs is at the courtyards of graves. In this there is the point that if it is meant that spirits do not leave the courtyards, it is an error refuted by the texts of the Book and the Sunnah. If it is meant that they are there at some times, as is reported from Mujahid: "The spirits are over the graves for seven days from the day the deceased is buried; the first of them is illumination over their graves, and they are in their abode." Then this is true, but one should not say that their abode is the courtyards of the graves. Some verifiers held that wherever spirits are, they have a connection whose reality none knows except Allah, the Exalted, and by this they return greetings and recognize the one who greets them, and their seat in Paradise or the Fire is displayed to them. Some of them said: there is no obstacle to their moving from their abode and returning to it very swiftly, wherever Allah, the Exalted, wills. Yes, in the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib there is what indicates that the spirits of believers settle in the earth and do not return to heaven after being displayed, where he said in describing the taking of the believer's spirit: "When it reaches the Throne, his book is written in 'Illiyyin." The Lord, exalted is His majesty, says: "Return My servant to his resting place, for I promised them that from it I created them, into it I return them, and from it I bring them out once more."

In another wording: "Return the spirit of My servant to the earth, for I promised them that I would return them into it." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "From it We created you" (Qur'an 20:55), to the end of the verse.

However, the Hafiz Ibn Rajab said: the hadith of al-Bara' alone does not contradict the many hadiths explicitly stating that spirits are in Paradise, especially those of the martyrs; and the Exalted's words "From it We created you" etc. refer to the bodies. Another group said: the abode of spirits in general is in the lowest heaven, on the right and left of Adam, peace be upon him. This is indicated by what is in the two Sahihs from Abu Dhar in the hadith of the Mi'raj, where it says: "When it was opened, we ascended to the lowest heaven, and behold, a man was sitting, with black figures on his right and black figures on his left. When he looked toward his right, he laughed, and when he looked toward his left, he wept. He said: 'Welcome, righteous prophet and righteous son.' I said to Jibril: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Adam. These black figures on his right and left are the souls of his offspring; those on the right are the people of Paradise, and the black figures on the left are the people of the Fire.'"

It is answered that the meaning is that he, peace be upon him, sees these two categories from his right and from his left, and this is compatible with the spirits of each group being in their abode in Paradise or the Fire. For the Prophet (ﷺ) saw Paradise and the Fire during the eclipse prayer while he was on earth; Paradise was not there, and he saw both while he was in heaven, and the Fire was not there. And in a hadith of Abu Hurayrah concerning the Night Journey there is what supports what we have said. Al-Nasafi in Bahr al-Kalam made the spirits into four categories: the spirits of the prophets, peace be upon them, leave their bodies and their likeness becomes like musk and camphor, and they are in Paradise eating, drinking, enjoying themselves, and at night they take refuge in lamps suspended beneath the Throne. The spirits of martyrs leave their bodies and are in the crops of green birds in Paradise, eating and enjoying themselves, and they take refuge in lamps like the spirits of the prophets. The spirits of obedient believers are at the outskirts of Paradise; they do not eat or enjoy, but they look upon Paradise. The spirits of disobedient believers are between heaven and earth in the air. As for the spirits of disbelievers, they are in Sijjin, in the crops of black birds beneath the seventh earth, and they remain connected to their bodies; so the spirits are tormented, and the bodies suffer from that. End.

[Page 163]

What he mentioned about the spirits of the obedient contradicts what is established: that they enjoy bliss in Paradise. In *al-Ifsah* it is stated that the spirits who are blessed occupy different states. Some of them fly among the trees of Paradise. Some are in the crops of green birds. Some take shelter in lamps beneath the Throne. Some are in the crops of white birds. Some are in the crops of birds like sparrows. Some are in figures of the forms of Paradise. Some are in a form created from the reward of their deeds. Some roam and move about to their bodies and visit them. Some receive the spirits of those who have died. Others, besides these, are under the care of Mika'il (peace be upon him), some are under the care of Adam (peace be upon him), and some are under the care of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). End of quotation. Al-Qurtubi said: "This is a good opinion that brings the reports together so that they do not conflict," and al-Jalal al-Suyuti approved it.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya transmitted from Malik, who said: "I was informed that the spirit is released; it goes wherever it wills." Even if this is authentic, it is not to be taken in its absolute sense.

Other opinions have been held about the resting place of the spirits, to the extent that some claimed that their resting place is pure non-existence. This is based on the view that the spirit is an accident (ʿaraḍ), and that it is life. This is a false, void, corrupt and worthless view, which is refuted by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus and sound reason. What pleases me in this section is what the gnostic imam Ibn Burjan mentioned in his commentary on the Beautiful Names of God, where he said: "The soul (nafs) is created from the innermost part of that from which the body was formed, and it is the spirit of the body. God, blessed and exalted, produced the spirit from the innermost part from which He created the soul. The spirit stands to the soul as the soul stands to the body, and the soul is its veil. The spirit is described as living by God's giving it life, and its death is extinction, except what God wills on the day when the spirits are extinguished. The body is described as dead until it is given life by the spirit, and its death is the separation of the spirit from it. When this servant, the spiritual one, departs from the body, he is raised with it. If he was a believer, the gates of heaven are opened for him until he ascends to his Lord, mighty and majestic, and he is commanded to prostrate, so he prostrates. Then he makes his soulish reality (haqiqatuhu al-nafsaniyya) inhabit the lower part from his grave up to where God, exalted, wills in the air. His spiritual reality (haqiqatuhu al-ruhaniyya) inhabits the higher part, from the lowest heaven to the seventh, in joy and bliss. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) met Musa (peace be upon him) standing in his grave praying, and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) beneath the tree before his ascent to the lowest heaven, and he met both of them in the high heavens. Those are their spirits, and these are their souls, and their bodies are in their graves. If he was wretched, it is not opened for him, and he is thrown from a height to the earth." End of quotation.

In this there is the statement of the distinction between the spirit and the soul, and by this verification many objections and numerous difficulties are resolved. It is known that the hadith "There is no one who passes by the grave of his believing brother whom he knew in this world, greets him with peace, except that he recognizes him and returns his greeting" is not explicit that the spirit is at the grave. This is because it is understood from it that what is in the grave is the soulish reality, which is connected to the spirit by a connection whose true nature none knows except God, exalted. The spirit, in addition to that, has states and phases known only to God, exalted. At times it is absorbed in witnessing the beauty and majesty of God, exalted and glorified, and similar things, and at times it awakens from that absorption. This is what is meant by the return of the spirit in the report: "There is no one who sends greetings upon me except that God, exalted, returns my spirit to me, so I return his greeting."

What should be relied upon, along with what has been mentioned, is that the spirits, although their resting places differ in the sense of their locations, which they have been given by God's grace as a recompense for their deeds, nevertheless have a roaming in God's dominion wherever He, majestic is His majesty, wills. This happens only after permission. They vary in this according to their variation in nearness and closeness to God, exalted. Indeed, some pure spirits appear, and whomever God wills among the living sees them while awake. The spirits of the dead meet, visit and converse with one another. Spirits of the dead and the living may also meet in sleep. Only one who regards dreams as mere imaginings with no basis denies this, and such a person is not to be heeded. Yet no legal ruling should be built upon this, because of the possibility that it is not sound, even if evidence supports it.

As for what is authentically reported, that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas went out with Khalid ibn al-Walid to the battle against Musaylima and was martyred, may God be pleased with him, and he was wearing a precious coat of mail. A man from among the Muslims passed by him and took it. Then, while a soldier was sleeping, Thabit came to him in his dream and said: "I enjoin you with a bequest, and beware of saying, 'This is a dream,' and neglecting it. When I was killed yesterday, a man from the Muslims passed by me and took my coat of mail. His dwelling is at the farthest end of the people, and beside his tent there is a horse neighing at its rope. A cooking pot has been placed over the coat of mail, and above the pot is a saddle. Go to Khalid and command him to send for my coat of mail, so that he may take it. When you reach Madina, go to the Caliph of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and say to him: 'I owe such and such a debt, and so-and-so among my slaves is freed.'" The man went to Khalid and informed him, so he sent for the coat of mail, and it was brought. He also related his dream to Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, and Abu Bakr permitted his bequest. Ibn Abd al-Barr and others have mentioned this. It is answered that this occurred with the permission of the heir, who was his daughter, because of the strong supposition that the dream was true, given the evidence that accompanied it. Had she not permitted it, it would not have been lawful for Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, to do that merely on the basis of a dream. It has also been said that Abu Bakr did not see it as a return of the property, and so he did that from the share of the public treasury (bayt al-mal). A story similar to this is the story of Mus'ab ibn Jathama and Awf ibn Malik. Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned it in *Kitab al-Ruh*, and it is far stranger than what has been mentioned. Perhaps the spirits of some people are permitted to visit their families, as has been reported in some narrations. Some spirits are detained in their graves, or wherever God, exalted, wills, from their station, such as the spirit of one who dies owing a debt that he incurred for something forbidden, not absolutely, as is the well-known view. Its verification is in the commentary on the *Shama'il* by the great scholar Ibn Hajar.

Then know that the connection of the spirit to the body is not restricted to one part rather than another. Rather, it is connected to and illuminates all its parts, even if they are dispersed, and one part is in the east and another in the west. Perhaps this illumination upon the original parts is because they are what a person rises from his grave with on the Day of Resurrection, according to the view chosen by a group. Know also that the spirit, according to the view of its immateriality, has no resting place. It cannot even be said that it is inside the world or outside it, as you have heard. The resting place in that case belongs only to the body to which it is attached. Some Sufis have stated that there is no barrier to a soul being attached to two or more bodies, and indeed that it actually happens among them. Some of them mentioned that one of the two bodies is the original body, and the other is an image (mithali) that appears to the eyes in a manner that breaks the customary order. Another said: the other is through the spirit's transformation and its appearance in a form, like the appearance of Jibril (peace be upon him) in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi, and the appearance of the Qur'an to its memorizer in the form of a pale man on the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 164]

The philosophers said: it is not possible for a single soul to be attached to many bodies, because it would follow that what is known by one of them is known by the other, and what is unknown to one of them is unknown to the other. It is evident that this is not the case. It is not hidden that this argument shows that any two persons, one of whom knows what the other does not, have two different souls. So why should it not be possible for two persons to whose bodies a single soul is attached, such that whatever one of them knows, the other necessarily knows, and whatever one of them does not know is unknown to the other? Since the impossibility lacks a proof, it stands. According to what these Sufis have mentioned, it is possible for the spirit to be attached to one body in Paradise and to another body wherever God, exalted, wills. Indeed, it is possible for it to appear in various forms in many places, in the same way they have said about Jibril (peace be upon him), that while he was appearing in the form of Dihya or some other Bedouin before the Prophet (ﷺ), he did not leave the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha). You know what they say about the manifestation of God, exalted, in forms, and you have heard the report: "God, exalted, created Adam in His form."

From here they said: "Whoever knows himself knows his Lord." So understand the allusion. By my life, it is only an expression. Then as for the spirits of all other animals, such as beasts and the like, it has been said that after their separation they remain in the air with no connection to bodies. It has also been said that they are annihilated, and nothing can overcome God, exalted. Some people said: if the animals have a gathering on the Day of Resurrection, as is the well-known view that the apparent meanings of the verses and reports require, then it is better to say that their spirits remain in the air or wherever God, exalted, wills. If they have no gathering, as al-Ghazali held when he interpreted the apparent meanings, then it is better to say that they cease to exist. This is what I have to say. Many other investigations remain, which I have left aside because of the narrowness of the cage and the breadth of the circle of anxieties. Perhaps what we have mentioned here, together with what we mentioned before, is sufficient for the people of beginning and guidance for those whom providence assists. God, mighty and majestic, is the Lord of generosity and bounty, and from Him, glorified is He, is the beginning of everything, and to Him, exalted is He, everything returns.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 86:

﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾ of the Qur'an, which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and that by which We made you firm when they almost tempted you away from it, and other of its attributes indicated by the context. He expressed it by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) to magnify its matter and to describe it by what follows the relative clause (fi hayyiz al-silah) from the outset, informing of its state from the very beginning, and that it is not of the kind of the speech of created beings. The first lam is a preparatory lam (muwatta'a) for the oath. "Wa-la-nadhhabanna" (and We would surely take away), whose answer takes the place of the answer of the conditional clause, so it dispenses with estimating it; it is not the answer of the condition because the lam has entered upon it, and this is evident. By this, the omission of the object of the will (mashi'ah) was made good. The meaning of "taking it away" is its erasure from the codices and the hearts, and this is more emphatic than the verbs. According to this, what is meant from the Qur'an, as has been said, is its form, whether it is in the written marks of the script or in the images in the retentive faculty (al-quwwah al-hafizah).

﴿Then you would not find for yourself﴾ concerning it, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿any guardian against Us﴾, that is: one who undertakes and binds himself to its recovery after its taking away, as a guardian (wakil) binds himself to that concerning which he is entrusted, while expecting that it will be preserved in the lines and in the hearts as it was before. Thus "wakil" is a metaphor for what has been mentioned.

﴿Illa rahmatan min rabbika﴾ ("except as a mercy from your Lord") is an *istithna' munqati'* (disjunctive exception), according to what Ibn al-Anbari, Ibn 'Atiyya and others chose. It is explained, in the well-known view, as meaning *lakin* ("but"). The sense is *istidrak* (correction), as al-Tibi and others stated explicitly. The apparent meaning of the words of a group of scholars concerning God's saying ﴿Wa-la'in shi'na lanadhhabanna﴾ ("And if We willed, We would surely take away...") also suggests this. But al-Kashshaf says that it is not an *istidrak* from that, because the exception's antecedent is ﴿wakilan﴾ ("a guardian"). This is a disjunctive exception, and it is impermissible to place it in the position of the first noun, which in the dialects of the Hijaz and Tamim must be in the accusative, as in God's saying ﴿La 'asima al-yawma min amri Allahi illa man rahima﴾ ("There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy") according to one opinion, and in the saying of the Arabs: *La takunanna min fulanin illa salaman bi-salamin* ("Do not be from so-and-so except in peace with peace"). Al-Radi and others have explicitly stated that both groups require the accusative and do not permit substitution (*ibdal*) in a disjunctive exception where there is no preceding noun that can validly be omitted. That the case at hand is of this type is evident to one who has discernment.

The meaning is: after the taking away, you will not find anyone who will take up the task of securing its restoration against Us, but (We have left it, as) a mercy from your Lord, not in the accusative. Thus there was no need for anyone to take up the task of restoring it. The loss is implied by the word *tajidu* ("you find"). The semantic difference between the two statements, in that the first implies the taking away and the second implies its opposite, is established, and it is sufficient. Understand this.

Some have chosen that it is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*) from *wakilan*, meaning: you will not find a guardian for its restoration except mercy, for you will find it restored. But you know that including mercy under the term *wakil* requires some kind of strained interpretation.
