Abu al-Baqa' said: *rahmatan* is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), the implied sense being: We preserved it for you for the sake of mercy. It may also be in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), meaning: "But We have shown you mercy, a mercy." End of quotation. As you see, this is not the case. On the assumption of disjunction, the verse is a favour (*imtinan*) by means of the preservation of the Qur'an after the favour of its revelation. They mentioned that on the other assumption it indicates non-preservation, so the favour then lies only in its revelation. The obscurity in this is not hidden, and what is offered in its explanation does not quench the thirst.

The verse clearly indicates that the will to take it away is not realised, and that the loss of what is restored except as mercy occurs only on the supposition that the will is realised. However, reports have come that the Qur'an will be taken away before the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Bayhaqi and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Majah with a strong chain, related from Hudhayfah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Islam will wear away as the embroidery of a garment wears away, until it is not known what fasting is, nor charity, nor ritual sacrifice. The Book of God, may He be exalted, will be carried away in a single night, and not a verse will remain on earth. The old man and the old woman will remain, saying: 'We found our fathers upon this word: there is no god but God, so we say it.'"

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, who both said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) delivered a sermon and said: 'O people, what are these books that I have been told you write alongside the Book of God, may He be exalted? It is near that God, may He be exalted, will become angry for His Book, and it will be carried away by night, so that not a letter of it will be left in heart or leaf. It was said: O Messenger of God, what of the believing men and believing women? He said: Whoever God, may He be exalted, wills good for, He will keep in his heart: there is no god but God.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Book of God, may He be exalted, will be carried away and raised to heaven, and no verse of the Qur'an will remain on earth, nor of the Torah, the Gospel or the Psalms. It will be removed from the hearts of men, and they will wake up in misguidance, not knowing what they are in."

Al-Daylami related from Ibn 'Umar, as a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Hour will not come until the Qur'an returns from where it came. It will have a humming around the Throne like the humming of bees. God, mighty and majestic, will say: 'What is the matter with you?' It will say: 'I came out from You, and to You I return. I am recited, but I am not acted upon.'" Muhammad ibn Nasr related something similar as a statement (*mawquf*) attributed to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.

Several related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The Qur'an will be lifted from the codices and from breasts," and then he recited: ﴿Wa-la'in shi'na﴾ ("And if We willed") to the end of the verse.

In al-Bahjah it is stated that it will first be lifted from the codices, and then it will be lifted from breasts in the briefest time. The one who takes it away is Jibril (peace be upon him), as Ibn Abi Hatim related through al-Qasim ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from his father, from his grandfather. So how great a calamity this is, and how grievous a trial!

If the verse indicates its taking away, then there is no contradiction between it and these reports. If it indicates its preservation, then the contradiction is evident, unless it is said that preservation does not necessitate permanence, and that it suffices for it to remain until near the establishment of the Hour. Reflect on this.

Among what points to the verse being a favour is His saying: ﴿Inna fadlahu kana﴾ ("Indeed His bounty has been") and still is and continues to be ﴿'alayka kabiran﴾ ("great upon you"). Among this is the sending down of the Qur'an, His choosing it over all creation, the sealing of the prophets (peace be upon them) through it, the granting of the praised station (*al-maqam al-mahmud*), and other things.

Abu Sahl said: "Except that it was brought to threaten someone other than him (ﷺ) with the taking away of what they were given, so as to prevent them from asking about what they were not given, such as the knowledge of the Spirit and the knowledge of the Hour."

The author of al-Tahrir said: It may be said that when he (ﷺ) was asked about the Spirit, Dhu al-Qarnayn and the People of the Cave, and revelation was delayed for him, this grieved him greatly and reached its extreme. So God, may He be exalted, sent down this verse to console him (ﷺ). The meaning is: "Does the delay of revelation grieve you? For if We will, We shall take away all that We have revealed to you." So what he (ﷺ) was feeling subsided, and his heart was content. End of quotation. Both opinions are as you see.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 88:

﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur'an,"﴾ that is, agree together, ﴿"they would not produce its like,"﴾ this Qur'an which is described with qualities of exalted rank that the intellects cannot grasp: eloquence (balaghah), excellence of composition (husn al-nazm), and perfection of meaning. The mention of the two weighty things (al-thaqalan, mankind and jinn) is specific because those who deny that it is from God, the Exalted, are from among them and not from others, and the challenge (al-tahaddi) was made to them. Although the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent to the angels as he was sent to them both, this is not because the others are capable of opposing it. The angels, peace be upon them, if they were to take it up, and far be it from them since they are infallible and do only what they are commanded, are incapable like others. ﴿"They would not produce its like."﴾ That is, this Qur'an. The explicit noun was preferred over using a pronoun referring back to the mentioned "like" (mithl), to avoid the assumption that it has a specific like, and to indicate that the intended meaning is the negation of producing a like of any kind; that is, they will not produce a speech similar to it in the exalted qualities mentioned, and among them are the Arabs, the pure Arabs, masters of eloquence and clear expression.

It has been said that the intended meaning is the incapacity of mankind, and the jinn were mentioned for emphasis in their incapacity, because if they are unable to produce its like while the jinn, who are capable of extraordinary acts, are with them, then they are even more incapable of producing its like alone. But this is not the right view. It has also been said that it is permissible that "the jinn" be understood to include the angels, peace be upon them, and the application of the term jinn to the angels has occurred, as in God's words: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾. Indeed, its most common use is for other than the angels, peace be upon them, and it is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Some have claimed that the angels, peace be upon them, since they were intermediaries in its descent, should not be included, for it would not fit with ﴿"they would not produce its like"﴾ then. In response: the negation here does not mean the negation of producing its like from God, the Exalted, in any way from those to whom the action is attributed.

The clause "they would not produce" (la ya'tun) is the answer (jawab) to the oath (qasam) which is indicated by the preparatory lam (al-lam al-muwatta'ah), and it stands in place of the answer of the conditional (jaza' al-shart). Were it not for that lam, ﴿"they would not produce"﴾ would be the answer of the conditional, even though it is in the nominative (marfu') on the view that when the conditional verb is in the past tense, the answer may be marked with raf' (nominative), as in the verse of Zuhayr:

"And if a friend comes to him on a day of hunger, saying: 'My wealth is not absent, nor is it forbidden [to you]'"

The reason is that when the conditional particle does not affect the conditional verb apparently even when it is near, it may also not affect the answer when it is further away. This view contradicts the school of Sibawayh, the school of the Kufans, and al-Mubarrad, as has been explained in its proper place. According to the Basrans, and contrary to al-Farra', it is not permissible, in the presence of this lam, to make the mentioned clause the answer of the conditional. As for the verse of al-A'sha:

"If you are struck with us after the aftermath of a battle, you will not find us deviating from the blood of creatures, we do not withdraw"

the lam there is not the preparatory lam but is an extra (za'idah) lam, as has been said, so understand.

Since the intended meaning of "gathering together" to produce the like of the Qur'an is absolute agreement upon that, whether the challenge is undertaken by each one of them individually or by the whole collectively, by gathering to fabricate one speech through successive thoughts and mutual support of opinions. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and even if some of them were helpers of others﴾, that is, assisting one another in achieving what they intend of producing its like. The clause is coordinated with an implied one; that is: "they would not produce its like, even if some of them were not helpers of others, and even if..." etc. It occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), like the omitted clause, and the meaning is: they will not produce its like in any supposed circumstance, even in this circumstance which is contrary to their not producing it, let alone in other circumstances. In this there is a refutation of the Jews or the Quraysh in their claim that they could produce its like.

It has been narrated that a group of the earlier people said: "Inform us, O Muhammad, about this truth that you have brought: is it truly from God, the Exalted? For we do not see it as harmonious as the harmony of the Torah." So the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Indeed, by God, you know that it is from God, the Exalted." They said: "We will bring you the like of what you bring." So God, the Exalted, revealed this verse.

In another narration: "A group of the Quraysh said to him (ﷺ): 'Bring us a strange sign other than this Qur'an, for we are capable of bringing its like,' and so it was revealed."

Perhaps their intended meaning by this "strange sign" is what is contained in the verses after it, which is God's words: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you"﴾ and so on. It has been said that this verse, together with the other verses, may be a refutation of everything they meant by this speech; however, it began with refuting their words "we are capable," and so on, out of concern for it, since their saying that is the source of their demand for the strange sign.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is said that in this verse there is a cutting off of their empty hopes of trying to replace some of its verses with others. It is not admissible that it is a confirmation of what precedes it, God's words: ﴿then you will not find for yourself against Us any advocate﴾, as has been said. But not for what has been said, that producing its like is more difficult than retrieving its very essence, and the negation of a thing is only confirmed by the negation of what is less than it, not the negation of what is greater than it, because the difficulty of retrieval without His, the Exalted's, command is more than the mentioned production, which is beyond doubt. Rather, it is because the oath clause is not directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), but to the obstinate ones before him, peace and blessings be upon him. End of quote. From this it is known what is in the view of some of them regarding the mode of confirmation: that the incapacity of the two weighty things to return it after it has been taken away is equivalent to their incapacity to produce its like, because returning it in its very form is not possible, since they cannot reach God, the Exalted, so only returning it by its like remains, so the negation of that is stated to confirm it from the perspective of reflection and futility. Moreover, the author of al-Kashshaf argued from the inimitability of the Qur'an for its createdness (huduth): for if it were eternal (qadim) it would not be capable of being done, and so it would not be inimitable, like the impossible. Al-Kashf responded to this by saying that there is no dispute about the createdness of the composition (al-nazm), even though the People of the Sunnah avoid applying the term "created" to it due to the possibility of misunderstanding. The one who is inimitable is it, and the dispute is only about the one who expresses it with this inimitable expression, which is called the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi). Therefore, this is an argument that does not benefit him. Ibn al-Munayyir mentioned something similar.

The author of al-Taqrib said: The response is to deny the implication, for what makes capability valid is possibility, and this is present, not createdness. Also, the inimitable is its wording, and it is not said to be eternal, while the eternal is the inner speech, and it is not said to be inimitable. Also, even if we concede that humans cannot produce the eternal itself, why can they not produce its like? Al-'Allamah al-Tibi chose this last point as the response. We have mentioned in the Introductions (al-Muqaddimat) some of the discussion that will benefit you in this matter, so reflect. And God, the Exalted, is the Bestower of favours and the Guide of understandings.

[p. 167]

[p. 168 begins at "الإعجاز" below]

﴿And We have certainly turned⁠﴾ (ṣarrafnā), i.e., We repeated and reiterated [it] in varied styles that bring about greater affirmation and firmness, ﴿for the people⁠﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah and others, as is the apparent meaning, ﴿in this Qur'an⁠﴾, which is described by the excellent attributes mentioned, ﴿with every kind of example⁠﴾, i.e., with every wondrous meaning which, in its beauty and strangeness and in its drawing of souls, is like an example. The object of ﴿ṣarrafnā⁠﴾, according to what Abu Hayyan preferred, is omitted, i.e., the clarification (al-bayān), and he estimated it as "the clear signs and lessons" (al-bayyināt wa'l-ʿibar). The word min is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtidāʾ al-ghāya). Ibn ʿAtiyya permitted that it be "a sword of an orator" (sayf khaṭīb), so that kull (every) is the object. This is based on the view of the Kufans and al-Akhfash, because they permit the addition of min in affirmative sentences, unlike the majority of the Basran grammarians.

Al-Ḥasan read ﴿ṣarafnā⁠﴾ with the letter rāʾ lightened, but the reading of the majority is more emphatic. Whichever it is, the meaning is: We did that for the people, so that they would submit and receive it with acceptance. ﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief⁠﴾, i.e., denial (juḥūd), and it was explained as such because the truthfulness [of the Qur'an] is established by the basis of its inimitability (iʿjāz). [p. 168 ends here.] The people mentioned first are meant, and the explicit noun was preferred over the pronoun for emphasis and clarification. As for "most" (al-akthar), it has been said it refers to those among the polytheists and People of the Book who were in his time ﷺ.

Al-Bahr [al-Baḥr al-Muḥīt] favored that they are the people of Makkah, on the evidence that the following pronouns refer to them. ﴿Kufūran⁠﴾ is in the accusative as the object of ﴿abā⁠﴾, and the exception is "emptied" (istithnāʾ mufarragh). This is valid here, although it is conditional on a preceding negation, so ḍarabtu illā Zaydan is not valid. But ﴿abā⁠﴾ is close in meaning to negation, so it is interpreted as such, and it is as if it were said: "Most of them accepted nothing except disbelief." There is in this more emphasis than in "they refused faith," because it adds that they were not content with any trait other than disbelief, such as faith, hesitation in the matter, and the like, and that they exaggerated in their non-acceptance until they reached the rank of outright refusal. This construction was not permitted in an affirmative sentence because the meaning would be corrupt, since there is no indication of a specific thing being omitted, and generality is not valid, because it is impossible in the example to strike everyone except Zayd. If generality is valid in an example, the emptied exception is permitted without interpretation by negation, so ṣallaytu illā yawma kadhā ("I prayed except on such-and-such a day") is permitted, since it is possible that you pray every day other than that day. It was also permitted that the verse be of this type, meaning that they refused everything they proposed except disbelief.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 17, verse 90:

﴿And they say﴾ when their incapacity became evident and their defeat was clear, through the revelatory miracle (*al-i'jaz al-tanzili*, the inimitability of the Qur'an) and other manifest miracles, offering pretexts that wisdom does not require to occur, and that are not dependent on the proof of the claim, some of which are rationally impossible: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth﴾ (*tafjura*) with the lightened form from the pattern of *nasara*, transitive. The Kufans recited it thus, meaning *taftahu* (you open up). The rest of the seven readers recited *tufajjira*, from *fajjara* with the doubled letter, and the doubling is for intensification, not for transitivity.

Al-A'mash and Abdullah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar recited *tufjira*, from *afjara* in the quadriliteral form, and it is a dialect of *fajara*. ﴿for us from the earth﴾, meaning the earth of Makkah, because of the scarcity of its water, so the definite article is anaphoric (*'ahdi*). ﴿a spring (*yanbu'an*)﴾ is an object (*maf'ul*) from *nabaʿa al-ma'u*, like *ya'bub* from *ʿabba al-ma'u*, when the water surged and its waves multiplied; the *ya'* is added for emphasis. The intended meaning is a spring whose water does not run dry.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that *al-yanbu'* is the river that flows from the spring. The first view is related from Mujahid, and Mujahid suffices as an authority.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 91:

﴿Or you have⟩ a garden especially for yourself, ﴿a garden⟩: an orchard whose trees cover what is beneath them of the open ground, ﴿of date palms and grapevines⟩. They singled out these two for mention because they were the predominant ones in those regions, along with the great stature of both. ﴿So that you cause rivers to gush forth⟩, that is, make them flow, ﴿through it⟩ (khilalaha): this is put in the accusative of place, meaning in the midst of that garden and within it. ﴿In abundance⟩ (tafjiran): "kathiran" (much). What is meant is either the causing of rivers to flow through it at the time of irrigating it, or the continuous flowing of them, as the fa' (so) indicates. ﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces⟩, the known body, ﴿as you claimed⟩ (kama za'amta) ⟨alayna kisafa⟩: the plural of kisfa, like qit'a and qita' in form and meaning. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the sky", and the kaf in "kama" is in the accusative position, being an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: a falling similar to what you claimed, they meaning by this:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 92:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾. Some have claimed that they mean what is in this surah in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you feel safe that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you, or send against you a squall of stones?﴾ But this is nothing. It was also said that the meaning is: "as you claimed, that your Lord, if He wills, does so." That will come, God willing, in the report of Ibn Abbas. Mujahid read «yusqata al-sama'» (with the yā' of the third person and the sky in the nominative). Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read «kisfan» with a sukun on the sin throughout the Qur'an, except in al-Rum; Ibn Amir read it so except in this surah; Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it so in other places; and Hafs read it so except in al-Tur in his saying. In al-Nashr (the book of Ibn al-Jazari, a work on the readings) it is stated that they agreed on the sukun of the sin in al-Tur. It is either a lightened form of the vowelled reading, since sukun is an unrestricted form of vowel, as in sidr and sadr, or it is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle, like al-tahn in the sense of al-matḥun, meaning a thing that is broken into pieces, that is, cut off.

﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a tribe (qabilan)﴾: that is, facing us, like the 'ashir (companion) and the mu'ashir (one who associates with another). They meant, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, "face to face" (iyanan). This is like their saying: ﴿Why are the angels not sent down to us, or do we not see our Lord?﴾ In another report from al-Habr (Ibn Abbas) and al-Dahhak, qabil is explained as kafil (guarantor), that is, a guarantor for what you claim, meaning a witness who testifies to the truth of what you said, and a surety who guarantees what follows from it. In both interpretations it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the Divine Name, and the ḥāl of the angels is omitted, because the stated ḥāl indicates it, that is: "as tribes (qubala')," just as the predicate is omitted in the saying of the poet:

"Whoever has his baggage in Medina tonight, then I and Qayyar in it are strangers."

Al-Tabarsi reported from al-Zajjaj that he explained qabilan as "facing and face to face," and said that the Arabs treat it in this sense as a verbal noun, so it is not made dual, nor plural, nor feminine. So do not be heedless. From Mujahid: al-qabil means a group, like al-qabila, and so it is a ḥāl from the angels. In al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari), he made it a ḥāl from the angels because of the closeness of the wording and the soundness of the meaning, since the meaning is "you bring God, exalted is He, and a group of angels," not "you bring the two together as a group," which would make it a ḥāl in the plural. The sense of being accompanied by Him, exalted is He, is not intended. Do you not see His saying, glorified is He, reporting them: ﴿or we see our Lord﴾? The Qur'an explains part of itself by part. End of quotation. Al-A'raj read «qibalan» from the root of confronting, and this supports the first explanation.

[Page 170]

﴿Or you have a house of gold﴾, as related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and others. The root meaning of *zukhruf* is adornment, and it came to denote gold because adornment with it is more desired and more admired. ʿAbd Allah [Ibn Masʿud] recited "min dhahab" (of gold), but al-Bahr [Abu Hayyan] treated that as an explanation rather than a recitation (*qira'a*), because it contradicts the consonantal text of the *mushaf* (the codex). ﴿Or you ascend into the sky﴾, meaning you climb its ascending paths; the noun governed is elided. One says *raqiya fi al-sullam* (he climbed the ladder) and *fi al-darajah* (on the stairway). The apparent meaning is that *al-sama'* (the sky) here is the canopy. It has also been said that the intended meaning is any high place, since everything that rises and is elevated is called *sama'*. The poet said:

*Every elevated thing may be called "sky,"*
*but true excellence lies where the sun and the moon are.*

﴿And we will not believe in your ascent﴾, meaning: we will not believe in it on account of your ascent alone, or: we will not affirm your ascent into it. ﴿Until you bring down upon us a book which we may read﴾ from it, in our own language and in the style of our speech, and which contains your confirmation. ﴿Say﴾ (this in wonder at the severity of their obstinacy and the extremity of their folly): ﴿Glory be to my Lord.﴾ Alternatively, say this to exalt the sacred majesty above what is hardly fitting for it, such as these proposals, which include some of the greatest impossibilities, such as bringing Allah Most High in the manner they proposed, or seeking that. This also alerts to the falsity of what they said.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAmir recited: "Qala subhana rabbi" (He said: "Glory be to my Lord"), meaning the Prophet ﷺ said: ﴿Am I but a human being, a messenger?﴾ like the other messengers, peace be upon them, who did not bring their peoples anything except what Allah Most High manifested through their hands, as wisdom required, without any delegation to them in it, nor any dictation by them over Him, glory be to Him. "Basharan" (a human being) is the predicate of *kana* and "rasulan" (a messenger) is its attribute, and this is the principal point of the statement. Mentioning his humanity serves as a preparatory introduction (*tawti'ah*) to that, in refutation of what they denied, namely the permissibility of a messenger being a human, and as an indication that the messengers before him were likewise. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "Am I anything but a messenger like the other messengers, a human like them?" Some have claimed that the mention of ﴿human﴾ is not a preparatory introduction, since their request of him, peace and blessings be upon him, may be understood as asking him to bring it by his own power, or as asking him to bring it by the power of Allah Most High. Thus the mention of "human" negates that he could bring it by his own power, as if he said: "Am I anything but a human?" and a human has no power to bring such things. And the mention of "messenger" negates that he could bring it by the power of Allah Most High, as if it were said: "Am I anything but a messenger?" and a messenger does not dictate to his Lord, glory be to Him.

[Page 170 continued]

This has been criticised: even with its deficiency in contradicting reports, as you will learn shortly, if Allah wills, it plainly treats the two nouns as two predicates, and this is something sound taste rejects. Al-Khafaji said: that the two nouns be two predicates is not sound, because it implies that each of them is independent, and that they denied each of the two, so that they were answered on that basis, whereas no one denied his humanity ﷺ. This has been answered: when they asked him, peace and blessings be upon him, for what is not possible for a human, such as ascending into the sky, they were in the position of one who denied his humanity. This, as you see, is weak.

Some permitted that "basharan" be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of the indefinite noun, and its being placed before it was deemed acceptable. This is feeble, because it implies that he ﷺ has a state other than humanity, and no one holds this, except perhaps the Wujudiyyah (the pantheistic school). Apparently the speaker of all that has preceded is one and the same. It is also possible that the speaker was not one and the same: some proposed one thing and others proposed another, but the statement was attributed to all of them because each was content with what the others proposed.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and others narrated from Ibn Jubayr that the words of Allah Most High, ﴿And they said: "We will not believe you"﴾ and so on, were revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah. This clearly indicates that he was the speaker, and the plural pronoun does not conflict with this, for the reason we have indicated.

Ibn Ishaq and a group narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabiʿah, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Zamʿah ibn al-Aswad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and other people gathered after sunset by the Kaʿbah. Some of them said to others: "Send for Muhammad and speak with him, so that you may have an excuse concerning him." They sent for him, and he ﷺ came to them quickly, thinking that they had perhaps changed their minds about his affair. He was eager for them, loved their guidance, and was distressed by their hardship, so he sat with them. They said: "O Muhammad, we have sent for you so that we may excuse you. By Allah, we know of no man among the Arabs who has brought upon his people what you have brought upon your people. You have reviled the forefathers, disparaged the religion, made foolish the forbearance of men, reviled the gods, and divided the community. Nothing evil remains that you have not done among us. If you came with this message seeking wealth, we will gather money for you from our wealth until you become the richest of us. If you seek nobility among us, we will make you our chief. If you want kingship, we will make you king over us. And if what comes to you is a spirit (*ri'y*) that has overcome you, we will spend our wealth seeking a physician to cure you of it, or until we are excused concerning you."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is nothing in me of what you say. I did not come with what I have brought seeking your wealth, nor nobility among you, nor kingship over you. But Allah Most High sent me to you as a messenger, revealed a book to me, and commanded me to be a bringer of good tidings and a warner to you. I have conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you. If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it, I will be patient regarding the command of Allah Most High until Allah Most High judges between me and you."

They said: "O Muhammad, if you will not accept from us what we have offered you, then you know that no people is more constricted in land, less in wealth, or harder in life than we are. So ask your Lord who sent you with what He sent you, to remove from us these mountains that have confined us, to spread out our land for us, to make rivers flow through it like the rivers of al-Sham and Iraq, and to raise up for us those of our forefathers who have passed away, and let Qusayy ibn Kilab be among those He raises for us, for he was an honest old man. We will ask them whether what you say is true or false. If you do what we have asked and they confirm you, we will confirm you, recognise your standing with Allah Most High, and know that He sent you as a messenger."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was not sent with this. I have come to you from Allah Most High with what He sent me with. I have conveyed to you what I was sent with. If you accept it, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it, I will be patient regarding the command of Allah Most High until Allah Most High judges between me and you."

They said: "If you will not do this for us, then ask your Lord for yourself to send an angel to confirm what you say, so that he may answer us on your behalf, and ask Him to give you gardens, treasures, and palaces of gold and silver, and to free you from what we see you seeking. For you walk in the markets and seek livelihood as we do, so that we may know your standing with your Lord, if you are a messenger as you claim."

[Page 171]

He ﷺ said: "I will not do it. I am not one who asks his Lord for this, and I was not sent to you with this. Rather, Allah Most High sent me as a bringer of good tidings and a warner. If you accept what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it, I will be patient regarding the command of Allah Most High until Allah Most High judges between me and you."

They said: "Then make the sky fall upon us, as you claimed that your Lord will do if He wills. We will not believe you unless you do so."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "That is up to Allah Most High. If He wills, He will do that to you."

They said: "O Muhammad, then inform your Lord that we will sit with you, ask you what we have asked, and demand of you what we demand. Then He will send to you and inform you of what we have argued about and of what He will do with us if we do not accept from you what you have brought us. For it has reached us that what teaches you this is a man in Yamamah called al-Rahman, and by Allah we will never believe in al-Rahman. We have made our excuse to you, O Muhammad. By Allah, we will not leave you and what you have done to us until we destroy you or you destroy us."

One of them said: "We will not believe you until you bring Allah and the angels as a multitude before us." When they said that, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rose from them, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah rose with him and said: "O Muhammad, your people offered you what they offered, and you did not accept it from them. Then they asked you for things by which they might recognise your standing with Allah Most High, and you did not do them. Then they asked you to hasten what they fear of punishment. By Allah, we will never believe you until you take a ladder into the sky and climb it while I watch, until you reach it, and bring with you a written scroll, with four angels bearing witness that you are as you say. By Allah, even if you did that, I would think that I might believe you."

Then he departed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to his household, grieved and distressed over what he had missed of what he had hoped for from his people when they had called him, and because of what he saw of their aversion. So Allah sent down these verses to him.

And the words of Allah Most High: ﴿Thus We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away﴾ and the verse. And His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And if a Qur'an were such that by it the mountains were set moving﴾ and the verse. End. And Allah Most High knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 94:

﴿And what prevented the people﴾ — that is, those whose falsehoods have been related — ﴿from believing﴾. ﴿An yu'minu﴾ is the object (maf'ul) of mana'a (prevented). The words of the Exalted, ﴿when there came to them the guidance﴾ (idhja'ahumu al-huda), are an adverbial clause (zarf) of mana'a. Alternatively, yu'minu is read as: what prevented them from believing at the time the revelation came accompanied by miracles that call for faith, [namely] believing in the Qur'an and in your prophethood. Or: what prevented them from believing at the time of the coming of what has been mentioned. ﴿Illa an qalu﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of mana'a, meaning: except their saying, ﴿"Has God sent a mortal as a messenger?"﴾, denying that the Messenger of God, upon him be blessings and peace, could be of the kind of mortals. It is not meant that this saying proceeded from some of them, thereby preventing others; rather, the preventing factor is the belief that encompasses all of them, which entails this saying from them.

The reason it is expressed as "saying" is to signal that it is merely a word they utter with their mouths, without it having any meaning or actual referent. The preventing factor is restricted to what has been mentioned, although they have many diverse obstacles, either because it is the greatest of them, or because it is the preventing factor according to the circumstances, namely at the hearing of the answer in the words of the Exalted, ﴿"Was I anything but a mortal messenger?"﴾, for it is what they cling to at that time, without any other of their feeble doubts occurring to them. In this there is, according to this view, a signal of the completeness of their obstinacy, since it indicates that the aforementioned answer, though decisive in cutting off the roots of their doubts and demanding faith, they reverse the matter and make it a preventing factor. This was said by some of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqin). It is evident from this that the people do not affirm the messengership of any of the well-known messengers, such as Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them, at all. Some have stated that they did not deny the sending of others besides him, upon him be blessings and peace, from among them, and that their saying was mere obstinacy; but this is contrary to the apparent meaning here. Perhaps the people were in doubt and hesitation, not holding steady to any state, so reflect.

The apparent meaning is that the verse is a report from Him, glorified is His majesty, about the matter that prevented them from faith. And it appears from the words of Ibn 'Atiyya that this statement from him, upon him be blessings and peace, was said in the sense of rebuke and grief; but far be it from anyone with even a little taste (for the Arabic language) to go to that.
Page 172

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 17, verse 95:

﴿Say﴾ to them first, from Us, as a clarification of the wisdom and a confirmation of the truth that removes doubt. ﴿If there were﴾, that is, if there existed ﴿on the earth﴾, in place of humans, ﴿angels walking﴾ as humans walk, and not flying up to the heaven, so that they would hear from its inhabitants and know what must be known, ﴿at peace﴾, that is, settled and dwelling there. Al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i) said: that is, at peace with this world and its pleasures, not fearing and not worshipping by a law, because the one at peace is one from whom fear has departed. ﴿We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾ who teaches them what their capacities cannot independently grasp, so that meeting him and receiving from him would be easy for them. As for the common run of humans, that is not easy for them, because of the distance between the angel and them. So he is not sent to them; he is sent only to their elite. This is because God Most High has given them pure souls, strengthened them with holy powers, and made for them two aspects: an angelic aspect, through which they draw from the angel, and a human aspect, through which they pour forth upon humans. Making all humans like this would violate wisdom. The angel was sent down to them in a manner that makes receiving from him easy, namely by appearing to them in the form of a human, as Gabriel (peace be upon him) appeared several times in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi.

It is established that a bedouin came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bearing traces of travel, and asked him about Islam, faith (*iman*), excellence (*ihsan*) and other matters. He (peace be upon him) answered him with what he answered, then the man left, and none of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) recognized him. So he (ﷺ) said: "This was Gabriel, who came to you to teach you the matters of your religion." This is of the kind that would not benefit those disbelievers, as the Exalted said: ﴿Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused for them what they [now] confuse.﴾

It has been said: the reason for sending the angel to them is that a kind is more inclined toward its own kind and more at ease with it. Yet perhaps the first explanation is better, even if others claim otherwise.

Al-Tabarsi related from some of them that he said about the verse: the Arabs said, "We were at rest and at peace, then Muhammad (ﷺ) came and disturbed us and confused our affair." So He (glorified be He) showed that if there were angels at peace, wisdom would require sending messengers to them, and their being at peace would not prevent the sending of messengers. Likewise, the fact that humans are at peace does not prevent the sending of messengers to them. You know that this is far from the context, and no reliable report supports it, as is clear to anyone who investigates.

The accusative of ﴿a messenger﴾ (*malakan*) may be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of *rasulan* ("messenger"), which is the object of *nazzalna* ("We sent down"), and the advancing of it permits this. It may also be the object of *nazzalna*, with *rasulan* as its attribute. Many scholars preferred the first, as it accords better and is more suitable to the context. Al-Qutb and the author of *al-Taqrib* explained this: on the circumstantial reading, it conveys the intended meaning through its explicit wording; on the attributive reading, it conveys the opposite of the intended meaning through its implication. As for the first: its explicit meaning is "Did Allah send a messenger who was a human and not an angel?" and "We sent down to them a messenger who was an angel and not a human," which is the intended meaning. As for the second: restricting by an attribute means "Did Allah send a human who is a messenger, rather than a human who is not a messenger?" and "We sent down to them an angel who is a messenger, rather than an angel who is not a messenger," which is contrary to the intended meaning, indeed not correct.

The author of *al-Kashf*, following his teacher al-Tibi, said: this is because fronting (*taqdim*) removes a word from its original place, indicating that it is the locus of denial. In the first phrase, "Did Allah send a human as a messenger?", it indicates that humanness is incompatible with this established fact, namely messengerhood. This is like your saying, "Did you strike [Zayd] standing?" (*a-darabta qa'iman Zaydan*). If you said, "Did you strike Zayd standing?" (*a-darabta Ziyadan qa'iman*) or "Did you strike Zayd, the standing one?" (*al-qa'im*), this would not yield that benefit. The first says that the denier struck him while standing, not that striking in general is denied. The second says that the denier denied striking Zayd because of his possessing this preventive attribute, and it does not indicate that the basic act of striking is good and accepted. The denial is directed at the attribute. This holds if the fronting is taken for restriction (*hasr*). [Page 173]

If the fronting is taken for emphasis (*ihtimam*), it indicates that the word is the locus of denial, though it does not indicate the establishment of its opposite. In either case, the benefit of the fronting is clear. He said this, and it is more precise.

Some scholars objected to this verse, claiming that it apparently indicates that He sends to each category only what is suitable to it and resembles it, such as humans to humans and angels to angels, and does not send to a category what is not suitable or similar to it. This contradicts his (ﷺ) being sent to the jinn as well as to humans, which is a consensus (*ijma'*) known by necessity from the religion, so whoever denies it is a disbeliever. Whoever disputes this is mistaken. It was answered: it is not apparent that the verse indicates this. Rather, the most it indicates is that they denied that Allah would send a human to humans, and they assumed that the one sent to them must be an angel. Their aim was to negate that the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent to them. So they were answered that wisdom requires sending an angel to angels, because of the existing relevance (*munasaba*) that makes receiving valid, and not to common humans, because that relevance is absent. Thus the obligation they claim is reversed. This indicates no more than that the matter of sending depends on the existence of relevance: when it exists, sending is valid, and when it does not, sending is not valid. Relevance exists between angel and angel, not between him and common humans like the deniers mentioned. This does not contradict his being sent to the jinn, because whenever relevance is valid for him with the angel, such that gathering with him and receiving from him is valid, then relevance with the jinn is also valid for gathering with them and conveying to them. How could it not be, when he (ﷺ) is the complete copy of Allah and His greatest manifest sign? When we say that his gathering with the jinn and his conveying to them occurs after they take a form for him, the matter of relevance is even more evident. And the angel's taking a form, if he were sent to humans, is of no benefit, for what you have just heard. The same is said of his sending to the angels, because of the strength of conveying to them, as receiving from them.

Among the Shafi'is, Taqi al-Din al-Subki, al-Barizi, and al-Jalal al-Mahalli in his *Khasa'is* went to the view that he (ﷺ) was sent to them. Among the Hanbalis, Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Muflih in *Kitab al-Furu'* did so. Among the Malikis, 'Abd al-Haqq did so. Ibn Taymiyya said: there is no dispute among scholars that they are addressed by the command and the prohibition.

Ibrahim al-Laqqani said: there is no doubt about the establishment of the principle of obligation to practical acts of worship for them. As for matters like faith, it is necessary for them, so obligating them with it is impossible. Al-Subki said in his *Fatawa*: the jinn are obligated with everything in this sharia, because if it is established that he (ﷺ) is sent to them as he is sent to humans, and the call is general, and the sharia is likewise general, then the obligations whose causes exist in them bind them, unless some evidence specifies some of them. So we say: prayer and zakat are obligatory for them if they possess the minimum amount (*nisab*) with its condition, and so are hajj, fasting Ramadan, and the other obligations. Every prohibition in the sharia is forbidden for them. This differs from the angels. We do not commit ourselves to the view that all these obligations are established for them if we hold that the messengership is general to them. Rather, it is possible, and it is also possible that the messengership is restricted to a specific matter.

There is no barrier to His obligating them all with what came to him from his Lord, the Majestic, through some of them. Moreover, not everything that he (peace be upon him) brought came through the mediation of an angel. So it is possible that what they were obligated with did not come through the mediation of any of them.

Some denied his sending to them. The denial of his being sent to them was affirmed by al-Halimi and al-Bayhaqi among the Shafi'is, and by Mahmud ibn Hamza al-Karmani in his book *al-'Aja'ib wal-Gharaib* among the Hanafis. Indeed, al-Nasafi (Burhan al-Din) and al-Razi in their tafsirs related a consensus on it. Among the later scholars, Zayn al-Din al-Iraqi in his notes on Ibn al-Salah, and al-Mahalli in his commentary on *Jam' al-Jawami'*, affirmed it. The explicit verse: ﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ (25:1), since "the worlds" (*al-'alamin*) are all that is other than Allah and His attributes. And the report of Muslim: "I was sent to all of creation" (*ila al-khalq kaffatan*) supports the first view. Yes, the proponents of this view relied on what they relied on, and there is what there is in it.

Some people claimed that the verse supports their view, because He specified in it the angel for sending to angels, so it is necessary that he be the one sent to them, not a human, whether or not there is any relevance between him and them. You have heard what was reported from al-Qutb and the author of *al-Taqrib*, that the intended meaning is: "We sent down to them a messenger who is an angel, not a human." It was answered: after loosening the reins, the verse indicates only that sending an angel is specified for angels when they are on the earth walking at peace instead of humans. It does not follow from this that sending humans to them is invalid when they are not in that condition. This is because the wisdom behind the specification in the first case may be something other than the relevance that results in the ease of gathering and receiving, which is a different matter that does not exist in the second case. That is, if the people of the earth were angels and a human, who has the strength to convey and to pour forth upon them, were sent to them, like the sending of human messengers (peace be upon them) to humans, it would be difficult by nature for that messenger to remain with them for a significant period of time, just as human messengers remain with humans. Unless he is made to share what they were created with and to join them, and that is nearly the same as taking him entirely out of human nature. So the shift from sending an angel to sending him would be nearest to futility, which contradicts wisdom. Reflect on this.

Perhaps Allah, glorified be He, will bestow upon you what quenches your thirst. Reflect upon all that has preceded, and perhaps, by the help of Allah Most High, you will be guided to the *jarh wa-ta'dil* (the scholarly science of evaluating the reliability of narrators).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 96:

﴿Say﴾ to them a second time, on your own part, after what you have said to them before, and you have explained to them what the wisdom of the mission requires, though they did not pay it any heed. ﴿Sufficient is Allah﴾, exalted and majestic, alone, ﴿as a witness﴾ that I have discharged the obligations of the message in the most complete manner, and that you have done what you have done of denial and obstinacy. It has also been said: "as a witness" that I am the Messenger of Allah, Exalted is He, sent to you, by manifesting a miracle in accordance with my claim. The first view is preferred because it better fits His words, ﴿between me and you﴾, and likewise His words, Glorified is He, giving the reason for sufficiency: ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants﴾, i.e., the Messengers and those to whom they were sent, ﴿Acquainted and Seeing﴾, i.e., encompassing their outward and inward states, so that He will recompense them for that. Al-Khafaji claimed that the second view fits the context better than the first, since the speech would then be like the preceding, a rebuttal of their denial that the Messenger could be a human being. To this view the Imam [al-Razi] also went. But that the first is better suited to His words ﴿Indeed He is﴾ and so on has no basis, because its meaning is a threat and warning that He, Glorified is He, knows their outward and inward states, and that they only raised this doubt out of envy, love of leadership, and disdain for the truth; and it contains consolation for His beloved ﷺ of what it contains. You know that denying that the first is better suited to this is something without basis, given the evident contrary. Nor does the inclusion of threat and consolation in the sentence negate it. Also, the matter of its suitability, "between me and you," remains in the context, and moreover, opening the speech with "Say" is a kind of support for the intention of the first, as is not hidden from the discerning. Here, He, Glorified is He, did not say "between us," in order to affirm separation and make clear the opposition. The accusative of ﴿as a witness﴾ is either a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) or a specifying accusative (tamyīz).

[p. 175]

﴿Whoever Allah guides﴾ is a new sentence (kalam mubtada', an independent clause), not included within the scope of (qul, "Say"). It separates what the preceding speech indicated about the recompense of the servants, because His knowledge, exalted is He, in such a context is used with the meaning of recompense. That is: whoever Allah, exalted is He, guides to the truth, ﴿then he is the one guided﴾ to Him and to what leads to Him of reward, or the one guided to every desired thing. Most of them omitted the yā' of al-muhtadī (the final yā' of "the one guided"). ﴿And whoever He leads astray﴾ means He creates misguidance in him because of his bad choice and the ugliness of his readiness, like these stubborn opponents. ﴿Then you will not find for them any awliyā'﴾, that is, helpers ﴿besides Him﴾, mighty and majestic, who guide them to the path of truth, or to a path that brings them to their worldly and otherworldly aims, or to the path of salvation from the punishment that their misguidance necessitates. The meaning is: you will not find for any one of them a protector, according to what is required by the matter of matching plural with plural, in the division of individuals over individuals, according to what is well known.

[p. 175 continued]

It has been said: He, glorified is He, said ﴿awliyā'﴾ (in the plural) for emphasis, because if the protectors do not benefit them, how much less a single protector. The pronoun in (lahum, "for them") refers to "man" (man) according to its meaning, just as (huwa, "he") refers to it according to its wording. Therefore the pronoun was made singular at one time and plural at another.

In the choice of the singular and plural in the places where each was chosen, there is an allusion to the oneness of the path of truth and the scarcity of its travelers, and to the multiplicity of the ways of misguidance and the abundance of the misguided. Abū Ḥayyān mentioned, and some of his followers after him, that the second clause is one of the places in which the reference is to the meaning first, without preceding reference to the wording, and that such places are few in the Qur'an. Al-Khafājī criticized this, saying that there is no basis for it, since in it the pronoun was referred to the wording first: in His saying ﴿yuḍlil﴾ (He leads astray) there is an omitted singular pronoun, its original estimate being yuḍillahu, and it refers to the wording of "man", so one cannot say that no reference to the wording preceded it. Then he said: More strange than that is what has been said, that it may be said that reference to the wording preceded it in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿whom Allah guides﴾, although that was in another clause. End of quote.

In this there is the objection that its basis is Abū Ḥayyān's making ﴿yuḍlil﴾ take an object, as he explicitly stated in al-Baḥr, and likewise he explicitly stated that in the first clause it is the object of "yahdi". In that case there is no omitted singular pronoun, as is not hidden, so consider this carefully. It has also been allowed that the two clauses fall within the scope of (qul), because "man" comes with a conjunction (wa, "and"). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We will gather them﴾, is more suitable to the first view. In it there is a shift from the third person to the first person, to show the complete concern with the matter of the gathering. According to the second possibility, it is taken as a report of what Allah, exalted is He, said to him, upon him be blessings and peace.

﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾, when they rise from their graves. ﴿On their faces﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the object pronoun, meaning: being upon them. This is either walking, by their crawling prone upon them, and this is supported by what al-Shaykhān and others narrated from Anas, who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, how will people be gathered on their faces? He said: The One who made them walk on their feet is able to make them walk on their faces."

What is meant is how this kind (of people) will be gathered on the face, because that is specific to the disbelievers, while others are gathered in another manner.

Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan (good), and Ibn Jarīr and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three categories: a category walking, that is, in the usual way; a category riding; and a category on their faces." It was said: O Messenger of Allah, how will they walk on their faces? He said: "The One who made them walk on their feet is able to make them walk on their faces. Indeed they will protect themselves with their faces from every rough ground and thorn." Or it is dragging, by the angels pulling them prone upon them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day they will be dragged into the Fire on their faces﴾.

This is supported by what Aḥmad, al-Nasā'ī, and al-Ḥākim narrated, and al-Ḥākim graded it ṣaḥīḥ (sound), from Abū Dharr, that he recited this verse: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection on their faces﴾, etc., and then said: The truthful, the one whose word is believed, ﷺ, told me: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three groups: a group eating, clothed and riding; a group walking and running; and a group the angels will drag on their faces."

Aḥmad, al-Nasā'ī, and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan, narrated from Mu'āwiyah ibn Ḥaydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, said: "Indeed you will be gathered walking and riding, and you will be dragged on your faces."

The way of reconciling these should be sought. If it is not found, then what is relied upon is what the hadith of the two Shaykhs bears witness to. The verse does not specify, I mean His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day they will be dragged into the Fire on their faces﴾ —

Second: because the Qur'an explains part of it by part, since that (verse) concerns their state after entering the Fire, while what is here concerns their state before it, so the two differ. Some have claimed that the speech is figurative, as is said of one who leaves a matter disappointed and distressed: "He left upon his face." So the meaning is: and We will drag them on the Day of Resurrection distressed and disappointed. It seems that the motive for this assumption is that he narrated from Ibn 'Abbās the interpretation of the present states as figurative, and then all the states would be of one pattern. This is not hidden from you. So beware of turning to an interpretation which the prophetic sunnah has spoken against, and do not heed people who do this.

﴿Blind, dumb, and deaf﴾: these are circumstantial phrases from the hidden pronoun in the preposition-and-object phrase that is the first circumstantial phrase. In Irshād al-'Aql al-Salīm it is said that they are circumstantial phrases from the object pronoun in the earlier circumstantial phrase. The first view is further from "what is said and what is repeated" (the gossip of disputes). Abū al-Baqā' permitted that this be a substitute for that earlier circumstantial phrase, and it is, as you see, far-fetched.

Abū Ḥayyān favored that what is meant by what was mentioned is its literal reality, and that this occurs at the beginning of the matter, then Allah, exalted is He, returns to them their sight, speech, and hearing, so they see the Fire, hear its roaring, and speak as Allah, exalted is He, related about them in more than one place.

Yes, their mouths may be sealed at a certain point. It has also been said that it is figurative, meaning that, because of extreme bewilderment and confusion, they resemble those possessing these attributes. Or it means that they do not see anything that would please them, nor hear it in the same way, nor speak with an argument, just as in the world they did not perceive insight, did not speak the truth, and did not hear it. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated this from Ibn 'Abbās, and it is also narrated from al-Ḥasan. So what they say, hear, and see is placed in the position of non-existence, because they gain no benefit from it. It is not objectionable to this that some verses indicate the removal of some faculties from them, due to differences in times. It has also been said: blind to looking at what Allah, exalted is He, has made for His friends; dumb from speaking with Him, glorified is He; deaf to what Allah, exalted is He, praised His friends for. It has been said: this happens to them literally after His saying, exalted is He, to them: ﴿Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me﴾. In this case the states are "assumed" (muqaddarah), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their abode is Hell﴾, meaning their place of settling, on the assumption that it is a circumstantial phrase. It may also be an independent new sentence (isti'nāf).

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whenever it subsides, We increase them in blaze﴾, it may also be an independent sentence, and it may be a circumstantial phrase from Hell, as Abū al-Baqā' said. He took the operating element of the circumstantial phrase to be the meaning of "abode". Al-Ṭabarsī said: it is a circumstantial phrase from it, because it is described as "blazing and flaming"; were it not so, it would not have been made a circumstantial phrase from it.

He permitted making it a circumstantial phrase from that from which the first clause was made a circumstantial phrase, but only after considering it within the structure, with the connecting element being the object pronoun in "We increase them". This is, as you see, far-fetched, and the independent sentence is less burdensome.

Al-khabw, and likewise al-khubū' with two damma-vowels and a shadda, are both verbal nouns of "khabat al-nār" (the fire subsided): the stilling of the flame. Al-Baḥr says: it is said "khabat al-nār" (the fire subsided) when its flame goes calm; "khamadat" when its embers are calm and weakened; and "hamadat" when it is completely extinguished. Al-Rāghib said: "khabat al-nār" means its flame calmed and there came over it a covering of ash, that is, a veil. In al-Qāmūs, "khabat" is interpreted as "sakanat" (calmed) and "ṭafi'at" (went out), and "ṭafi'at" is interpreted as "dhahaba lahabuhā" (its flame went away). This differs from what is in al-Baḥr, but most agree with what is in it.

Among the strange things is what Ibn al-Anbārī narrated from Abū Ṣāliḥ, interpreting "khabat" in the verse as "ḥamiyat" (became heated), which contradicts what is well known and transmitted. Al-Sa'īr is the flame. The meaning is: whenever its flame calms, by consuming their skins and flesh and there remains nothing for the fire to take hold of and burn, We increase them flame and blazing, by returning them to what they were, so that the fire is kindled and blazes with them. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said about the verse: the disbelievers are the fuel of the Fire. When it burns them and nothing remains, it becomes embers glowing; that is its subsiding. Then when they are changed into a new creation, it returns to them.

Perhaps that, as some of the eminent scholars said, is a punishment for them for their denial of resurrection after annihilation, by its repetition again and again, so that they may see it with their own eyes, since they did not see it as proof, as what follows makes clear.

What has been mentioned is objected to on the ground that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whenever their skins are cooked, We exchange them for other skins﴾ indicates that the Fire does not go beyond cooking them to burning and annihilating them, so this contradicts that. Some answered that the exchange of skins for others means burning and annihilating them and creating others in their place, as if it were said: whenever their skins are cooked, We burn them and annihilate them and create other skins for them. Others answered that what is meant is: whenever their skins are cooked to the full degree of cooking, so that their roasting reaches a point where, if they remained in it, their owner would not feel the punishment; this is the level of burning, and then We exchange them. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that they may taste the punishment﴾.

Al-Khafājī said: It was answered that it is possible that for their skins there sometimes occurs cooking and sometimes annihilation, or each of them in the case of a particular people. And it is not closed to figurative speech, by making "cooking" an expression for the general effect of the fire, since at the beginning of entering there occurs nothing but burning, not cooking. End of quote.

There is no hiding what is in His saying "by making cooking an expression for the general effect of the fire" of leniency, and in His saying "since at the beginning of entering there occurs" ... there is a clear prohibition. It was mentioned that an objection was raised to the first answer, that the word "whenever" (kullamā) contradicts it. In this there is discussion, so reflect.

Perhaps it is imagined that there is a contradiction between this verse and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, because the subsiding entails lightening. This is rejected by the fact that subsiding means the stilling of the flame, as you have heard, and its entailing the lightening of the punishment of the Fire is denied. Furthermore, even if we concede the entailment, the punishment that is not lightened is not restricted to punishment by fire and pain by its heats. In that case it is possible that what was lost of it through the stilling of the flame is compensated with another kind of punishment which no one knows but Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Imām mentioned that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We increase them in blaze﴾ apparently indicates that the second state is greater than the first state, so the first state would be a lightening compared to the second. He answered that in the first state there arose the fear of the second occurring, so the punishment was severe. It may be said that when the punishment became great, the difference occurring within it became unperceived. We seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, from it. End of quote.

It may be said: the verse contains nothing more than the increase in their blazing, and perhaps this does not entail an increase in their punishment. The meaning of the verse is: whenever they are burned, they are restored, except that it was expressed in this way for emphasis. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We increase them﴾ rather than "We increase it", so reflect.

﴿That﴾, i.e. the punishment understood from His words, "Whenever it abates, We increase them in the Blaze" (17:97), or referring to all that was mentioned of their being gathered upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf, etc. What has been understood from what we mentioned is included in it.

﴿Their recompense is because﴾, i.e., because of the fact that they ﴿disbelieved in Our signs﴾, the Qur'anic and the cosmic signs that clearly indicate the possibility of resurrection (al-i'adah), or the truth of what We sent you with in general, so that it includes what has been mentioned. (ذلك) is a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), ﴿their recompense﴾ is its predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate), and the adverbial phrase is connected to it. It has been permitted that ﴿their recompense﴾ be a second subject, with the adverbial phrase as its predicate, and the whole clause a predicate of (ذلك). It has also been permitted that ﴿their recompense﴾ be an apposition (badal) or an explanatory elaboration (bayan) of (ذلك), with the predicate being the adverbial phrase. It was also said that (ذلك) is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "the matter is that," and what follows is a subject and predicate, but this is worthless.

﴿And they said﴾, denying in the strongest terms, ﴿"When we are bones and crumbled fragments?"﴾ The word (رفات, rufat) originally, as al-Raghib said, means like the crumbs (الفتات) of what has broken and scattered of straw, and what is meant here is that they have decayed and become scattered. ﴿"Shall we indeed be resurrected as a new creation?"﴾ It is either an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkad) from a verb of its own kind, i.e., "shall we indeed be resurrected with a new resurrection," or a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., "created anew, in a fresh form."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 99:**

﴿Have they not seen that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, have they not reflected and not known that Allah, exalted is He, who has power to create these massive, strong, great bodies and forms, of which humankind is only a small part, ﴿is able to create the likes of them﴾ from among mankind? That is: whoever is able to do that, how could He not be able to restore them, and restoration is easier for Him, majestic and exalted is He? Some of the verifying scholars said: here the likeness is used as in the expression "someone like you does not stinginess," meaning: He is able to create them. The intended meaning of creation is restoration, as it is expressed in ﴿a new creation﴾, or it is not meant that way, since it was said: ﴿a new creation﴾. This has some distance. Some claimed that the intended meaning is: He is able to create other servants who affirm His oneness, acknowledge the perfection of His wisdom and power, and abandon the mention of these corrupt doubts, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and bring a new creation﴾
Page 178
and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and replace you with another people﴾. But this does not fit the context, as is not hidden from those of refined taste.

Then know that the apparent meaning of the verse is that the disbelievers denied their restoration on the Day of Resurrection, in the sense of gathering their scattered parts and their crumbled bones, assembling them, and breathing life into them again as they were in the world. This is what they meant by their saying: ﴿Shall we indeed be resurrected as a new creation?﴾ after their saying ﴿When we are bones and crumbled dust?﴾ So He answered them by establishing that through a demonstrative argument. On this basis, the verse is one of the proofs of those who say that the gathering (hashr) is by restoring the parts of the bodies that disperse, like the bodies of all except the Prophets, peace be upon them, and those who never committed a sin, the muezzins who did so for the sake of reward, and others whose bodies were forbidden to the earth, as has come in the reports; and their gathering after dispersal. By this they meant the original parts (al-ajza' al-asliyyah), which are those present at the very beginning of the natural disposition (fitrah) at the time of the breathing of the spirit. They hold these to be preserved from becoming part of another body, let alone becoming an original part of it. Those who go to this view are the minority, and al-Amidi related it with the wording "it was said," but al-Fakhr al-Razi preferred it, and mentioned that the majority hold that Allah, glorified is He, annihilates the essences entirely and then restores them, and he said: this is the correct view. Likewise al-Badr al-Zarkashi said. Al-Laqqani mentioned that it is the view of the People of the Sunnah and of the Mu'tazilah who affirm the possibility of annihilation (fana') and nonexistence (adam) upon bodies, indeed the occurrence of it, although they differed as to whether that is by the occurrence of an opposite (didd), or by the absence of a condition, or by neither. The latter view was taken by al-Qadi from the People of the Sunnah and Abu al-Hudhayl from the Mu'tazilah. They said: Allah, exalted is He, annihilates whatever He wills to annihilate in the manner of His bringing it into being, so He says to it, according to Abu al-Hudhayl: "Perish," and it perishes, just as He says to it "Be," and it is.

The majority of the Mu'tazilah took the first view and said: the annihilation of the substance (jawhar, indivisible particle or atom) is by the occurrence of an opposite to it, which is annihilation. Then they differed. Ibn al-Ikhshid held that Allah, exalted is He, creates annihilation in one direction of the substances, so all the substances are annihilated together. Ibn Shabib said: He, exalted is He, produces in each specific substance an annihilation that requires the substance's non-existence in the second moment. Abu 'Ali, Abu Hashim, and their followers held that Allah, exalted is He, annihilates the substance by creating an annihilation not in any specific locus of it. Then they differed: Abu 'Ali and his followers said: Allah, glorified is He, creates one annihilation not in any locus, by which He annihilates all the substances. Abu Hashim and his followers said: He, exalted is He, creates for each substance an annihilation not in any locus.

Imam al-Haramayn, the majority of the People of the Sunnah, Bishr al-Marisi, and al-Ka'bi of the Mu'tazilah took the second view. Then they differed about specifying the condition. Bishr said: it is a continuance (baqa') that He, glorified is He, creates not in any locus; if He does not create it, the substance is annihilated. The majority and al-Ka'bi said: it is a continuance subsisting in the substance, which He, majestic and exalted is He, creates in it moment by moment; when He, exalted is He, does not create it in it, the substance ceases. Imam al-Haramayn said: it is the accidents (a'rad) which the body must be described by; Allah, exalted is His state, creates them in the body moment by moment, so whenever He, glorified is He, does not create them in it, it ceases to exist. Al-Nazzam said: it is Allah, exalted is He, creating the substance moment by moment, for substances in his view have no continuance but are renewed with the renewal of accidents. So if He, mighty is His glory, does not continue to create the substance, it perishes.

You know that most of these sayings belong to the category of falsehoods, especially the claim that annihilation is a realized matter outside the mind, an opposite to continuance, subsisting by itself or in the substance, and that continuance exists without a locus. The reason for their falsity is too clear to need explanation. They argued for this view with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Everything perishes except His face﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾. They answered regarding the verse that the disbelievers were satisfied with the least necessary implication and intended exaggeration in denial, for if, by their claim, restoration is not possible after they become bones and crumbled dust, then its impossibility after complete annihilation is even more evident and more evident. But in this there is that the perishing of everything is its departure from the qualities required of it, and dispersal is likewise, so it is called perishing, and it is also called annihilation (fana') in common usage. So the argument by the two verses is not complete, and what they said in answer to the verse is contrary to the apparent meaning.

It is not objected against them that the restoration of the non-existent is impossible, because of
Page 179
what the philosophers mentioned as proofs, against what the Muslims mentioned in refuting them. Some people said: the coccyx bone (ajb al-dhanab) does not perish, even if everything else of the body's parts perishes, because of the authentic hadith of the two Shaykhs: "Nothing of the human being is not decayed except one bone, and it is the coccyx bone; from it the creation is made on the Day of Resurrection."

In the narration of Muslim: "All of the son of Adam is eaten by the earth except the coccyx bone; from it he was created and from it he is assembled."

Al-Muzani affirmed that it also perishes, and he interpreted the hadith to mean that the intent is that all of the human being decays by the earth and that this is the cause of his annihilation, except the coccyx bone, for Allah, exalted is He, causes it to perish without earth, just as He causes the Angel of Death to cause death without an angel of death. The creation from it and the assembling from it can be after its restoration, so what was mentioned is not a clear text regarding its continuance. Ibn Qutaybah agreed with him on that. You know that the apparent meanings of the reports indicate its non-perishing absolutely. Some scholars stopped short of definitively deciding in favour of either of the two previous views about the manner of the gathering.

Al-Sa'd said: it is the truth, and it is the choice of Imam al-Haramayn. In al-Mawaqif and its commentary by al-Sayyid al-Sanad: Does Allah, exalted is He, annihilate the bodily parts and then restore them, or does He disperse them and restore the assembling within them? The truth is that nothing has been established regarding that, so there is no definitive affirmation or negation of it, because there is no evidence for anything on either side.

Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali said in the book al-Iqtisad: If it is said: what do you say? Are the substances and accidents annihilated and then both restored together, or are the accidents annihilated without the substances, and then only the accidents are restored? We say: all of that is possible, and the truth is that there is no decisive evidence in the Law determining one of the two possible matters.

Some of them said: the truth is the occurrence of both matters together: the restoration of what was annihilated with its very self, and the restoration of what was dispersed with its accidents. This is good. The discussion of this matter is very long, and perhaps Allah, glorified and exalted is He, will bestow upon us its completion, even in several places.

﴿And He appointed for them a term﴾: and it is the appointed time of their restoration and gathering, or their death. On this view it is a generic noun, since each person has a term of death specific to him. The term has come to be applied to death, and its basis is that it is applied to the duration of life and to its end, and death is adjacent to that.

﴿there is no doubt in it﴾: that is, there should be no doubt in it, and denial is for the one who reflects upon it; or the negation is on its apparent sense. The sentence is conjoined to: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. Although it is an imperative (insha'iyyah) and there is debate about conjoining a declarative (khabariyyah) to it, which is interpreted as a declarative sentence. Conjoining to the relative clause (silah) in what passed is impossible because of the separation by the predicate of inna.

Likewise, it is conjoined to what follows anna, the verbal and semantic one. The meaning, as in al-Kashf and elsewhere, is: they already knew by the evidence of reason that Allah, exalted is He, is able to restore them, and He has appointed a term for it, about which there is no doubt, so it must come to pass; that is, if that is possible in itself and obligatory to occur by the report of the Truthful, denial has no meaning. If the term means the appointed time of their restoration, that is the Day of Resurrection, due to their saying: ﴿When we are bones and crumbled dust?﴾ and this is the apparent meaning, then it is clear. If it means death, then its basis is that they have known its possibility and that they are certainly going to die and depart from this life, and that they must have a recompense, so they were not created in vain nor left neglected; so why the denial? It seems he was content with death instead of what comes after it, because it is the beginning of the Resurrection, and whoever dies has had his resurrection established. So the conjunction is, in estimation, upon "they already knew." It is known from this explanation that the connection between the two sentences for the correctness of the conjunction is extremely strong.

Al-Qutb claimed that it is better to conjoin to what follows the verbal anna. As for first, it is closer; and as for second, the appointing of the term then falls under His power, exalted is He, and under their knowledge, unlike when it is conjoined to His saying, glorified is He: "Have they not seen," etc.
Page 180
What is in it is not hidden from one who has turned round and round upon the axis of verification. ﴿But the wrongdoers refused﴾: those who disbelieved in the signs and said what they said. He placed the apparent noun in the place of their pronoun, to record upon them wrongdoing and transgressing the limit entirely. ﴿except disbelief﴾: that is, denial.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 100:

﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would surely withhold them."﴾ That is, the treasuries of His bounties which He has bestowed upon all existing things.
