So "mercy" is a metonymy (majaz) for bounties, and "treasuries" is a metaphor (isti'arah), either realistic (tahqiqiyyah) or imaginative (takhyiliyyah). The "antum" (you) is, according to what al-Hufi, al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Baqa', Ibn 'Atiyyah and others have held, the subject (fa'il) of a deleted verb which the mentioned verb explains, because "law" (if/even if) cannot be followed directly by a noun. The original is: law tamlikuna tamlikuna, and when the verb was deleted the pronoun became detached. A similar case is the words of Hatim when he was taken captive and a slave-girl slapped him: "Law dhat siwarin laṭamatni" (If a woman with bracelets had slapped me...), and the words of al-Mutalammis:

"Wa law ghayru akhwali aradu naqisati / ja'altu lahum fawqa al-'iranini mismama"
(And if other than my maternal uncles had wished to diminish me, I would have branded for them a mark above the noses.)

The benefit of the deletion and explanation, as is said, is brevity (ijaz). For after the intention of emphasis, if it were said "tamlikuna tamlikuna," it would be prolixity and repetition on the surface. The emphasis lies in the repetition of the predication or in the repetition of the condition, as it requires the repeated consequence of the apodosis upon it, and it indicates exclusivity. This is based on the view that "antum" itself is the pronoun of the postponed "tamlikuna," so it is in meaning a fronted subject, and fronting the semantic subject conveys exclusivity when the context suits, so the statement then conveys the consequence of withholding. What is meant by it will come shortly, God willing, as their being alone in possessing the treasuries, and it is known from it that the consequence follows their possession of them in common by a fortiori reasoning. To this analysis of such a construction in this pattern the Basrians went, except that Abu al-Hasan Ibn al-Sa'igh and others stated explicitly that they prohibit "law" from being followed by a deleted verb in the eloquent usage, and permit it in necessity (poetic license) and in rare speech. Perhaps the poetry of al-Mutalammis and the proverb of Hatim are, in their view, among such cases, but the truth is otherwise.

Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Fadalah al-Mujashi'i said: the estimate is "law kuntum antum tamlikuna" (if you were yourselves the possessors), and its apparent meaning is that "antum" for him is an emphasis of the pronoun deleted with the verb, and this is not correct. Abu al-Hasan Ibn al-Sa'igh said: the original is "law kuntum tamlikuna," so the verb "kana" was deleted alone and the pronoun became detached. So it is for him the subject of a deleted "kana," and the clause "tamlikuna" is its predicate, and its parallels are construed on this basis.

Abu Hayyan said after citing what preceded: this analysis is better, because deleting "kana" after "law" is well known in the language of the Arabs. It is not hidden that the statement according to what you first heard is more expressive, although the apparent sense is that withholding on this view is continuous possession. What is meant by "withholding" is stinginess (bukhl), because stinginess is a specific kind of withholding. When the object was deleted and the act was directed to the verb itself, meaning "you would surely do withholding," it was made a kinaya (allusion) for its most eloquent and most ugly kind. Al-Sahib of al-Fara'id and others went to the view that it is a kinaya for what has been mentioned.

It was allowed that it may be implicitly containing the meaning of stinginess, and this was objected to as being nothing in wording or meaning. On what we have mentioned is based the saying of people about the stingy person: "mumsik" (a withholder), ﴿for fear of spending﴾, that is, for fear of poverty, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, and something similar was narrated from Qatadah. al-Raghib went to this view and said: it is said "anfaqa fulan" when he became poor. Abu 'Ubaydah said: anfaqa, amlaqa, a'dama and asrama have one meaning. Some said: infaq has its well-known meaning, which is the disbursement of wealth, and in the speech there is an estimated element, that is, for fear of the consequence of spending.

It was allowed that it may be a metonymy for its concomitant, which is exhaustion (nafad). "Khashyata" is put in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). Making it a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, as Abu al-Baqa' allowed, is contrary to the apparent sense. This verse has reached in describing them with miserliness the utmost extreme which imagination cannot reach, since it conveys that if they had possessed the treasuries of God's mercy, which are not exhausted, and had been alone in possessing them without any competitor, they would have withheld them without any reason except fear of poverty. If you wish, compare it with the words of the poet:

"Wa-law anna dāraka anbatat laka arduha / ibaran yadiqu bihā finā'u al-manzili"
"And if your house had made its soil grow needles for you, the courtyard of the dwelling would be too narrow for them,

Wa-atāka Yusufu yasta'iruka ibratan / liyakhiṭa qadda qamisihi lam taf'ali"
And Joseph came to you asking to borrow a needle to sew the rent of his shirt, you would not have done it."

Along with that, it contains exaggerations exceeding ten; you see the disparity that cannot be counted. Many made the address in it general, which requires that each one of mankind be stingy, as is evident from what follows, even though it affirmed preference for some of them despite need.

It was answered that this is in relation to the true Generous One and the absolute Bestower, glorified is His majesty. For a human being is either withholding or spending, and spending occurs only for a purpose for the sensible person, such as a material or immaterial return, like a fine praise, or service and enjoyment, as in providing for one's family, or the like. What is for a return is an exchange, not a sacrifice. Or it is with regard to the majority, and the rest is treated as nonexistent, as is said:

"We have returned in our age / away from the tale of noble deeds.
Whoever spares people his evil / is in the generosity of Hatim."

This answer, in my view, is preferable to the first. On this is to be understood His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and man has always been stingy﴾, exaggerating in stinginess. "Qatr" came to mean reducing expenditure, and it stands opposite to extravagance, and both are blameworthy. It is said: "qattartu al-shay'a" and "iqtartuhu" and "qattartuhu," meaning I reduced it, and "fulan muqattir" (a stingy, needy man). The root of this, as al-Raghib said, is from "al-qutar" and "al-qatr," which is the smoke rising from roasted meat, wood and the like, so it is as if the one who reduces and the one who is reduced is the one who takes from a thing its smoke. It is also said: the address is to the people of Mecca, who proposed what they proposed of springs, rivers and other things. The intended "man" is, as in the first view, the species, and there is no doubt that the human species is created with a tendency to stinginess, because the basis of its affairs is need. It is also said: "al-insan" here refers to a specific person, and Ali is the one meant. The connection of the verse with what precedes, on the specification of the address, is that the people of Mecca asked for springs and rivers so that their provisions would increase and expand for them, so God, glorified is He, explained that if they possessed the treasuries of God's mercy they would have been stingy and miserly, and would not have hastened to give benefit to anyone. The intent is to condemn them, that they are at the utmost extreme of miserliness, and they propose what they propose. Or the intent is that this is their attribute, so there is no benefit in granting them what they asked for. So said al-'Askari and others. Thus the verse for them is connected with His saying: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth."﴾ And it suffices, in generality, that the people of Mecca are included in it.

Abu Hayyan said: the appropriate connection is to say that he, peace and blessings be upon him, had been granted by God what He had granted to no one of prophethood and messengership to mankind and jinn. So he (ﷺ) was the most eager of people to convey good to them and rescue them from error, persevering in that and risking himself in calling them to God, presenting that to the tribes and clans of the Arabs, generously, asking no wage from them. Yet these, his kinsmen, scarcely any of them responded except one after another, having persisted in their opposition and hostility, so nothing reached him from them but harm. So God, exalted is His dignity, by this verse pointed out his generosity, peace be upon him, and his giving of what God had given him, and the refusal of these people that any good should reach him from them. So it came clarifying the difference between his, peace be upon him, and theirs in his eagerness for their benefit and the absence of any good coming from them to him. The connection between the verse and the whole of the preceding verses is that they indicate his eagerness for their guidance. And by my life, this is something that sound taste and upright mind reject.

It may be that the connection is their inclusion of condemnation of them for excessive stinginess, just as what precedes includes condemnation of them for disbelief, so both are two evil attributes, the harm of one is limited, and the harm of the other is transgressive. So reflect; the path of the mind is broad, and God Most High knows best what He means.

When He, glorified is He, related what He related of the Quraysh regarding their obstinacy and opposition toward His Messenger (ﷺ), He consoled him, exalted is His majesty, with what happened to Musa, peace be upon him, with Pharaoh, and what He, glorified is He, did to Pharaoh and his people. So He, mighty is He, said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 101:

﴿And We certainly gave Musa nine clear signs.﴾ The apparent sense of the context and of parallel passages requires that the meaning is nine proofs, clearly indicating the prophethood of Musa, peace be upon him, and the truth of what he brought from Allah, exalted is He. It does not contradict this that he was given more than what is mentioned, because specifying a number in the text does not indicate the negation of anything beyond it, as has been verified in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). Many scholars held this view. However, they differed about the specification of these nine. In some tafsir works, they are, as in the Torah: the staff, then blood, then frogs, then lice, then the death of livestock, then hail, like fire, sent down together with a blazing fire that destroyed the plants and animals it passed over, then locusts, then darkness, then a death that afflicted the adult humans and all animals.

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that they are: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the years (of drought) and a decrease in fruits. This was also related from Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah and Ikrimah.

This was criticized on the grounds that "the years (of drought) and the decrease in fruits" are one sign, as was related from al-Hasan.

It was answered that this is not what al-Hasan said, since the apparent meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years (of drought) and a decrease in fruits﴾ requires that they be different. So the first is interpreted as drought in their deserts, and the second as shortage in their farms, or something similar. This has already been discussed, so there is no harm in counting them as two signs.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related in another narration from al-Habr (Ibn Abbas) that they are his hand, peace be upon him, his tongue, his staff, the sea, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood. In al-Kashshaf, from him, may Allah be pleased with him, [it is related] that they are: the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the stone, the sea, and the mount that Allah, exalted is He, lifted over the Children of Israel. Al-Kashf commented on this, saying: "The stone and the mount are not among the signs that were brought to Pharaoh, and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people﴾. And in this surah He mentioned: ﴿You certainly know that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear proofs﴾, and the reference is to the signs." Then he said: "The answer is that the nine clear signs may be some of them, different from some of those nine. And there is nothing in this verse indicating that all of them were for Pharaoh and his people. As for the reference, it is to some of them by necessity, since all of them did not occur at once but gradually, and the splitting of the sea did not occur in the context of a challenge, but when destruction had become certain." End of quotation.

This does not avoid departing from the apparent meaning, and what was related from Ibn Abbas at first is clearly worded but has a problem, and al-Kashshaf attributed it to al-Hasan, which contradicts what we have found in the books relied upon in such matters. It is related that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, asked Muhammad ibn Ka'b about these signs, and he counted what he counted and mentioned in it the effacement (tams). Umar said: "How could a jurist be other than this?" Then he said:
Page 183
"Boy, bring out that bag." He brought it out and shook it, and there were broken eggs in halves, broken walnuts, garlic, chickpeas, lentils, all of them stones. This, however, and the apparent meaning of some reports require something different from that.

Ahmad, al-Bayhaqi, al-Tabarani, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Tirmidhi, who said "hasan sahih", and al-Hakim, who said "sahih, we do not know of any defect in it", and others related from Safwan ibn Assal: "Two Jews said to one another, 'Come, let us go to this Prophet and ask him.' So they came to him (ﷺ) and asked him about the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly gave Musa nine clear signs.﴾ The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do not associate anything with Allah, do not commit adultery, do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, do not steal, do not practise sorcery, do not consume usury, do not hand an innocent person over to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not slander a chaste woman, and do not flee from the battlefield.'"

In another narration: "Or he said: 'Do not flee from the battlefield' - Shu'bah was in doubt - and upon you, O Jews, specifically, is that you do not transgress on the Sabbath." So they kissed his hands and feet and said: "We testify that you are a prophet." The report continues.

From here it has been said: the meaning of "signs" is the rulings (ahkam). Al-Shihab al-Khafaji said: "This is the correct interpretation." The reason for calling them signs is that they are indicators of happiness for whoever complies with them and of wretchedness for others. It has also been said: they are called signs because they were revealed within verses, meaning expressions that indicate meanings, like the verses of the Book. This would be an instance of naming the indicator and meaning the indicated. It has also been said: there is no harm in meaning by the signs here the divine expressions that indicate those rulings, insofar as they indicate them. In this there is, and similarly in the earlier view, the application of the term "signs" to what was revealed to other than our Prophet (ﷺ) of divine expressions, just as it is applied to what was revealed to him, peace be upon him.

It was objected that the signs in the narration, about which there is no doubt, are ten, while those in the verse asked about are nine. It was answered that the last one in it, namely "do not transgress on the Sabbath," is not one of the signs, because what is meant by signs are general rulings established in all the sharia, and this is not so in that case. For this reason the style changed there. So it is a concluding statement (tadhyil) and a completion of the speech with an addition beyond what they asked him (ﷺ). In al-Kashf it is said that it is of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), because when he (ﷺ) mentioned the nine general signs found in every sharia, he mentioned one specific to them, to show the comprehensiveness of his knowledge (ﷺ) of all of them. This is good, and the wise style here is not in the commonly known sense. So the claim that it is not of the wise style, as al-Khafaji did, is not in its proper place.

One of the eminent scholars said: "These things have no connection to Pharaoh; rather, they were given to the Children of Israel. Perhaps his (ﷺ) answer with what was mentioned was because it was what was most important to the questioner, and because it was accepted since it was written in the Torah. It is known that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew it only through revelation." End of quotation.

It was criticized: we do not accept that the signs mentioned in the verse must be ones connected to Pharaoh, and what follows is not explicit on that. Yes, it is almost apparent in that sense, but apparent meanings are often set aside in favour of sound reports. Even if we grant that they must have a connection, we do not accept that those rulings have no connection, since it is possible that all or some of them were addressed to Pharaoh and the Children of Israel together. Negating that requires evidence. It seems that his intended meaning in the phrase "perhaps his (ﷺ) answer..." is that this answer is of the wise style: Musa, peace be upon him, was given nine clear signs, in the sense of manifest miracles, and these are what is meant in the verse, and he was given nine others in the sense of rulings, which are not what is meant, but the answer came concerning them for the reason mentioned. This, as you see, is weak, so reflect.

Thus the supports of each of the two interpretations, namely interpreting the signs as proofs and miracles, and interpreting them as rulings, are in conflict. The strongest support for the second is the report: ﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾. A group read it as "fa-sal" (so ask). The apparent meaning is that it is addressed to our Prophet (ﷺ), and the asking has its well-known meaning. However, the majority hold that it is addressed to Musa, peace be upon him, and the asking is either in the sense of requesting or in its well-known sense. The reading of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supports this, and Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and others related it from Ibn Abbas as "fa-sa'ala" in the past tense without a hamza, like "qala," which is the dialect of Quraysh, since they replace the moving hamza. This is because this reading indicates that the one who asked was Musa, peace be upon him, and that it follows the giving. So "fa-sal" cannot be addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), lest the two readings contradict each other. Then a supposition is necessary, so that they do not differ in being a report and a command. That is: "So We said to him, ask them from Pharaoh, and say to him, send the Children of Israel with me," or "ask them that they support you, and that their hearts and hands be with you," or "ask them about their faith and the state of their religion, and inquire of them whether they remain firm in it or followed Pharaoh." The clause ﴿when he came to them﴾ is connected to the supposed verb "say," and on the reading of the Prophet (ﷺ) it is connected to "ask." The evidence for that supposition in the wording is His words: ﴿Pharaoh said to him﴾, because if "fa-sal" were addressed to our Prophet, peace be upon him, the structure would be broken. Also, the following would not be evident, nor would its causation from Musa's giving. Yes, those who favour the first view made "fa-sal" a parenthetical clause, like: "Zayd, know, is a jurist," and the fa' can be parenthetical just like the waw. On this basis is his saying:
"Know, for the knowledge of a man benefits him, that everything decreed will certainly come."
This view needs no supposition, and ﴿when he came to them﴾ is connected by it, as an adverbial clause, to "our signs." It cannot be connected to "sal," since his (ﷺ) asking did not take place at the time of Musa's coming, peace be upon him. In al-Kashf: "The meaning: so ask, O Muhammad, the believers among the People of the Book about that. Either because the concurrence of proofs is stronger, or as a stimulus and incitement, or to indicate that it is a matter established among them and firmly in their Book. The intent is not the literal asking, but that they, that is those asked, are people of knowledge of it. For this reason someone like you is commanded to ask them." This is the view by which the parenthetical position is justified. It was also permitted that it be governed by "udhkur" (mention), supposed as an object, and on this view it is permissible not to make "fa-sal" a parenthetical clause, and to make "udhkur" a substitute for "as'al," since, as you have heard, the asking is not literal. Likewise it was permitted that it be governed in the same way by "yukhbirukum" (they will inform you), supposed as the answer to the imperative, i.e., "ask them, they will inform you, when he came to them."

On this view the parenthetical position is not permitted. However, the parenthetical position may be objected to on this view by saying that "akhbara" (to inform) is transitive with the preposition "bi" or "an" and not by itself, so the mention or something similar that is transitive by itself must be supposed instead of informing. To make it a temporal adverb of it is not valid, since the informing did not occur at the time of coming. It was also objected that asking about the signs, and answering with informing about the time of coming or mentioning it, is not suitable to it. The answer may be that what is meant is: they will inform you of that reality at the time of its coming to them, or they will mention that to you. But this, as you see, is weak. Some of them permitted that it be governed by "yukhbirukum," with "idh" being causal, and on this view it is permissible to be governed by "udhkur." The meaning on the rest of the possibilities, when the address is to our Prophet, peace be upon him, is: when he came to their fathers, since the Children of Israel at that time were the ones existing in his time, and Musa, peace be upon him, had not come to them. So the speech is either by omitting a noun (hadhf mudaf) or by employing a kind of double reference (istikhdam). The possibilities on the supposition that the address is to whoever hears are the same possibilities that were heard on the supposition that it is to the master of the hearers, peace be upon him.

The "fa" in ﴿so he said﴾ is, on the rest of the possibilities and views, an eloquent connective (fasiha), and the meaning is: when he came to them, he went to Pharaoh, claimed prophethood, displayed the miracle, and such and such happened, and he said: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Musa, are bewitched﴾, meaning you have been bewitched, so your mind has become disturbed, and for this reason your speech has become disturbed, and you claimed what you claimed. This is like His words: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is certainly mad﴾.

Al-Farra' and al-Tabari said: "Mashur" (bewitched) means "sahir" (sorcerer), either by way of the relative adjective (nisba) or literally. This fits the transformation of the staff and the like, on the interpretation of the signs as miracles.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 102:

﴿Said﴾ Moses, peace be upon him, in reply to his statement mentioned above: ﴿"You certainly know, O Pharaoh,﴾ ﴿that none has sent down these"﴾, i.e., the nine signs or some of them. The reference to them by "these" is in the manner of his saying, according to one of the two narrations: "And life after those days..." (this has been discussed before). ﴿"Except the Lord of the heavens and the earth"﴾, i.e., their Creator and their Governor. The gist of the reply is that your knowledge that these signs are from Allah, the Exalted, since none other than Him, the Exalted, has power over them, necessitates that I am neither bewitched nor a sorcerer, and that my speech is not deranged. But the love of leadership (riyasah) has driven you to obstinacy in claiming lordship, as an indication that sending them down is among the effects of that. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's exegesis): How excellent is the attribution of sending them down to the Lord of the heavens and the earth. For when Pharaoh asked him at the start of their dialogue, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?", he said, "The Lord of the heavens and the earth," as a reminder of his deficiency and that he has no control over existence, so his claim to lordship is a claim of impossibility. Thus he rebuked him and informed him that he knows the signs of Allah, the Exalted, and who sent them down, but he is arrogant and obstinate, like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"And they denied them, while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance"﴾ (27:14). He addressed him thus by way of reproach, meaning: You are in the state of one who knows these, or they are so clear that you know them. His address is not in the manner of informing him about his own knowledge or about the knowledge of his knowledge, so that it would convey a necessary implication of the statement, like your saying to someone who has memorized the Torah: "You have memorized the Torah."

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and al-Kisa'i read "laqad 'alimtu" with a dammah on the tā' (I certainly know). In that case Moses, peace be upon him, informs about himself that he is not bewitched, as the enemy of Allah and his enemy claimed; rather he knows that none sent down those signs except the Creator of the heavens and the earth and their Governor. It is narrated from the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "By Allah, the enemy of Allah did not know, but it was Moses, peace be upon him, who knew." Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that it is not sound, because it was narrated by Kulthum al-Muradi, who is unknown (majhul). And how could the Gate of the City of Knowledge, may Allah ennoble his face, say such a thing? The reason for attributing knowledge to him is clear.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned in al-Durr al-Manthur that Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he used to read with the dammah and would say so. He did not follow this with anything. Perhaps this unknown transmitter whom Abu Hayyan mentioned is in their chains of narration. And Allah knows best.

The clause ﴿"what has sent down"﴾ and so on is a suspended clause (mu'allaq) that takes the place of the object of ﴿"you know"﴾. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"clear proofs"﴾ (basa'ir) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from ﴿"these"﴾, and the governing element for it, according to al-Hufi, Abu al-Baqa' and Ibn 'Atiyyah, is the mentioned verb "sent down". Nothing that comes before the exception (illa) acts upon what follows it, if it is the exception from something or a follower of it (tābi'). Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i explicitly permitted: "Nobody struck Hind except Zayd, laughing." The school of the majority (al-Jumhur) does not permit it. If something apparently of that kind occurs, they interpret it as implying a verb supported by what precedes it. The estimate here is: "He sent them down as clear proofs," i.e., manifest evidences that make you see my truthfulness. It is said that basa'ir is the plural of basirah in the sense of mubsirah, i.e., clear. The word basa'ir is also applied to arguments, as if they were insights of the intellects; i.e., He sent them down only as arguments and proofs of my truthfulness. It may also mean lessons (i'bar), as al-Raghib mentioned. Moreover, you should not be unaware that if the intended meaning of the nine signs is what the earlier report of Safwan implies, then "these" may be a reference to the miracles that he, peace be upon him, displayed, and the display of that is considered in what the eloquent fa' (al-fa' al-fasihah, the "fa" that reveals an implied condition) reveals. If you insist on taking it as a reference to the mentioned signs in that sense, because all of them were established from the beginning and existed at the time of the dialogue, and because the sending down fits them so well, you would need to resort to some kind of artificial interpretation, which is not hidden from you.

﴿"And indeed I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed"﴾ (mathbur), i.e., perishing, as was narrated from al-Hasan and Mujahid, taking it as from thabara in the intransitive sense meaning "perished." The word is a maf'ul fihi (adverbial object) for attribution, on the basis that it comes both intransitive and transitive. Some interpreted it as "destroyed" (muhlakan), which is obvious. It is narrated from al-Farra' that he said: i.e., turned away from good, inclined to evil, from their saying: "What has turned you away from this?", i.e., what has prevented you from it. To this returns what al-Tasti transmitted from Ibn Abbas in explaining it as "cursed" (mal'unan), restrained from good.

Al-Shirazi in al-Alqab and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the route of Maymun ibn Mihran from him, may Allah be pleased with him, the explanation of it as "deficient in intellect." Similar to this is the explanation of al-Dahhak as "bewitched." He said: Moses, peace be upon him, replied with the same words Pharaoh had said to him, with a difference in wording. Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Dhamm al-Ghadab transmitted from Anas ibn Malik that he was asked about "mathbur" in the verse, and he said: "Opposing." Then he said: The prophets, peace be upon them, are too exalted to curse or revile. You know that this is a metaphorical meaning for it, and likewise "deficient in intellect," and there is no reason to resort to it. As for what Imam Malik mentioned, there is much to be said about it. Indeed, it has been said that explaining it as "doomed" and similar expressions that contain harshness contradicts His saying, the Exalted, addressing Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both: ﴿"Speak to him with gentle speech"﴾ (20:44). Abu Hayyan pointed to its answer: Moses, peace be upon him, at first feared harm from Pharaoh, as he said: ﴿"Indeed we fear that he will hasten against us, or that he will transgress"﴾ (20:45). So he was commanded to speak to him gently. When the Glorified said to him: ﴿"Do not fear"﴾ (20:46), he trusted in the protection of Allah, the Exalted, and he assaulted him with the assault of one under protection, and answered him with speech that he would not have answered with before that. There is discussion of this which you will come to know, Allah willing, in its place. In sum, the first explanation is the most apparent of the explanations, and there is no harm in it, especially with Moses, peace be upon him, expressing it as a supposition (zann). Then he, peace be upon him, countered his supposition with his own supposition, and how vast is the difference between the two suppositions! For Pharaoh's supposition is "manifest falsehood," while Moses', peace be upon him, supposition hovers around certainty.

Ubayy and Ibn Ka'b read: "Wa in ikhalaka, O Pharaoh, la-mathbur" (And indeed I consider you, O Pharaoh, to be doomed), with the light (mukhaffafah) "in" and the distinguishing lam (lam al-fariqah). Ikhal means the same as azunn, with a kasrah on the hamzah in the eloquent usage, and it may be pronounced with a fathah in one dialect, as in al-Qamus (the dictionary).
