Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 103:

﴿Then he (Pharaoh) intended﴾ to ﴿drive them out﴾, i.e., Musa and his people. The root of al-istifzaz (driving out, uprooting) is al-izaj (disturbing, unsettling), and it is used here as a metaphor for expelling them ﴿from the land﴾, i.e., the land of Egypt in which they were, or from the whole earth. Driving them out from it entails killing them and annihilating them, and this is what is meant. ﴿So We drowned him and those with him, all together.﴾ I.e., We turned his scheme back upon him, since he intended that for them but not for himself, so it befell him rather than them. Thus he and his people were driven out by drowning. This reversal is as clear as the sun on the second reading, and apparent on the first, because he intended to expel them from Egypt, and he himself was expelled in the most severe manner, through destruction. The addition does not harm the reversal; rather, it confirms it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 104:

﴿And We said﴾ on the tongue of Musa, upon him be peace, ﴿after him﴾, i.e., after Pharaoh, in the sense of after his drowning; or the pronoun refers to the drowning understood from the preceding verb, i.e., after his drowning and the drowning of those with him. ﴿To the Children of Israel﴾ who
صفحة 187
Pharaoh wanted to provoke (istifzaz) ﴿Dwell in the land﴾ from which he wanted to expel you. This is the land of Egypt. This is evident if it is established that they entered it after they had left it, and Pharaoh and his armies followed them and were drowned. But if it is not established, then the intended "Children of Israel" are the descendants of those whom Pharaoh wanted to provoke. More than one scholar has chosen that the intended "land" is the Holy Land, which is the land of al-Sham. ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾, i.e., the return (al-karrah), or the life, or the Hour, or the Last Abode; and what is intended by all of that is the establishment of the Hour. ﴿We will bring you together in a mass (laffifan)﴾, i.e., mingled, you and they; then We will judge between you and distinguish your happy ones from your wretched ones. The root of laffif is a gathering from various tribes; it is a collective noun like jami', with no singular, or it is a verbal noun that includes the few and the many, since it is said: laffa laffan and laffifan. What is meant by it is what has been indicated. Ibn Abbas explained it as "jamian" (all together). In any case, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive in "bikum." Some have stated that in "bikum" the addressees take precedence over the absent ones; and what is meant by them and by "bikum," and how subtle it is, together with ﴿laffifan﴾.

﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended﴾: this returns to describing the state of the Noble Qur'an. It is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn were to gather...﴾ and the verse that follows. This is the manner of the Arabs in their speech: they take up one matter, digress from it to another, then to another, and then return to what they mentioned first, for "discourse has its branches" (al-ḥadīth shujūn). So the pronoun of absence refers to the Qur'an. Whoever holds that it refers to Musa (peace be upon him) is far off the mark. The verse is connected to what comes before it. The sending down (al-inzāl) here is like His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾. Some have understood it in this sense as referring to what came before, or to the Nine Signs, and it has been mentioned that it refers to the meaning, or to the promise mentioned just above.

The apparent meaning is that the bā' (al-bā', the preposition "with") in both places indicates accompaniment (al-mulābasa), and the prepositional phrase in both places is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a circumstantial accusative describing the state of the subject) relating to the pronoun of the Qur'an. The possibility that the first is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun of God, Exalted is He, contradicts the apparent meaning. By "the first truth," as has been said, is meant the divine wisdom requiring its sending down, and by "the second" is meant what it contains of beliefs, rulings and the like. That is: We did not send it down except accompanied by the truth that required its sending down, and it did not descend except accompanied by the truth that it contains. It has also been said that the first bā' indicates causation and relates to the verb that follows, and the second indicates accompaniment. It has also been said that both indicate causation, so both relate to the verb. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: the first truth is monotheism, and the second is the promise and threat, the command and the prohibition. It has also been said that "truth" in both places means the preserved, established matter, and the meaning is: We did not send it down from heaven except preserved by the guard of the angels, and it did not descend upon the Messenger except preserved by them from the confusion of the devils. The sum of this is that it is preserved at the time of sending down, at the time of descent, and after that; falsehood does not come to it from before it or from behind it.

Whoever permitted that the second truth refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that its descending with him means its descent upon him and its arrival with him, from the saying "a guest descended upon so-and-so," is far off the mark. On all the other views, the benefit of mentioning the second clause after the first is not hidden, and the apparent repetition is removed. Al-Tabari inclined to the view that the second clause is an emphasis of the first in meaning, because it is said: "We sent it down and it descended," and "We sent it down and it did not descend," when some obstacle to its descent arises. So the second clause comes to remove this possibility. Some have shied away from calling it an emphasis because of the difference between sending down and descent, and claimed that if the second were an emphasis of the first, the conjunction would not be permissible, due to the complete connection between them.

﴿And We did not send you except as a bringer of good tidings﴾ to the obedient of reward, ﴿and a warner﴾ to the disobedient of punishment. So upon you is only the conveying of good tidings and warning, not guiding the disbelievers who make demands, nor compelling them to the religion. Perhaps the sentence is to establish the truth of his mission (ﷺ) right after establishing the reality of the Qur'an. The word after illā (except) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 17, verse 106]**

﴿وَقُرْآنًا﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a suppressed verb which is explained by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فَرَقْنَاهُ﴾ (We have divided it). It is therefore of the type called *al-ishtighal* (الاشتغال, "the verb being occupied"; a construction in which a noun is governed by a verb that is elided and explained by another verb that governs a pronoun referring to that noun). He preferred the accusative over the nominative [reading], since it is coordinated with the verbal sentence. Had it been put in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*) in other than the Qur'an, it would have been permissible; however, according to those who do not suffice with an indefinite noun for the validity of a subject (*ibtida'*) unless a benefit is achieved, one must take into account a justifying factor (*musawwigh*). On this basis al-Hufi cited it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the view of Sibawayh. al-Farra' said: It is governed by "arsalnaka" (We sent you), meaning: ﴿أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا مُبَشِّرًا وَنَذِيرًا﴾ (We did not send you except as a bearer of good tidings and a warner), and [We sent] the Qur'an, just as you say "a mercy," because the Qur'an is a mercy. It is not hidden that this is a laboured grammatical analysis, which a learned scholar hardly says. Among the things that cause wonder is what Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted, namely that it is governed by coordination with the kaf (the pronoun "ka," "you") in "arsalnaka."

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is inferior to the first [view] but superior to the rest; it is governed by a suppressed verb indicated by the preceding "atayna" (We gave), or by "arsalnaka." The clause ﴿فَرَقْنَاهُ﴾ is in the place of an attributive modifier (*sifah*) of it, i.e.: "We gave you a Qur'an which We have divided," that is: We sent it down in portions, separated, or We made a separation in it between truth and falsehood. The preposition is then elided, and its object is put in the accusative as a direct object by way of extension (*tawassu'*), as in his saying: "And a day We witnessed Sulaym and 'Amir [as enemies]."

This was narrated from al-Hasan, and from Ibn 'Abbas, [who read] "bayyana" (We explained) its lawful and unlawful [matters]. al-Farra' said: "We made it firm and detailed," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فِيهَا يُفْرَقُ كُلُّ أَمْرٍ حَكِيمٍ﴾ (therein is made distinct every wise matter).

'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy, 'Abdullah, Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Sha'bi, Humayd, 'Umar ibn Qa'id, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Amr ibn Dharr, 'Ikrimah, and al-Hasan (according to a variant from him) recited: "farraqnahu" with a doubled *ra'*. Its meaning is like the unemphasized form; i.e., We sent it down divided into portions, except that the doubling indicates intensity in the act, which is division. It was said: "faraqa" (unemphasized) indicates a close separation, and "farraqa" (emphasized) a distant separation. The first is more apparent. Since His saying, exalted is He, later: ﴿عَلَى مُكْثٍ﴾ (at a gradual pace) indicates the multiplicity of its installments, the two readings have the same meaning. It was also said: its meaning is that We divided its verses between command and prohibition, rulings and laws, admonitions and parables, stories and reports of unseen matters that have come and will come. The majority hold the first [interpretation].

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Qur'an was sent down all at once from Allah, exalted is He, from the Preserved Tablet to the noble scribe-angels (*al-safarah*) in the lowest heaven. Then the scribe-angels revealed it to Jibril, peace be upon him, in twenty nights, and Jibril revealed it to the Prophet ﷺ over twenty years.

In another narration: it was sent down on the Night of Power in Ramadan and placed in the House of Honour (*Bayt al-'Izzah*) in the lowest heaven; then it was sent down in installments over twenty [years].

In another narration: over twenty-three years.

In another: over twenty-five.

This disagreement, as stated in *al-Bahr*, is based on the disagreement about the age of the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn al-Durays narrated through Qatadah from al-Hasan, who used to say: Allah sent down the Qur'an to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ over eighteen years: eight years in Makkah and ten years after he emigrated.

Ibn 'Atiyyah criticised this, saying it is a corrupt statement that is not authentically from al-Hasan. A group relied on the view that between its beginning and its end there were twenty-three years, and that Jibril, peace be upon him, used to bring it down, it is said, five verses at a time, five verses at a time. Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Learn the Qur'an five verses at a time, five verses at a time, for Jibril, peace be upon him, used to bring it down five by five.

Ibn 'Asakir narrated through Abu Nadrah, who said: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri used to teach us the Qur'an five verses in the morning and five verses in the evening, and he would report that Jibril, peace be upon him, descended with it five verses at a time. This was meant generally, for it is authentically established that it descended with more than that and with less.

Ubayy and 'Abdullah recited: "farraqnahu 'alayka li-taqra'ahu 'ala al-nas 'ala muktin" (We divided it for you, that you might recite it to the people at a gradual pace). *Muktin* means deliberation and unhurriedness, for that is easier for memorisation and more helpful for understanding. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It was also said: it means over a lengthy period of time, dispensing it little by little.

The apparent view is that ﴿لِتَقْرَأَهُ﴾ is connected to ﴿فَرَقْنَاهُ﴾, ﴿عَلَى النَّاسِ﴾ to ﴿تَقْرَأَهُ﴾, and ﴿عَلَى مُكْثٍ﴾ also to it [i.e., to *taqra'ahu*]; but in this there is the connection of two prepositional phrases to one single governing element with the same meaning. It is answered that the connection of the second comes after considering the connection of the first to it, so the governed element differs. In *al-Bahr* it is said that one need not be concerned with the connection of these two prepositions to what has been mentioned, because their meanings differ: the first is in the position of a direct object, and the second is in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*), i.e., "slowly, deliberately." Because of the disputation involved in this, some chose to connect it to ﴿فَرَقْنَاهُ﴾. al-Khafaji permitted its connection to a suppressed element: i.e., "dividing or division upon deliberation," or "reciting upon deliberation from you, like the deliberation of its revelation." Abu al-Baqa' made it a circumstantial state of the pronoun in the accusative in ﴿فَرَقْنَاهُ﴾, i.e., "unhurried." It is strange that al-Hufi said it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿عَلَى النَّاسِ﴾. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying it is not valid, because ﴿عَلَى مُكْثٍ﴾ is an attribute either of the reciter or of the recited, and not an attribute of "the people," so that it could be a substitute for them. The noun *muktheun* has three vowel options for its *mim*; it was read with a *damma* and with a *fatha*, and it was not read with a *kasra*, which is a rare dialectal form. Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed a consensus of the readers upon the *damma*.

﴿وَنَزَّلْنَاهُ تَنْزِيلًا﴾ (And We sent it down in gradual revelation), according to the occurrences and the interests. Thus the mention of this after His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فَرَقْنَاهُ﴾ etc., is beneficial: the first indicates the gradualness of its descent so that it may be easy to memorise and understand, without regard to what requires that; and this is more specific than that, for it indicates its gradualness according to what the circumstances require.

﴿قُلْ﴾ (Say) to those who disbelieve: ﴿آمِنُوا بِهِ﴾ (Believe in it), i.e., in the Qur'an, ﴿أَوْ لَا تُؤْمِنُوا﴾ (or do not believe), i.e., in it, in the sense that your belief in it and your non-belief in it are the same, for your belief does not add to its perfection, and your non-belief does not bring it any deficiency.

﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِ﴾ (Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it), i.e., the scholars who read the earlier scriptures before the descent of the Qur'an, and who knew the reality of revelation and the signs of prophethood, and were able to distinguish truth from falsehood and the righteous from the wrongdoer; or who saw your description and the description of what was sent down to you. ﴿إِذَا يُتْلَى﴾ (When it is recited) i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (to them), ﴿يَخِرُّونَ لِلْأَذْقَانِ﴾ (they fall down upon their chins). *Kharr* means to fall rapidly. *Al-adhqan* is the plural of *dhaqan*, which is the joint of the two jaws, and it is also applied, metaphorically, to what hair grows upon it; and likewise it is applied to the face, by expressing the part for the whole. It was said: this is what is meant. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. So it is as if it were said: they fall quickly upon their faces ﴿سُجَّدًا﴾ (prostrating), in glorification of the command of Allah, exalted is He, or in thanks for the fulfilment of what was promised in those scriptures concerning your mission. The apparent view is that here "kharru" and "sujudan" are in their literal sense. It was said: none of that is meant; rather, what is intended is that they submit to what they heard and humble themselves to it with complete submission and humility, so the statement is put in the manner of an illustrative metaphor (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*). Al-Zamakhshari interpreted "kharr li-l-adhqan" as falling upon the faces. Then he said: The chin is mentioned because it is the first thing with which the prostrating person's face meets the earth. It was said: there is a problem with this, because the first [part to meet the ground] is the forehead and the nose. It was answered that when one begins to fall, the nearest part of his face to the ground is the chin; and it seems that what is meant is the first thing that comes close to the encounter. It is also permitted that the chins remain in their literal sense, and that what is meant is intensification in humility, namely rubbing the beards in the dust; or that they sometimes fell upon the chin like one who has fainted, out of fear of Allah, exalted is He. It was said: perhaps their prostration was like this, other than what we know; and that is, as you see, weak.

The author of *al-Fara'id* said: What is meant is exaggeration in pressing down upon the forehead and the nose, until it is as if they were pressing their chins to the ground; and this is an extremely good interpretation. The *lam* [in *li-l-adhqan*], according to what al-Zamakhshari explicitly stated, is for specialisation (*ikhtisas*), and he mentioned that the meaning is: they made their chins for falling and specialised them for it.

The meaning of this specialisation, according to *al-Kashf*, is that the falling does not go beyond the chins to other corresponding limbs; and he verified this with what cannot be improved upon. This specialisation has been objected to on the ground that it contradicts what preceded, namely his saying that the chin is the first thing with which the prostrating person meets the earth. It was answered with what was answered. al-Khafaji criticised this, saying that it is based on the premise that the specialisation indicated by the *lam* means exclusivity (*hasr*), and that is not the case; rather it means a particular connection. Even if it were granted, the meaning of specialisation to the chin would be specialisation to its direction and what is opposite it, namely the direction of the bottom; and there is no doubt in its specialisation to it, since it does not belong to anything else. ﴿يَخِرُّونَ لِلْأَذْقَانِ﴾ means: they fall upon the ground, in precise terms. The intent is to depict that state, as in his saying: "So he fell prostrate, [his face] to the two hands and the mouth." So reflect.

Some chose that the *lam* means *'ala* (upon). Some claimed that the pronouns in "bihi" (by it) and "qablihi" (before it) refer to the Prophet ﷺ, but the context and the following text reject this.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Jarir narrated that the pronoun in "yutla" (is recited) refers to their book. Its status is not hidden. The apparent view is that the nominal sentence falls within the scope of

﴿Say﴾. This is a reason (ta'lil) for what is understood from His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Believe in it or do not believe﴾, namely, a disregard for that. The meaning is: if you do not believe in it, then those who are better than you have believed in it in the best manner of belief. It is also permissible that the phrase ﴿Say﴾ is not within the scope of the command to "say," but rather that the statement "Those who were given knowledge..." is a reason for it by way of consolation (tasliya) for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as if it were said: Find consolation in the belief of the scholars in place of the belief of the ignorant, and do not concern yourself with their belief and their aims. Al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary) mentioned both views. He said in al-Kashf (by al-Tibi): The summary is that the intended purpose is consolation, contempt, and disregard, which conveys rebuke and reproach. This is a consequence of it, incorporated into it, or the reverse. The form of expression in the second case is clearer, and the reason given by His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge﴾ is for the first.

Ibn Atiyya said: Another meaning is apparent in the verse, namely that His words, glorified is He: ﴿Say, believe in it or do not believe﴾ came as a threat (wa'id). The meaning is: Do whichever of the two matters you wish, and you will see what you will be recompensed for. Then he set forth for them an example by way of reproach through those among the People of the Book who came before them, namely: People were not like you in disbelief; rather, those who were given the Torah (al-Tawrat), the Gospel (al-Injil), the Psalms (al-Zabur), and the revealed books, when what was revealed to them was recited to them, would humble themselves and believe. (End of quotation.) This is very far-fetched and cannot avoid the use of metaphor (majaz, figurative usage).

Perhaps in the discussion of it there is istikhdam (a figure in which one word is used in two senses).

"They say, 'Glory be to our Lord! Indeed the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled.'" [Note: translate exactly as given below]

Actually, I must translate the given passage faithfully. Here it is:

﴿And they say﴾ — i.e., in their prostration, or in general — ﴿Glory be to our Lord﴾ — exalted above breaking His promise, or above what the disbelievers do of denial — ﴿Indeed, the promise of our Lord was ever to be fulfilled﴾. "Inna" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of "inna" (mithqalah), its noun is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr sha'n), and the "lām" is the lām that distinguishes (lām fāriqah), i.e., "Indeed, the matter is this." ﴿And they fall down upon their faces weeping﴾. He repeated "they fall down upon the chins" because the causes differ: the first is for glorifying the command of God Most High, or thanksgiving for the fulfilment of the promise; the second is for what the admonitions of the Qur'an have affected in them. The prepositional phrase is either attached to what precedes it, or to an omitted verb that serves as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from what comes before or after, i.e., "prostrating." The clause ﴿weeping﴾ is also a circumstantial clause, i.e., "weeping out of the fear of God Most High." Since the weeping arises from fear, which arises from reflection that is continually renewed, the verbal sentence, which indicates renewal, is used. Numerous reports have come in praise of weeping out of the fear of God Most High.

Al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī narrated from al-Naḍr ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If a servant weeps among a community, God Most High will save that community from the Fire by the weeping of that servant. There is no deed except that it has a weight and a reward, except the tear; for it extinguishes seas of Fire. No eye wells up with its water out of the fear of God Most High except that God Most High forbids its body to the Fire. If it overflows onto his cheek, no dust nor humiliation will cover his face."

He also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Two eyes will not be touched by the Fire: an eye that wept out of the fear of God Most High, and an eye that spent the night guarding in the way of God Most High."

He, al-Nasa'i and Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No man who weeps out of the fear of God Most High will enter the Fire until the milk returns to the udder. Nor will dust gathered on a servant in the way of God Most High and the smoke of Hell gather together." Al-Nasa'i added: "in his nostrils," and Muslim added: "ever."

It is fitting that this be the state of the scholars; for Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from 'Abd al-A'la al-Taymi that he said: "Whoever has been given knowledge that does not make him weep is surely one who has been given knowledge that does not benefit him; for God Most High described the people of knowledge, saying: ﴿They fall down upon their chins weeping, and it increases them﴾ — i.e., the Qur'an, by their hearing it — ﴿in humility﴾, because it increases them in knowledge and certainty regarding the command of God Most High beyond what they already possessed of the evidences."

"They say, 'Glory be to our Lord! Indeed the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled.'" [Note: translate exactly as given below]

Actually, I must translate the given passage faithfully. Here it is:

﴿And they say﴾ — i.e., in their prostration, or in general — ﴿Glory be to our Lord﴾ — exalted above breaking His promise, or above what the disbelievers do of denial — ﴿Indeed, the promise of our Lord was ever to be fulfilled﴾. "Inna" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of "inna" (mithqalah), its noun is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr sha'n), and the "lām" is the lām that distinguishes (lām fāriqah), i.e., "Indeed, the matter is this." ﴿And they fall down upon their faces weeping﴾. He repeated "they fall down upon the chins" because the causes differ: the first is for glorifying the command of God Most High, or thanksgiving for the fulfilment of the promise; the second is for what the admonitions of the Qur'an have affected in them. The prepositional phrase is either attached to what precedes it, or to an omitted verb that serves as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from what comes before or after, i.e., "prostrating." The clause ﴿weeping﴾ is also a circumstantial clause, i.e., "weeping out of the fear of God Most High." Since the weeping arises from fear, which arises from reflection that is continually renewed, the verbal sentence, which indicates renewal, is used. Numerous reports have come in praise of weeping out of the fear of God Most High.

Al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī narrated from al-Naḍr ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If a servant weeps among a community, God Most High will save that community from the Fire by the weeping of that servant. There is no deed except that it has a weight and a reward, except the tear; for it extinguishes seas of Fire. No eye wells up with its water out of the fear of God Most High except that God Most High forbids its body to the Fire. If it overflows onto his cheek, no dust nor humiliation will cover his face."

He also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Two eyes will not be touched by the Fire: an eye that wept out of the fear of God Most High, and an eye that spent the night guarding in the way of God Most High."

He, al-Nasa'i and Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No man who weeps out of the fear of God Most High will enter the Fire until the milk returns to the udder. Nor will dust gathered on a servant in the way of God Most High and the smoke of Hell gather together." Al-Nasa'i added: "in his nostrils," and Muslim added: "ever."

It is fitting that this be the state of the scholars; for Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from 'Abd al-A'la al-Taymi that he said: "Whoever has been given knowledge that does not make him weep is surely one who has been given knowledge that does not benefit him; for God Most High described the people of knowledge, saying: ﴿They fall down upon their chins weeping, and it increases them﴾ — i.e., the Qur'an, by their hearing it — ﴿in humility﴾, because it increases them in knowledge and certainty regarding the command of God Most High beyond what they already possessed of the evidences."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 110 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful (al-Rahman).﴾

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed at Mecca one day and called upon Allah, the Exalted, and in his supplication he said: 'O Allah, O Merciful (Ya Rahman).' The polytheists said: 'Look at this Sabian (saabi'), who forbids us to call upon two gods, yet he calls upon two gods.' So this verse was revealed."

And from al-Dahhak that he said: The People of the Book said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "You mention the name al-Rahman very little, though Allah the Exalted has mentioned this name very often in the Torah." So this verse was revealed.

According to the first report, the intended meaning is equating the two terms, that they are two expressions for one essence, although the perspective differs. The oneness (tawhid) belongs to the Essence who is the one worshipped, and this fits His saying, exalted be He, later: ﴿And say: Praise belongs to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has not had a partner in the dominion﴾. According to the second report, the equality is in the goodness of the usage and in its leading to the intended meaning. The People of the Book understood the superiority of al-Rahman because He loves it more, since He mentioned it often in their book. It seems that the wisdom behind this is that Musa (peace be upon him) was quick-tempered (ghadub), as the reports indicate, so He mentioned al-Rahman to him often, so that he would treat his community with greater mercy, because the prophets (peace be upon them) take on the character traits of Allah, the Exalted. The judge al-Baydawi said: This is a better answer to His saying, blessed be His name: ﴿Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, because describing the names as "most beautiful" implies that those addressed by this believe in the superior goodness of one name over another, not in their difference. Sahib al-Kashf said: The purpose in both perspectives is equality between the two terms in goodness, and the difference lies in this: equality in goodness is a rebuttal of the one who said "You mention so little..." etc., to the effect that using either of the two good names is sufficient; or of the one who said "He forbids us to call upon two gods, yet he calls upon two," to the effect that the difference between the two terms indicates His perfection, not a difference between two perfect beings, so the objection is refuted. End of quotation.

It has been criticized: the suitability of describing the second as "most beautiful" is apparent and hardly deniable. Al-Tibi justified the answer (al-ajwibiyya) by saying that the objection of the Jews was an expression of Muslims' preference for one of the two names over the other, while the objection of the polytheists was an objection to combining the two terms. The saying of Allah, exalted be He, "Whichever you call upon" corresponds to the rebuttal of the Jews, because the meaning is: whichever of the two names you call upon, it is good. This does not apply to the objection of the polytheists. Then he said: This is accepted if "aw" (or) is for choice (takhyir), but it may be for permission (ibahah), and the correspondence then is clear, since the polytheists forbade combining the two names, so their rebuttal is the permission of combining many names, let alone combining two names. Moreover, the answer by choice (takhyir) in rebuttal to the People of the Book is not matching, since they objected by preference. It was answered that equality is what "aw" requires. The ready answer would have been: "We preferred Allah over al-Rahman in mention because He comprises all the attributes of perfection, unlike al-Rahman." The complete discussion of this will come shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills.

Al-Jalabi also rejected the answer by ajwibiyya, saying that the fronting of the predicate in His saying, "To Him belong the most beautiful names," requires the ajwibiyya of the first, since its meaning is: these names belong to Allah, the Exalted, not to other than Him, as the polytheists claimed. Unless it is said that "aw" is for choice, and this is not accepted; rather it is necessarily for permission, because, as al-Radi and others said, combining the two coordinated items is permitted in it, and restricting to one of them is also permitted; whereas in choice combining is not permitted, and here it is permitted. It was rebutted that the meaning is: "To Allah belong names agreeing in goodness, because their referents do not differ in essence, unlike others, glory be to Him, whose names differ." So the restriction, when the fronting is not merely for suspense, looks at the attribute and not the names. This does not depend on accepting the choice interpretation. Moreover, there is no obstacle to intending it; rather "ayy" requires it, because it is for one of two things. When you say to someone, "Whichever of the two matters you do, do it," you do not command him to do both but to do one of them. As for the proof of permissibility of combining, it comes from outside the wording and from reason: since they are not contradictory, combining them is permitted. From here you know there is no need to read "choice" in the words of one who used it as other than the well-known technical meaning, which is the grammarians' usage, when it is contrasted with permission, namely that it means equality between the two names in indicating one essence, whether in singular or plural. In al-Talwih it says: "In choice, combining may be permitted by the original permissibility (al-ibahah al-asliyya), and this is called choice by way of permission." End of quotation.

The apparent truth lies with the one who blocks the ajwibiyya and with the one who holds permission, so reflect.

As for "calling" (al-du'a), according to what Abu Hayyan and a group chose, it means "addressing" (al-nida'). Al-Zamakhshari said: it means "naming" (al-tasmiya), not "addressing," and it takes two objects: you say "I called him Zayd," then one of the two is omitted for brevity, so you say "I called Zayd." The original, as is said, is that it transitively reaches the second with the preposition "bi," but it is widened so the preposition is dropped. The second object here is omitted; that is, "name Him with this name" or "with this name," and the same applies to the second call. This was explained by saying that if it is taken in its well-known literal sense, it would entail either homonymy (ishtirak) if the two names' referents differ, or conjoining a thing to itself with "aw," which is only permitted with "wa" if they are identical. This was examined: we choose the second, and what was mentioned does not follow, since he intended the wording itself, as you say: "Address the Prophet (ﷺ) as Muhammad or as Ahmad," even though the difference of their concepts suffices for its validity. As for the report about the occasion of revelation, "or do not address (Him)," according to what is said, it is in the sense of addressing. It was also said: if the verse is a rebuttal of the polytheists, it means naming; if it is a rebuttal of the Jews, it means addressing. Al-Tibi took al-Zamakhshari's explanation as naming as indicating his inclination to the view that it is a rebuttal of the polytheists, and in that there is room for reflection.

"Ayyan" is a conditional noun in the accusative, governed by "tad'u," and as a conditional it is also a jussive governor, so it is both governing and governed from two directions. The tanwin is a substitute for the omitted genitive complement; the estimate is: "whichever of these two names." "Ma" is an extra particle for emphasis. It was also said that it is a conditional noun emphasized by it. Talha ibn Musarrif read "man" in place of "ma," and this is explained by its being extra according to al-Kisa'i's view, or by taking it as a conditional particle; combining two conditional particles is like combining two prepositions in the verse "fa-asbahna la yas'alnani 'an bima bihi," which is anomalous.

The clause "To Him belong the most beautiful names" stands in the place of the answer of the condition, and in reality it is an explanation for it. The original sense seems to be: "Whichever you call Him by, it is good, because to Him belong the most beautiful names, of which these two are." Departing from the expected form of the answer, placing the proof in place of the claim, has an exaggeration that is not hidden. This estimate is evident on the second view regarding the occasion of revelation, and it can be estimated on the first view as well, where its meaning is one and similar. There is no need for this; rather it can be estimated on both views, and it is good according to what you heard from the author of al-Kashf.

Al-Tibi said: "Aw" has been taken as permission, and the address has been made to the polytheists. The estimate: "Say: Name His Holy Essence with Allah and with al-Rahman; the two are equal in the appropriateness of naming Him with either. So with whichever of them you name Him, you are right, and if you name Him with both together, you are more right, because to Him belong the most beautiful names, and He has commanded us to call upon Him with them, in His saying: ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾." So the answer to the first condition is our saying "you are right," and the second condition and its answer are indicated by His saying: ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ On this reading the verse is one of the arts of concision (al-ijaz), which is among the ornaments of the revelation; and on the estimate "it is good," as you heard first, it is of the type of elaboration (al-itnab). He said: "And that is, as you see..." (It is as you see.)

Al-Bahr reports that some of them paused at "ayyan," meaning: "Whichever of the two terms you call Him by is permissible," then began anew: "Whatever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names." He criticized this, saying it is not valid, because "ma" is not used for individual rational beings, and because a condition entails generality, which is not valid here. The pronoun in "fa-lahu" refers to the named one or the one addressed, understood from the speech, and the indicator is rational, namely that names belong to the named or the addressed, not to the name itself or the word by which one addresses. Later, if Allah the Exalted wills, something other than this will come from Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified, in the chapter on allusion.

The describing of the names as "most beautiful" is because they indicate that which comprises all attributes of perfection, such that nothing of them is excluded, and that which belongs to the attributes of majesty, beauty and generosity.

Furthermore, know that the apparent meaning of what is reported about the Jews is that they do not deny the goodness of all of Allah's names, the Exalted; they only claim that al-Rahman is the most beloved of His names to Him, the Exalted, and the greatest and most noble of them, because of the frequency of His mention of it in the Torah. The differing of His names, may His names be honored, in nobility and greatness is also what the Muslims hold.

This is indicated by his (ﷺ) singling out some names as "the Greatest Name."

It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man supplicating, saying: "O Allah, I ask You, for I bear witness that You are Allah, there is no god but You, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is begotten, and to whom no one is equal." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, he has asked Allah by His Greatest Name, which when called upon with it, He answers, and when asked by it, He gives."

It is also narrated that he (peace be upon him) said: The name of Allah, the Exalted, is in these two verses: ﴿Your God is one God; there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ and the opening of Al 'Imran: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾.

Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali explicitly stated at the beginning of his book "al-Maqsad al-Asna" that Allah is the greatest of the ninety-nine names, because it indicates the Essence comprising all the attributes of divinity, whereas the rest of the names, each of them, indicate only individual meanings, such as knowledge, power, act, or other. Also because it is the most specific of the names, since no one applies it to other than Him, the Exalted, neither literally nor figuratively, whereas the other names may be applied to others, such as al-Qadir (the Able), al-Alim (the Knowing), al-Rahim (the Merciful) and others. His name al-Rahman, the Exalted, is also not applied to other than Him, and in this respect it is close to the name Allah, glory be to Him, although it is derived from mercy, certainly. That is why He, the Mighty and Majestic, combined the two in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful.﴾ End of quotation.

He said at its end: If it is asked: why are ninety-nine of His names singled out in that whoever counts them enters Paradise, although all of them are the names of Allah, the Exalted? We say: names may differ in excellence according to the differing of their meanings in majesty and nobility, so ninety-nine of them comprise kinds of meanings that indicate majesty, which others do not comprise, and so they are specially distinguished by an additional nobility. End of quotation.

[p. 194 page break omitted; keeping marker:] [Page 194]

Imam al-Razi said regarding this verse: The singling out of these two names, Allah and al-Rahman, for mention indicates that they are more excellent than the rest of the names. Mentioning the name Allah before the name al-Rahman indicates our saying: "Allah is the greatest of the names," among other things that have been mentioned by more than one of the eminent scholars. The verse, on its apparent meaning, is only suitable as a rebuttal of what the Jews understood, if its intended meaning is the negation of the disparity they alleged. In that case, a contradiction arises between it and the reports that indicate disparity. This may be taken as a reason for preferring that the occasion of revelation was the statement of the polytheists, and perhaps its report is more authentic. What we quoted earlier from al-Allamah al-Tibi supports what we have said. Al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) argued from the verse that He, exalted is He, is not the creator of injustice, for otherwise it would be valid to derive a name for Him, glorified is He, from it, and then what the verse indicates would be nullified, namely that all His names, exalted is He, are most beautiful.

It is answered that the implication is denied, because injustice is not an attribute of His, mighty and majestic is He. And His being its creator does not make it valid to derive a name from it; otherwise it would be valid to derive names from tallness and shortness, blackness and whiteness, since He, exalted is He, is by consensus the creator of these. Yes, it is not fitting to say of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, "the creator of the ugly," because of the obligation of good manners toward Him, glorified is He; rather, it is said: "the Creator of everything." 

[Page 195 marker, as in source: [Page 194]] 

And what is among His names, exalted are His names, is "al-Khaliq" (the Creator), not "creator of such-and-such." So understand this. May Allah, exalted is He, guide us and you upon the most upright path.

This verse, according to what has been said, is among the verses of protection, based on what al-Bayhaqi reported in al-Dala'il through the chain of Nahshal ibn Sa'id, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His saying, exalted is He: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon al-Rahman…" to the end of the verse: "It is a protection from theft."

And a man from among the Emigrants recited it when he lay down on his bed. A thief entered upon him, gathered what was in the house and carried it off, while the man was not asleep, until the thief reached the door and found it closed. He set down the bundle and did this three times. The owner of the house laughed and then said: "I have secured my house."

[Verse:] "And do not raise your voice in your prayer, nor lower it, but seek a way between that." 

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and others reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: It was revealed while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was hiding in Makkah. When he led his companions in prayer, he raised his voice with the Qur'an. When the polytheists heard that, they reviled the Qur'an, the One who revealed it, and the one who brought it.

So Allah, exalted is He, said to His Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: "And do not raise your voice in your prayer," meaning in your recitation, lest the polytheists hear and revile the Qur'an. "Nor lower it," meaning from your companions, so that you do not make them hear the Qur'an until they take it from you. "And seek a way between that," meaning: between loud and whispered. 

Its apparent meaning is that the intended sense of "prayer" is the recitation, which is one of its parts, by way of metonymy. It is also possible that the speech is on the assumption of an elided genitive, meaning: "with the recitation of your prayer." The apparent meaning of "recitation" is what covers the basmalah and other things, though some reports, on their apparent meaning, indicate that it is restricted to the basmalah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf reported from Sa'id, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to raise his voice with 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' Musaylimah had named himself al-Rahman, so when the polytheists heard that from the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, they said: 'Musaylimah has mentioned the god of Yamamah!' Then they opposed him with whistling, clapping and hand-clapping, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

It is not hidden on this report how strongly the verse is connected to what precedes it.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Rabi', who said: "Abu Bakr, when he prayed at night, lowered his voice greatly, and Umar, when he prayed at night, raised his voice greatly. Umar said: 'O Abu Bakr, if only you raised your voice a little!' And Abu Bakr said: 'O Umar, if only you lowered your voice a little!' Then the two came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of their matter, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse. The Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, sent for them both and said: 'O Abu Bakr, raise your voice a little,' and said to Umar: 'Lower your voice a little.'"

In another report, it was said to Abu Bakr: "Why do you do this?" He said: "I am conversing with my Lord, and He knows my need." And it was said to Umar: "Why do you do this?" He said: "I drive away the devil and awaken the drowsy."

The matter of metonymy or of elision of the genitive on this interpretation is like its counterpart in the first. Likewise on what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, that the meaning is: "Do not raise your voice in all your prayer, nor lower it in all of it, but seek a way between that," by loudness in some of it, such as Maghrib and 'Isha', and quietness in some of it, as in the rest of the prayers.

It has also been said: "Prayer" here means supplication. This is because al-Shaykhan and others reported from 'A'ishah, who said: "This verse, 'And do not raise your voice in your prayer, nor lower it,' was revealed concerning supplication." Ibn Abi Shaybah reported something similar from Mujahid. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group also related this from Ibn Abbas, and they used to raise their voices saying: "O Allah, have mercy on me."

They also reported from Abd Allah ibn Shaddad that "some Bedouins from the Banu Tamim, whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) finished the salam, would say, aloud: 'O Allah, grant us camels and children,' so this was revealed."

In another report from 'A'ishah, the "prayer" here is the tashahhud. Ibn Sirin reported that the Bedouins used to raise their voices with their tashahhud, so this was revealed.

It was also said that "prayer" is in its literal Shari'ah sense. Ibn 'Asakir reported from al-Hasan that he said: "The meaning is: do not pray for show, and do not abandon it out of shame." Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported something similar from Ibn Abbas as well.

Most scholars hold to the interpretation transmitted from him first. "Mukhafatah" (quiet speech) is the concealment of speech so that the speaker himself does not hear it. From here, Ibn Mas'ud said, as reported from him by Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir: "He who makes his own ears hear is not quiet." "Kharafat" (to be quiet) is of the pattern of "daraba," and "khafata" has the same meaning. It is said: "Khafata yakhfitu khaftan wa khufutan," and "khafata mukhafatah" when one speaks softly and conceals. The expression of the middle course as "the way" is in view of the fact that it is a matter toward which seekers turn, which those who follow aim at, and which brings them to the goal. It has come from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir and Abu Qilabah: "The best of matters are their middle course."

The verse, according to what the majority's statements require, is muhkam (not abrogated). It has also been said that it is "mansukhah" (abrogated), based on what Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded in Makkah to take a middle course: not to raise his voice greatly, nor to lower it so that he did not make even his own ears hear. When he emigrated to Madinah, that was dropped.

It has also been said: it is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: "Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly." But this, as you see, is weak.

No ruling is hidden from you regarding raising the voice in recitation beyond what is needed, and regarding quietness in the sense you have heard, which are recorded in the books of jurisprudence. So refer to them, if this is not already in your memory. 

Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif reported from Abu Razin, who said: "Abd Allah recited: 'And do not be quiet with your voice, nor be loud with it.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 17, verse 111 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: "Praise be to God, who has not taken a son."﴾ This is a refutation of the Jews, the Christians, and the Banu Malih, who said: "Uzayr is the son of God," "the Messiah is the son of God, exalted is He," and "the angels are the daughters of God, glory be to Him, high exalted above what they say." The negation of taking a son is explicit in denying adoption, and from it is known the negation of a begotten son for Him, glory be to Him, all the more so. This is stated explicitly in His words: ﴿He has not begotten﴾ and ﴿nor has He had a partner in the dominion.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it refutes the dualists (al-thanawiyya), who are polytheists in lordship (rububiyya). It is also possible that it is a metaphor for the negation of partnership in divinity (uluhiyya), in which case it refutes the idolaters (al-wathaniyya).

﴿Nor has He had any protector out of weakness.﴾ That is, no helper or defender for Him, glory be to Him, from humiliation, since He is mighty in Himself. Here "min" is connected to "waliyy," and "waliyy" is taken to imply the meaning of protection and support. Or the meaning is: He does not take anyone as a friend because of abasement, so "wilaya" keeps its basic sense of love and "min" is causal. The meaning in both cases is not the negation of humiliation and support in the first, and of friendship and humiliation in the second, in the manner of "one is not guided by its beacon." Rather, the intended meaning is that when He takes a servant as a friend, this is pure favour toward the servant, not that there is any need. Likewise, God's support is a perfection for the one who supports, not that there is any need. Do you not see His words, glory be to Him: ﴿If you support God, He will support you﴾? This is the view of the author of al-Kashf, and it is good. The learned Tayyibi took both meanings to fall under this same figure of speech. In the Shihabi glosses, in explaining the second of the two meanings, it is said that the intended negation is that He has no master to whom He might have recourse. As for the "waliyy" by which the believer is described, the sense of "wilaya" there is not in this meaning, but in the meaning of one who manages his affairs out of love for him, by His grace and mercy, mighty and majestic is He. Thus the two senses of "wilaya" are distinguished. Perhaps the truth lies with the author of al-Kashf. Among the strangest things said is that "min al-dhull" is in the position of a qualifier for "waliyy," with "min" partitive, and that the speech has an elided noun, meaning: "He has no protector from among the people of humiliation, by whom are meant the Jews and the Christians." By my life, one should not give heed to this.

It may be imagined that the context is one of declaring God free from imperfection, not one of praise, because praise is for a voluntary act, and the attributes mentioned are negative. This is answered by saying that it is appropriate to describe Him by what has been mentioned with the word of praise, because it indicates the negation of possibility, which requires need, and affirms that He is the Necessary Existent in His essence, self-sufficient, needing nothing else while everything else needs Him. Therefore He is the Bountiful, who gives to every receptive thing what it deserves. So He alone is worthy of praise, mighty and majestic is He. This is what al-Zamakhshari intended, and he said in al-Kashf: "You may take the negation of these attributes, which are means of withholding good, as follows: as for a son, it is a cause of stinginess; as for a partner, he prevents one from acting as one wills; and as for needing one who gives one strength or defends one, this is more evident as a companion of affirming their opposites, by way of metaphor." [p. 196]

This is a good view. Even if the speech is taken in its apparent sense, it also has a valid basis. The saying "Praise be to God" contains an indication that divinity requires praise. So when you say "Praise be to God, who is exalted above imperfections," for example, you have strengthened the meaning of divinity understood from the word. Thus it becomes a fitting description that supports His worthiness of praise, without regard to the description's independent role in the praise. This is clear and evident. However, al-Zamakhshari tried to draw attention to the place of the additional benefit. [End of quotation from al-Alusi's source, as cited.]

It has been objected that his statement, that "praise be to God" contains an indication that divinity requires praise, is not complete according to those who deny derivation of the noble name (Allah). But there is room to consider this. According to the learned Tayyibi, the verse is a division that exhausts all possibilities: the one who prevents the giving of blessings is either above Him, glory be to Him, or below Him, or equal to Him, mighty and majestic is He. So the speech is built on ascent, beginning with the lowest and ending with the highest, and negating all of them. Thus it includes ﴿has not taken a son﴾ and ﴿has not had a partner﴾, and for Him is the few and the many, the small and the great. Exalted is His greatness and abundant are His favours. And because what preceded indicates that He, exalted is He, is the Perfect, and that everything else is deficient, He deserves glorification. For this reason the words that follow are joined to it: ﴿and magnify Him with full magnification.﴾ "Takbir" is the most eloquent word in Arabic for the meaning of exalting and honouring. The command to do this after what has preceded, emphasised with a indefinite verbal noun without specifying what one magnifies Him with, indicates that it is something which speech cannot contain and human power cannot fulfil, even if the servant goes to great lengths in declaring Him free from imperfection and glorifying Him, and strives in worship and praise. Nothing remains but to stand with the feet of humility in the depths of deficiency, and to acknowledge one's inability to fulfil His right, exalted is He, however long the deficiency may be.

It has been related by more than one narrator that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to teach a boy from the Banu Abd al-Muttalib, once he could speak clearly, to say "Praise be to God" through to the end of the verse, seven times. He (ﷺ) called it the verse of might (ayat al-izz), as Ahmad and al-Tabarani reported from Mu'adh.

Abu Ya'la and Ibn al-Sunni reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "I went out with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), my hand in his, and he came upon a man of shabby appearance. He said: 'O so-and-so, what has brought you to what I see?' He said: 'Sickness and harm.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Shall I not teach you words that will remove from you the sickness and the harm? Say: I have put my trust in the Living One who does not die. Praise be to God who has not taken a son...' to the end of the verse." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came back to him, and his condition had improved, so he said: "Mahyam?" (an Arabic interrogative meaning "What is the matter with you?"). The man said: "I have not ceased to say the words you taught me."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in the Book of Relief and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat reported from Isma'il ibn Abi Fudayk, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No matter has distressed me but that Jibril (peace be upon him) appeared to me and said: 'O Muhammad, say: I have put my trust in the Living One who does not die, and praise be to God who has not taken a son,'" to the end of the verse.

Ibn al-Sunni and al-Daylami reported from Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), may God be pleased with her, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "When you take your resting place, say: 'Praise be to God, the Sufficient. Glory be to God, the Most High. God is sufficient for me, and He suffices. What God wills comes to pass. God hears whoever calls upon Him. There is no refuge from God, and no shelter beyond God. I have put my trust in my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed my Lord is upon a straight path. Praise be to God who has not taken a son,'" through to: "and magnify Him with full magnification." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim who recites these at his sleep and then sleeps amid the devils and vermin will be harmed by them."

Now, how subtle is the correspondence between the beginning of this surah and this conclusion! This is no novelty in the speech of the Subtle, the All-Knowing.

* * *

"From the way of indication in the verses": ﴿And indeed they almost tempted you﴾ to the end of the passage is an admonition to His beloved (ﷺ) against falling into what harms the preservation of the conditions of love. It also contains an indication of bringing him to the station of establishment (tamkin, the stage of firm settledness in God).

﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾ to the end of the verse. It has been mentioned that prayer is of five kinds: the prayer of union and intimate converse (al-muwasala wa'l-munaghat), in the station of the hidden (al-khafi); the prayer of witnessing (al-mushahada), in the station of the spirit (al-ruh); the prayer of secret intimate discourse (al-munajat), in the station of the secret (al-sirr); the prayer of presence (al-hudur), in the station of the heart (al-qalb); and the prayer of obedience and submission, in the station of the soul (al-nafs). Thus the decline of the sun is an indication of the passing of the sun of unity (shams al-wahda) from its standing over the existence of the servant, through complete annihilation (fana', the passing away of the self in God). For there is no prayer in the state of standing overhead, since then the servant has no existence and no awareness of himself. Prayer becomes obligatory only with the decline and the appearance of a shadow, which is the existence of the servant, whether in the state of veiling by creation, which is the state of differentiation before unification (farq, the state of distinction before the unity of the Real), or in the state of persistence, which is the state of differentiation after unification (jam', the unifying perception in which all things are seen as coming from the One). The darkness of the night is an indication of the darkness of the night of the soul. The Qur'an of dawn is an indication of the Qur'an of the dawn of the heart. The most guiding and subtle of the prayers is the prayer of union; the most excellent is the prayer of witnessing, indicated by the afternoon prayer; the lightest is the prayer of the secret, indicated by the sunset prayer; the most effective in firming up the soul is the prayer of the soul, indicated by the night prayer; and the most effective in driving away Satan is the prayer of presence, indicated by the dawn prayer.

﴿Indeed the Qur'an of dawn is ever witnessed﴾, that is, witnessed by the angels of the night and the day. This is an indication of the descent of the attributes of the heart and its lights, and the departure and passing away of the attributes of the soul.

﴿And from the night, perform the tahajjud with it as a supererogatory prayer for you﴾, that is, in addition to the five obligatory prayers, specific to you. It was said: because it is the sign of the station of the soul, it is necessary to single it out for extra devotion, because this station needs prayer more than the other stations do. It was also said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was singled out for tahajjud because the night is the time of the lover's private retreat with the Beloved, and he (ﷺ) is the greatest Beloved and the most honoured Intimate Friend (khalil).

﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾, which is the station of raising the deficient to the perfect and the perfect to the most perfect. ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter﴾ the presence of unity within the vision of plurality (hadrat al-wahda fi 'ayn al-jam') ﴿by a sincere entrance﴾, a pleasing entry, free from the calamity of the eye's deviation toward attention to others at all. ﴿And cause me to exit﴾ into the wide expanse of multiplicity, upon returning to differentiation through the existence bestowed by the Real ﴿with a sincere exit﴾, safe from the calamity of fluctuation (talwin, changing spiritual states) and deviation from the path of uprightness. ﴿And grant me from Yourself a supporting authority﴾, a helping proof, through firm establishment and empowerment (tamkin). ﴿And say﴾, when the point of the ghayn has moved away from the eye: ﴿Truth has come﴾, that is, the abiding existence has become manifest, which is necessary existence (al-wujud al-wajibi), ﴿and falsehood has vanished﴾, which is contingent existence (al-wujud al-imkani).

In the authentic hadith: "The truest word spoken by a poet is the word of Labid:
Surely everything other than God is vanity."

It is said: the truth is knowledge and falsehood is ignorance. The truth is what appears of inspiration (ilham), and falsehood is the whisperings of the soul and the suggestions of Satan. Faris said: everything that carries you to follow the way of reality (haqiqa) is truth, and everything that veils you and divides your time is falsehood. ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing﴾ from the diseases of blameworthy attributes, ﴿and a mercy for the believers﴾ who believe in the unseen, which brings them perfections and great virtues. The first is an indication of purification (takhliya, emptying the self of vices), and the second an indication of adornment (tahliya, filling the self with virtues). It is also said: it is a healing from the disease of doubt for the weak believers, from the disease of ignorance (nakira) for the knowers (arifun), from the pain of longing for the lovers, and from the disease of despair for the seekers and those who aim (for God). And they recited:

Your books surround me and do not leave my resting place,
and in them is a healing for what I conceal.

﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers﴾ who diminish their own share of perfection by inclining toward carnal desires ﴿except in loss﴾, by the increase in the manifestation of their selves with their attributes, such as denial and the like.

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and withdraws to one side﴾, so he is veiled by the blessing from the Giver and does not give thanks. ﴿And when evil touches him, he is in despair﴾, because of his ignorance of the great power of God, and he does not endure patiently. ﴿Say: Each acts according to his own manner﴾, according to his way which accords with his readiness, and every vessel drips with what is in it.

﴿And they ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾, that is, from the world of origination (alam al-ibda'), which is the world of essences sanctified from shape, colour, direction, and place, so those veiled from it cannot perceive it. ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾, which is the knowledge of sensible things. (Whom God guides, by His light, according to the eternal providence) ﴿then he is the one guided﴾ and no other. ﴿And whom He leads astray﴾ by withholding that light from him ﴿you will not find for them any protectors﴾ apart from Him, exalted is He, who might guide them or protect them from His subjugation, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾, because they are drawn toward the lowest direction, ﴿blind, dumb, and deaf﴾, because these conditions match their state in this world. ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down upon their faces in prostration﴾.

[p. 198]

because of their knowledge of its truth and their awareness of the secrets deposited in it. ﴿And they fall down on their faces weeping﴾ — out of awe at its greatness, or out of longing for its Revealer and love for meeting Him. Abu Ya'qub al-Susi said: Weeping is of several kinds: weeping from Allah Most High, which is to weep out of fear of what the pen wrote in the Opening (al-Fatiha) and which appears in the Conclusion (al-Khatima); weeping for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is to weep in sorrow over what of the Real (al-Haqq, Most High) one has missed; weeping to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, which is to weep when His name is mentioned, and the mention of His promise and His threat; and weeping through Allah Most High, which is to weep without any share of oneself in one's weeping.

Al-Qasim said: Weeping is of various forms: the weeping of the ignorant over what they did not know, the weeping of scholars over what they fell short in, the weeping of the righteous out of fear of missing out, the weeping of the imams out of fear of being outstripped, and the weeping of the knights among the people of the hearts out of awe and reverence; and there is no weeping for the monotheists (al-muwahhidin).

In the verse there is also an allusion to listening (al-sama'), and there is nothing more noble than listening to the Qur'an; it is the Spirit and the fragrant herb.

﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)﴾. It has been said: calling upon Allah is by annihilation in the Essence (al-fana' fi'l-dhat), and calling upon the Most Merciful is by annihilation in the Attribute (al-fana' fi'l-sifa). The attribute of the Most Merciful (al-rahmaniyya) is the mother of the attributes, and by it He, glory be to Him, established Himself upon His Throne. From this it is known that the purpose of existence (al-ijad) is nothing but the mercy of those who exist.

﴿Whichever you call﴾ — that is, whichever of these two stations you seek — ﴿to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ — Most High, in these two stations — not to you, for you are not existent there. As for annihilation in the Essence, it is evident; and as for annihilation in the mentioned attribute, it is because al-Rahman is not suitable as a name for anything other than that Essence, and that attribute cannot be established for anything other than It. And it is not hidden from you that the pronoun in "lahu" (to Him), on this interpretation, refers back to what it referred to on the (previous) explanation.

In the Futuhat al-Makkiyya (Meccan Openings) it is stated that He, Most High, made the most beautiful names belong to Allah just as they belong to al-Rahman, except that the name has a meaning and a form. So Allah is called by the meaning of the name, and al-Rahman is called by its form, because al-Rahman is the one described by the Self (al-nafs), and by the Self the divine words appeared in the levels of the void (al-khala') in which the world appeared. So we do not call Him except by the form of the name. He has two forms: one form is with us, from our breaths and the composition of our letters, and it is the one by which we call Him, and these are the names of the divine names, and they are like a robe bestowed upon them, and we, in the form of these names, translate the divine names. And He has forms from the very Self of al-Rahman, from His being speaker and described by speech; and behind those forms are the meanings, which are like spirits to the divine names by which the Real mentions Himself, and these are from the very Self of al-Rahman. So to Him belong the most beautiful names. And the spirits of those forms are those which belong to the name Allah, outside the judgment of the Self, not described by modality (al-kayfiyya); and they are to the forms of the self-named Rahmanic names as meanings are to letters. When we knew this, and we were commanded to call upon Him, Glory be to Him, and given the choice between the two sublime names, then if we wish we call Him by the forms of the self-named Rahmanic names, which are the cosmic resolves (al-himam al-kawniyya) that are in our spirits; and if we wish we call Him by the names that come from our breaths, by the rule of translation. Then when we pronounce them, we bring into our selves either Allah, so we contemplate the meaning, or al-Rahman, so we contemplate the form of the divine self-named Rahmanic name, however we wish we do. For the indication of the two forms from us and from al-Rahman upon the meaning is one, whether we know this or do not know it. End of quotation. It is a statement whose understanding is difficult except for whom Allah wills. However, there is in it no application of the supplication to what you have heard.

﴿And say: Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son﴾ — far less that He, Glory be to Him, should have a son by way of begetting — ﴿and has had no partner in the dominion﴾ — so there is no entry for anyone other than Him, Most High, into the ownership of anything in the true sense; and whatever comes to be through a cause, the cause is only an instrument for it, and an instrument owns nothing. Rather, there is nothing except that it is His creation, in the true sense. A bed, for example, though it is attributed to the carpenter in terms of craftsmanship, is in reality an instrument like the adze, and work is not attributed to an instrument in the true sense; so it is said. The Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, has a statement on this station that reveals part of this; he mentioned it in the 198th chapter, so return to it and reflect. Likewise he has a statement on His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿and has had no protector out of weakness﴾, but what we have previously presented suffices for it. ﴿And magnify Him with magnification﴾. Some of them said: His magnification, Most High, is that you know that you cannot magnify Him except through Him. Ibn 'Ata' said: His magnification, Mighty and Majestic, is by exalting His favor and His beneficence in the heart, with the knowledge of one's shortcoming in gratitude; and how can anyone render Him His due thanks, when His blessings are uncountable and His bounties cannot be exhausted. This is all; and by the grace of Allah Most High, the tafsir of this noble surah is complete.
